t: Among adults, inflammatory arthritis was the most common new autoimmune disease diagnosed after SARS-CoV-2 infection, and Sjögren's disease also showed high incidence.

Thyroid disease, psoriasis or psoriatic arthritis, and inflammatory bowel disease were among the most common new-onset autoimmune diseases consistently observed across all three EHR networks after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Inflammatory arthritis/rheumatoid arthritis was the most common newly diagnosed autoimmune disease among adults after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
Incident type 1 diabetes and hematological autoimmune diseases were specifically found among the most common new autoimmune diagnoses in the pediatric population after SARS-CoV-2 infection.
In PEDSnet, the largest incidence-rate gap between COVID-19 severity levels for any single autoimmune disease was for type 1 diabetes, comparing moderate to severe COVID-19.

The authors propose that neutrophil extracellular traps (NETs), which are elevated in severe COVID-19 and stimulate type I interferon production, contribute mechanistically to autoimmune disease pathogenesis by priming dendritic cells and promoting autoantibody formation.
Patients with the most severe acute COVID-19 illness had a higher baseline prevalence of pre-existing autoimmune disease than those with milder illness across all three networks.

A MAUDE injury report described a 35-year-old female with a known seizure disorder who developed muscular rigidity, anxiety, neck pain, sleep dysfunction, and seizures after using Somryst, a prescription digital therapeutic for chronic insomnia, despite epilepsy being a labeled contraindication.
A MAUDE malfunction report for EndeavorRx, a digital therapeutic for pediatric ADHD, described a lack of therapeutic effect reported by a male user, with no clinical symptoms or physical harm noted.
No adverse event reports were identified in the MAUDE database for CT-132, an FDA-cleared digital therapeutic for episodic migraine, among the 13 evaluated PDTs through April 2025.
No adverse event reports were identified in MAUDE for Parallel, an FDA-cleared digital therapeutic for irritable bowel syndrome, among the PDTs evaluated.
No adverse event reports were identified in MAUDE for Regulora, an FDA-cleared digital therapeutic for irritable bowel syndrome, among the PDTs evaluated.

Across all 13 FDA-cleared prescription digital therapeutics searched in MAUDE through April 30, 2025, only two verified adverse event reports were identified, with no deaths, hospitalizations, or life-threatening outcomes reported for any of them.
Cluster headache is rare (~0.1% prevalence) and more common in men, while migraine affects about 12% of the population and is more common in women.
5-HT2A receptor activation has opposing effects on pain depending on anatomical location: pro-inflammatory in the peripheral nervous system but antinociceptive in the central nervous system.

In a retrospective survey of 53 cluster headache patients, psilocybin terminated acute attacks within 20 minutes in 85% of users and stopped cluster periods in 52%, while LSD stopped cluster periods in 88% of cases.
In an online survey of 496 cluster headache patients, psilocybin showed efficacy comparable to high-flow oxygen and was superior to oral and intranasal triptans for remitting attacks.
An Italian survey of 54 patients with drug-resistant cluster headache found psilocybin had a high perceived efficacy of 77.8%, even at subhallucinogenic doses.

A Dutch cross-sectional study of 643 cluster headache patients found lifetime psychedelic drug use was higher than in the general population, with psilocybin and LSD reducing attack frequency by 56-60%.

In a double-blind crossover study of 18 healthy volunteers, psilocybin doses of 0-30 mg/70 kg produced dose-dependent increases in headache incidence, duration, and severity, all mild-to-moderate and resolving within 24 hours.

In a Phase 1 placebo-controlled trial (NCT02981173), low-dose psilocybin in a pulse regimen reduced weekly cluster attack frequency more in chronic than episodic CH, though the reduction did not reach statistical significance.
In the blinded extension phase of the same trial, a repeated psilocybin pulse regimen produced a significant 50% reduction in cluster attack frequency regardless of response during the first round.

A case report describes a 33-year-old man with episodic migraine who self-administered 1.2 g of Psilocybe cubensis at aura onset, resulting in markedly reduced headache intensity and vomiting compared with prior conventionally treated migraines.

In a double-blind, placebo-controlled Phase 1 trial (NCT03341689) of 10 adults with frequent migraine, a single low dose of oral psilocybin significantly reduced weekly migraine days, attack frequency, pain severity, and functional impairment compared to placebo.
In an open-label Phase 1b study (NCT04905121) of four SUNHA patients receiving escalating oral psilocybin doses, two of four participants experienced a greater than 50% reduction in attack frequency.
Early research by Kast and Collins found that 100 μg LSD provided superior pain relief compared to opioids in 50 severely ill patients.

A qualitative study of 11 participants self-medicating with classic psychedelics for chronic pain found significant pain reductions during and after use, along with positive reframing of pain and enhanced somatic awareness.

An online survey of 250 chronic pain sufferers found macrodoses of psychedelics provided greater and longer-lasting pain relief than microdoses, opioids, and over-the-counter drugs, with 33.7% experiencing benefits over 3 days versus 21.4% for microdoses.

A cross-sectional survey of 354 North Americans with fibromyalgia found nearly 30% had used psychedelics (mainly LSD and psilocybin), with 11 of 12 pain-relief users reporting symptom improvement, and most participants supported further clinical trials.

A case report described a patient using microdose (0.2-0.5 g) and macrodose (2-3 g) psilocybin for phantom limb pain, achieving significant pain reduction and decreased paroxysmal episodes for 3 weeks, exceeding effects of mirror-visual feedback and phantom massage alone.

Three patients with neuropathic and musculoskeletal pain treated with microdosed psilocybin (250 mg-1 g dried mushrooms) experienced 80-100% pain relief with improved functional capacity and effects lasting up to 4 weeks without tolerance.

In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover trial of 24 healthy volunteers, 20 μg LSD significantly increased pain tolerance and reduced pain intensity and unpleasantness on the Cold Pressor Test.

In a Phase 2 open-label pilot trial (NCT05128162), five adults with fibromyalgia receiving two oral psilocybin doses (15 mg and 25 mg) with psychotherapy showed clinically significant improvements in pain severity, interference, sleep disturbance, and psychological resilience with no serious adverse events.

2-Br-LSD (BOL-148) is a nonhallucinogenic LSD derivative that acts as a partial agonist at 5-HT2A (Ki=0.5-2.2 nM) via Gq and β-arrestin2 pathways but lacks 5-HT2B agonism, reducing cardiac valvulopathy risk associated with LSD.

In an open-label case series of five patients with treatment-resistant cluster headache, three oral doses of 2-Br-LSD over 10 days produced substantial improvement in four patients, including one complete 6-month remission, without hallucinogenic effects.

In mouse chronic pain models, ibogaine-derived analogs tabernanthalog (TBG), ibogaminalog (IBG), and DM506 alleviated mechanical and thermal hypersensitivity, with these antinociceptive effects fully reversed by the 5-HT2A antagonist ketanserin, confirming a serotonergic mechanism.

Oxa-noribogaine and its stereoisomer epi-oxa-noribogaine produced pronounced antinociceptive effects in the tail-flick assay that were abolished in kappa opioid receptor (KOR)-deficient mice, confirming a KOR-dependent mechanism.

PET imaging in healthy volunteers showed psilocybin doses of 3-30 mg occupied 43-72% of 5-HT2A receptors one hour after ingestion, with a subperceptual 10 mg/70 kg dose producing about 39.5% average occupancy.

Psychedelics exhibit anti-inflammatory properties, reducing the release of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as interleukin-6 and tumor necrosis factor alpha that are implicated in neuropathic and inflammatory pain.

Classic psychedelics such as LSD promote synaptic plasticity via 5-HT2A receptor activation, leading to release of BDNF and activation of TrkB signaling that facilitates dendritic growth and synapse formation, with LSD shown to directly bind TrkB.
5-HT2A receptor activation has opposing effects on pain depending on anatomical location: pro-inflammatory in the peripheral nervous system but antinociceptive in the central nervous system.
LSD and DMT have been shown to increase dendritic arbor complexity, promote dendritic spine growth, and stimulate synapse formation.
Activation of 5-HT2A receptors by psychedelics promotes release of BDNF and engages TrkB signaling, facilitating synaptic growth and strengthening.
Classic psychedelics such as LSD directly bind to the TrkB receptor and enhance BDNF signaling.
Psychedelics exhibit anti-inflammatory properties, reducing release of the pro-inflammatory cytokine IL-6, which is implicated in neuropathic and inflammatory pain.
Psychedelics reduce release of the pro-inflammatory cytokine TNF-alpha, implicated in neuropathic and inflammatory pain.

Psychedelics influence the default mode network, which is involved in self-referential thinking and pain-related rumination, and disrupting its connectivity may reduce the emotional distress associated with chronic pain.
LSD interacts with dopamine (D1R and D2R), adrenergic (α1R), and histaminergic (H1R) receptors, which can lead to cardiovascular side effects.
Psilocin does not strongly bind D2R but indirectly increases dopaminergic activity, influencing reward processing and emotional responses.
Agonistic activity at the 5-HT2B receptor, shared by all classic psychedelics discussed, has been associated with a risk of cardiac valvulopathy, particularly with chronic use.

PET imaging in healthy volunteers showed that psilocybin doses of 3-30 mg occupied 43-72% of 5-HT2A receptors 1 hour after ingestion, with a subperceptual dose (10 mg/70 kg) producing approximately 39.5% average occupancy.
2-Bromo-LSD (BOL-148) shows high-affinity partial agonism at 5-HT2A receptors via both Gq and β-arrestin2 pathways.
2-Br-LSD acts as an antagonist at 5-HT2B receptors in both Gq and β-arrestin2 pathways, which is thought to prevent the valvulopathy risk linked to 5-HT2B agonism seen with LSD.

In mouse models of chronic pain, tabernanthalog (TBG), ibogaminalog (IBG), and DM506 alleviated mechanical and thermal hypersensitivity, and these effects were fully reversed by the 5-HT2A antagonist ketanserin, confirming a serotonergic mechanism.

Oxa-noribogaine and its stereoisomer epi-oxa-noribogaine produced antinociceptive effects in the tail-flick assay that were abolished in kappa-opioid receptor-deficient mice, confirming a KOR-dependent mechanism.
Benzofuran ibogalogs reduced nociceptive behaviors in the formalin pain model and reversed neuroinflammatory markers (substance P, CGRP, COX-2) while restoring the neurotrophic factors BDNF and GDNF.
IBG and nor-IBG required coadministration with the mGlu2 agonist LY379268 at subtherapeutic doses for analgesic efficacy, suggesting synergistic 5-HT2A-mGlu2 receptor crosstalk.
A randomized, placebo-controlled trial (NCT06180759) is underway investigating the acute analgesic effects of DMT on experimentally induced pain compared to racemic ketamine and placebo.
A Phase 1/2 trial (NCT04280055) assessing the safety and efficacy of psilocybin for cluster headache has been terminated and is no longer recruiting.
A Phase 1 study (NCT03806985) analyzing psilocybin's effects on postconcussion headache has been terminated and is no longer enrolling participants.
Females with Loeys-Dietz syndrome had a significantly higher rate of obesity than males.
Females with Loeys-Dietz syndrome had a significantly higher rate of migraines than males.
Females with Loeys-Dietz syndrome had significantly more easy bruising than males.
Dolichocephaly was significantly more common among male Loeys-Dietz syndrome patients than females.
Ascending aortic aneurysms were significantly more common in males than females with Loeys-Dietz syndrome.
Males with Loeys-Dietz syndrome had a higher rate of abdominal aortic aneurysms than females.
Males with Loeys-Dietz syndrome had a higher rate of aneurysms at locations other than the ascending or abdominal aorta compared to females.
Males with Loeys-Dietz syndrome had higher rates of Type A and Type B aortic dissections than females.
Males with Loeys-Dietz syndrome underwent aortic root replacement surgery more frequently than females.
Females with Loeys-Dietz syndrome underwent tricuspid valve repair more frequently than males.

A 47-year-old man with diabetes and a smoking history presented with an isolated severe, migraine-like headache—without chest pain—as the sole manifestation of inferior ST-segment elevation myocardial infarction.
ECG revealed ST-segment elevation in leads II, III, and aVF with reciprocal ST depression in V2–V4, consistent with inferior STEMI and first-degree AV block.
Serum troponin I was markedly elevated, supporting the diagnosis of myocardial infarction.

Coronary angiography demonstrated total thrombotic occlusion of the mid-right coronary artery and up to 80% long-segment stenosis of the proximal-to-mid left anterior descending artery, confirming multivessel coronary artery disease.
Echocardiography showed a preserved ejection fraction of 55% but with regional wall motion abnormality in the inferior wall and no pericardial effusion.

The patient's headache began improving approximately 30 minutes after initial ACS treatment and resolved completely following percutaneous coronary intervention (stenting of RCA and LAD), with concurrent normalisation of the ECG.
Diabetic autonomic neuropathy causes sensory denervation of cardiac afferents, which may blunt typical anginal pain and result in atypical presentations of myocardial ischaemia such as headache.
One proposed mechanism for cardiac cephalalgia is convergence of afferent cardiac vagal fibres with cranial pain afferent pathways, producing referred headache during myocardial ischaemia.
Release of proinflammatory neurotransmitters such as bradykinin, histamine, adenosine, and serotonin during myocardial ischaemia may cause cerebral vasodilation and provoke headache.
Headache in cardiac cephalalgia may also arise from increased venous congestion secondary to acute heart failure following myocardial ischaemia.

Recent upper respiratory tract infection is a recognised trigger for acute coronary syndrome, particularly within two weeks of infection, via inflammatory and prothrombotic destabilisation of atherosclerotic plaques; the patient had a URTI two days before presentation.

The patient had received diclofenac (an NSAID) for two days prior to admission; NSAIDs, especially diclofenac, are associated with increased cardiovascular risk and may precipitate ACS in patients with pre-existing risk factors.

Triptans and ergot derivatives, commonly used to treat migraine, are vasoconstrictors and are contraindicated in patients with myocardial ischaemia, making distinguishing cardiac cephalalgia from primary migraine clinically crucial.

Inclusion of ECG, along with serial ECGs and cardiac biomarker testing, in the initial evaluation of patients presenting with acute headache and cardiovascular risk factors is recommended to aid diagnosis of cardiac cephalalgia and avoid misdiagnosis as primary migraine.
Time-restricted eating (TRE) significantly improved SF-36 physical function scores after 12 weeks.
TRE significantly improved SF-36 energy/fatigue scores after 12 weeks.
The Malmö POTS Symptom Score (MAPS) overall severity score decreased by approximately 19 points after 12 weeks of TRE, reaching a post-intervention mean of 40.65.
TRE was associated with reductions in multiple individual POTS symptoms including dizziness, palpitations, difficulty breathing, nausea, gastrointestinal issues, exhaustion, and insomnia.
The orthostatic increase in heart rate (supine-to-standing delta) decreased by approximately 11 bpm after 12 weeks of TRE.
Standing heart rate significantly decreased following the 12-week TRE intervention.
Mitochondrial stress test parameters (oxygen consumption rate profile) in C2C12 myoblasts did not significantly differ between cells treated with pre- versus post-TRE patient plasma.

Under physiological (non-stress) conditions, C2C12 cells treated with post-TRE plasma showed significantly increased mitochondrial-derived ATP production compared to cells treated with pre-TRE plasma.
TRE was safe and well-tolerated, with no adverse events reported and high adherence (20 of 23 enrolled participants completed the 12-week intervention).
Anaemia was significantly more common among female VVS patients than male VVS patients.
Emergency department visits for syncope increased significantly with age, reaching 15% in patients older than 70.
Males presented more frequently with first-time syncope and had fewer recurrent episodes compared to female patients.
Female patients were more likely than males to have an identifiable and avoidable trigger for vasovagal syncope.
Crowded or warm environments were the most common trigger for syncope in both sexes and were significantly more frequent in females than males.
Sight of blood as a syncope trigger was equally common in males and females, in contrast to all other triggers assessed.
Older patients had a lower probability of having specific identifiable triggers before syncope compared with younger patients.
More than 80% of patients experienced prodromal symptoms before vasovagal syncope, slightly more common in females than males.
The likelihood of experiencing prodromal symptoms before syncope decreased significantly with increasing age.
Seizure-like movements during syncope were notably more common in younger females than other groups, raising misdiagnosis risk with epilepsy.
Post-syncopal symptoms including palpitations, drowsiness, headache, and chest pain were significantly more prevalent among females than males.
Overall positive head-up tilt test rate was 40% with no significant difference between males and females.
During the passive phase of the tilt test, females showed a significantly greater diastolic blood pressure drop than males.
During the active phase of the tilt test, females exhibited a significantly greater heart rate reduction than males.
Cardioinhibitory syncope during the passive phase was more prevalent among younger patients and progressively declined with age.
Mean heart rate reduction during the active tilt phase was highest in the youngest patients and progressively declined with advancing age.
Among patients with positive HUTT, palpitations were the only tilt-induced prodromal symptom significantly more common in females than males.
Agreement between prodromal symptoms during spontaneous syncope versus those induced during head-up tilt testing was low, with McNemar's test showing significant discrepancies for several symptoms.

Cohen's kappa values for agreement between spontaneous and HUTT-induced prodromal symptoms ranged from 0.06 to 0.32, indicating slight to fair agreement overall, with diaphoresis, palpitation, and light-headedness showing the best (fair) agreement.

The authors suggest cardioneuroablation may be preferable for younger patients with predominant cardioinhibitory syncope to avoid lifelong pacemaker dependence, whereas pacemakers may be more suitable for older patients due to reduced autonomic adaptability.
Among fibromyalgia patients with concomitant immune-mediated rheumatic disease, HLA-B27-negative spondyloarthritis was the most common IMRD, present in 53% of cases.
Sjögren's syndrome was the second most common IMRD among fibromyalgia patients with concomitant immune-mediated rheumatic disease, occurring in 16% of cases.
In the majority of fibromyalgia patients with a concomitant IMRD, the underlying rheumatic disease was clinically inactive at the time of assessment.
No significant clinical or epidemiological differences were found overall between fibromyalgia patients with versus without concomitant IMRD in either diagnostic cohort.
Fibromyalgia patients with concomitant IMRD showed a higher prevalence of enthesopathies compared to those without IMRD.
A history of childhood pain was more prevalent among fibromyalgia patients with concomitant IMRD than those without.
Sjögren's syndrome was the second most common immune-mediated rheumatic disease concomitant with fibromyalgia, present in 16% of FM patients with IMRD.
In the large majority of fibromyalgia patients with concomitant immune-mediated rheumatic disease, the underlying rheumatic disease was clinically inactive at the time of assessment.
Migraine patients took significantly longer to complete the Trail Making Test A than healthy controls, indicating slower psychomotor/processing speed.

During cognitive testing, beta-wave brain activity increased physiologically in healthy controls but showed a significant decrease in migraine patients, with a large effect size for the Stroop Color Test.

Healthy controls showed a marked increase in low-frequency HRV power (sympathetic activity) during cognitive tasks, whereas migraine patients showed minimal change, with a large effect size for the between-group difference.

Parasympathetic activity (HF power) decreased from baseline in healthy controls during cognitive testing, reflecting normal parasympathetic withdrawal, but remained essentially unchanged in migraine patients.
Overall cognitive test performance did not differ significantly between untreated migraine patients and healthy controls.
Prior studies cited in the discussion reported an association between migraine and a higher risk of dementia.
Prior papers cited in the discussion reported that reduced HRV in migraine patients was associated with poorer performance on attention and processing speed tests.
Rates of previous comorbidities such as alcohol consumption, smoking, and hypertension were similar between the migraine and control groups.
The Movement Disorder Society MSA diagnostic criteria achieve maximum specificity of 99%-100% for the clinically established MSA category.
The clinically probable MSA diagnostic category offers a balanced sensitivity of 64%-77% and specificity of 74%-100%.
A video case demonstrates one patient's clinical progression from possible prodromal MSA to clinically established MSA-parkinsonian subtype, later confirmed neuropathologically.
Migraine with aura is associated with approximately double the risk of ischemic stroke compared to migraine without aura.
A meta-analysis of 1600 hemorrhagic stroke patients found increased hemorrhagic stroke risk among women under 45 with migraine.
The same meta-analysis found an increased hemorrhagic stroke risk among patients with any type of migraine, but no significant association specifically for migraine with aura.
A separate meta-analysis including 654 patients found no association between migraine and hemorrhagic stroke, contradicting other meta-analyses.
Patent foramen ovale prevalence is markedly higher in patients with migraine with aura than in those with migraine without aura.
In CADASIL, caused by NOTCH3 mutations, migraine-with-aura-like headache is often an early clinical manifestation preceding recurrent ischemic strokes.
MTHFR gene polymorphisms, associated with elevated homocysteine levels, have been implicated in both increased stroke risk and migraine pathogenesis.

In a population-based study, migraine with aura was significantly associated with increased prevalence of major cardiovascular events including angina, MI, and stroke even after adjusting for traditional risk factors, whereas migraine without aura was not independently associated with elevated cardiovascular risk.
Migraine was highly prevalent among patients with acute coronary syndrome due to spontaneous coronary artery dissection, with a lifetime prevalence of 42%, particularly among women.
In an Australian cohort study, both women and men with migraine had approximately twice the likelihood of a prior myocardial infarction compared to those without migraine.
In a large US study of individuals with physician-confirmed migraine, the risk of chest pain suggestive of MI was found to be nearly twice as high compared to individuals without migraine.

A large prospective cohort study of female healthcare workers and male physicians found no increased risk of MI or angina pectoris in individuals who self-reported a history of migraine, in either sex.
A prospective study with 5-year follow-up reported that migraine was associated with an approximately 1.42-fold increased risk of developing hypertension.

In a study of 15,176 hypertensive patients followed for a mean of 12.2 years, the risk of persistent or worsening hypertension was 9% higher in women with migraine with aura, 21% higher in women with migraine without aura, and 15% higher in women with any history of migraine, compared to controls.
A population-based study found migraine patients had higher diastolic but lower systolic blood pressure than controls, with no significant overall association between migraine and hypertension.
A large cohort of Polish migraine patients showed that low blood pressure, rather than hypertension, was common, found in 26.9% of patients.
Among young adults with ischemic stroke, the risk of atrial fibrillation was five times higher in those with migraine with aura compared to those with migraine without aura.

A Korean nationwide cohort study found migraine with severe aura increased atrial fibrillation risk in women by 48% compared to controls, with no association observed in men, while migraine without severe aura was associated with a 16–21% increase in both sexes.

A 9-year follow-up study based on the HUNT cohort found no increased risk of atrial fibrillation in individuals with migraine, and migraine was associated with lower AF risk among participants over age 55.
GWAS analysis identified PHACTR1 as a shared genetic risk locus between migraine and coronary artery disease, replicated across two independent CAD GWAS.
The variant rs9349379 in PHACTR1 shows pleiotropy between migraine and large artery ischemic stroke.
The variant rs1058587 in GPD1L shows pleiotropy between migraine and cardioembolic stroke.
Flow-mediated dilation, a marker of endothelial function, was reduced in patients with chronic migraine compared to both episodic migraine patients and healthy controls.
The Genetic Epidemiology of Migraine Study found an unfavorable lipid profile in patients with migraine with aura, including elevated total cholesterol and TC/HDL ratio.
A meta-analysis found that smoking was associated with a nine-fold increased risk of stroke among people with migraine.

A meta-analysis of 126,173 participants found that alcohol drinkers had a lower risk of migraine than non-drinkers, likely reflecting migraine-related alcohol avoidance rather than a protective effect.
Clinical trials have shown that cognitive behavioral therapy reduces migraine attack frequency by 35–50% and lowers cardiovascular risk by reducing sympathetic overactivation.
A prospective follow-up study reported increases in both systolic and diastolic blood pressure in patients treated with erenumab, with some individuals requiring antihypertensive therapy.
A systematic review and meta-analysis did not find a significant association between erenumab and increased systemic blood pressure, though evidence was fragile.
Major depressive disorder is estimated to occur in 47–50% of patients with migraine, significantly higher than in the general population.
CBT reduces migraine attack frequency by 35-50%, improves stress resilience, and may lower cardiovascular risk by reducing sympathetic overactivation.
A prospective follow-up study reported increases in systolic and diastolic blood pressure among patients treated with erenumab, with some requiring antihypertensive therapy.
A systematic review and meta-analysis found no significant association between erenumab and increased systemic blood pressure, though it noted evidence fragility.
A systematic review and meta-analysis found that poor social relationships were associated with a 29% increase in risk of coronary heart disease and a 32% increase in risk of stroke.
The prevalence of major depressive disorder in patients with migraine is estimated at 47-50%, significantly higher than the general population.

Generalized anxiety disorder occurs in up to 50% of patients with chronic migraine and is associated with higher resting heart rate, increased blood pressure variability, and heightened sympathetic activation.
Patients with chronic migraine commonly exhibit high levels of CRP, IL-6, and TNFα, biomarkers of systemic inflammation and endothelial dysfunction.
An RCT evaluating clopidogrel 75 mg daily in migraine patients found no significant reduction in headache days or disability compared to placebo.
A small study of dual antiplatelet therapy with aspirin and dipyridamole versus placebo showed improvement in reducing migraine frequency and severity.
Clinical trials evaluating PFO closure for migraine prevention have failed to meet their primary endpoints, though some studies suggest a tendency toward improvement in aura symptoms.
Women with migraine with aura using combined hormonal contraceptives have a six-fold increased risk of ischemic stroke compared to women without migraine.
Preeclampsia risk is two to three times higher in women with migraine, and migraine has been linked to increased peripartum cardiovascular complications.

In a NHANES study of 4560 never-smoking adults, heavy secondhand smoke exposure (serum cotinine 1-10 ng/mL) was significantly positively associated with severe headache or migraine, especially among sedentary individuals and those with BMI <25.
A meta-analysis found that smoking was associated with a nine-fold increased risk of stroke among people with migraine.

The Genetic Epidemiology of Migraine Study of 5755 people including 620 migraine patients found an unfavorable lipid profile in migraine with aura, including total cholesterol ≥240 mg/dl and TC/HDL ratio >5.0.

A meta-analysis of 126,173 participants found the risk of migraine in alcohol drinkers was approximately 1.5 times lower than in non-drinkers, likely reflecting alcohol avoidance by migraineurs rather than a protective effect.
A meta-analysis of 15,402 patients found headache prevalence in OSA was 33% (16% migraine), suggesting OSA did not increase the risk of headache.
The GPD1L variant rs1058587 showed significant pleiotropy, being associated with both migraine and cardioembolic stroke.
The PHACTR1 variant rs9349379 showed significant pleiotropy, being associated with both migraine and large artery ischemic stroke.

González-Quintanilla et al. found reduced flow-mediated dilation in patients with chronic migraine compared to both episodic migraine patients and healthy controls, consistent with earlier findings of decreased FMD in new-onset migraine.
Lower levels of flow-mediated dilation predicted incidence of cardiovascular events at 36 months, per Shimbo et al.

Specific miRNA expression profiles appear dysregulated in individuals with migraine, implicated in neurovascular inflammation, endothelial dysfunction, and pain modulation, and are being explored as biomarkers and precision therapy targets.

Women with higher Framingham Risk Scores were more likely to report a past history of migraine but less likely to experience active or new-onset migraine, indicating a paradoxical inverse relationship between current cardiovascular risk and active migraine.

A population-based study using the Rotterdam Study cohort found that the association between migraine and cardiovascular disease does not follow a traditional risk factor model, supporting migraine as a distinct vascular phenotype.
Contemporary cardiovascular guidelines, including the UK's QRISK3 calculator, now incorporate migraine with aura as a risk variable in cardiovascular risk assessment.
Women with migraine, particularly with aura, are at higher risk of pregnancy-related hypertensive disorders including gestational hypertension and preeclampsia.
Late-life migraine accompaniments, characterized by prolonged aura symptoms without headache, can be misinterpreted as transient ischemic attacks, posing a diagnostic challenge in older patients.
Migraine with aura is specifically associated with diffuse carotid thickening, whereas migraine without aura may be linked to a lower risk of carotid plaques and arterial stiffening.

Some studies report a higher prevalence of white matter hyperintensities in individuals with migraine, particularly those with aura, though other investigations found no significant differences compared to controls.
Individuals with migraine and insulin resistance experienced more severe attacks, with greater pain intensity, longer duration, and increased disability compared to those without insulin resistance.

Weight loss, whether through surgical or non-surgical approaches, significantly reduced migraine attack frequency and intensity, with surgical interventions yielding greater and more sustained improvements.

A meta-analysis showed diabetes mellitus was negatively associated with migraine occurrence, while migraine was positively associated with subsequent diabetes occurrence, though evidence quality was low.

Propranolol reduces both migraine attack frequency and hypertension while improving anxiety and panic disorder symptoms, though beta-blockers should be used cautiously in depression due to fatigue and mood disturbance risk.
CGRP monoclonal antibodies show a favorable safety profile with no evidence of increased cardiovascular or psychiatric risk, and treatment may improve depressive symptoms.

Patients with chronic ocular pain had significantly lower visual photosensitivity discomfort thresholds (greater photosensitivity discomfort) than controls as measured by the Ocular Photosensitivity Analyzer.
VPDT did not differ significantly between inflammatory (Sjögren's disease) and neuropathic ocular pain subtypes of chronic ocular pain.
COP patients reported higher (worse) VLSQ-8 scores than controls, indicating greater subjective light sensitivity symptom burden.
COP patients had markedly higher OSDI scores than controls, indicating greater overall ocular surface disease symptom burden.
COP patients scored higher on the OSDI light-sensitivity item than controls.
Visual photosensitivity discomfort thresholds did not differ significantly between the inflammatory (Sjögren's disease) and neuropathic ocular pain subtypes of chronic ocular pain.
Lower photosensitivity discomfort thresholds (measured by OPA) were strongly correlated with higher VLSQ-8 light sensitivity symptom scores.
Lower photosensitivity discomfort thresholds were also correlated with higher OSDI Question 1 (light sensitivity) scores.

Adding chronic fatigue to the regression model that already included fibromyalgia improved prediction of visual photosensitivity discomfort threshold, raising the explained variance from 19.6% to 26.5%.
A study using machine learning on genetic data to diagnose migraine achieved statistically significantly better results than the currently established polygenic risk scoring approach.
Across AI diagnostic studies for headache disorders, classification accuracy ranged widely from 62% to 99.7%.
An AI model predicted migraine patients' response to CGRP-targeted treatments with accuracy ranging from 70% to 84%.
An AI model predicted the effect of NSAIDs as acute migraine treatment with 74% accuracy.
An AI model predicted the preventive effect of verapamil for cluster headache with AUC = 0.689.

A multi-dimensional Bayesian classifier predicted BoNT-A treatment response in chronic migraine patients with average accuracies of 73%, 83%, and 77% across three treatment stages, though test-set evaluation details were not reported.

A TabNet deep-learning representation combined with an AutoML pipeline predicted migraine preventive treatment response with accuracies of 80% for CGRP mAb, 73% for beta-blockers, 66% for gabapentin, 63% for topiramate, 63% for onabotulinumtoxinA, 60% for tricyclic antidepressants, and 60% for verapamil, using data from 4260 patients.

Imaging-based machine learning models predicted CGRP monoclonal antibody treatment efficacy, with the random forest model achieving 40%-65% accuracy in an external testing cohort of 93 patients, depending on the month of prediction after treatment.

Resting-state fMRI-derived neuroimaging biomarkers predicted NSAID treatment response for episodic migraine with 61% accuracy on a held-out test cohort of 39 participants, using a random forest model.
An ML model using demographic and clinical questionnaire data predicted with 87% accuracy which patients with medication overuse headache would become medication overuse-free.

Machine learning models combining genetic and clinical/demographic data outperformed models using only genotype data or only clinical data in predicting new-onset migraine, suggesting genotype-phenotype interactions contribute to migraine onset.

In an analysis of 459 individuals using the Boruta feature-importance algorithm, self-reported headache data showed stronger associations with migraine than genetic variant data, although some genetic variants were also possibly associated.
In a cohort of 61,826 individuals, migraine sufferers were more likely to seek medical care with increasing interictal burden, disability, and allodynia.
A multivariate logistic regression analysis of 178 individuals with migraine without aura identified factors influencing mild depression in this population.

Five large language models tested on 30 migraine-related queries each were rated predominantly appropriate by three independent migraine specialists, who considered LLMs valuable tools for clinical practice in headache.
A comprehensive big data analytics (CBDA) protocol combined with machine learning predictors achieved migraine diagnostic prediction accuracies exceeding 90%.

Resting-state fMRI data from 100 individuals were used to develop a linear regression model relating cortical/subcortical alterations to migraine frequency, achieving modest performance (ICC=0.33), while the model for migraine duration was not significant.

Analysis of ambulatory and hospitalization records from 116,136 patients using density estimation algorithms found migraine to be associated with mental, cardiovascular, neurological, gastroenterological, hepatological, musculoskeletal, metabolic, endocrinological, and otolaryngological comorbid disorders.
Brain MRI analysis of 51 subjects using decision tree regression suggested that damage to the superficial white matter structure is a pathological feature of new daily persistent headache.

Wearable-derived data showed that during migraine and tension-type headache days, patients slept more, had reduced physical activity, and had lower maximum heart rates, with migraine patients experiencing a greater everyday burden than tension-type headache patients.
Contrary to an initial hypothesis of pre-ictal hyperactivity, wearable-measured activity energy expenditure was found to be decreased during the pre-ictal and cluster headache phase.

Patients with double-positive anti-Ro/anti-La antibodies had a lower prevalence of hypertension and diabetes compared to single-positive patients.
Age at pSS diagnosis differed significantly across the 16 participating Egyptian rheumatology centers, with the oldest age at diagnosis in Aswan and the youngest in Giza.
The Minia rheumatology center had the highest rates of double anti-Ro/anti-La, ANA, and RF positivity among the 16 participating centers.
Intravenous galcanezumab reduced spontaneous trigeminocervical complex neuronal firing compared to control IgG in the durovascular-evoked model, reaching a maximal 73% reduction at 4 h 30 min.
Galcanezumab reduced spontaneous trigeminocervical complex neuronal activity compared to control IgG in the superior salivatory nucleus (SSN)-evoked model, reaching a maximal 67% reduction at 4 h.
In the durovascular model, galcanezumab reduced cutaneous noxious-evoked neuronal responses by up to 38% at 4 h 30 min.
In the durovascular model, galcanezumab reduced cutaneous non-noxious (brush)-evoked neuronal responses by up to 50% at 4 h 30 min.
In the SSN-evoked model, galcanezumab reduced cutaneous noxious-evoked neuronal responses by up to 34% at 4 h 30 min.
In the SSN-evoked model, galcanezumab reduced cutaneous non-noxious-evoked neuronal responses by up to 47% at 4 h 30 min.
Galcanezumab significantly reduced durovascular-evoked nociceptive Aδ-fiber activation in the trigeminocervical complex, with a maximal 48% reduction at the last time point.

Galcanezumab significantly reduced SSN-evoked nociceptive trigeminal activation in the trigeminocervical complex, with a maximal 32% decrease that did not return to baseline within the recording window.
Galcanezumab did not significantly alter mean arterial blood pressure compared to control IgG in the durovascular-evoked model.
Galcanezumab showed no significant change in mean arterial blood pressure compared to control IgG in the SSN-evoked model, though the effect approached significance.

Unlike galcanezumab, fremanezumab was reported in prior work to inhibit only high-threshold (not wide dynamic range) neurons in the trigeminocervical complex and to have no effect on cutaneous responses.

Prior distribution studies found monoclonal antibodies against CGRP reach highest levels in the dura mater and spleen, followed by trigeminal ganglion, with lower levels in hypothalamus, spinal cord, prefrontal cortex, cerebellum, and cerebrospinal fluid.
Galcanezumab has been reported to decrease hypothalamic activation in migraine patients, most robustly in treatment responders, a response not seen with CGRP receptor-targeted antibodies.
Clinical data show that CGRP-targeted antibodies can access the cerebrospinal fluid at a 1:1000 ratio compared to plasma and bind CGRP in the CSF over a one-month period in humans.

Fluorophore-labeled galcanezumab persisted in the dura mater and trigeminal ganglion for at least 30 days after subcutaneous injection, with an accompanying reduction in capsaicin-evoked CGRP release, specifically observed in females.

A phase 3 randomized controlled trial of galcanezumab for chronic cluster headache failed to meet its primary and key secondary endpoints, despite clinical practice reports of benefit in chronic cluster headache patients.
Cluster headache had the highest five-year prevalence among the trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias at 56.7 per 100,000.
Paroxysmal hemicrania had a five-year prevalence of 22.0 per 100,000 in the US EHR cohort.
Hemicrania continua had a five-year prevalence of 7.2 per 100,000.
SUNCT had the lowest five-year prevalence among the TACs at 2.3 per 100,000.

Prevalence of paroxysmal hemicrania and cluster headache was highest in the Midwest census region, while hemicrania continua and SUNCT prevalence was highest in the Northeast, and the West had the lowest prevalence of all four TACs.
All four TAC subtypes showed a higher prevalence in women, with the highest female-to-male ratio in hemicrania continua (2.4:1) and the lowest in cluster headache (1.3:1).
Prevalence of all four TACs peaked in patients aged 50-65 years, while the lowest prevalence age group varied by subtype; cluster headache had the lowest average patient age.

Race-ethnicity was associated with differences in TAC prevalence, with American Indian or Alaska Native-Hispanic/Latino individuals having the highest prevalence for all four TACs and Asian subgroups generally having the lowest.
Comorbid migraine diagnosis was common among TAC patients, most frequently in hemicrania continua, where 51.8% of patients also carried a migraine diagnosis.
Depression, anxiety, and irritable bowel syndrome were commonly comorbid in hemicrania continua patients, who had the highest rates of these comorbidities among the TAC subtypes.
SUNCT patients had the highest rate of comorbid cerebrovascular disease among the TACs, while cluster headache patients had the lowest.
Cluster headache patients had the highest rates among TACs of nicotine use disorder, alcohol-related disorders, and cannabis-related disorders.
Among cluster headache patients, men had notably higher rates of nicotine use disorder and alcohol-related disorders than women, while women had higher rates of anxiety and depression.
The vast majority of TAC patients received at least one commonly used treatment medication, ranging from 64.9% in paroxysmal hemicrania to 86.1% in hemicrania continua.
Steroids (methylprednisolone, prednisone, dexamethasone) were broadly used across all four TAC subtypes, with usage ranging from 57.3% to 62.6%.
Lamotrigine was prescribed to 21.8% of SUNCT patients, consistent with its recognized use for this condition.
Verapamil was prescribed to 18.9% of cluster headache patients.
Despite being the diagnostic and gold-standard treatment, indomethacin was underutilized in both hemicrania continua (46.6%) and especially paroxysmal hemicrania (only 14.7%).
Sumatriptan and zolmitriptan prescriptions were most frequent among cluster headache patients.
OnabotulinumtoxinA and galcanezumab were used most frequently among TAC patients with hemicrania continua.

A very high proportion of hemicrania continua patients receiving onabotulinumtoxinA also had a concurrent migraine diagnosis, raising the possibility that migraine coding was used to facilitate insurance coverage of the treatment rather than reflecting confirmed comorbid migraine.
Women with recent (past 2 years) midlife migraine had 30% greater odds of reporting vasomotor symptoms compared to women without migraine.
Among women reporting vasomotor symptoms, those with recent midlife migraine had higher odds of severe vasomotor symptoms than those without recent migraine.
Among women reporting vasomotor symptoms, recent midlife migraine was associated with prolonged vasomotor symptoms lasting 5 years or longer.
Migraine phenotype (with versus without aura) was not associated with vasomotor symptom frequency or duration.

Migraine with aura and self-reported clinician-diagnosed migraine were more strongly associated with severe vasomotor symptoms than migraine without aura or self-reported (non-clinician-diagnosed) migraine.
Mendelian randomization analysis found that genetic liability to depression was causally associated with increased risk of Sjögren's syndrome.
Mendelian randomization analysis found that genetic liability to depression was causally associated with a markedly increased risk of fibromyalgia syndrome.
Mendelian randomization analysis found that genetic liability to depression was causally associated with increased risk of psoriasis.
Mendelian randomization analysis found that genetic liability to depression was causally associated with increased risk of psoriatic arthritis.
No causal association was found between depression and risk of rheumatoid arthritis, systemic lupus erythematosus, polymyalgia rheumatica, systemic sclerosis, gout, polymyositis, or Behçet's disease.
Reverse Mendelian randomization found no significant causal effect of any autoimmune rheumatic disease on risk of depression.
Botulinum toxin cleaves SNAP-25, a SNARE complex component, blocking vesicle exocytosis and neurotransmitter/neuropeptide release, underlying its analgesic mechanism in headache disorders.

Botulinum toxin blocks release of nociceptive neuropeptides including CGRP, substance P, and other neurotransmitters from sensory neurons and reduces surface expression of nociceptive receptors, contributing to analgesia.
In the PREEMPT 1 trial, there was no statistically significant difference between onabotulinumtoxinA and placebo on the primary outcome of change in headache episode frequency at week 24.
OnabotulinumtoxinA produced a significantly greater decrease in mean number of headache days than placebo in the PREEMPT 1 chronic migraine trial.

In PREEMPT 2 (705 patients), onabotulinumtoxinA significantly reduced headache days versus placebo (primary outcome) and improved migraine days, moderate-severe headache days, triptan use, and headache impact.
Open-label follow-up of the PREEMPT trials demonstrated onabotulinumtoxinA is safe with a sustained effect over 56 weeks.
A systematic review found no difference in the number of migraine days between BoNT-A and placebo in the single available episodic migraine trial.
A meta-analysis of four chronic migraine studies found a decrease of 3.1 migraine days per month favoring BoNT-A over placebo.
A systematic review of 44 real-world studies found decreases of 10.6 headache days/month at 24 weeks and 10 fewer days at 52 weeks after onabotulinumtoxinA treatment.

Patients with excellent response to onabotulinumtoxinA for chronic migraine had a higher baseline prevalence of medication overuse compared with non-responders, and were more likely to have excellent responses in subsequent treatment cycles.

Among 235 elderly patients treated with onabotulinumtoxinA for chronic migraine, response to treatment, discontinuation rate, and adverse event incidence did not differ from non-elderly patients, and no serious adverse events occurred.
A meta-analysis of observational studies in children and adolescents showed decreased headache intensity and frequency in chronic migraine after onabotulinumtoxinA treatment.

In a class I trial of patients aged 12-17 with chronic migraine, onabotulinumtoxinA 155 U (n=45), 74 U (n=43), and placebo (n=37) all showed similar improvement in headache day frequency, with no significant difference between groups, reflecting a large placebo effect in this age group.

In a study of 397 pregnancies exposed to BoNT-A (95% in the first trimester or before conception, 30% for migraine/headache), fetal loss (19%) and major fetal defects (0.7%) rates were considered within the expected range for the general population of the same age.

In a prospective study of 126 pregnant people using onabotulinumtoxinA for chronic migraine (97 continuing treatment during pregnancy), there were no fetal malformations and only 3 (2.4%) fetal losses, a rate lower than expected for the general population.

In an early open-label study of 12 patients (9 with chronic cluster headache) treated with 50 U of onabotulinumtoxinA applied ipsilateral to the headache site, three of the chronic cluster headache patients showed improved headache frequency and intensity compared to baseline.

Lampl et al. found that applying the PREEMPT injection paradigm in 12 patients with refractory chronic cluster headache significantly reduced headache day frequency, total headache duration, and headache intensity compared to baseline, with 59% experiencing a ≥50% reduction in total headache duration.

Sphenopalatine ganglion blockade with 25-50 U of onabotulinumtoxinA in refractory chronic cluster headache decreased attack frequency compared to baseline through 6 months, with a ≥50% reduction seen in five of seven analyzed patients.

Long-term follow-up of repeated sphenopalatine ganglion blockade with onabotulinumtoxinA showed decreased attack frequency and severe/unbearable attack frequency, and increased headache-free days at months 18 and 24 compared to baseline.

A larger series of 31 patients undergoing repeated sphenopalatine ganglion blockade with onabotulinumtoxinA for refractory chronic cluster headache showed decreased attack frequency after each of four applications, with a favorable safety profile.

An open trial of ipsilateral otic ganglion blockade with 12.5-25 international units of onabotulinumtoxinA for intractable chronic cluster headache showed a favorable safety profile but did not prove effective.
Eleven reported cases of hemicrania continua showed improvement in headache intensity and frequency after treatment with BoNT-A, mostly using the PREEMPT protocol.
A male adolescent with SUNCT treated with subcutaneous BoNT-A into the area of pain had no recurrence of pain at 17 months of follow-up.

A 55-year-old man with treatment-refractory SUNCT had significant improvement in attack frequency and intensity within weeks of periorbital onabotulinumtoxinA injections and remained stable over two and a half years, while continuing lamotrigine and gabapentin.
A 65-year-old woman with SUNA treated with subcutaneous BoNT-A in the painful area, followed by a second treatment cycle, remained pain-free during 16 months of follow-up.

A patient with new daily persistent headache treated with 100 U of BoNT-A across multiple cranial/cervical muscles remained headache-free for 8 to 10 weeks after each application cycle during one year of follow-up.
A second case of new daily persistent headache treated with 195 units of BoNT-A had only partial improvement and the patient was never pain-free.

A retrospective cohort of 19 patients with new daily persistent headache treated with onabotulinumtoxinA (PREEMPT protocol) showed improved headache frequency in 50% at 6 months and 64% at 12 months, and improved intensity in 15%, 50%, and 78% of patients at 3, 6, and 12 months respectively.

In an open-label trial of 53 patients with nummular headache treated with onabotulinumtoxinA applied in a cross pattern to the painful area, headache frequency significantly improved from a baseline of 24.5 days to 6.9 days per month at weeks 20-24.

A double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled crossover trial of Abobotulinum toxin A (PREEMPT protocol) in 40 patients with persistent post-traumatic headache found a significantly greater decrease in pain frequency and intensity in the BoNT-A group than placebo.

A prospective cohort study found that BoNT-A treatment of cervical dystonia decreased the impact of headache attributed to craniocervical dystonia (measured by HIT-6) but did not affect other headache types experienced by these patients.
Four small open-label studies (8 to 15 patients each) of BoNT-A for trigeminal neuralgia showed improvement in pain intensity and frequency.
An open-label clinical trial found that onabotulinumtoxinA significantly reduced headache frequency in patients with nummular headache, from a baseline of 24.5 days to 6.9 days during weeks 20-24.
A randomized placebo-controlled crossover trial found no statistically significant reduction in headache frequency with AbobotulinumtoxinA versus placebo in persistent post-traumatic headache.
In the same trial, AbobotulinumtoxinA significantly reduced headache intensity compared to placebo in patients with persistent post-traumatic headache.
Sixty percent of patients with craniocervical dystonia experience headache as a comorbid symptom.

A prospective cohort study found that treating cervical dystonia with botulinum toxin A decreased the impact of headache attributed to craniocervical dystonia, as measured by the Headache Impact Test, but did not affect other headache types in the same patients.
Four small open-label studies including 8 to 15 patients with trigeminal neuralgia showed improvement in both pain intensity and frequency after BoNT-A treatment.

Larger open-label studies of 40 to 100 patients with trigeminal neuralgia corroborated improvement in pain intensity and frequency with BoNT-A, benefiting both paroxysmal and continuous pain phenotypes.

Four double-blind, randomized, placebo-controlled trials (n = 20, 36, 42, and 84 patients) found that BoNT-A significantly reduced pain intensity, and in some studies frequency, in trigeminal neuralgia compared to placebo, with only mild-to-moderate adverse reactions.
NDPH patients had a numerically lower rate of ≥30% improvement in moderate-to-severe headache days than daily chronic migraine patients, but this difference was not statistically significant.
NDPH patients had a significantly lower response rate for moderate-to-severe headache days compared to non-daily chronic migraine patients.
Improvement in overall monthly headache days was rare in NDPH and daily CM but common in non-daily CM.
Headache severity did not differ significantly between the NDPH, daily-CM, and non-daily-CM groups following treatment.
Patient-estimated improvement was lowest in NDPH, intermediate in daily-CM, and highest in non-daily-CM.
Patient-estimated improvement was strongly correlated with objective improvement in moderate-to-severe headache days.
Response rates to erenumab and galcanezumab were similar across the whole study population, suggesting drug choice did not bias the main results.
Approximately half of all patients experienced at least one adverse effect from CGRP monoclonal antibody treatment, with constipation the most common, affecting nearly a quarter overall.
Two patients experienced serious adverse events (severe allergic rash in daily-CM; severe flare of inflammatory arthritis in NDPH) after starting erenumab, both resolving after treatment cessation.
One patient reported worsening of PoTS symptoms as an adverse event during CGRP monoclonal antibody treatment.
At baseline, the NDPH group had fewer females and less medication overuse than the chronic migraine groups.
The authors hypothesize that CGRP may play a smaller pathophysiological role in NDPH than in chronic migraine, given the poorer treatment response observed.

A prior similarly designed study found no significant difference in headache diary outcomes or patient-reported improvement between NDPH and chronic migraine groups treated with onabotulinumtoxinA, in contrast to the CGRP monoclonal antibody findings of the present study.

In a prior retrospective study of adolescents with mixed chronic headache disorders (including NDPH) treated with CGRP monoclonal antibodies, about 30% of the total population had a significant benefit, though NDPH-specific response was not separately reported.

A prior retrospective study of 82 patients with abrupt-onset continuous daily headache disorders (53 with NDPH) found that about a third of NDPH patients had subjective improvement in headache/migraine symptoms with erenumab.

Preclinical evidence suggests CGRP monoclonal antibodies may preferentially affect A-delta pain fibres, whereas onabotulinumtoxinA selectively inhibits C-fibres, a mechanistic difference proposed to explain divergent efficacy in NDPH.

Despite limited objective reduction in headache frequency, over half of NDPH patients reported subjective improvement and a third had clinically meaningful improvement in disability scores after CGRP monoclonal antibody treatment.
About 30% of patients had a ≥30% reduction in headache severity, suggesting reduced pain intensity may contribute to perceived clinical benefit even without reduced headache frequency.
Radiofrequency ablation of the SPG reduces cluster headache days by approximately 50% while preserving sensory and motor function.

Cryoablation of the posterior nasal nerve significantly reduced nasal symptoms and improved quality of life in a large cohort of chronic rhinitis patients, with a favorable safety profile, suggesting possible extrapolation to SPG cryoablation.

SPG-targeted onabotulinumtoxinA injections have produced substantial reductions in pain intensity and attack frequency in patients with chronic migraine, chronic cluster headache, and trigeminal neuralgia.
In the multicenter randomized sham-controlled Pathway CH-1 trial, SPG stimulation aborted 67% of cluster headache attacks compared to 7% with sham stimulation.
64% of participants in the Pathway CH-1 trial experienced acute relief from chronic cluster headache attacks within 15 minutes of SPG stimulation.
43% of participants in the Pathway CH-1 trial showed a ≥50% reduction in cluster headache attack frequency with SPG stimulation.
Long-term data show that over 60% of patients maintained a therapeutic response to SPG stimulation at 24 months.

Jürgens et al. (2017) reported that over 80% of patients experienced a therapeutic response of at least 30% at 24-month follow-up, with most responders achieving a ≥75% reduction in attack frequency, classifying them as extreme responders to SPG neuromodulation.

A model-based economic analysis using data from the Pathway CH-1 trial found SPG stimulation for chronic cluster headache yields an incremental cost-effectiveness ratio of EUR 2736 per quality-adjusted life year over 5 years in the German healthcare system, well below typical willingness-to-pay thresholds.

SPG stimulation implantation carries risks such as transient sensory disturbances (e.g., maxillary nerve numbness), facial swelling, or pain, typically resolving within three months, with rare complications including lead migration and contralateral 'side shift' of cluster attacks.

The ONSTIM trial, a randomized controlled study of occipital nerve stimulation in chronic migraine, reported modest reductions in headache days but failed to achieve its primary efficacy endpoint, with a high placebo response.

The PRISM trial and various case series on peripheral nerve stimulation demonstrated inconsistent outcomes and high device-related complication rates, including lead migration, infection, and hardware malfunction.

No randomized controlled trials or large case series currently support the use of SPG blocks for tension-type headache, as TTH lacks significant autonomic features and the rationale for SPG involvement is weak.

A prospective observational study of 14 patients with refractory trigeminal neuralgia who received 40 units of onabotulinumtoxinA per side to the SPG showed a 50% reduction in pain scores and daily attack frequency by 60 days, with transient hemifacial weakness in 77% of patients that resolved within three months.

In a study of 34 patients with persistent idiopathic facial pain, CT-guided dual-target neurolysis of the SPG and trigeminal ganglion resulted in significantly higher rates of ≥50% pain relief at one month compared to SPG-only blocks, with better response in patients with positive neuropathic screening (DN4 > 4).

Mojica et al. (2017) found consistent short-term relief with SPG blocks for migraine and cluster headache in a narrative review, though variability in technique and outcome measures limited pooled analysis.

Sánchez-Gómez et al. (2021) reviewed clinical trials on SPG neurostimulation and concluded it is a safe and effective therapy for chronic cluster headache, with mostly minor adverse events in the immediate postoperative period.

Láinez et al. (2014) conducted a randomized sham-controlled trial in 32 implanted patients with chronic cluster headache; 68% experienced an acute or preventive response, SPG stimulation achieved 67% pain relief in treated attacks compared to 7% with sham, and over 40% achieved a ≥50% reduction in attack frequency.

In a study of 34 patients with persistent idiopathic facial pain, CT-guided dual-target neurolysis of the sphenopalatine ganglion and trigeminal ganglion produced significantly higher rates of ≥50% pain relief at one month than SPG-only neurolysis, with better response in patients with positive neuropathic screening (DN4>4).

A narrative review by Mojica et al. (2017) found consistent short-term relief from sphenopalatine ganglion blocks for migraine and cluster headache, though variability in technique and outcome measures limited pooled analysis.

Sánchez-Gómez et al. (2021) reviewed clinical trials on sphenopalatine ganglion neurostimulation and concluded it is a safe and effective therapy for chronic cluster headache, with mostly minor adverse events in the immediate postoperative period.

In a randomized sham-controlled trial by Láinez et al. (2014), sphenopalatine ganglion stimulation in 32 implanted chronic cluster headache patients produced a 67% rate of pain relief in treated attacks versus 7% with sham stimulation, with 68% of patients showing an acute or preventive response and over 40% achieving a ≥50% reduction in attack frequency.

A systematic review by Ho et al. (2017) of 83 studies found the strongest evidence for SPG block, radiofrequency ablation, and neurostimulation in cluster headache, moderate evidence for SPG blocks in trigeminal neuralgia, migraine, and postoperative sinus pain, and only case-report-level evidence for conditions like persistent idiopathic facial pain, postherpetic neuralgia, and cancer pain; SPG radiofrequency ablation showed longer-lasting relief than blocks, and most studies lacked replication.
Among 957 individuals screened, 69 were HTLV-positive, comprising 56 HTLV-1 cases (5.9%), 12 HTLV-2 cases (1.2%), and 1 undetermined case (0.1%).
Of the HTLV-infected individuals, 15 were referred for rheumatology evaluation due to complaints suggestive of rheumatological disease, 11 with HTLV-1 and 4 with HTLV-2.
Arthralgia was the most common joint manifestation, reported in 13 of 15 patients (10 with HTLV-1 and 3 with HTLV-2).
Two cases of arthritis (as opposed to arthralgia alone) were observed, and both occurred exclusively in HTLV-1-infected patients.
Myalgia was reported in eight of the 15 patients, five with HTLV-1 infection and three with HTLV-2 infection, split evenly between localized and diffuse pain presentations.

All four patients with diffuse muscle pain (two HTLV-1, two HTLV-2) fulfilled clinical characteristics suggestive of fibromyalgia (chronic pain, tender points, sleep disorders, and mood disorders) and were diagnosed with fibromyalgia, including patients with HTLV-2 infection.
A previously published epidemiological study cited in the discussion found fibromyalgia diagnosed in 38% of an HTLV-infected population compared with 4.8% of a control population.
The majority (86.7%) of patient samples were nonreactive for ANA, rheumatoid factor, and anti-CCP testing.

Two HTLV-1-infected patients had high-titer ANA reactivity: one with a fine speckled nuclear pattern at 1:3200 and one with a homogeneous nucleolar pattern at 1:320, without reactivity for other specific autoantibodies.
None of the samples tested for rheumatoid factor and anti-CCP were reactive.
Psoriatic arthritis, diagnosed via CASPAR criteria, was the only inflammatory autoimmune rheumatological disease identified in the cohort, occurring in one HTLV-1-infected patient.
A case of low back pain in an HTLV-2-infected patient is reported, described by the authors as the first such report in the literature.

The authors conclude that HTLV-1 infection is associated with rheumatological disease manifestations and, as a novel finding, HTLV-2 infection is also associated with rheumatological/rheumatoid-arthritis-like symptoms.
Female sex predominated among HTLV-infected patients presenting with rheumatological manifestations (12 of 15, 80%).
Substance P is released from primary afferent neurons and binds neurokinin-1 receptors expressed in both peripheral tissues and central pain-processing regions.

In the meninges, substance P contributes to vasodilation, plasma protein extravasation, mast cell degranulation, and immune cell recruitment, facilitating neurogenic inflammation and possibly lowering the activation threshold of meningeal nociceptors.
In the central nervous system, substance P promotes excitatory neurotransmission by potentiating glutamatergic activity and attenuating inhibitory GABAergic signaling, amplifying pain transmission.
Preclinical studies consistently show that neurokinin-1 receptor antagonists inhibit substance P-induced neurogenic inflammation and neuronal activation.
Randomized controlled trials of neurokinin-1 receptor antagonists were not superior to placebo in treating migraine.

Randomized controlled trials of neurokinin-1 receptor antagonists failed to show superiority over placebo for migraine treatment, and re-appraisal suggests this may reflect methodological shortcomings such as underpowered samples and suboptimal efficacy endpoints rather than a true lack of biological effect.
In a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled, two-way crossover study, intravenous infusion of substance P potently induced headache and arterial dilation in healthy adults.
Repeated nitroglycerin (NTG) administration in rats increased c-fos expression in the trigeminal nucleus caudalis, consistent with central sensitization.
Repeated NTG administration increased CGRP levels in the trigeminal nucleus caudalis, indicating a role in migraine pathophysiology in this model.

Repeated NTG exposure induced chronic mechanical and thermal hypersensitivity in the rat migraine model, evidenced by reduced paw and periorbital mechanical thresholds and altered paw withdrawal latency.
Stellate ganglion block (SGB) treatment alleviated hyperalgesic symptoms and decreased CGRP and c-fos levels in the trigeminal nucleus caudalis in the migraine model.
Machine learning analysis of transcriptomic data identified a significant increase in Romo1 (reactive oxygen species modulator 1) expression in the NTG-induced migraine model.
Romo1 expression, elevated in the migraine model, notably decreased following stellate ganglion block treatment, suggesting Romo1 mediates part of SGB's therapeutic effect.
The paper proposes a distinct clinical phenotype of migraine with associated myofascial pain that bridges corpalgia, fibromyalgia, and chronic migraine.
Dry eye patients, including those with Sjögren's syndrome, showed significantly cooler ocular surface and central upper lid temperatures on infrared thermography than normal eyes.
Initial ocular surface temperature positively correlated with tear film break-up time and with the initial time-segmented cooling rate in dry eye patients.

A case report found that infrared thermography performed at different ambient temperatures improved characterisation of thermoregulatory sweating abnormalities in a patient with Ross syndrome associated with Sjögren's syndrome.
In women with fibromyalgia, thermographically measured core body temperature was significantly associated with overall symptom impact, daytime dysfunction, and reduced physical activity.
Hypothenar eminence skin temperature in women with fibromyalgia was significantly associated with pressure pain thresholds at the greater trochanter and with sleep medication use.
Resting skin temperature measured by infrared thermography did not differ meaningfully between women with fibromyalgia and healthy women, indicating limited diagnostic value.

In a cross-sectional study of 103 participants, computerised infrared thermography showed low sensitivity and specificity for detecting pain at tender points, suggesting it is not a reliable diagnostic method for fibromyalgia.
Health Belief Model (HBM) constructs added in Step 3 of the regression explained a substantial and significant additional 40% of variance in intent to wear a mask in public.
HBM constructs added in Step 3 explained a substantial and significant 24.2% of variance in intent to test for COVID-19 after exposure.
HBM constructs added in Step 3 explained a substantial and significant 27% of variance in intent to test before attending a social event.
HBM constructs added in Step 3 significantly explained 19.5% of variance in intent to obtain a COVID-19 booster vaccine among vaccinated individuals.

Higher perceived susceptibility to Long COVID predicted greater intent to carry out all four COVID-19 preventive behaviors (masking, testing after exposure, testing before events, and booster uptake).
Higher self-efficacy to carry out preventive behaviors was a significant predictor of intent for all four COVID-19 preventive behaviors.
Higher perceived benefits of a given preventive behavior predicted higher intent to carry out that corresponding behavior.
High perceived barriers to mask wearing and to getting the booster vaccine were significant predictors of lower intent to carry out these two behaviors.
Perceived severity of Long COVID was a significant predictor only for intent to test after COVID-19 exposure, not for the other three behaviors.
Cues to action (healthcare provider discussion of Long COVID) was a significant predictor only for intent to test before attending a social event.
Black respondents were more likely than White respondents to express intent to carry out COVID-19 preventive behaviors across all models except intent to get the booster vaccine.
Hispanic respondents were more likely than White respondents to express intent to wear a mask in public and to test after COVID-19 exposure.
Age, sex, education, and rurality did not significantly predict intent to carry out any of the four COVID-19 preventive behaviors in the final models.
No significant racial or ethnic differences were observed in booster vaccine uptake intent.
About half of patients with anti-IgLON5 disease had co-existing dysautonomia as a non-sleep-related feature at initial evaluation, alongside bulbar dysfunction and cognitive impairment.
Elastic compression stockings did not significantly reduce the proportion of participants with at least one vasovagal syncope recurrence compared with sham stockings over 12 months.
Time to first vasovagal syncope recurrence (VVS-free survival) did not differ significantly between active and sham compression stocking groups.
Adherence and discontinuation rates for compression stockings were similar between the active treatment and sham groups.
The median number of recurrent vasovagal syncope episodes was similar between the active ECS and sham groups.
Significantly fewer vasovagal syncope episodes occurred specifically while participants were actively wearing the compression stockings.
Total hypothalamic volume was significantly smaller in migraine patients (combined episodic and chronic) compared with healthy controls.
Inferior tubular hypothalamic subregion volume was smaller in migraine patients than in healthy controls and remained significant after multiple-comparison correction.
Anterior inferior hypothalamic subregion volume was smaller in migraine patients than in controls at nominal significance, but this did not survive correction for multiple comparisons.
Lateralized analyses showed significant volume loss in the left inferior tubular, right superior tubular, and right anterior inferior hypothalamic subregions in migraine patients versus controls.
Whole hypothalamic and inferior tuberal subregion volumes differed significantly across the three-group comparison of healthy controls, episodic migraine, and chronic migraine.
Chronic migraine patients had significantly smaller total hypothalamic and inferior tubular volumes than healthy controls after adjusting for age, gender, BMI, and TIV.
Lateralized hypothalamic subregion volumes were significantly smaller in chronic migraine patients than healthy controls in pairwise comparisons.

Smaller inferior tubular hypothalamic volume was correlated with higher monthly migraine attack frequency after adjustment for covariates.
Mendelian randomization showed that genetically reduced total hypothalamic volume causally increases the risk of migraine.
Mendelian randomization showed that genetically reduced inferior tubular hypothalamic volume causally increases migraine risk.
Reduced total hypothalamic volume was causally associated with increased risk specifically of migraine without aura (MO) in MR analysis.
Reduced inferior tubular hypothalamic volume was causally associated with elevated risk of migraine without aura (MO) in MR analysis.
No significant causal association was found between hypothalamic volume (total or subregional) and migraine with aura (MA) in MR analysis.

Reverse MR suggested migraine without aura was nominally associated with reduced total hypothalamic volume, but this did not remain significant after FDR correction, indicating no robust reverse causal effect.
Reduced total hypothalamic volume was causally associated with lower abundance of the gut bacterial genus Eubacterium ruminantium group.
Reduced total hypothalamic volume was causally associated with lower abundance of the gut bacterial genus Defluviitaleaceae UCG011.
Decreased inferior tubular hypothalamic volume was causally associated with increased abundance of gut bacterial family FamilyXIII.

Higher abundance of gut bacterial family FamilyXIII was causally associated with decreased risk of migraine without aura (MO).

The genus Eubacterium ruminantium group partially mediates the causal effect of total hypothalamic volume on migraine without aura (MO) risk, accounting for 11.8% of the total effect.
Reverse Mendelian randomization suggested migraine without aura was nominally associated with reduced total hypothalamic volume, but this association did not survive FDR correction.
Mendelian randomization showed reduced total hypothalamic volume was causally associated with lower abundance of the gut bacterial genus Eubacterium ruminantium group.
Mendelian randomization showed reduced total hypothalamic volume was causally associated with lower abundance of the gut bacterial genus Defluviitaleaceae UCG011.
Mendelian randomization showed decreased inferior tubular hypothalamic volume was causally associated with increased abundance of the gut bacterial family FamilyXIII.
Reduced abundance of genus Defluviitaleaceae UCG011 was causally associated with an increased risk of migraine.
Lower abundance of genus Eubacterium ruminantium group was causally associated with elevated risk of migraine without aura.
Higher abundance of family FamilyXIII was causally associated with decreased risk of migraine without aura.
Two-step mediation analysis showed genus Defluviitaleaceae UCG011 partially mediated the causal effect of total hypothalamic volume on migraine risk, accounting for 5.2% of the total effect.

Two-step mediation analysis showed genus Eubacterium ruminantium group partially mediated the causal effect of total hypothalamic volume on migraine without aura risk, accounting for 11.8% of the total effect.
Family FamilyXIII exhibited a suppressive mediation effect, accounting for 20.9% of the association between inferior tubular hypothalamic volume and migraine without aura risk.

Sensitivity analyses found no evidence of heterogeneity or horizontal pleiotropy among the significant hypothalamus-migraine Mendelian randomization associations, supporting the robustness of the causal estimates.
Before exercise, blood exposed to the superantigen SEB from ME/CFS patients showed elevated levels of CXCL5, GM-CSF, IL-1β, IL-2, IL-6, IL-8, IL-23, and TNF-α compared to healthy controls.
Similar but marginally significant (padj<0.10) elevations were seen for IFN-γ, IL-13, and IL-17 in SEB-stimulated blood from ME/CFS before exercise.
SEB-induced cytokine responses were greater in female than male ME/CFS patients, consistent with known sex differences in immune responses to microbial stimuli.

Female ME/CFS patients younger than 45 years had significantly higher SEB-induced CXCL5, IL-1β, IL-6, and IL-8 than age-matched female HC before and after exercise, with IL-23 elevated before exercise; differences in older females (>45y) were not significant.
Plasma testosterone levels were negatively associated with age in female participants, independent of ME/CFS status.
In response to heat-killed Candida albicans (HKCA), ME/CFS subjects had elevated baseline levels of IFN-γ and TNF-α compared to controls.
Baseline IL-1β levels in response to HKCA were elevated in ME/CFS but did not reach statistical significance.
