After exercise, HKCA-induced GM-CSF, IFN-γ, IL-1β, IL-6, IL-10, and TNF-α decreased in female ME/CFS patients but not in males, possibly reflecting immune exhaustion.

TruCulture responses to LPS and poly I:C showed higher cytokine secretion than unstimulated controls in both groups, but no significant case-control differences were observed at the single dose/time point tested.

In a small subset of pre-exercise PBMC samples tested across multiple doses and durations, LPS and poly I:C induced dose- and time-dependent IL-6 responses that were higher in ME/CFS than HC, most evident at lower doses and 24-hour incubation.
Baseline plasma levels of CSF1 and LRP8 were lower in ME/CFS compared to HC, consistent with earlier reports.
Plasma levels of protein C (proC) and BATF3 were elevated in ME/CFS both before and after exercise.
Post-exercise plasma levels of the endogenous retrovirus ERVV1 were elevated in ME/CFS, potentially linked to inflammation and neurological dysfunction.
Integrative pathway analysis showed that analytes involved in integrin cell surface interactions, VEGF signaling, and leukocyte adhesion/diapedesis pathways were reduced in ME/CFS before exercise.
ECM degradation pathway analytes were elevated in ME/CFS after exercise per integrative pathway analysis.
Plasma citrate increased after exercise in ME/CFS but decreased in healthy controls, suggesting impaired TCA cycle flux and mitochondrial dysfunction in ME/CFS.
ChemRICH chemical enrichment analysis showed higher plasma triglycerides and diglycerides in ME/CFS both before and after exercise.
Plasma acylcarnitines, particularly CAR(12:0), were lower after exercise in ME/CFS, indicating reduced flux of fatty acids for mitochondrial β-oxidation.
Before exercise, ME/CFS patients had lower plasma levels of 12,13-diHOME compared to healthy controls.
After exercise, levels of 12,13-diHOME and its precursor linoleic acid were increased in ME/CFS compared to healthy controls, with the shift significant for linoleic acid.
KYN:TRP ratios were lower in ME/CFS before exercise but increased after exercise, suggesting exercise-induced overactivation of the kynurenine pathway diverting tryptophan from serotonin synthesis.
KYNA:KYN ratios were higher in ME/CFS before exercise and decreased after exercise, indicating reduced kynurenine aminotransferase activity post-exercise.
Baseline plasma levels of the gut-microbiota-derived metabolite indole-3-lactate were depleted in ME/CFS.
Plasma propionic acid, a short-chain fatty acid, was elevated after exercise in ME/CFS and may contribute to mitochondrial disruption, neuroinflammation, and cognitive impairment.
Before exercise, plasma levels of the neuronal proteins EPHA4 and CNTN4, both involved in synaptic plasticity, were lower in ME/CFS.
After exercise, plasma levels of ELAVL2, which regulates post-transcriptional expression of neuronal genes, were elevated in ME/CFS.
In response to exercise, plasma NRXN1 levels decreased in ME/CFS, suggesting reduced synaptic adhesion and neuronal transmission that may contribute to PEM-related cognitive impairment.
ORN:CIT and ARG:CIT ratios were elevated in ME/CFS before exercise, reflecting impaired early urea cycle steps, and decreased after exercise, reflecting impairments in later urea cycle stages.
Plasma glucuronic acid was higher in ME/CFS both before and after exercise, concordant with increased gut β-glucuronidase activity and dysbiosis.
Before exercise, plasma levels of EIF1 and UBE2D3, both involved in protein translation and quality control, were higher in ME/CFS, consistent with a proposed hypometabolic state.
After exercise, plasma levels of the copper-dependent enzyme AOC2 and copper-transport protein CUTC were higher in ME/CFS, indicating increased oxidative stress from reactive oxygen species.
Post-exercise plasma levels of MAPK6, induced by oxidative stress and linked to IL-8 production, were elevated in ME/CFS.
Lower baseline levels of 12,13-diHOME correlated with higher Multidimensional Fatigue Inventory scores of physical fatigue and reduced activity in both ME/CFS and healthy controls.
Higher post-exercise plasma GDF15 levels in ME/CFS positively correlated with MFI scores of general fatigue, physical fatigue, and reduced activity.
Reduced baseline CNTN4 levels, a neuroplasticity-related protein, correlated with higher general fatigue scores in ME/CFS.
Reduced pre- and post-exercise tetranectin (CLEC3B) levels in ME/CFS correlated with higher MFI scores of physical fatigue and reduced activity/motivation respectively.
Elevated post-exercise levels of S100A8 and C1r in ME/CFS correlated with MFI scores of reduced activity/motivation, consistent with dysregulated calcium signaling and complement activation.
Plasma phosphate decreased after exercise in healthy controls but not in ME/CFS, consistent with impaired phosphate utilization for ATP generation in ME/CFS.
Plasma testosterone levels were negatively associated with age in female subjects, while no significant age-hormone association was seen in males after BMI adjustment.
Female ME/CFS subjects showed amino acid abnormalities indicative of glutathione depletion both before and after exercise, a subgroup-specific finding distinct from male ME/CFS subjects.
Male ME/CFS subjects had lower plasma levels of plasmalogens, suggesting peroxisomal dysfunction distinct from the female subgroup pattern.

In long duration (>3 years) ME/CFS, post-exercise levels of IL-6, BMP1, and WNT5A were elevated, reflecting impaired leukocyte adhesion, ECM homeostasis and non-canonical WNT signaling promoting adipogenesis and inflammation.
Plasma citrulline levels were reduced specifically in the long-duration (>3 years) ME/CFS subgroup, consistent with urea cycle and gut mucosal integrity impairment.
Plasma aspartic acid levels increased after exercise specifically in the long-duration ME/CFS subgroup, reflecting urea cycle impairment.
Across nine studies reviewed, the reported frequency of migraine in people with FND ranged from 6% to 53%.
In the three largest case-control studies comparing functional seizures with epilepsy, migraine was more common in the functional seizure group, with odds ratios of 2.6, 3.0 and 3.3.
One smaller case-control study of 170 patients found no difference in migraine frequency between functional seizures and epilepsy.
In an international online study of 456 FND patients with mixed symptoms, 13% reported having migraines before their FND diagnosis.
In a case series of 42 individuals with both functional seizures and headache, 65% had migraine, and 73% reported reductions in both functional seizures and headache during migraine treatment.
A prospective study of 51 individuals with functional movement disorders found that 78% had headache, of whom 23 met diagnostic criteria for migraine.
A 14-month prospective study of 1200 young adults reported approximately twice as many functional neurological (conversion) symptoms in migraineurs compared to non-migraineurs.
In a single-centre Indian study of 1000 migraineurs (800 adults, 200 children), functional seizures were found in 16.5% overall (19.3% of adults and 5.5% of children), with nearly all cases female.

In a study of 897 children with migraine, functional neurological symptoms (nonepileptic shaking spells, tremor, functional gait disorder) occurred in 4.3% of chronic migraine patients and 0.9% of episodic migraine patients.

A systematic review of 34 case-control studies including 1405 people with FND found increased odds of childhood/adulthood stressors compared with controls: OR 5.6 for emotional neglect, OR 3.9 for physical abuse and OR 3.3 for childhood sexual abuse.

A meta-analysis of 28 studies involving over 150,000 participants found adverse childhood experiences associated with migraine, at a pooled OR of 1.48 for one or more experiences, rising to OR 2.1 for four or more.
PTSD is comorbid with migraine at a frequency of 14-25% versus 1-12% in population controls, and is more prevalent in chronic migraine (43%) than episodic migraine (9%).
A meta-analysis of 4272 people with FND found chronic pain in 55%, irritable bowel syndrome in 16% and fibromyalgia in 10%, all higher than control populations.
A meta-analysis of 4.2 million individuals with primary headache (at least 82% migraine) found fibromyalgia in 26%, three to six times higher than population estimates of 2-8%.
A German insurance data study of 56,597 adolescents found that those with migraine had a higher risk of developing back pain (OR 1.6) and irritable bowel syndrome (OR 1.5) over a 10-year follow-up.

In genetically confirmed hemiplegic migraine, limb weakness during aura lasted between 20 minutes and 24 hours in all cases studied, and was almost always accompanied by at least one other reversible aura symptom.
In the original paper describing the CACNA1A genetic variant in hemiplegic migraine, 6 of 89 patients had auras lasting up to 5 days.
In childhood-onset hemiplegic migraine cases with PRRT2 gene variants, 4 of 49 patients had auras lasting more than 24 hours, up to 10 days in the longest case.
Another study found that 8 of 65 patients with hemiplegic migraine had motor symptoms lasting longer than 24 hours.

Both migraine and functional neurological disorder show a female preponderance of approximately three times more common in women, with similar age-of-onset distributions peaking in the twenties and thirties.
Migraine is moderately heritable, with heritability estimates of up to 60%, whereas heritability of functional neurological disorder has not yet been studied.

A systematic review of 34 case-control studies involving 1405 people with functional neurological disorder found increased odds of childhood emotional neglect (OR 5.6), childhood sexual abuse (OR 3.3), and physical abuse (OR 3.9) compared with controls.
In the same meta-analysis, recent stressful life events were less strongly associated with functional neurological disorder (OR 2.0-2.5) compared with neurological or healthy controls.

A meta-analysis of 28 studies involving over 150,000 participants found that one or more adverse childhood experiences was associated with a pooled odds ratio of 1.48 for migraine, rising to 2.1 for four or more adverse experiences.
PTSD is comorbid with migraine at a frequency of 14-25% compared with 1-12% in population controls, and is more prevalent in chronic migraine (43%) than episodic migraine (9%).
Migraine has been associated with an increased risk of depression (two to three times more common) and anxiety (two to five times more common) compared with the general population.

A meta-analysis of 4272 people with functional neurological disorder found that 55% had chronic pain, 16% had irritable bowel syndrome, and 10% had fibromyalgia, all higher than in control populations.
A meta-analysis of 4.2 million individuals with primary headache (at least 82% with migraine) found that 26% had fibromyalgia, three to six times higher than population estimates of 2-8%.

A German insurance data study of 56,597 adolescents found that migraine was associated with a higher risk of developing back pain (OR 1.6) and irritable bowel syndrome (OR 1.5) over a 10-year follow-up.
A multicentre US and Canada study of 1348 people with migraine found fibromyalgia in 10% of patients.
A Swedish study of 151 migraine patients found irritable bowel syndrome in 7% and chronic fatigue syndrome in 3%, with odds ratios of 3-6 compared to 3255 controls.
A Taiwanese registry-based study found that 6902 migraine patients had a 1.5-fold increased risk of developing chronic fatigue syndrome compared with 27,608 controls.
The same Taiwanese database found a 1.9-fold increased risk of irritable bowel syndrome in 14,117 migraine patients compared with controls, an association especially strong in people under 30.
In a study of 59 individuals with persistent postural perceptual dizziness, 53% met formal diagnostic criteria for migraine.
In epilepsy, up to 5% of patients may also have comorbid functional seizures.

Impaired prepulse inhibition of the R2 response of the blink reflex has been found in functional movement disorder compared to controls, and similar brainstem gating abnormalities have also been reported in migraine and fibromyalgia.

Randomized trials of intensive physiotherapy for functional motor disorders (average symptom duration 5 years), which capitalized on features such as improvement with distraction, have shown benefit on clinical global outcome measures and activities of daily living.

Patients with migraine show reduced habituation on median nerve somatosensory evoked cortical recordings, reflecting deregulated cortical excitability, a finding paralleled by impaired sensory attenuation in motor functional neurological disorder.
Cluster headache has an estimated overall prevalence of approximately 124 per 100,000 individuals.
Only 3.5-13.7% of cluster headache patients manifest the chronic subtype (CCH), which underlies its classification as a rare disease.
The prevalence of chronic cluster headache satisfies both FDA and European Medicines Agency criteria for designation as a rare disease.
Chronic cluster headache imposes a substantial economic burden, with annual per-patient costs exceeding €20,000.
The rarity of chronic cluster headache creates clinical and research challenges including prolonged diagnostic delays, limited research funding, and a scarcity of approved treatments.
Migraine is associated with increased risk of cervical artery dissection compared to healthy controls, with moderate certainty of evidence.
MTHFR TT homozygosity is associated with increased risk of cervical artery dissection, with moderate certainty of evidence.
Matrix metalloproteinase (MMP) concentration was identified as a genetic/familial-predisposition-related risk factor for cervical artery dissection.
Connective tissue disorders were identified as a genetic/familial risk factor for cervical artery dissection.
Recent infection was identified as an external risk factor associated with cervical artery dissection.
Winter or autumn-winter season was identified as an external risk factor associated with cervical artery dissection compared to healthy controls.
Oral contraceptive use was identified as an external risk factor associated with cervical artery dissection compared to healthy controls.
Minor trauma was identified as a risk factor for cervical artery dissection, with low certainty evidence.
Hypertension was identified as a cardiovascular risk factor associated with cervical artery dissection.
Hypercholesterolaemia was identified as a cardiovascular risk factor associated with cervical artery dissection.
Relative vasodilatation of the internal carotid artery was identified as a cardiovascular factor associated with cervical artery dissection.
Coronary artery disease was identified as a cardiovascular factor associated with cervical artery dissection.
Other cardiac diseases were identified as cardiovascular factors associated with cervical artery dissection.

Eosinophilia was present in 12.3% of patients undergoing spinal cord stimulation or intrathecal pump implantation for chronic pain, far exceeding the <1% prevalence reported in the general population.
Patients meeting eosinophilia criteria had a mean absolute eosinophil count of 547 cells/uL compared to 138 cells/uL in the non-eosinophilic group.
Patients with eosinophilia had a higher eosinophil percentage (6.3%) compared with the non-eosinophilic group (1.9%).
Total white blood cell counts did not differ significantly between eosinophilic and non-eosinophilic chronic pain patients.
C-reactive protein levels did not differ significantly between eosinophilic and non-eosinophilic chronic pain patients.

Age, sex, implant type, and preoperative diagnoses (chronic neuropathic pain, persistent spinal pain syndrome type 1, complex regional pain syndrome) were comparable between patients with and without eosinophilia.
Migraine was present in 21.4% of patients with eosinophilia, a comorbidity rate not significantly different from the non-eosinophilic group.
Asthma was present in 21.4% of patients with eosinophilia, comparable between eosinophilic and non-eosinophilic groups.
Fibromyalgia was present in 7.10% of patients with eosinophilia, similar to the non-eosinophilic group.
Rheumatoid arthritis was present in 7.10% of patients with eosinophilia, comparable to the non-eosinophilic group.
No patients with eosinophilia experienced complications within 30 days or one year after spinal cord stimulator or intrathecal pump implantation, nor required revision surgery or device removal.
Participants with facial/sinus pain or pressure (FPP+) were significantly younger than those without FPP (FPP-).
Female sex was more prevalent among FPP+ participants than FPP- participants.
Frequent nasal symptoms (runny nose or congestion) were reported at a much higher rate in FPP+ participants than FPP- participants.
History of vestibular symptoms (dizziness, imbalance, spinning sensation) was more common in FPP+ than FPP- participants.
History of otologic symptoms (tinnitus, ear pressure/pain, blocked ears, hearing difficulty) was more common in FPP+ than FPP- participants.
History of frequent or severe headache was very common overall but significantly more prevalent in the FPP+ group than the FPP- group.
Headache-associated nausea/vomiting was more common in FPP+ than FPP- participants.
Light sensitivity with headache was more common in FPP+ than FPP- participants.
A positive migraine screen using the ID Migraine tool was significantly more prevalent in FPP+ than FPP- participants.
FPP+ participants were more likely to report a family history of migraine or frequent headache than FPP- participants.
FPP+ participants reported greater rates of daily functional interference overall, and specifically due to FPP and headache, than FPP- participants.
FPP+ participants more often named headache as their most disabling symptom, whereas FPP- participants more often named vestibular or otologic symptoms as most disabling.
FPP+ participants reported higher rates of allergies, allergy testing, sinus infection/sinusitis, and antibiotic use for FPP symptoms than FPP- participants.

Despite more frequent antibiotic use in FPP+ participants, there was no significant difference between FPP+ and FPP- groups in antibiotic effectiveness, indication, frequency, or duration, raising concern for misdiagnosis.
Within the FPP+ group, ID Migraine+ participants were younger and more likely female than ID Migraine- participants.
Temporomandibular joint pain and unexplained tooth pain were more common in the ID Migraine+ subgroup than the ID Migraine- subgroup among FPP+ participants.
Pain or pressure occurring over the forehead and eyes was more frequent in ID Migraine+ participants than ID Migraine- participants, suggesting a neurogenic contribution to FPP location.
ID Migraine+ participants were more likely than ID Migraine- participants to report that their FPP symptoms felt distinct from their headache symptoms.
ID Migraine- participants were more likely than ID Migraine+ participants to describe their FPP symptoms as always more severe and always lasting longer than their headache.
ID Migraine+ participants had a higher proportion with MIDAS grade IV and a higher median MIDAS score than ID Migraine- participants.
Co-occurrence of headache and photophobia was significantly more common in the ID Migraine+ subgroup than the ID Migraine- subgroup.
Co-occurrence of headache and phonophobia was significantly more common in the ID Migraine+ subgroup than the ID Migraine- subgroup.
Co-occurrence of headache and nausea/vomiting was significantly more common in the ID Migraine+ subgroup than the ID Migraine- subgroup.
In a comparison of participants with FPP but no migraine to those with migraine but no FPP, frequent nasal symptoms were more than twice as common in the isolated FPP subgroup.

The isolated-FPP subgroup (FPP+/ID Migraine-) reported more allergies, more history of sinus infection, and higher antibiotic effectiveness for FPP symptoms than the isolated-migraine subgroup (FPP-/ID Migraine+).

A cited Mendelian randomization study found no causal relationship between allergic rhinitis and migraine in either direction, suggesting their epidemiological overlap may instead reflect shared underlying mechanisms.
PACAP is expressed in a smaller proportion of trigeminal ganglia neurons than CGRP, with limited co-expression between the two peptides.
PACAP is poorly expressed in trigeminal C-fibers in the dura mater near the middle meningeal artery, whereas CGRP is richly expressed in trigeminal C-fibers.
PACAP is highly expressed in the parasympathetic sphenopalatine ganglia, suggesting a role in triggering autonomic migraine symptoms.

In satellite glial cells of the trigeminal ganglia, CGRP gene transcripts predominantly encode procalcitonin rather than CGRP itself, a product possibly involved in inflammation whose role in migraine is unknown.
PACAP activation of the Mas-related G-protein coupled receptors Mrgprb2 (mouse) and MrgB3/Mrgprb3 (rat) induces mast cell degranulation.

Human mast cells were reported not to express CGRP receptors and CGRP did not release histamine from human or porcine dural mast cells, though a later study reported CLR/RAMP1 expression in primate mast cells.
Chronic PACAP-38 administration induced mechanical allodynia in RAMP1 knockout mice comparable to that in wild-type mice, indicating PACAP receptor signaling does not require RAMP1.
PACAP couples more strongly to Gq-mediated calcium/IP3 signaling than CGRP, with CGRP's IP3 stimulation being over 200-fold weaker than its cAMP effect, versus only 4-10-fold weaker for PACAP.
PACAP-deficient mice show reduced mechanical hyperalgesia and nocifensive responses, yet enhanced thermal allodynia, indicating a dual, modality-specific role for PACAP in pain modulation.
Neuronal PAC1 receptors mediate delayed activation and sensitization of second-order neurons in the trigeminocervical complex, an effect blocked by a PAC1 receptor antagonist.
PACAP-38 injection into the mouse dura mater produced a sustained increase in periorbital allodynia lasting up to 24 hours, dependent on the MrgprB2 receptor.

PACAP-induced periorbital allodynia was unaffected by CGRP-blocking antibodies and chronic PACAP sensitization was not reversed by the CGRP receptor antagonist olcegepant, indicating PACAP and CGRP act via distinct, independent mechanisms.
Dural (but not intraplantar) administration of CGRP in mice and rats produced mechanical cephalic allodynia only in females, contrasting with PACAP-induced allodynia occurring in stress-primed males.

Chronic CGRP-induced periorbital allodynia sensitization was not significantly attenuated by the PAC1 receptor antagonist M65, indicating this CGRP effect occurs predominantly through a PACAP-independent pathway.

PACAP-38 produced concentration-dependent release of CGRP in the trigeminal nucleus caudalis but not in the trigeminal ganglia, suggesting possible convergence of PACAP and CGRP pathways at second-order neurons.

VPAC1 and VPAC2 knockout mice both showed reduced PACAP-38-induced mechanical hindpaw allodynic responses versus wild-type, while PAC1 knockout mice showed no difference, indicating PACAP mediates plantar allodynia through VPAC1/VPAC2 rather than PAC1.

Intrathecal injection of 1 nmol CGRP significantly increased paw withdrawal frequency in nestin/hRAMP1 mice with elevated hRAMP1 expression, while control mice required a higher 5 nmol dose, indicating RAMP1 expression is rate-limiting for CGRP-induced mechanical nociception.
Intraperitoneal PACAP-38 induced photophobia and meningeal vasodilation in wild-type CD1 mice but not in PACAP knockout mice.
PACAP knockout mice exhibit significantly reduced nitroglycerin-induced light aversion compared to wild-type, suggesting PACAP has a crucial role in mediating photophobic migraine-related behavior.
About one-third of outbred CD1 mice showed resilience (no light aversion response) to PACAP, a stable and inheritable trait, distinct from CGRP which induced light aversion in almost all mice.

PACAP-induced photophobia was not blocked by an anti-CGRP antibody, and CGRP-induced photophobia was not blocked by an anti-PACAP antibody, indicating the two peptides mediate photophobia via parallel, non-redundant pathways.
Optogenetic stimulation of CGRP-expressing cerebellar medial nucleus neurons increased light aversion selectively in female mice, but did not significantly increase squinting behavior.
The PACAP monoclonal antibody Lu AG09222 showed efficacy in a phase 2 clinical trial for migraine, consistent with preclinical PACAP-targeting insights.

A clinical trial of the PACAP monoclonal antibody LY3451838 was discontinued primarily due to recruitment issues that precluded a decision on efficacy, possibly reflecting heritable variability in PACAP responsiveness.
In a clinical study, PACAP-38 could still trigger migraine attacks in patients treated with the CGRP monoclonal antibody eptinezumab, demonstrating independence of PACAP and CGRP signaling in humans.
The PAC1 receptor antibody AMG 301 failed in a phase 2 clinical trial for migraine, although the reasons were unclear.

CGRP receptor antagonists (rimegepant, ubrogepant, atogepant, zavegepant) and CGRP monoclonal antibodies (erenumab, eptinezumab, fremanezumab, galcanezumab) have demonstrated clinical efficacy for both acute and preventive treatment of migraine, validating translational strength of preclinical CGRP research.
Telcagepant was discontinued as a migraine treatment due to liver toxicity observed with long-term use, despite demonstrating clinical efficacy.
Olcegepant demonstrated clinical efficacy for migraine but never reached commercialization because it could not be administered orally, though it remains widely used preclinically.
Among 392 patients scheduled for elective CABG, 80 (about 20%) met formal diagnostic criteria for orthostatic hypotension on preoperative testing.
In multivariable Cox regression, the presence of preoperative orthostatic hypotension was not an independent predictor of long-term mortality after elective CABG.

Backward stepwise Cox regression identified older age, male sex, heart failure, and renal failure—but not orthostatic hypotension—as factors independently associated with long-term mortality after CABG.
Patients with orthostatic hypotension had significantly higher supine systolic and diastolic blood pressure at baseline than those without orthostatic hypotension.
After 3 minutes of standing, systolic and diastolic blood pressure did not differ significantly between OH+ and OH− patients.

OH+ and OH− patients did not differ in prevalence of self-reported symptoms potentially attributable to orthostatic hypotension, including fatigue, unsteady gait, dizziness, excessive sweating, and falls.
About 30% of patients in each group (OH+ and OH−) reported a history of transient loss of consciousness (syncope), with no significant difference between groups.

During a median follow-up of approximately 9.7 years after elective CABG, 38% of the overall cohort died, with mortality rates similar between OH+ and OH− groups at 30 days, 1 year, and end of follow-up.

The ARIC Study, cited by the authors for their sample-size calculation, found that mortality in middle-aged adults was four times higher in those with orthostatic hypotension compared with those without it, a much larger effect than observed in this CABG cohort.

The authors hypothesize that some patients without a preoperative BP fall may have had elevated catecholamine levels masking underlying autonomic dysfunction, potentially associated with worse long-term outcomes, but this was not measured.
Migraine occurs in 8.4%-23% of people with epilepsy and epilepsy occurs in 1%-17% of migraineurs, rates higher than in the general population.
A 2014 meta-analysis found a 52% increased prevalence of migraine among people with epilepsy compared to controls.
The same 2014 meta-analysis found a 79% increased prevalence of epilepsy among people with migraine.
A more recent random-effects meta-analysis reported an 80% increase in lifetime prevalence of each condition when the other is present.
Headache occurs in up to 79% of people with epilepsy, with migraine in up to 25% and tension-type headache in up to 40% of cases.
Women with epilepsy are more likely than men to report comorbid migraine.

A large population-based cohort study found no significant difference in migraine or non-migraine headache prevalence between people with epilepsy and controls, contradicting the meta-analytic findings of increased comorbidity.

Mutations in CACNA1A, encoding the P/Q-type calcium channel α1A subunit, cause familial hemiplegic migraine type 1 and confer susceptibility to epilepsy by enhancing calcium influx and glutamate release.

Loss-of-function mutations in ATP1A2 (FHM2) reduce astrocytic potassium uptake, impairing ionic buffering and promoting a hyperexcitable extracellular environment relevant to both migraine and epilepsy.

Mutations in SCN1A, associated with Dravet syndrome and other epileptic syndromes, disrupt sodium channel function and lower thresholds for both cortical spreading depression and epileptiform activity.

Loss-of-function mutations in TRESK potassium channels increase trigeminal sensory neuron excitability contributing to migraine susceptibility, and experimental evidence suggests TRESK dysfunction also enhances hippocampal excitability and seizure severity.
KCNQ2, TRESK, and PRRT2 gene variants have been linked to both benign familial neonatal seizures and some forms of migraine.
Extracellular potassium rises to 8-10 mM during seizures but often exceeds 20 mM during cortical spreading depression, reflecting differing magnitudes of ionic dysregulation.

MELAS patients are susceptible to both migraine with aura and epileptic seizures, with pathological studies revealing cytochrome oxidase deficiency in meningeal vessel smooth muscle and endothelial cells.
The Visual Aura Rating Scale (VARS) has been validated to distinguish visual migraine aura from other transient visual disturbances with high sensitivity and specificity.
Pre-ictal headaches occur in 1%-10% of epilepsy patients, presenting as migraine-like in 30-60% and tension-type in about 20% of cases.
A video-EEG study found pre-ictal headache without concurrent epileptic discharges in 3% of epilepsy patients, and reclassified some cases as ictal seizure aura.
A review of 50 previously reported migralepsy cases found that only two actually satisfied the stringent ICHD-II definition, indicating most historical cases were misdiagnoses.

In a video-EEG cohort, six of 831 epilepsy patients had headache as the sole seizure manifestation with concurrent epileptiform discharges lasting under 35 seconds, fulfilling criteria for ictal epileptic headache.
Meta-analytic data suggest one-third of people with epilepsy develop postictal headache, with postictal migraine occurring in about 16% of cases.
Risk factors for postictal headache include younger age, longer epilepsy duration, higher seizure severity or frequency, and antiseizure medication polytherapy.

Children with self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes show a higher prevalence of migraine, and this higher prevalence is also seen in their relatives, suggesting shared genetic susceptibility.
Children with migraine with aura have a higher risk of developing unprovoked seizures, and up to 25% of pediatric epilepsy patients also report migraine.
Women with epilepsy are more likely than men to report comorbid migraine.
Among individuals with epilepsy, up to 79% report headaches, with migraine occurring in up to 25% and tension-type headache in up to 40% of cases.

A video-EEG study found pre-ictal headache in 3% (25 of 831) of epilepsy patients without concurrent epileptic EEG discharges, and reclassified five of these cases as headache-as-seizure-aura (ictal epileptic headache).

In the same 831-patient video-EEG cohort, six patients had headache as the sole seizure manifestation with concurrent epileptiform discharges lasting under 35 seconds, meeting criteria for ictal epileptic headache.
A review of 50 previously reported migralepsy cases found that only two actually satisfied the stringent ICHD-II definition, indicating most historical migralepsy diagnoses were likely misdiagnoses.
Meta-analytic data indicate that about one-third of people with epilepsy develop postictal headache, with postictal migraine occurring in approximately 16% of cases.
Risk factors identified for postictal headache include younger age, longer epilepsy duration, higher seizure severity or frequency, and antiseizure medication polytherapy.

Hemicrania epileptica, a rare subtype of ictal epileptic headache characterized by strictly unilateral headache ipsilateral to the ictal EEG discharge, has debated existence due to the rarity of obtaining EEG during isolated headache episodes.

Migraine with brainstem aura, more common in children but also seen in adults, presents with dysarthria, vertigo, tinnitus, diplopia, paresthesia, ataxia, and altered consciousness, with EEG sometimes showing encephalopathy-like features or occipital epileptiform abnormalities, and may respond to antiepileptic drugs or calcium channel blockers.

In migraine, especially with aura, EEG may show nonspecific transient focal or diffuse slowing in 11%-74% of patients and enhanced photic driving (the 'H response'), but these findings lack diagnostic specificity.

Other antiseizure medications such as gabapentin, pregabalin, lacosamide, zonisamide, and carbamazepine show variable efficacy in migraine prevention and lack formal approval for this indication, with off-label use now rare given newer anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies and gepants.
CGRP has been postulated to contribute to epileptogenesis by promoting excitotoxic death of hippocampal neurons in kainate-induced seizure animal models, though this remains unconfirmed in humans.

A higher prevalence of migraine is observed in children with self-limited epilepsy with centrotemporal spikes (benign rolandic epilepsy) and in their relatives, suggesting shared genetic susceptibility.

Children with migraine with aura have a higher risk of developing unprovoked seizures, up to 25% of pediatric epilepsy patients report migraine, and postictal migrainous headaches affect up to 40% of cases in self-limited focal epilepsies.
Patients with POTS had significantly lower measured blood volume than healthy controls.
POTS patients showed a significantly greater orthostatic heart rate increase upon standing than healthy controls, consistent with the POTS diagnostic criterion.
Supine resting heart rate was significantly higher in POTS patients than in healthy controls.
Resting systolic blood pressure was higher in POTS patients than in healthy controls.
Resting diastolic blood pressure was higher in POTS patients than in healthy controls.
POTS patients had significantly lower RMSSD, a time-domain marker of cardiovagal modulation, with a non-significant trend toward lower logHFRRI, another cardiovagal index.
Resting MSNA burst rate and burst incidence did not differ between POTS patients and healthy controls.
During the Valsalva maneuver, POTS patients had a significantly higher heart rate than healthy subjects at both baseline and early phase 2.
Absolute MSNA spike rate during Valsalva baseline and early phase 2 did not differ between POTS patients and healthy subjects.

Overall, several Valsalva-derived sympathetic markers (SBP overshoot, PRT, DBPVM2l_rise, csBRS, psNVT, Valsalva ratio) did not differ between the whole POTS group and healthy controls, indicating that POTS as a group is not distinguishable from controls by these Valsalva metrics.
In healthy subjects, the percentage change in MSNA spike rate during Valsalva phase 2 strongly correlated with the DBPVM2l_rise, supporting its use as a surrogate marker of sympathetic activation.

In POTS patients overall, the correlation between percentage MSNA spike rate change and DBPVM2l_rise was significant but weaker than in healthy controls, attributed to greater heterogeneity within POTS.
Among POTS patients with DBPVM2l_rise ≥15 mmHg (hyperadrenergic subgroup), the correlation between percentage MSNA change and DBPVM2l_rise was very strong.
Among POTS patients with DBPVM2l_rise <15 mmHg (non-hyperadrenergic subgroup), the correlation between percentage MSNA change and DBPVM2l_rise was moderate but significant.
All POTS patients classified as hyperadrenergic by DBPVM2l_rise ≥15 mmHg reported at least one hyperadrenergic symptom, with high rates of palpitations, sweating, and flushing.
There were no significant differences in age, orthostatic blood pressure, orthostatic plasma norepinephrine, or blood volume status between the hyperadrenergic and non-hyperadrenergic POTS subgroups.
The correlation between beat-to-beat MSNA spike rate percentage change and DBPVM2l_rise was weaker in POTS patients than in healthy subjects, likely reflecting greater physiological heterogeneity.

In POTS patients with DBPVM2l_rise ≥ 15 mmHg, the correlation between beat-to-beat MSNA spike rate change and DBP rise was very strong (n=6), while it was more modest in those below the cutoff (n=13).

All POTS patients identified as hyperadrenergic (DBPVM2l_rise ≥15 mmHg) reported at least one hyperadrenergic symptom, with palpitation, profuse sweating, and flushing reported by 86%, 71%, and 57% respectively.
There were no significant differences in age, orthostatic blood pressure, orthostatic plasma norepinephrine, or blood volume status between the hyperadrenergic and non-hyperadrenergic POTS subgroups.
At Valsalva baseline, the hyperadrenergic POTS group had higher SBP and heart rate than the non-hyperadrenergic POTS group.
The hyperadrenergic POTS group had higher SBP throughout the end of late phase 2 and at the peak of phase 4 of the Valsalva maneuver compared to the non-hyperadrenergic group.
The magnitude of SBP drop during early phase 2 of Valsalva was similar between hyperadrenergic and non-hyperadrenergic POTS groups.

The duration of the early phase 2 of Valsalva (to the point of SBP nadir) was shorter in the hyperadrenergic POTS group than in the non-hyperadrenergic group, suggesting faster or more efficient vasoconstriction.
Absolute MSNA spike rate during baseline and early phase 2 of Valsalva did not differ between hyperadrenergic and non-hyperadrenergic POTS patients.

Peripheral sympathetic neurovascular transduction (psNVT) was significantly higher in the hyperadrenergic POTS group than in the non-hyperadrenergic group, supporting enhanced neurovascular coupling rather than primary elevated sympathetic tone.
Central sympathetic baroreflex sensitivity (csBRS) was not significantly different between hyperadrenergic and non-hyperadrenergic POTS groups.
Pressure recovery time (PRT) was significantly shorter in the hyperadrenergic POTS group compared to the non-hyperadrenergic group, consistent with higher sympathetic vascular function.
SBP overshoot during Valsalva phase 4 tended to be higher in the hyperadrenergic POTS group compared to the non-hyperadrenergic group, though the difference did not reach statistical significance.
DBPVM2l_rise was significantly correlated with Valsalva baseline SBP, pressure recovery time, and SBP overshoot, but not significantly with resting SBP low-frequency power.
No correlation was found between DBPVM2l_rise and blood volume deviation among POTS patients.

The identified hyperadrenergic POTS patients had an average upright plasma norepinephrine level exceeding 600 pg/mL, consistent with a hyperadrenergic phenotype, although this was not significantly different from non-hyperadrenergic patients.

Using a golden section search optimization method, a DBPVM2l_rise cutoff of 15 mmHg was identified as optimal for distinguishing hyperadrenergic from non-hyperadrenergic POTS, classifying 32% (6 of 19) of patients as hyperadrenergic, a prevalence similar to a prior study using baseline MSNA quartiles.

Preliminary results suggest that moxonidine, a central sympatholytic, could selectively suppress sympathetic Valsalva responses including DBPVM2l_rise in hyperadrenergic POTS patients, despite the limited sample size.
The central sympatholytic drug guanfacine has previously been shown to improve symptoms in hyperadrenergic POTS.

Functional hyperadrenergic POTS patients and other POTS patients had similar degrees of blood volume deficit, indicating hypovolemia does not contradict the hyperadrenergic subtyping given the known inverse relationship between blood volume and blood pressure in orthostatic intolerance.
Most participants showed improvements in at least four outcome measures following the digital behavioural treatment, whereas two participants (P-9, P-10) improved in only one outcome.
The most substantial treatment effects were seen in three participants, who improved across 12, 8, and 11 outcomes respectively.
More than half of participants showed improvement in pain catastrophising and in the sleep pattern item 'waking up frequently/too early' following treatment.
One participant (P-10) exhibited deterioration in four outcomes, representing the main instance of negative treatment effects observed.
All participants who completed treatment showed a meaningful (≥0.5 SD) improvement in pain intensity as measured by the BSI-SF from pre- to post-treatment.
No meaningful positive change was observed on the fusion subscale of the Psychological Inflexibility in Pain Scale (PIPS), and two participants showed meaningful negative change.

Momentary digital diary ratings of pain intensity showed improvement in only four participants, whereas retrospective pre-/post-treatment questionnaires showed meaningful pain-severity improvement in all treatment completers, indicating a discrepancy between momentary and retrospective measures.
Two of 11 enrolled participants withdrew before completing treatment, citing being too busy or not finding the treatment helpful.
Blocking visual input with opaque contact lenses abolished the green-light-induced increase in paw withdrawal threshold in naive rats, showing the effect depends on the visual transmission system.
Green light exposure significantly increased paw withdrawal latencies in naive rats, indicating a physiological antinociceptive effect.

In naive mice, green light elevated bilateral paw withdrawal thresholds and latencies, with the left side responding earlier (day 5) than the right side (day 7), suggesting differential activation of retino-recipient brain regions.

Green light produced a dose-dependent but non-monotonic analgesic effect across intensities, with 330 lux producing only a suboptimal (half-maximal) effect while 4 lux produced the maximal antinociceptive response.
Green light completely inhibited thermal hyperalgesia and strongly reversed mechanical hyperalgesia in rats with spinal nerve ligation-induced neuropathic pain.
Seven days of green light treatment elevated bilateral paw withdrawal thresholds and latencies in a partial sciatic ligation neuropathic pain mouse model.
In chronic constriction injury mice, only 200-lux green light produced antinociceptive effects, whereas 50-lux and 500-lux intensities did not.

Green light exposure reduced anxiety-like behavior associated with neuropathic pain in chronic constriction injury mice, as measured by increased time spent in a conditioned place preference chamber paired with green light.

Green light treatment increased spinal cord expression of the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 while decreasing proinflammatory cytokines IL-18, IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α in a spinal cord injury pain model.
Expression of the microglial activation marker CD68 was significantly reduced after green light application in a spinal cord injury pain model, suggesting decreased microglial activation.
Green light treatment increased β-endorphin and pro-enkephalin levels in the cerebrospinal fluid but not serum of naive rats, while dynorphin was unchanged in either compartment.

The thermal analgesic effect of green light was reversed by genetic deletion of δ- or μ-opioid receptors, and by intrathecal or subcutaneous naloxone (a μ-opioid receptor antagonist), indicating opioid receptor dependence of the effect.
Green light reduced both thermal and mechanical hypersensitivity in a model of HIV-related chronic neuropathic pain, an effect requiring activation of spinal δ- and μ-opioid receptors.

In osteoarthritic rats, green light reversed hind paw mechanosensitivity after only two sessions and elevated serum levels of the analgesic fatty acid amides PEA and N-acyl glycines, while classic endocannabinoids anandamide and 2-arachidonoylglycerol were unchanged; the antinociceptive effect was blocked by the CB1/GPR18 antagonist AM281.
Green light exposure inhibited N-type channel-mediated Ca2+ influx in ATP-responsive dorsal root ganglion sensory neurons, a peripheral mechanism implicated in neuropathic pain.

Green light increased bilateral pain thresholds/latencies in partial sciatic ligation mice mainly through activation of vLGN glutamatergic neurons, whereas red light exacerbated neuropathic pain via vLGN GABAergic neuron activation.

Green light increased excitability of V2M glutamatergic neurons and ACC GABAergic neurons while decreasing ACC glutamatergic neuron excitability, consistent with a V2MGlu-ACCGABA-Glu inhibitory circuit contributing to analgesia.

Unlike red light which promotes pain, bright light suppressed nocifensive behaviors via disinhibition of the lateral/ventrolateral periaqueductal gray through activation of a RGC-vLGN/IGL GABAergic-l/vlPAG GABAergic circuit.
Low-intensity green light reduced headache pain scores, whereas higher-intensity green light (100 cd/m2) exacerbated migraine.
High-intensity bright light (18,000 lux) caused thermal hyperalgesia in naive rats, mediated by activation of RVM ON cells and suppression of OFF-cell firing.

Microinjection of lidocaine diminished the thermal analgesic effect of green light, and proteomic analysis found 65 DRG proteins with decreased structural molecule activity and increased antioxidant activity associated with green light-induced thermal analgesia.

The green light-induced antinociceptive effect is conveyed by retinal rod and cone cells but not by ipRGCs, with enkephalin neurons in the vLGN (vLGNENK) transmitting signals to the dorsal raphe nucleus to mediate analgesia via μ-opioid receptors in an inflammatory pain model.

In a colorblind patient (unable to differentiate green, yellow, orange, and red), green light exposure significantly decreased headache pain intensity but not headache frequency, suggesting intensity is modulated via non-image-forming ipRGCs while frequency depends on cone/rod input.

Green light therapy has been reported to reduce pain in migraine, fibromyalgia, and headache patients, though its analgesic effect has not yet been evaluated in patients with clinical neuropathic pain.
Fibromyalgia symptom severity decreased after 2 weeks of green light therapy administered 4 hours per day.
CGRP receptor antagonists significantly reduced monthly migraine days compared to placebo.
CGRP monoclonal antibodies significantly reduced monthly migraine days compared to placebo.
CGRP antagonist achieved the highest p-score ranking (0.71) for reduction in mean migraine days among all treatments compared.
Triptans were found to be highly effective for relieving migraine pain, photophobia, phonophobia, and nausea, but carried a higher risk of adverse events.
CGRP antagonists excelled at reducing monthly migraine days but were also associated with increased side effects.
BPRT completers showed a significant reduction in average pain intensity across the 1-, 2-, and 3-month follow-up assessments.
BPRT completers reported significant reductions in pain interference with daily functioning across follow-up.
BPRT completers reported significant reductions in pain-related fear across follow-up assessments.
The vast majority of enrolled participants (33 of 35) completed the full three-session BPRT protocol, supporting feasibility of the intervention.
Participants rated BPRT as highly acceptable using a standardized treatment acceptability measure.
A substantial proportion of BPRT completers reported marked global improvement at 3-month follow-up.
A KIT mutation was detected in 14 of the 16 patients with available testing (87.5%) among the advanced systemic mastocytosis cohort.
Median bone marrow mast cell burden decreased substantially from pre-transplant baseline to one year after allogeneic haematopoietic cell transplantation.
Median serum tryptase levels declined markedly from pre-transplant baseline to one year following alloHCT.
At one year after alloHCT, progression-free survival and overall survival for the entire advanced systemic mastocytosis cohort were 59% and 74% respectively.
In the subset of patients with SM with associated haematological neoplasm (SM-AHN), 1-year PFS and OS were higher, at 74% and 79% respectively.
The cumulative incidence of relapse or progression for the whole cohort was low at 100 days and increased by one year post-alloHCT.
Among patients with an associated haematological neoplasm, cumulative incidence of relapse/progression was higher than in the overall SM cohort.
In the entire cohort of 27 patients with advanced systemic mastocytosis, the cumulative incidence of relapse/progression after alloHCT was 4% at 100 days and 15% at 1 year.
Among patients with SM and an associated haematological neoplasm (AHN), the cumulative incidence of relapse/progression was higher, at 11% at 100 days and 21% at 1 year.
Relapse or progression of underlying disease was the leading cause of death, accounting for half of the deaths observed post-alloHCT.
KIT inhibitors were used both before and after alloHCT, including for treatment of post-transplant relapse/progression, reflecting increasing integration of targeted therapy with transplant.
Post-transplantation cyclophosphamide (PTCy) was used as GVHD prophylaxis in approximately half of the transplant cohort.
Despite expert evaluation and comprehensive workup including cardiovascular autonomic testing, 10-20% of syncope patients remain undiagnosed.
Among approximately 4400 observations from implantable cardiac monitor use in unexplained syncope, about half of monitored patients still lacked a final diagnosis.
Current AI models did not outperform emergency department physicians when both assessed the Canadian Syncope Risk Score retrospectively.
Grant et al. found no statistically significant benefit of AI-based predictive models over traditional risk scoring methodology for syncope risk assessment.
A hybrid model combining an XGBoost machine-learning algorithm with knowledge-based rules outperformed the standalone XGBoost model in predicting 30-day severe outcomes after syncope.
ML-based ECG interpretation can predict both past and future atrial fibrillation, potentially identifying tachy-brady syndrome-related syncope in patients with previously undiagnosed paroxysmal AF.
AI-based ECG signal processing reduced clinician workload by 42% among patients monitored with implantable cardiac monitors.
The median emergency department wait time is 6.58 hours at 85% capacity, with 10% of patients leaving without being evaluated, a burden that may be worse for syncope patients.
Hospital costs associated with inpatient evaluation of syncope patients exceed $2.4 billion per year in the USA.
Patients preferred chatbot-generated responses over physician responses nearly 80% of the time in a 2023 JAMA Internal Medicine study.
A 2024 PNAS study found that AI chatbots were perceived as more empathetic than human responders because they avoided common conversational pitfalls.
Deep neural networks outperformed traditional automated methods in interpreting 12-lead ECGs in emergency department and other clinical settings.
Neural networks have been used to predict positive head-up tilt table test results.

In a study of ED syncope patients predicting hospitalization, ICU admission, and in-hospital mortality, ML models outperformed unaided physician classification for ICU admission and mortality predictions.
Photoplethysmography-based wearable technology is inherently unable to detect ventricular ectopy, only inferring atrial fibrillation via rhythm irregularity as a proxy.
Wearable sensors can capture heart rate variability as a proxy for autonomic tone, along with blood pressure-heart rate temporal relationships to capture autonomic changes relevant to syncope.
AI can already accurately predict conditions that cause syncope, including concealed long QT syndrome, Brugada syndrome, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, aortic stenosis, and ventricular dysfunction.
Administration of CGRP monoclonal antibody for three months was not associated with an overall change in plasma cytokine profile in patients with chronic migraine.
IL-5 plasma levels significantly decreased following three months of CGRP monoclonal antibody therapy in chronic migraine patients.
No statistically significant change was observed in IFNγ, IL-10, IL-12p70, IL-1β, IL-22, IL-4, IL-6, IL-8, or TNFα levels following three months of CGRP monoclonal antibody therapy.
Baseline plasma IL-8 levels were significantly lower in patients with chronic migraine compared to age- and sex-matched healthy controls.
There was no significant baseline difference between chronic migraine patients and healthy controls for the remaining measured cytokines (IFNγ, IL-1β, IL-4, IL-5, IL-6, IL-10, IL-12p70, IL-22, TNFα).
A 2023 meta-analysis found that IL-8 levels are higher in migraine patients than in healthy controls, contrasting with the present study's finding of lower IL-8 in migraine.
A 1998 study by Munno and colleagues reported increased IL-5 levels in migraine patients compared to healthy controls, a finding not replicated by subsequent studies including the present one.

A previously published case series described patients who developed new inflammatory complications—including flares of psoriasis/psoriatic arthritis, autoimmune hepatitis, and granulomatosis with polyangiitis—temporally related to initiation of a CGRP monoclonal antibody, which improved after cessation of the drug.

Pre-clinical evidence indicates CGRP limits the response of group 2 innate lymphoid cells (ILC2), a mediator of IL-5 secretion, suggesting a possible mechanistic link to the observed reduction in IL-5 with CGRP inhibition.

CGRP is expressed on trigeminal C-fibres while its receptors are located on Aδ fibres of the trigeminal ganglion, cranial blood vessels, and the trigeminal nucleus caudalis, implicating it in migraine pathophysiology.

PET studies found significant brain elevations of the TSPO radioligand 11C-PBR28 in migraine patients, suggesting increased glial activation/neuroinflammation, though correlation with headache frequency was inconsistent across studies.

PET studies reported an overall decrease in mu-opioid receptor binding potential (μOR BPND) in limbic brain structures of migraine patients compared with healthy controls, suggesting altered opioid signalling contributes to hyperalgesia/allodynia.

Migraine patients show distinct D2/D3 dopamine receptor availability patterns differentiating them from healthy controls, and dopamine receptor hypersensitivity is proposed as a hallmark of migraine, supported by increased sensitivity to dopamine agonists and improvement with dopamine antagonists.
Dopamine is elevated during prodromal symptoms of nausea, vomiting and dizziness in migraine patients relative to controls.
Plasma glutamate levels are higher in migraine patients and are suspected markers of neuronal hyperexcitability, hypothesized to play a role in aura.

Cortical spreading depression, driven by massive extracellular potassium and glutamate increases with reduced sodium and calcium, is believed to underlie migraine aura and activates the trigeminal nucleus caudalis via c-Fos expression and release of substance P, NKA and CGRP.

Reduced serotonin release is thought to influence migraine aura by activating the trigeminovascular nociceptive pathway, whereas high 5-HT levels are theorized to help prevent attacks and aura via receptor desensitization.

Patients with episodic migraine show decreased functional connectivity between the thalamus and S1, premotor cortex, occipital cortex, precuneus, insula, operculum and temporal lobe compared with healthy controls, alongside increased thalamic connectivity with primary motor and orbitofrontal cortex and parietal areas.

Chronic migraine patients show increased functional connectivity to the amygdala, insula, dorsolateral prefrontal cortex, thalamus and precuneus relative to episodic migraine patients, implicating pain-matrix network involvement in migraine chronification.
Regional homogeneity in the rostral anterior cingulate cortex (part of the pain matrix) is negatively correlated with duration of migraine disease.
Default mode network abnormality is associated with the duration of migraine attacks, suggesting a role for this network in migraine chronification.

Migraine with aura patients show abnormalities in perfusion and thickness of the occipital cortex, supporting a central role for the visual cortex in aura symptoms, although some studies report an absence of such changes.

Gepants and CGRP monoclonal antibodies block CGRP or CGRP-receptor binding, causing vasoconstriction and receptor internalization, thereby impairing CGRP-induced nociceptive signalling for migraine treatment.

Triptans act as selective 5-HT1B/1D receptor agonists on blood vessels and trigeminal nerves, inducing vasoconstriction and inhibiting neuropeptide release by preventing calcium influx needed for neurotransmitter exocytosis.
Botulinum toxin degrades the SNARE complex needed for synaptic vesicle fusion, thereby inhibiting release of CGRP, glutamate and substance P from the trigeminal ganglion to reduce headache.

Following sumatriptan injection in migraine patients, abnormal brainstem activation persists despite symptom relief, supporting the hypothesis that migraine pathogenesis relates to an imbalance among brainstem nuclei regulating antinociception and vascular control.
Approximately one third of migraine patients experience migraine with aura, manifesting as visual, sensory, speech and language disturbances.
Chronic migraine is defined as headache occurring on ≥15 days/month with at least 8 migraine days/month for more than 3 months, whereas episodic migraine is defined as <15 headache days/month.
Existing headache treatments show limited efficacy in some patients, with reported numbers needed to treat (NNT) ranging from 3 to 10.
PACAP and VIP are highlighted as promising prospective molecular targets for new headache therapies currently under investigation.
CGRP, along with IL-2, NO, VIP, dopamine, glutamate, histamine and PACAP, is elevated during cluster headache attacks and decreases after the attack resolves.
CGRP release is higher in cluster headache patients in remission compared to those with chronic cluster headache, possibly reflecting CGRP depletion in trigeminal fibres of chronic patients.
Somatostatin levels are lower during and between bouts of cluster headache, which may contribute to pathophysiology by reducing inhibition of CGRP release.

Kynurenine metabolism, the tryptophan breakdown pathway, is altered during cluster headache attacks and bouts, and is thought to contribute to neuronal sensitization and altered glutamate transmission.
Elevated CGRP and VIP levels in the jugular bulb of patients with paroxysmal hemicrania and hemicrania continua decrease to normal levels after successful treatment.
Compression or trauma of the occipital nerve increases release of glutamate and substance P into the trigeminal nucleus caudalis, contributing to allodynia and headache pain in occipital neuralgia.
Release of glutamate, CGRP, PACAP and cytokines from glial cells is involved in central sensitization underlying occipital neuralgia.

During the interictal phase of migraine, increased functional connectivity of the PAG with prefrontal cortex, insula, thalamus, parahippocampal gyrus, amygdala and other cortical regions is found alongside decreased FC of insula and prefrontal subregions.

Studies report both decreased and increased functional activity of the anterior cingulate cortex in migraine, likely reflecting heterogeneity in cingulum function; FC to the middle frontal gyrus is negatively correlated with migraine attack intensity.

During the preictal phase of migraine, increased functional activity and connectivity in the hypothalamus, tegmental area, PAG, pons, occipital, temporal cortex and PFC are reported compared to the ictal phase.

Comparing ictal to interictal migraine phases shows increased functional activity of the pons and increased connectivity between pons and hypothalamus, S1 and nucleus accumbens, alongside decreased visual cortex connectivity during attacks.

In episodic migraine, decreased thalamic functional connectivity with S1, premotor cortex, occipital cortex, precuneus, insula, operculum and temporal lobe is found relative to healthy controls, while chronic migraine shows decreased connectivity within the default mode, salience and central executive networks.
Regional homogeneity in the rostral ACC (pain matrix) is negatively correlated with duration of migraine disease, supporting a role for this network in migraine chronification.

In migraine with aura, altered occipital cortex perfusion and thickness, together with increased functional connectivity in visual-related gyri, support a central role of the visual cortex in aura symptoms, though evidence on functional activity changes is inconsistent.

During cluster headache bouts, increased functional connectivity of the hypothalamus with ventral tegmental area, dorsal raphe nuclei, substantia nigra, red nucleus and subthalamic nucleus is found relative to healthy controls, with reduced hypothalamic salience-network coactivation also reported in-bout.

Out-of-bout, cluster headache patients show decreased hypothalamic functional connectivity with frontal and temporal-parietal pain control regions, and altered functional activity in dorsal attention, sensorimotor, visual and pain matrix networks correlated with disease duration.

In episodic cluster headache, increased hypothalamic functional connectivity with medial frontal gyrus, occipital cuneus, thalamus, temporal and frontal cortex and multiple large-scale networks is found compared to healthy controls, along with altered diffusivity and reduced cingulate gyrus volume.

In chronic cluster headache, reduced functional connectivity in the right frontal pole-right amygdala pathway is reported, alongside increased functional activity in perigenual ACC, hypothalamus, thalamus, insula and hypothalamic connectivity with VTA, SN, RN and STN.

In paroxysmal hemicrania and hemicrania continua, increased functional activity is found in bilateral PFC, thalamus, amygdala, insular cortex and anterior olfactory cortex during headache versus headache-free states.

Functional imaging following occipital nerve stimulation shows decreased activity in the amygdala, bilateral primary visual, auditory and somatosensory cortex, alongside increased activity in bilateral thalamus, cerebellum, frontal and parietal areas.

Gepants (Ubrogepant, Rimegepant, Zavegepant) and CGRP-targeting monoclonal antibodies (Erenumab against the receptor; Eptinezumab, Fremanezumab, Galcanezumab against the ligand) impair CGRP-induced nociceptive signalling as a treatment strategy for headache disorders.
Triptans act as selective 5-HT1b,d receptor agonists on blood vessels and the trigeminal nerve, preventing calcium influx needed for neuropeptide release, thereby reducing headache.

Botulinum toxin inhibits release of CGRP, glutamate and substance P by impairing the SNARE complex required for synaptic vesicle fusion, thereby constraining neurotransmitter release in the trigeminal nerve.
Occipital nerve stimulation is theorized to cause diffuse noxious inhibitory control via the trigeminal nucleus caudalis, preventing activation of second-order neurons and the spinothalamic tract.
Non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation is thought to modulate pain matrix activity through its connections to the trigeminal nerve and trigeminal spinal tract.

Deep brain stimulation electrodes are often placed in the hypothalamus due to its central role and connectivity to the pain matrix, leading to reduced activation of pain matrix areas usually activated via the spinothalamic tract.
SPG stimulation applies electrical stimulation to the sphenopalatine ganglion, interfering with the trigeminal-autonomic pain reflex that plays a major role in headache pathology.

Melatonin and the hypothalamus may play a role in timing cluster headache attacks, as circadian rhythmicity and altered melatonin levels are described specifically for cluster headache and not other headache disorders in this review.

IgG4-related disease with hypertrophic pachymeningitis primarily affects the cavernous sinus and orbital apex, causing multiple cranial nerve palsies and mimicking secondary trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia.
Concomitant extrapulmonary tuberculosis complicated the diagnostic picture, as it is a frequent clinical mimic of IgG4-related disease in tuberculosis-endemic regions.
Accurate diagnosis of IgG4-related hypertrophic pachymeningitis mimicking secondary trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia requires integrating advanced neuroimaging with serological markers.
Performing a head-up tilt test first led to a significantly higher proportion of patients receiving an etiologic diagnosis of syncope within one year compared to first implanting a cardiac monitor.
By the end of follow-up, the proportion of patients with a syncope diagnosis remained higher in the HUTT-first group than in the ICM-first group.
Patients undergoing HUTT first reached a syncope diagnosis much faster than those undergoing ICM implantation first, with a nearly fourfold higher hazard of earlier diagnosis.
At baseline, the ICM group had more patients with mild cardiomyopathies, injury history, and use of beta-blocker and diuretic therapies compared to the HUTT group.
Approximately 70-90% of cluster headache patients have a history of smoking, which correlates with increased attack frequency and bout duration.
A Mendelian randomization study demonstrated a causal relationship between smoking and cluster headache.
Presence of side-shifting of headache pain was associated with significantly increased odds of having chronic rather than episodic cluster headache.

An Italian cohort found significant association between the HCRTR2 G1246A polymorphism (rs2653349) and cluster headache, but a subsequent meta-analysis could not confirm this association, instead showing only a weak association with rs9357855.
A study exploring CLOCK gene SNPs reported a significant association between CH and the rs12649507 variant.
A Swedish cluster headache cohort showed a strong genetic association between the CRY1 variant rs8192449 and CH.
Italian studies found significant associations between ADH4 polymorphisms (rs1126671, rs1800759) and cluster headache, but replication attempts in Swedish, Chinese, and Greek cohorts failed.
A genetic variant in RAMP1, part of the CGRP receptor complex, has been linked to cluster headache in a Swedish cohort.
A large meta-GWAS spanning 10 European cohorts and one East Asian cohort identified eight genetic risk loci for cluster headache, three of which (FHL5, PLCE1, LRP1) overlap with known migraine loci.
MERTK, the top GWAS hit gene involved in microglia-mediated neuroinflammation, showed increased mRNA levels in patient-specific tissue from CH participants.
Serum levels of Galectin-3, the ligand for MERTK, are increased in cluster headache participants.
A GNB3 polymorphism significantly influenced the likelihood of responding to triptan treatment in cluster headache patients.
Plasma CGRP is elevated during acute cluster headache attacks, both spontaneous and triggered, and normalizes with oxygen or sumatriptan treatment.
CGRP concentrations are elevated in saliva and tears during CH attacks compared to healthy controls.
Galcanezumab 300 mg subcutaneously effectively reduced attack frequency in episodic cluster headache.
Galcanezumab was not effective for the chronic variant of cluster headache.
Fremanezumab was ineffective in a placebo-controlled trial for episodic cluster headache, and its chronic CH trial was discontinued after an interim analysis showed no efficacy.
Eptinezumab 400 mg IV did not significantly reduce attack frequency versus placebo in episodic cluster headache, but showed a greater 50% responder rate.
Infusion of PACAP38 provokes cluster headache-like attacks in episodic CH patients during the active phase and in chronic CH patients, but not in episodic CH patients in remission.
VIP levels are elevated during CH attacks, and infusion of VIP induces CH-like attacks in episodic CH active phase and chronic CH patients.
Nitrite and nitrate (NO oxidation products) are elevated in CSF and plasma of CH patients during the active period compared to remission and healthy controls.
Infusion of the KATP channel opener levcromakalim induced cluster headache attacks in episodic CH patients during the active phase and in chronic CH patients.
Sphenopalatine ganglion volume is larger on the painful side in episodic cluster headache and correlates with the number of cranial autonomic symptoms.

PET imaging showed increased regional cerebral blood flow in the posterior hypothalamic grey matter ipsilateral to the attack side during nitroglycerin-induced and spontaneous cluster headache attacks.
Automated segmentation revealed an increased ipsilateral volume of the paraventricular nucleus and preoptic area of the hypothalamus in chronic compared to episodic cluster headache patients.

Chronic cluster headache patients showed increased anterior hypothalamic volume ipsilateral to the headache side compared to healthy controls, and bilateral hypothalamic volumes were larger in cluster headache patients than in both healthy controls and migraine patients.
Diffusion tensor imaging showed cluster headache patients had lower fractional anisotropy and higher mean diffusivity in the hypothalamus relative to healthy subjects.

Magnetic resonance spectroscopy demonstrated reduced N-acetyl aspartate levels and a decreased choline/creatine ratio in the hypothalamus of episodic and chronic cluster headache patients compared to healthy controls.
In-bout interictal episodic cluster headache patients showed reduced functional connectivity between the hypothalamus and the salience network compared to healthy controls.

Task-specific fMRI found the posterior hypothalamus in episodic cluster headache showed higher activation out of bout but decreased activation during the in-bout state, contrasting the prior PET-based hyperactivity hypothesis.
Deep brain stimulation of the posterior hypothalamic grey matter produced significant long-term benefit in about half to over three-quarters of patients with intractable chronic cluster headache.

PET imaging with an opioidergic radioligand showed an inverse relationship between cluster headache duration and opioid receptor binding in the ipsilateral hypothalamus, suggesting descending opioidergic mechanisms contribute to attack maintenance.

Ventral tegmental area deep brain stimulation demonstrated greater efficacy than posterior hypothalamic stimulation in reducing both frequency and intensity of attacks in severe chronic cluster headache.
Chronic cluster headache patients showed reduced thickness of the anterior cerebellar lobe compared to healthy individuals.

Two studies documented a lateralized habituation deficit of the nociceptive blink reflex on the symptomatic side during the active phase of episodic cluster headache, though a later study found no differences from controls.

Greater occipital nerve blockade reduced the nociceptive blink reflex R2 area and increased its latency on the injection side only in chronic cluster headache patients, without significant clinical improvement.

Although high-flow oxygen therapy effectively aborted cluster headache attacks, it did not alter nociceptive blink reflex parameters, indicating dissociation between clinical efficacy and brainstem reflex modulation.
Dynamic pupillometry showed altered pupillary constriction and dilation velocities during active cluster headache periods, consistent with autonomic imbalance.
Obstructive sleep apnea has been found in 20-90% of cluster headache patients, though whether this is coincidental or causal remains uncertain.

In an open-label case series, sodium oxybate reduced nocturnal pain frequency by up to 90% and pain intensity by more than 50%, and improved sleep quality, in all four refractory chronic cluster headache patients treated.
Cluster headache patients scored significantly higher on alexithymia, a construct reflecting difficulty identifying and expressing emotions, than comparison groups.

A large GWAS of 4,777 cluster headache patients found that genetic risk variants for cigarette smoking, risk-taking behaviour, ADHD, depression, and musculoskeletal pain were significantly associated with cluster headache.

A multicentre controlled study found no increase in outward-directed aggression in cluster headache patients but a significant rise in self-directed aggression, especially in chronic cases, closely linked to greater headache-related disability.
In a randomized controlled trial, 78% of participants breathing 100% oxygen at 12 L/min for 15 minutes became pain-free compared to 20% of those breathing regular air.
Subcutaneous sumatriptan 6 mg had a number needed to treat of 3.3 in one trial and 2.4 in another for acute cluster headache treatment.
Subcutaneous octreotide 100 µg achieved headache relief in 57% of cluster headache patients at 30 minutes compared to 36% with placebo.
In a large RCT of 118 patients, 100 mg prednisone reduced the mean number of cluster headache attacks by 25.3% within the first week, significantly outperforming placebo.
A placebo-controlled trial found active greater occipital nerve block reduced weekly attack frequency significantly more than placebo in episodic cluster headache patients.
In a multicenter randomized placebo-controlled crossover trial, 80% of participants were responders to verapamil compared to no responders in the placebo arm.
Obstructive sleep apnea is highly prevalent among cluster headache patients, though whether this represents a causal relationship or coincidence remains uncertain.
In an open-label case series, sodium oxybate reduced nocturnal pain frequency and intensity and improved sleep quality in four patients with refractory chronic cluster headache.
Cluster headache attack risk is highest in the early night, peaking around 2 a.m., coinciding with REM sleep or the end of the first sleep cycle.
Melatonin levels are reduced in cluster headache patients, prompting studies of prophylactic melatonin administration.
Cluster headache patients scored significantly higher on alexithymia, a trait characterized by difficulty identifying and expressing emotions, compared to reference populations.
Cluster headache patients with an 'emotionally overwhelmed' personality profile on the MMPI-2 reported higher affective pain scores regardless of headache severity.

Over 90% of cluster headache patients showed clinically significant personality traits, predominantly obsessive-compulsive, histrionic, narcissistic, and avoidant features, on the Millon Clinical Multiaxial Inventory-III.

Comparing CH and migraine patients, CH patients most frequently exhibited Cluster A (odd/eccentric) personality traits including anankastic and schizoid tendencies, while migraineurs more often showed Cluster C (anxious/fearful) traits.

A multicentre controlled study found no increase in outward-directed aggression but a significant rise in self-directed aggression among chronic cluster headache patients, linked to greater disability.
The Danish Cluster Headache Survey found elevated substance use among CH patients compared to controls, suggesting a propensity toward impulsivity or compulsivity.
A large GWAS in cluster headache patients identified genetic risk variants significantly associated with cigarette smoking, risk-taking behaviour, ADHD, depression, and musculoskeletal pain.
Methysergide reduced cluster headache attack frequency in the first published trial in 1961, but was ultimately abandoned due to adverse effects including fibrotic complications.
A large 2019 survey found a small minority of cluster headache patients used caffeine as an acute treatment, with a minority reporting high effectiveness.
The first double-blind, placebo-controlled crossover study in 1975 showed prednisone decreased cluster headache attack frequency in the majority of previously treatment-refractory patients.
A retrospective study found prednisone gave at least 50% headache relief in most treated CH patients, but the majority relapsed once the drug was tapered.
Lee Kudrow first reported in 1981 that inhalation of 100% oxygen at 7-10 L could abort cluster headache attacks within minutes.
In a randomized trial, high-flow oxygen at 12 L/min for 15 minutes rendered the majority of CH patients pain-free, far exceeding the effect of regular air.
Randomized trials of subcutaneous sumatriptan 6 mg for acute cluster headache attacks demonstrated low numbers needed to treat.
Intranasal zolmitriptan produced pain-free responses within 30 minutes in a dose-dependent manner in episodic cluster headache patients.
In a small crossover RCT, intranasal lidocaine and cocaine were both superior to placebo in stopping nitroglycerin-induced cluster headache attacks.
Subcutaneous octreotide 100 µg significantly outperformed placebo for headache relief in an RCT of acute cluster headache treatment.

A large RCT of transitional prednisone therapy (n=118) showed significantly greater reduction in mean weekly cluster headache attacks compared to placebo, with over a third of patients achieving complete cessation of attacks within one week.

The first clinical study of methysergide in 1961 showed a reduction in cluster headache attack frequency compared with baseline, but it was later abandoned due to adverse effects including fibrotic complications.
In a large 2019 survey, 2.5% of CH patients reported using caffeine as an acute treatment and 17% of those found it highly effective.
Lithium is proposed to act in cluster headache via facilitation of presynaptic GABA release and upregulation of postsynaptic GABA-A receptors, mechanisms borrowed from its use in bipolar disorder.
In the first double-blind placebo-controlled crossover study (1975), prednisone decreased cluster headache attack frequency in 17 of 19 treated patients who had failed prior therapies.
A retrospective study found 14 of 19 CH patients treated with 10-80 mg/day prednisone had at least 50% headache relief, but 79% relapsed when the drug was tapered.
