An RCT of 12 L/min oxygen for 15 minutes found 78% of participants pain-free versus 20% with regular air inhalation.
In an RCT, subcutaneous sumatriptan 6 mg achieved pain freedom in 36% of patients at 10 minutes and 48% at 15 minutes post-injection.
Numbers needed to treat for subcutaneous sumatriptan 6 mg were 3.3 and 2.4 across two studies.
Intranasal zolmitriptan achieved pain-free response within 30 minutes in 63% of patients on the 10 mg dose and 48% on the 5 mg dose across two RCTs.
Sumatriptan 20 mg nasal spray produced pain freedom at 30 minutes in 47% of participants in an RCT.
In a small crossover RCT of nitroglycerin-induced CH attacks, intranasal lidocaine and cocaine both stopped pain faster than placebo.
Subcutaneous octreotide 100 µg achieved headache relief at 30 minutes in 57% of subjects versus 36% with placebo in an RCT.
A large RCT (n=118) found 100 mg prednisone reduced mean cluster headache attacks by 25.3% within the first week, significantly outperforming placebo.
A large placebo-controlled trial found active greater occipital nerve block reduced weekly cluster headache attack frequency significantly more than placebo injections.
In a retrospective study, most patients became headache free within two days of transitional treatment with 1 mg DHE given 2-3 times daily, with 16% headache free after the first dose.
Intranasal DHE showed insufficient efficacy in one RCT for transitional treatment of cluster headache.

A multi-center, placebo-controlled RCT of frovatriptan 5 mg in episodic cluster headache was discontinued early due to infeasibility and showed no significant difference from placebo on primary or secondary endpoints.
In a multicenter randomized placebo-controlled crossover study, verapamil 120 mg tid produced significantly more responders than placebo for cluster headache attack frequency.
A double-blind crossover trial comparing verapamil to lithium carbonate for chronic cluster headache found both effective, but verapamil had fewer adverse effects and a shorter latency to response.
Erenumab, a CGRP receptor antibody, failed to show efficacy in a randomized, double-blind, placebo-controlled phase 2 trial (CHERUB01) for chronic cluster headache.
Fremanezumab showed futility in interim analyses of Phase 3 trials (ENFORCE) for both episodic and chronic cluster headache.
Eptinezumab failed to meet the primary efficacy outcome in the phase 3 ALLEVIATE trial for prevention of episodic cluster headache, although it showed numerically higher responder rates.

In the open-label CHRONICLE trial, eptinezumab treatment for chronic cluster headache prevention was associated with improvements in attack frequency, pain severity, and patient-reported outcomes over twelve months.
Circannual urinary melatonin concentrations are lowered in individuals with episodic cluster headache.

In a double-blind placebo-controlled pilot study, melatonin 10 mg at night reduced attack frequency in 5 of 10 episodic CH participants within 3-5 days, while chronic CH patients and placebo recipients showed no response.
OnabotulinumtoxinA has shown benefit in small case series for chronic cluster headache using an adapted PREEMPT protocol, but controlled trials are lacking.
MELAS syndrome patients had a significantly higher overall disease burden (NMDAS score) than non-MELAS patients with the same m.3243A>G variant.
Headaches/migraines were a common clinical feature reported in both MELAS syndrome (67%) and non-MELAS (60%) m.3243A>G patients.
Hearing impairment was reported in all MELAS syndrome patients compared to less than half of non-MELAS patients.
Gait instability was more frequently reported in MELAS syndrome than non-MELAS patients.
Self-reported autonomic symptom scores (COMPASS-31) did not significantly differ between MELAS syndrome and non-MELAS patients despite the higher disease burden in MELAS.
Moderate-to-severe autonomic dysfunction (COMPASS-31 ≥20) was present in all MELAS syndrome patients who completed the questionnaire and in the majority of non-MELAS patients.
Severe or excessive fatigue was reported by all MELAS syndrome patients but only half of non-MELAS patients.
MELAS syndrome patients had significantly lower body weight than non-MELAS patients.
Absolute peak VO2, anaerobic threshold and peak power were significantly lower in MELAS syndrome patients than non-MELAS, but the difference disappeared after adjusting for body weight.

MELAS syndrome patients had lower peak cardiac output, cardiac index, stroke volume, and stroke volume index than non-MELAS patients, suggesting cardiovascular rather than muscle oxidative impairment.

Objectively measured accelerometry showed MELAS syndrome patients spent less time in moderate and moderate-vigorous physical activity than both non-MELAS patients and healthy controls, despite no difference in self-reported activity.
MELAS syndrome patients averaged significantly fewer daily steps than both non-MELAS patients and healthy controls.
MELAS syndrome patients had significantly longer sleep duration than non-MELAS patients and healthy controls, with no difference in sleep efficiency.
Increasing age was strongly correlated with higher measured inactivity in both MELAS syndrome and non-MELAS patients.
In non-MELAS patients, higher blood/urine mtDNA heteroplasmy levels correlated with lower objective and self-reported physical activity, longer sleep, and poorer perceived mobility/ADLs.

Age-adjusted blood mtDNA heteroplasmy was not associated with any clinical, subjective, or performance outcome measure in MELAS syndrome patients, contrasting with its associations in non-MELAS patients.
Cognitive impairment (NMDAS cognitive sub-score ≥2) was far more common in MELAS syndrome than non-MELAS patients.
Only a minority of carriers of the m.3243A>G MT-TL1 pathogenic variant go on to develop MELAS syndrome, illustrating incomplete penetrance.
Peak handgrip strength was below population norms in the majority of both MELAS syndrome and non-MELAS patients, with no significant difference between the two groups.
Both MELAS syndrome and non-MELAS patients had notably lower mental well-being scores than published population norms.
Headaches/migraines were a common clinical feature reported in both MELAS syndrome (67%) and non-MELAS (60%) m.3243A>G patients.

Gastrointestinal disturbance, hearing impairment, diabetes mellitus, exercise intolerance and gait instability were frequently reported comorbidities in m.3243A>G patients, with hearing impairment and gait instability notably more prevalent in MELAS syndrome.
All MELAS syndrome participants had a documented history of seizures, whereas none of the non-MELAS participants had a history of seizures.
Cognitive impairment, defined as an NMDAS cognitive sub-score ≥2, was substantially more common in MELAS syndrome patients than non-MELAS patients.
In both MELAS syndrome and non-MELAS patients, increasing age correlated with higher accelerometer-measured inactivity.
In MELAS syndrome, increasing age was inversely correlated with peak VO2 (ml/kg/min) and cardiac index.
In non-MELAS patients, increasing age was associated with lower peak heart rate, higher peak stroke volume/stroke volume index, longer TUG time and reduced objective physical activity.
Age negatively correlated with mental well-being (WEMWBS) in non-MELAS patients, but positively correlated with perceived energy/fatigue (NMQ) in MELAS syndrome patients.

In MELAS syndrome, BMI was inversely correlated with peak cardiac index, and higher body weight was associated with lower peak exercise capacity, greater handgrip strength and poorer perceived mobility.
Age-adjusted blood mtDNA heteroplasmy level was not associated with any clinical, subjective or objective outcome measure in MELAS syndrome patients.
In non-MELAS patients, higher blood mtDNA heteroplasmy correlated with lower moderate/MVPA activity, longer sleep, poorer perceived mobility/ADLs, and lower self-reported physical activity.

In non-MELAS patients, disease severity (NMDAS) positively correlated with fatigue (FIS) and both were inversely correlated with well-being, perceived mobility/energy-fatigue, and positively associated with autonomic dysfunction (COMPASS-31).
In MELAS syndrome patients, disease severity showed no significant association with patient-reported outcomes except that fatigue was inversely correlated with activities of daily living.

MELAS syndrome patients showed a 'weekend warrior' activity pattern, completing approximately twice as many steps on weekend days compared to weekdays, whereas non-MELAS patients maintained similar activity levels throughout the week.
Neither MELAS syndrome nor non-MELAS patients showed strong correlations between objectively measured (accelerometry) and self-reported (IPAQ) physical activity.
A positive correlation between well-being (WEMWBS) and MVPA in 10-minute bouts was the only shared significant PRO-PerfO relationship observed in both MELAS syndrome and non-MELAS patients.

In MELAS syndrome patients, PerfO-PRO associations were fewer and often reversed relative to expected directions, including inverse correlation between well-being and peak VO2/anaerobic threshold, perceived mobility and MVPA, and energy/fatigue and anaerobic threshold.

Autonomic dysfunction (COMPASS-31) was inversely associated with perceived mobility, energy/fatigue and ADLs in non-MELAS patients, while no such associations were observed in MELAS syndrome patients.

Across 40 included studies, PANS was found to affect children's occupational performance most consistently in the domains of communication, nutrition, education, rest/sleep, social participation, and toileting.
The reviewed literature contained limited data on how PANS affects bathing, dressing, personal hygiene, and play/leisure occupations in children.
Assessment tools used in the PANS literature primarily evaluated client factors (e.g., skills/impairments) rather than occupation-based participation.
Only two of the 40 included studies mentioned occupational therapy interventions for children with PANS, indicating a major gap in the intervention evidence base.

PANS causes sudden, severe neuropsychiatric symptoms including obsessive-compulsive behaviors, eating difficulties, sensory and motor changes, and developmental regression, which significantly disrupt children's ability to perform daily activities.

Agreement between non-specialist and specialist interviewers for diagnosing post-traumatic headache (PTH) was very good by proportion of concordance and PABAK, but only fair by simple kappa coefficient.
Among the 63 patients, 94% experienced migraine-like headaches after mTBI, including 19% classified as probable migraine-like.
Tension-type-like, primary stabbing-like, and cervicogenic-like headache phenotypes were also diagnosed among the cohort, though far less frequently than migraine-like headache.
Autonomic features consistent with trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia (TAC) were reported in only 11% of patients, and no other features supported a TAC-like phenotype in this cohort.
Just under half of patients with migraine-like post-traumatic headache reported an aura, most commonly visual and/or vestibular in nature.
Nearly all patients (all but one) had definite PTH, meaning their headache began within seven days of head injury, consistent with the ICHD-3 definition.
Patients reported a high burden of headache with a mean of 19.5 headache days per month and a mean maximum severity of 5.5 out of 10.
A large proportion (70%) of the cohort had experienced repeated concussions, averaging 2.1 prior concussions, likely reflecting the high proportion of sports-related injuries.
A notable minority of patients had a pre-existing history of migraine, childhood migraine, or family history of migraine prior to their head injury.

When classifying sub-phenotypes, agreement between non-specialist and specialist was very good for distinguishing migraine-like from TTH-like headache, and good for migraine-like versus other phenotypes.
Diagnostic agreement for PTH improved across the three iterative refinement cycles of the classification interview, reaching 100% PABAK-adjusted concordance by cycle three.

For PTH diagnosis and for differentiating migraine-like from TTH-like headache, the 95% confidence interval for the kappa coefficient included negative values, meaning agreement could be worse than chance by this metric, although PABAK indicated good-to-very-good agreement.
The single patient with suspected trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia in the cohort was correctly identified as such by both the non-specialist and the specialist doctor.
The authors note that an ongoing open-label study of the CGRP-targeting drug erenumab has shown preliminary efficacy for post-traumatic headache, though placebo-controlled RCTs are still needed.
One patient queried as having a trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia underwent an indomethacin trial but showed no response, arguing against that diagnosis.
A prior systematic review found topiramate produced the smallest effect size among chronic migraine preventives, reducing monthly migraine days by 1.49 days compared with placebo.
The same systematic review found fremanezumab produced the largest effect size among reviewed preventives, reducing migraine days per month by 2.77 days compared with placebo.

Stakeholders ranked Candesartan versus placebo as the top research priority because it is commonly used for chronic migraine despite an absence of clinical- and cost-effectiveness evidence identified by the team's prior systematic review.

Flunarizine, an unlicensed drug typically prescribed only through specialist headache services, was also ranked as a top priority for a placebo-controlled trial due to lack of existing evidence despite being commonly used.

CGRP monoclonal antibodies and OnabotulinumtoxinA (BTA) dominated the stakeholder group's prioritised head-to-head drug comparisons, each appearing in six of the eleven top drug-drug comparisons proposed.

The stakeholder group identified a research need to compare differing clinical effectiveness between different CGRP MAbs, MAbs with different molecular targets, and the combination of MAbs with BTA versus each drug alone.

Topiramate, BTA, and CGRP MAbs did not appear in the top five drug-placebo comparisons prioritised, reflecting the group's view that existing evidence already establishes their superiority over placebo.

Melatonin, not a commonly used chronic migraine drug, was nonetheless ranked in the top five drug-drug comparisons by stakeholders; a cited study found it outperformed placebo but was not superior to amitriptyline, though that study was in an episodic (not chronic) migraine population.
Doxycycline was proposed by one small group based on a small open-label study of four patients but was rejected by the wider stakeholder group and excluded from the final list of research priorities.

The stakeholder group raised the possibility that combining OnabotulinumtoxinA with a CGRP monoclonal antibody could produce additive effects, hypothesising a combined mean reduction of 4-5 headache/migraine days per month if the effects add without negative interaction.
Dysautonomia was significantly more frequent among adult anti-NMDAR encephalitis patients than paediatric patients.
Migraine was the most frequent primary headache diagnosis among patients consulting in primary care, accounting for 60% of cases.
Tension-type headache was the second most frequent primary headache diagnosis, accounting for 38.5% of cases.
Trigeminal autonomic headaches were the least frequent primary headache diagnosis at 1.5% of cases.
Primary headache accounted for 2.2% of all demand consultations in primary care.
The majority of primary headache patients (58%) received an incomplete or incorrect diagnosis in primary care.
Using the MIDAS scale, 33% of primary headache patients showed at least a moderate decrease in quality of life.
Using the HIT-6 scale, 50.8% of primary headache patients showed at least a moderate decrease in quality of life.
Quality-of-life impact was greater among migraine patients than the overall headache cohort, with moderate-or-greater decreases seen in 40.8% (MIDAS) and 72.5% (HIT-6) of migraine cases.
Work or activity absenteeism due to headache occurred in 12% of patients over the previous year.
Among patients reporting absenteeism due to headache, the large majority (87.5%) had migraine as the underlying diagnosis.
More than half of primary headache patients (58%) had at some point been referred to Neurology.
Preventive pharmacological treatment for primary headache had been initiated in Primary Care in only 5.5% of patients, indicating a management gap.

Genomic SEM modeling of six BMS-related GWASs revealed substantial shared genetic covariance among Sjögren's syndrome, anxiety, depression, fibromyalgia, migraine, and dysphagia, supporting a common latent BMS factor with good model fit.
The multivariate genomic SEM analysis identified nine genome-wide significant loci associated with the latent BMS factor.
Fine-mapping of the latent BMS factor signal highlighted credible causal variants at the MRPL49P1 locus.
Fine-mapping of the latent BMS factor signal highlighted credible causal variants at the R3HDML locus.
Transcriptome-wide association analysis prioritized LRP1 expression as associated with lower risk for the latent burning mouth syndrome factor.
Enrichment analyses of the latent BMS factor implicated evolutionarily conserved regions and enhancer elements as functionally relevant.
Cell-type enrichment analyses suggested neuronal and immune-related cellular contributions to the latent BMS factor's genetic architecture.
Polygenic risk score analyses indicated that chromosomes 1 and 2 carry a higher polygenic risk burden for the latent BMS factor than other chromosomes.
Ultrasound-guided superior cervical ganglion (SCG) block combined with standard triptan produced significantly higher rates of sustained headache relief at 2 hours than triptan alone.
SCG block plus triptan resulted in significantly higher rates of freedom from pain within 2 hours compared to triptan alone.
Sustained headache relief at 24 hours was significantly more common with SCG block plus triptan than triptan alone.
Sustained freedom from headache within 24 hours was significantly more frequent with SCG block plus triptan than with triptan alone.
At 1 month, moderate-to-severe migraine-related disability (MIDAS) was far less common in patients treated with SCG block plus triptan compared with triptan alone.
Monthly migraine days at 1 month were significantly lower in the SCG plus triptan cohort compared with triptan alone.
Migraine-specific quality of life (MSQ) scores improved significantly more with SCG block plus triptan than with triptan alone at 1 month.
Use of rescue analgesics (celecoxib and oxycodone-acetaminophen) at 2 hours, 24 hours and 1 month was significantly lower in the SCG plus triptan cohort compared with triptan alone.

No serious adverse events (allergic reaction, arrhythmia, vascular injection, hematoma, local anesthetic intoxication) occurred in either treatment group, and minor dizziness/somnolence rates did not differ significantly between groups.
Minor procedure-related complications from steroid and local anesthetic injection (nausea, vomiting, facial flushing) occurred in a small proportion of SCG-treated patients but all resolved quickly.
Both connective tissue massage (CTM) and manual lymphatic drainage (MLD) significantly reduced Neck Pain and Disability (NPAD) scores after six weeks of treatment in migraine patients.
Connective tissue massage produced a greater reduction in neck disability scores than manual lymphatic drainage, despite similar effects on pain, quality of life, and pressure pain thresholds.
Migraine pain duration decreased more (was shorter) in the MLD group than in the CTM group after treatment.

Pain duration, number of headache days, and medication use showed no significant difference between the CTM and MLD groups, but all three parameters improved significantly within each group after treatment.

Pressure pain thresholds increased significantly in the anterior scalene, trapezius, and suboccipital muscles after treatment in both the CTM and MLD groups, with no significant between-group difference post-treatment.
Pressure pain thresholds increased considerably in the temporalis, levator scapulae, and sternocleidomastoid muscles after treatment in both groups.
Energy/vitality subscale scores of the SF-36 significantly improved after treatment in both the CTM and MLD groups.
Mental health subscale scores of the SF-36 significantly improved after treatment in both the CTM and MLD groups.
Social functioning subscale scores of the SF-36 significantly improved after treatment in both the CTM and MLD groups.
Physical role subscale scores did not significantly improve after CTM (p=0.083) but did significantly improve after MLD (p=0.046).
Emotional role subscale scores did not significantly improve after CTM (p=0.257) but did significantly improve after MLD (p=0.038).
SF-36 pain subscale scores significantly increased after treatment in both the CTM and MLD groups.
SF-36 total quality-of-life scores significantly increased after treatment in both the CTM and MLD groups.
General health perception subscale scores of the SF-36 significantly increased after treatment in both the CTM and MLD groups.
In a retrospective cohort of 68 PSH patients, 90% had concomitant migraine, with 65% meeting criteria for chronic migraine, 25% for episodic migraine, and 18% reporting aura.
In the same cohort, 10% of PSH patients had comorbid cluster headache and 7% had hemicrania continua.
Only 3% of the PSH cohort had isolated stabbing headache with no other primary headache disorder present.
Among patients where reason for attendance was documented, almost all attended primarily for their underlying headache disorder rather than for the stabbing headache itself.
Among patients with available data, the mean frequency of stabs was 7 ± 9 per day.
The number of days per month with stabbing headache averaged 17 ± 12 among the subset with available data.
Among patients with documented location data, 58% reported that stabbing pains co-localized with the underlying primary headache.
Among patients assessed, 69% reported that stabbing pains occurred predominantly during migraine or cluster attacks, while 31% did not report this temporal association.
Among the subset with data on treatment impact, 86% reported some improvement of stabbing pains when treated for the underlying primary headache disorder, whereas 14% noted no benefit.
Lansche's original 1964 description of PSH (as ophthalmodynia periodica) reported comorbid migraine in 66% of cases.
Across subsequent adult PSH studies identified in the systematic review, migraine comorbidity ranged from 25% to 83%.

In Atalar and colleagues' population study, only 32% of PSH cases met criteria for definite migraine, but a migrainous biology was supported by high rates of accompanying symptoms: nausea in 68%, photophobia in 76%, and phonophobia in 84%.

Seleker and colleagues found 88% topographical concordance between stabbing and migraine headache locations, with 79% of stabbing episodes occurring during migraine attacks and a further 21% occurring immediately adjacent to attacks.
Migraine-based cohorts showed a markedly elevated prevalence of stabbing headache, reported between 38% and 45%, compared with the general population lifetime prevalence.
Raskin and colleagues reported that PSH occurred in 42% of migraineurs versus only 3% of controls, with a strict temporal correlation to migraine attacks in 69% of cases.
Silva and colleagues reported that PSH was experienced by 44.7% of migraine sufferers compared to 10.3% of non-migraine subjects.
Stabbing paroxysms characteristic of PSH occur in 36-41% of hemicrania continua series and 2-33% of cluster headache series.

By contrast, when PSH is the index diagnosis, accompanying TACs are uncommon: hemicrania continua appears in only 0-8% of adult PSH cohorts, and cluster headache has not been reported in this direction.
In paediatric PSH cohorts, comorbid migraine prevalence was lower than in adults, ranging from 0% to 27%.
Family history of migraine was prominent in paediatric PSH cohorts, ranging from 35% to 78% across series.
Monte and colleagues reported that 72% of children with PSH also experienced migraine-related episodic syndromes such as cyclic vomiting and recurrent abdominal pain.
A population-based study reported a lifetime prevalence of primary stabbing headache of 35.2%, suggesting roughly one in three people have experienced these sharp head pains.

Although PSH is not formally classified among indomethacin-responsive headache disorders, nearly two-thirds of patients achieve partial or complete relief with indomethacin, making it the mainstay of treatment.
Indomethacin uniquely lowers cerebrospinal-fluid pressure, reduces cerebral blood flow, and interferes with nitric-oxide signalling, distinguishing it from other NSAIDs.
In the trigeminal ganglion, nitric-oxide synthase colocalises with CGRP, and experimental models show that nitric oxide can drive CGRP release, a mechanism proposed to link PSH with migraine biology.

Nitric oxide facilitates glutamate-mediated activation of NMDA receptors and promotes central sensitisation, a mechanism increasingly recognised as pivotal in migraine and proposed as a substrate linking PSH to migraine.

A study of 424 cluster headache patients found short-lasting jabs ("cluster stabs") affecting 47% of cases independently of trigeminal neuralgia, triggerable in only 17% of cases, which the authors of this review suggest simply represent PSH occurring in the context of cluster headache.
Raskin and colleagues found that primary stabbing headache occurred far more often in migraineurs than in controls, with most stabs temporally linked to migraine attacks.
Silva and colleagues found that PSH was substantially more common among migraine sufferers than among people without migraine.
Stabbing paroxysms characteristic of PSH were reported in over a third of hemicrania continua case series.
Stabbing paroxysms characteristic of PSH were reported across a wide range (2-33%) of cluster headache case series.
Lance and Ekbom noted that short-lasting jabs resembling PSH occurred during an ongoing cluster headache attack.

When PSH is the primary/index diagnosis rather than a comorbidity, trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias are rarely seen: hemicrania continua occurs in only 0-8% of adult PSH cohorts and cluster headache has not been reported at all.
Paediatric PSH cohorts showed a lower rate of comorbid migraine than adult cohorts.
A family history of migraine was common among children with PSH, despite lower rates of the child themselves meeting migraine criteria.
Monte and colleagues reported that most children with PSH in their cohort also experienced migraine-related episodic syndromes such as cyclic vomiting and recurrent abdominal pain.

Nearly two-thirds of PSH patients achieve partial or complete relief with indomethacin, making it the mainstay of treatment even though PSH is not formally classified as an indomethacin-responsive headache disorder.
Indomethacin has the unique property among NSAIDs of lowering cerebrospinal-fluid pressure.
Indomethacin reduces cerebral blood flow, a property distinct from typical cyclo-oxygenase inhibition and relevant to its efficacy in indomethacin-responsive headaches.
Indomethacin blocks nitric-oxide-induced vasodilatation and, unlike other NSAIDs, also suppresses neuronal firing triggered by NO donors.
In the trigeminal ganglion, nitric oxide synthase colocalises with calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP), suggesting a shared pathway relevant to migraine biology.
Experimental models show that nitric oxide can drive the release of calcitonin gene-related peptide (CGRP).
Nitric oxide facilitates glutamate-mediated activation of NMDA receptors, a mechanism increasingly recognised as pivotal in migraine.

Nitric oxide promotes central sensitisation in migraine, producing a hyperexcitable state in peripheral and central pain circuits; the authors propose that spontaneous discharges from such hyperexcitable neurons may surface as PSH's brief stabbing pains.

In cluster-tic syndrome (first described by Klimek), patients have both cluster headache and a separate trigeminal neuralgia component whose stabs, unlike PSH, do not respond to indomethacin but do respond to carbamazepine.

A study of 424 cluster headache patients (excluding those with trigeminal neuralgia) found short-lasting jabs, newly termed "cluster stabs," in nearly half of cases, with triggerability in only a minority, and proposed these be considered part of the cluster headache symptomatology; the authors interpret this as likely representing PSH occurring within cluster headache.

Epicrania fugax, a disorder of dynamic short-lasting paroxysms of stabbing or electric quality that spread over the head, is frequently described occurring alongside migraine or cluster headache and may be best regarded as an endophenotype of PSH.
Pooled proportions of MIDAS Grade IV (severe disability) increased across population-based studies from low-frequency episodic migraine to high-frequency episodic migraine to chronic migraine.
Pooled overall work productivity impairment scores from WPAI increased with headache frequency across population-based studies.
Pooled activity impairment scores from WPAI increased with headache frequency across population-based studies.
Pooled proportions of MIDAS Grade IV disability increased with headache frequency across clinic-based studies.
Pooled overall work productivity impairment scores increased with headache frequency across clinic-based studies.
Pooled activity impairment scores increased with headache frequency across clinic-based studies.
In clinic-based studies, pooled mean MIDAS scores increased progressively across low-frequency episodic migraine, high-frequency episodic migraine, and chronic migraine subgroups.
Across the meta-analyses, a substantial proportion (42%-44%) of individuals with high-frequency episodic migraine experienced a severe level of disability, regardless of study setting.
Meta-analysis of 16 studies (1123 participants) found reduced intraepidermal nerve fibre density at the distal leg in people with non-neuropathic chronic pain compared with pain-free controls.
Meta-analysis of 12 studies (896 participants) found reduced intraepidermal nerve fibre density at the proximal thigh in people with non-neuropathic chronic pain compared with pain-free controls.
Meta-analysis of 8 studies (768 participants) found reduced corneal nerve fibre density on corneal confocal microscopy in people with non-neuropathic chronic pain compared with pain-free controls.
Other intraepidermal nerve fibre density and corneal confocal microscopy metrics beyond the primary density measures also differed between people with non-neuropathic chronic pain and controls.
Associations between clinical features such as pain and disability and IENFD/CCM measures were examined less often and mostly showed no relationship.
A weak recommendation was issued for the SAVI Dual non-invasive neuromodulation device in the treatment of acute migraine attacks based on GRADE evaluation of randomized controlled trials.
A weak recommendation was issued for Cefaly in the treatment of acute migraine attacks based on GRADE evaluation of randomized controlled trials.

Overall, women with systemic sclerosis were found to be similar to healthy women regarding sexual dysfunction, though psychosocial health was an important contributing factor.
Women with Sjögren's disease showed significantly lower FSFI scores across desire, arousal, orgasm, lubrication, and pain domains compared with healthy individuals.

Vaginal dryness was a predominant factor in SD among Sjögren's disease patients, leading to increased lubricant use compared with normal individuals.

Physiological and psychological factors including exhaustion, depressive symptoms, unhappy relationships, and diminished mental quality of life contribute to sexual dysfunction in primary Sjögren's disease.
Karakus found that sexual functionality in Sjögren's disease patients decreased with longer disease duration.
Vaginal dryness in primary Sjögren's disease was associated with more significant inflammation and atrophy on cervical smears compared with controls.

A qualitative study by Rebel et al. (2025) found that sexual dysfunction was prevalent in both female (64%) and male (67%) Sjögren's disease patients, with six key themes influencing sexual experience.
Isik et al. (2024) found that vaginal and vulvar dryness and dyspareunia were significantly more common in Sjögren's disease patients, particularly primary SjD, compared to healthy controls.
SLE can potentiate ovarian failure or ovarian insufficiency through a mechanism that remains idiopathic.

A survey by Jin et al. found that males had a higher predilection towards developing sexual dysfunction than females.

Reduced sexual desire was seen in 50-60% of RA patients, with decreased frequency of sexual activity in up to 73% of patients compared with normal individuals.

Gutweniger et al. found that female RA patients with higher morning stiffness were more self-conscious about their bodies and less satisfied with their sexual experiences than those with lower morning stiffness.

El Miedany's study of 231 rheumatoid arthritis patients found sexual dysfunction in 53.8% of men and 45.7% of women, with orgasm, arousal, and satisfaction issues predominating in women and erectile dysfunction in men.

Men with ankylosing spondylitis experience considerably lower sexual function scores compared to healthy controls.

Erectile dysfunction is more prevalent in ankylosing spondylitis patients, with prevalence rates ranging from 41% to 58%, influenced by age, disease duration, and severity.

Women with axial spondyloarthritis frequently experience sexual dysfunction influenced by disease activity, anxiety, depression, and impaired quality of life.
The impact of non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis on sexual function remains unclear for both men and women.
Women with fibromyalgia syndrome had significantly worse sexual function than healthy controls, with a mean FSFI score of 13.2±8.1 versus 32.1±5.2 in controls.

Peripheral neuropathy in Sjögren's disease may impair vasodilation, resulting in insufficient vaginal lubrication and contributing to sexual dysfunction.
In perimenopausal women with Sjögren's disease, gradual decline in sex hormones may worsen vaginal dryness and tissue atrophy, increasing pain and reducing sexual desire.
The effect of non-radiographic axial spondyloarthritis on sexual function has not been clearly established for men or women.

Hormone replacement therapy is suggested as a beneficial intervention for patients with SARD-related endocrine dysfunction contributing to sexual dysfunction.

In axial spondyloarthritis, fatigue, sleep disturbances, anxiety, depression, and stress contribute to impaired quality of life and sexual health.

Chronic respiratory alkalosis reduces cerebral blood flow via vasospasm and left-shifts the oxygen-hemoglobin dissociation curve, decreasing tissue oxygen delivery and contributing to headache disorders.
Right-to-left shunts, commonly occurring through a patent foramen ovale, are associated with migraine, particularly migraine with aura.
Hypoxic echocardiography with bubble contrast is described as a novel diagnostic paradigm for identifying clinically significant right-to-left shunts and orthodeoxia-platypnea.
A time-limited course of a carbonic anhydrase inhibitor is used to normalize acid-base status and tissue carbon dioxide stores, thereby reducing neuromuscular irritability and headache symptoms.
Rehabilitation measures aimed at normalizing breathing patterns are used to correct acid-base status and reduce neuromuscular irritability and headache symptoms.

Common causes of clinically symptomatic chronic respiratory alkalosis include sleep disordered breathing, right-to-left shunting (anatomic and capillary), post-concussive states, and post-viral or postoperative acid-base derangements linked to altered autonomic function.
A case-control study found that negative stressful life events in the year preceding disease onset were more common among Chinese women with primary Sjögren's syndrome than controls.
A separate study found more major negative life events among Sjögren's syndrome patients compared with both healthy controls and lymphoma controls.
A Quebec cohort study found that long-term PM2.5 exposure was associated with an increased risk of incident Sjögren's syndrome.
A case-control study of 175 Sjögren's syndrome cases and 350 controls found significant associations between multiple occupational solvents and disease risk.

The same case-control study found additional elevated odds ratios for perchloroethylene and benzene, and an overall increased risk from any solvent exposure or chlorinated/aromatic solvents in Sjögren's syndrome.
The same case-control study found no significant association between pesticide exposure and Sjögren's syndrome.

In a population-based cohort of over 7.4 million adults, long-term PM2.5 exposure was associated with a small but statistically significant increased risk of autoimmune inflammatory rheumatic diseases including SLE, Sjögren's syndrome, and systemic sclerosis.

Case-control and prospective studies found an increased risk of chronic widespread pain (fibromyalgia) following motor vehicle accidents and other physical injuries, particularly when accompanied by psychological distress.
A case-control study found that more fibromyalgia patients reported significant physical trauma in the 6 months prior to disease onset compared to controls.
A cross-sectional study found fibromyalgia in 21.6% of patients with cervical spine injury compared to 1.7% of leg fracture controls.

In contrast to other studies, one study found a low incidence of chronic widespread pain following motor vehicle accidents, attributing modest associations to psychological distress rather than the accident itself.
A large population-based sample found that a history of physical or sexual abuse was associated with significantly higher odds of reporting a fibromyalgia diagnosis.
Following a national disaster, acute stress exposure was associated with fibromyalgia disease onset.
In a male veteran cohort, nearly half of those with PTSD met fibromyalgia criteria.
A 2018 systematic review of 31 studies reported consistent associations between fibromyalgia and early-life trauma, particularly sexual and physical abuse.

In SEQUOIA, changes in the OHQ composite, OHSA composite, and OHSA item 1 scores correlated strongly with the Patient Global Impression of Change (PGI-C), supporting their use as anchors for MCID estimation.

In REDWOOD, changes in OHSA composite and OHSA item 1 scores correlated moderately-strongly with the Patient Global Impression of Severity (PGI-S), while the OHQ composite correlation was somewhat lower but still adequate.

The OHDAS activity-impact composite showed weak and inconsistent correlation with symptom-based anchors, making it unsuitable for anchor-based MCID derivation, with some patients reporting symptomatic improvement on PGI-S while worsening on OHDAS.
In SEQUOIA, the anchor-based minimal clinically important difference for the OHQ composite score was a −0.9 point change for improvement and a +0.7 point change for worsening.
In REDWOOD, the anchor-based threshold for minimal worsening of the OHQ composite score was a +1.1 point change.
In SEQUOIA, the OHSA composite MCID was −1.3 points for minimal improvement and +1.1 points for minimal worsening.
In REDWOOD, a +0.7 point change in the OHSA composite score represented the anchor-based threshold for minimal worsening.
In SEQUOIA, the anchor-based MCID for OHSA item 1 (dizziness/lightheadedness) was −3.0 points for minimal improvement and +1.0 points for minimal worsening.
In REDWOOD, the anchor-based MCID for OHSA item 1 was −1.0 for improvement and +1.0 for worsening.

Standard error of measurement/half-standard deviation estimates of measurement error were calculated for the OHQ, OHSA composite scores, and OHSA item 1 at both trial baselines, and all proposed anchor-based MCID thresholds exceeded these error estimates.

ROC curve analysis in SEQUOIA identified optimal score-change thresholds for detecting a ≥1-category improvement on PGI-C: −1.2 for OHQ composite, −0.9 for OHSA composite, and −2.0 for OHSA item 1, each with good discriminative accuracy.
ROC curve analysis in REDWOOD identified optimal worsening thresholds of +0.8 for the OHQ composite score and +1.0 for OHSA item 1 for detecting a ≥1-category worsening on PGI-S.
The ROC-derived worsening threshold for the OHSA composite score in REDWOOD fell below the measurement error estimate (SEM) and was therefore excluded as not clinically interpretable.
Combining anchor-based and ROC-based methods, the final MCID range for the OHQ composite score was −0.9 to −1.2 points for improvement and +0.7 to +1.1 points for worsening.
The final MCID range for the OHSA composite score was −0.9 to −1.3 points for improvement and +0.7 to +1.1 points for worsening.
The final MCID for OHSA item 1 was −2.0 to −3.0 for improvement and +1.0 for worsening.
Almost half of patients with chronic migraine reported vertigo associated with their migraine attacks.
Patients with baseline aura had over twice the odds of reporting vertigo compared with those without aura, after adjustment for other variables.
Patients reporting allodynia had nearly three times the odds of also reporting vertigo, after adjustment for other variables.
Unlike aura and allodynia, the sensory sensitivities of photophobia, phonophobia, and osmophobia showed no significant association with vertigo in the adjusted regression model.
Premonitory symptoms were highly prevalent in this chronic migraine cohort, most commonly concentration difficulty, mood change, and neck discomfort.
Cranial autonomic symptoms were common in this chronic migraine cohort, most often facial flushing or pallor, lacrimation, and nasal congestion.
Allodynia was reported by nearly two-thirds of the chronic migraine cohort.

A multivariate logistic regression model including age, sex, aura, headache days, photophobia, phonophobia, osmophobia, allodynia, CAS, and PS significantly predicted vertigo reporting, explaining 16% of variance and correctly classifying 65% of cases.

At baseline before sit-to-stand, older adults had higher systolic, diastolic, and mean arterial blood pressure and systemic vascular resistance than younger adults.
At baseline before sit-to-stand, older adults had lower heart rate, cardiac output, and stroke volume than younger adults.
Immediately after sit-to-stand, older adults showed a greater drop in SBP, DBP, MAP, and SVR compared to younger adults.
Immediately after sit-to-stand, older adults showed lower HR and CO peaks but a larger SV peak than younger adults.
During sit-to-stand, SBP, DBP, and MAP compensatory responses did not differ between older and younger adults in the first 60 seconds, but were higher in older adults from 60 s onward (except DBP).
During sit-to-stand, older adults had lower SVR compensatory response values than younger adults in the first 60 seconds, with no differences after that.
During sit-to-stand, older adults had lower heart rate and higher stroke volume than younger adults across all four compensatory phases.
During sit-to-stand, cardiac output was lower in older adults in phases 1 and 4 but showed no difference in phases 2 and 3.
In younger adults during sit-to-stand, CO and SVR were not significantly correlated in the first 30 seconds but showed a significant strong negative correlation from 30 seconds to 7 minutes.
In older adults during sit-to-stand, CO and SVR showed significant moderate-to-strong negative correlations across all four phases, indicating faster CO-SVR matching than younger adults.
At baseline before lie-to-stand, older adults had higher SBP, DBP, MAP, and SVR, lower CO and SV, and no difference in HR compared to younger adults.
Immediately after lie-to-stand, older adults had a greater drop in SBP, DBP, MAP, and SVR, a lower HR peak, a higher SV peak, and no difference in CO peak compared to younger adults.
During lie-to-stand, older adults' SBP, DBP, MAP, and SVR short-term compensatory responses were lower than younger adults' in the first 60 seconds but became similar from 60 seconds onward.
During lie-to-stand, older adults had lower heart rate and higher stroke volume compensatory values than younger adults in phases 1-3, but not in phase 4.
During lie-to-stand, cardiac output showed no statistically significant differences between older and younger adults across all four phases.
In younger adults during lie-to-stand, CO and SVR showed moderate to strong significant negative correlations across all four phases, indicating rapid coupling.

In older adults during lie-to-stand, CO and SVR were not significantly correlated in the first 30 seconds but showed strong significant negative correlations from 30 seconds to 7 minutes, indicating delayed CO-SVR matching under higher orthostatic stress.

The percentage drop in SVR after standing was larger in older adults (44% sit-to-stand, 45% lie-to-stand) than younger adults (33% for both transitions), contrasting with prior studies that reported the opposite pattern.

A substantial proportion of older adult participants were taking cardiovascular medications (calcium channel blockers, beta-blockers, diuretics, ACE inhibitors, angiotensin receptor blockers), which were recorded but not controlled for and could have influenced the cardiovascular responses observed.

Overall, older adults exhibited delayed and less effective short-term cardiovascular compensatory responses during active standing compared to younger adults, which may contribute to increased risk of orthostatic hypotension, orthostatic intolerance, or falls in daily life.
TLR4 knockout male mice did not develop significant STZ-induced thermal hyposensitivity, while wild-type male mice did.
STZ-treated wild-type male mice lost about 40% of intraepidermal nerve fibers, whereas TLR4-knockout male mice were protected from this loss.
Dermal Iba1+ macrophage intensity increased in STZ-treated wild-type male mice but not in TLR4-knockout male mice.
TLR4 deletion did not alter the severity of STZ-induced hyperglycemia in either sex, indicating protective effects on neuropathy were independent of glycemic control.
Male mice of both genotypes developed more severe STZ-induced hyperglycemia than female mice.
STZ induced significant weight loss only in male mice of both genotypes, and TLR4 deletion partially protected males from this weight loss.
Final blood glucose strongly correlated with thermal hyposensitivity in wild-type male mice, but this relationship was absent in TLR4-knockout males.
IENFD was strongly negatively correlated with final blood glucose in wild-type male mice, but this correlation was not present in TLR4-knockout males.

STZ treatment lowered mechanical thresholds overall, and TLR4-knockout mice showed higher mechanical thresholds as a main effect of genotype, although no individual group comparisons reached significance.
Serum IL-23 and IL-1α levels were not significantly altered by STZ treatment or TLR4 genotype, though IL-23 trended higher in wild-type versus TLR4-knockout mice.
In TLR4-knockout male mice, serum IL-23 significantly correlated with both intraepidermal nerve fiber density and dermal Iba1 macrophage intensity, though the measured ranges were narrow.

Female mice of both genotypes developed a milder diabetic neuropathy phenotype overall, with less severe hyperglycemia, no significant weight loss, preserved epidermal nerve fiber density, and no increase in dermal macrophages.
In females, STZ-treated wild-type mice had significantly higher thermal latency than STZ-treated TLR4-knockout mice at six weeks, although neither group differed from its own vehicle-treated control.

According to cited prior work, TLR4 mRNA and protein expression are significantly higher in patients with diabetic peripheral neuropathy compared to those with type 2 diabetes alone, suggesting potential use as a diagnostic marker.
A cited clinical study reported that low-dose naltrexone, a TLR4 inhibitor, provided symptom relief in patients with painful diabetic peripheral neuropathy.
Adding a 12-week pranayama and relaxation program to standard care produced a significantly greater reduction in monthly headache frequency than standard care alone.
Pain intensity measured by VAS decreased significantly more in the pranayama and relaxation group than in the control group.
Migraine-related disability scores (HIT-6) improved significantly more in the intervention group than the control group.
Quality of life improvements, particularly in the physical and vitality domains, were more pronounced in the group receiving pranayama and relaxation.

The pranayama and relaxation group showed increased heart rate variability indices (higher RMSSD and HF_nu, lower LF/HF ratio), indicating enhanced parasympathetic tone, whereas the control group did not.
The pranayama and relaxation intervention group showed increased RMSSD, a time-domain heart rate variability index, reflecting greater parasympathetic activity compared to controls.
Normalized high-frequency power (HF_nu), a marker of vagal/parasympathetic tone, increased in the intervention group relative to controls.
The LF/HF ratio, an index of sympathovagal balance, decreased in the intervention group, consistent with a shift toward parasympathetic dominance.
Resting heart rate was significantly reduced only in the intervention group, consistent with enhanced parasympathetic tone.
Resting blood pressure was significantly reduced only in the intervention group, indicating a broader autonomic and cardiovascular benefit of the program.
The pranayama and relaxation program was well tolerated, with no adverse events reported and high adherence rates among participants.
The KIT D816V mutation is the key driver mutation found in up to 95% of systemic mastocytosis cases.
Serum tryptase is one of the key laboratory parameters assessed from peripheral blood as part of the diagnostic workup of systemic mastocytosis.

Variant allele frequency of KIT D816V in bone marrow and peripheral blood, along with bone marrow mast cell infiltration and cytogenetic analysis, is used to characterize disease burden and subtype in systemic mastocytosis.
Two patients with KIT D816V-positive systemic mastocytosis (one with advanced SM, one with indolent SM) were managed with KIT-targeted therapies.

Systemic mastocytosis is classified into nonadvanced SM (indolent SM, bone marrow mastocytosis, smoldering SM) and advanced SM (aggressive SM, SM with an associated hematological neoplasm, and mast cell leukemia), reflecting heterogeneous clinical presentations.
The supraorbital nerve (SON) was found to be significantly more superficial in the skin than the infraorbital (ION) and mental (MN) nerves.
The SON had a higher ratio of nerve tissue to connective tissue than the mental nerve (MN).
Finite element modeling showed that nerve depth was a key determinant of neural activation and sensitivity to skin impedance properties during simulated transcutaneous trigeminal nerve stimulation.
Preferential activation of low-threshold nociceptors relative to nerve trunks may cause treatment-limiting off-target side effects during transcutaneous stimulation of the trigeminal nerve.
The SON is proposed as the most accessible and anatomically favorable target among the examined branches for non-invasive transcutaneous trigeminal nerve stimulation due to its superficial location.
CT imaging was used to localize the supraorbital nerve's exit foramen and measure its distance to midline as part of characterizing trigeminal branch anatomy.
Microdissection was used to quantify infraorbital nerve circumference and depth relative to the skin surface.
Histological analysis described the number of fascicles and fascicular tissue area for the mental nerve as part of comparing trigeminal branch tissue composition.
Finite element modeling showed that nerve depth strongly influenced sensitivity of neural activation to skin impedance properties during transcutaneous stimulation.

Cadaveric measurements, histological analyses, and imaging together characterized the depths, branching patterns, and fascicular organization within the trigeminal nerve branches, providing an anatomical framework for electrode design and modeling.
Among 267 Italian patients with Sjögren's disease, a concomitant diagnosis of fibromyalgia was identified in 30% of patients.
SjD patients with concomitant fibromyalgia had a significantly longer disease duration than those without fibromyalgia.
The follow-up period was significantly longer for SjD patients with fibromyalgia compared to those without.
Mixed anxiety-depressive disorder was significantly more frequent among SjD patients with fibromyalgia than among those without.
Arthralgias were more commonly reported in SjD patients with fibromyalgia than those without.
Patients with fibromyalgia reported a significantly higher overall symptom burden on the ESSPRI compared to those without fibromyalgia.
The ESSPRI fatigue domain was significantly higher in SjD patients with fibromyalgia.
The ESSPRI pain domain was significantly higher in SjD patients with fibromyalgia.
The ESSPRI dryness domain was significantly higher in SjD patients with fibromyalgia.
Physician-assessed disease activity (ESSDAI) did not differ significantly between SjD patients with and without fibromyalgia, despite markedly higher patient-reported symptom scores in the FM group.
Platelet counts were significantly higher in SjD patients with fibromyalgia, although this was not considered clinically relevant and thrombocytosis frequency did not differ.
Prior corticosteroid use was significantly more common in SjD patients with fibromyalgia than in those without, though current use and dose were similar.
Antidepressant use was markedly more frequent among SjD patients with fibromyalgia compared to those without.
Muscle relaxant use was markedly more frequent among SjD patients with fibromyalgia compared to those without.
Pilocarpine use trended higher in SjD patients with fibromyalgia but did not reach statistical significance.
Biologic DMARD use trended higher in SjD patients with fibromyalgia but did not reach statistical significance.

Univariate logistic regression showed corticosteroid use was significantly associated with the presence of fibromyalgia in SjD.
Univariate logistic regression showed the ESSPRI score was significantly associated with the presence of fibromyalgia in SjD.

Pain VAS score was independently associated with fibromyalgia in univariate analysis.
Dryness VAS score was independently associated with fibromyalgia in univariate analysis.

Use of biologic DMARDs tended to be more frequent among SjD patients with concomitant FM than those without, but this difference was not statistically significant.
Prior corticosteroid use was significantly more common in SjD patients with concomitant FM than in those without.
Pilocarpine use was numerically more frequent among SjD patients with FM but the difference did not reach statistical significance.

The association between the ESSPRI dryness domain and FM was attenuated and lost statistical significance after adjusting for antidepressant or muscle relaxant use, suggesting confounding by symptomatic treatment.
A nationwide Taiwanese study reported that fibromyalgia patients have an increased risk of subsequently developing Sjögren's disease, particularly among those aged 20-49 years.

A meta-analysis found fibromyalgia is diagnosed more frequently among patients with autoimmune rheumatic diseases, with pooled prevalence of 18-24% in rheumatoid arthritis, 15% in axial spondyloarthritis, and 18% in psoriatic arthritis.
Sedda et al. demonstrated shared pro-inflammatory cytokines and neurochemical mediators as potential mechanisms underlying the overlap between fibromyalgia and autoimmune disease.

Contrary to a Dutch study suggesting SjD patients with widespread pain form a benign subset with lower anti-SSB positivity and less polyneuropathy, this cohort found no such association, with anti-SSA/SSB profile and polyneuropathy prevalence comparable regardless of FM status.

In a cohort of fibromyalgia patients with sicca symptoms, one-third tested positive for tissue-specific autoantibodies associated with early-stage Sjögren's disease, suggesting a possible autoimmune component in fibromyalgia.
Novel antibodies such as anti-aquaporin-5 have been implicated in Sjögren's disease and may influence its clinical expression.

A pilot study using salivary gland ultrasonography in fibromyalgia patients found a high prevalence of sicca symptoms and structural glandular changes, suggesting a subset of FM patients may harbor subclinical or misdiagnosed Sjögren's disease.
A Brazilian study identified pain and fatigue as the main predictors of poor quality of life in Sjögren's disease, independent of age or disease activity.
An Italian study found that Sjögren's disease patients have substantially greater healthcare utilization, with healthcare costs three times higher than the general population.
Quality of life in Sjögren's disease patients is significantly impaired and comparable to that observed in patients with systemic lupus erythematosus.

Some medical officers reported logistical barriers to accessing ECHO training, including inconvenient session days (25.5%), poor internet connectivity (23.5%), and session frequency (20.1%).
External trigeminal nerve stimulation is a non-invasive neuromodulation device with evidence supporting safety and efficacy in treating migraine and other headache disorders.
Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) is highlighted as a non-invasive neuromodulation modality with growing evidence for treating headache disorders.

Single-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation (sTMS) is described as a non-invasive neuromodulation device with evidence of safety and efficacy for headache disorders including migraine and trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias.
Non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation (nVNS) is presented as a safe and effective non-pharmacologic option for managing headache disorders.
Remote electrical neuromodulation (REN) is listed among non-invasive devices with supporting evidence for safety and efficacy in headache treatment.
External concurrent trigeminal and occipital nerve neurostimulation (eCOT-NS) is listed as a non-invasive device modality for headache management.
Non-pharmacologic neuromodulation options are proposed as particularly appealing for patients vulnerable to or wishing to avoid pharmacologic side effects.

A 21-year-old man developed anti-NMDA receptor encephalitis 34 days after presenting with Murray Valley encephalitis virus infection, with anti-NMDAR antibodies subsequently detected in serum and CSF.
The patient developed autonomic instability accompanied by orofacial and hand dyskinesia and decreased consciousness as part of his anti-NMDAR encephalitis presentation.
The patient's pre-existing medical history included level 1 autism spectrum disorder prior to developing MVEV-associated anti-NMDAR encephalitis.
The patient had a pre-existing history of migraine prior to the onset of MVEV infection and subsequent anti-NMDAR encephalitis.

Prior mechanistic studies showed that NMDA receptor activation following Japanese encephalitis virus infection increases neuronal damage in vitro (mouse neuron/glial cultures) and in vivo (mouse infection models), suggesting a role for NMDAR in flavivirus neuropathogenicity.

In a prospective observational study of 65 patients with CSF-confirmed Japanese encephalitis, 7.9% (5/65) developed autoimmune encephalitis, with anti-NMDAR antibodies detected in the CSF of three of these cases.

Following two doses of rituximab (1,000 mg each, 2 weeks apart) combined with a weaning course of corticosteroids, the patient made a steady neurological recovery with improvement in autonomic and cognitive symptoms.
Treatment with intravenous immunoglobulin (100 g daily for 5 days) did not result in clinical improvement.
Intravenous methylprednisolone (1 g daily for 5 days) was administered but did not lead to clinical improvement.

The median time to development of autoimmune encephalitis following viral encephalitis reported by Armangue et al. was 32 days (range 7-61 days), a timeframe consistent with this patient's symptom onset at 34 days.

At 11-month follow-up after discharge, the patient had ongoing mild short-term memory loss and mild bilateral parkinsonism with cogwheel rigidity and decrementing bradykinesia, without significant functional impairment.
A serum sample collected on day 20 demonstrated a high titer of MVEV-specific total antibody, supporting a probable diagnosis of Murray Valley encephalitis virus infection.

Across the molecular probe screen for 185 virus genomes, more distinct viruses (17 total) were detected in cell-free blood from healthy controls than from ME/CFS patients, and no virus was found uniquely in the patient group.

A molecular probe targeting human alphaherpesvirus 3 (varicella-zoster virus) showed the strongest overall signal in the screen, being elevated in six ME/CFS patients and completely absent in healthy controls.

Molecular probes designed against human herpesvirus 7 (HHV-7) failed to detect the virus in any clinical sample, despite HHV-7 being reported as the most frequently detected blood virus in a prior healthy-donor cohort.

Postural tachycardia syndrome (POTS) can complicate the differential diagnosis of orthostatic headache because it presents with orthostatic headache in the absence of a CSF leak and is diagnosed via head-up tilt-table testing.
Migraine is a key differential diagnosis for the frontal headache seen in SIH but, unlike SIH, migraine does not exhibit postural (orthostatic) variation.
Connective tissue disorders such as Marfan syndrome and Ehlers-Danlos syndrome may predispose individuals to spontaneous CSF leaks because of inherent dural weakness.
Spontaneous intracranial hypotension has an estimated incidence of 3.7 to 5 cases per 100,000 per year, likely an underestimate due to underdiagnosis.
SIH affects women approximately twice as often as men and has a peak incidence around age 40.
Diagnosis of SIH is frequently delayed, with misdiagnosis rates reported to exceed 70% and a median time from presentation to diagnosis of two months.
Lumbar puncture in SIH typically shows a low CSF opening pressure (usually <60 mm H2O), occasionally with mild pleocytosis or elevated protein due to meningeal irritation.
Blind epidural blood patch, used when conservative management fails, has a reported efficacy of over 70% in non-pregnant SIH populations.

In this pregnant patient, two blind epidural blood patches (40 mL then 21 mL at L3/4, 10 days apart) provided only transient relief before headache recurrence, and symptoms ultimately resolved spontaneously without a planned third targeted patch.

Diagnosis of SIH in this pregnant patient was established from thunderclap orthostatic headache combined with MRI findings of meningeal thickening, bilateral shallow subdural collections, extradural spinal fluid, and lumbar puncture showing xanthochromia and lymphocytic pleocytosis.

The patient's Sjögren's syndrome with positive anti-Ro antibodies was speculated by the authors to have predisposed her to meningeal fragility and susceptibility to spontaneous CSF leak, though this association is unproven and previously unreported.
Caesarean delivery under general anaesthesia (rather than neuraxial anaesthesia) was chosen because neuraxial techniques could worsen the CSF leak and symptoms in a patient with SIH.
Recognised complications of SIH include cerebral venous thrombosis, superficial siderosis (with cerebellar ataxia and sensorineural hearing loss), subdural collections, and subarachnoid haemorrhage.
Nociplastic pain is defined as a third mechanistic pain descriptor, alongside nociceptive and neuropathic pain, arising from altered nociception not fully explained by either of those mechanisms.
The authors caution that nociplastic pain should not be equated with chronic primary pain or with central sensitization, and is not merely a new label for pain of unknown origin.
The authors note that fibromyalgia syndrome is not always the prototypical example of a pure nociplastic pain condition, challenging its default use as the paradigm case.

The paper argues that 'nociplasticity' may be better understood as a continuous dimension present across pain conditions rather than a categorically separate diagnosis, questioning the requirement to exclude nociceptive and neuropathic pain before diagnosing nociplastic pain.
The concept of nociplastic pain has expanded beyond pain medicine into other specialties such as gynaecology and rheumatology.
A headache occurred as a hangover symptom in 57.3% of the 96 monitored alcohol consumption episodes.
A prior history of headaches was the only variable that remained independently associated with the occurrence of delayed alcohol-induced headache after multivariable adjustment.

In univariate analysis, a higher average amount of alcohol regularly consumed on weekdays was associated with lower odds of hangover headache, but this did not remain significant in multivariable analysis.
A more prolonged duration of thirst as a hangover symptom was associated with increased odds of headache in univariate analysis.
A more prolonged duration of difficulty thinking or speaking normally was associated with increased odds of hangover headache in univariate analysis.
The presence of difficulty in reading or writing normally was associated with increased odds of hangover headache in univariate analysis.
Higher headache intensity was associated with shorter headache duration in univariate Cox regression.
Presence of photophobia was associated with shorter headache duration in univariate Cox regression.
Presence of dizziness/vertigo was associated with shorter headache duration in univariate Cox regression.
Precipitation of headache by standing up was the only variable independently associated with headache duration in multivariate Cox regression, corresponding to a 75% shorter duration.

The clinical phenotype of delayed alcohol-induced headache was predominantly holocranial and frontal with a pressing or stabbing quality, but a throbbing quality (required by ICHD criteria) was reported in only 5.5% of cases, contradicting formal diagnostic criteria.
Most participants reported worsening or precipitation of the hangover headache with orthostatic changes, suggestive of a low cerebrospinal fluid pressure pattern.

Eating food during the alcohol consumption episode did not significantly reduce the odds or duration of hangover headache, failing to support the popular belief that food consumption prevents hangover headache.
Consumption of non-alcoholic beverages during the alcohol episode was not associated with lower frequency or milder severity of hangover headache.

Migraine-associated symptoms, including phonophobia, photophobia, and nausea, were common accompaniments of delayed alcohol-induced headache, and worsening with physical activity occurred in all episodes with headache.
Fludrocortisone is reported as an effective treatment for vasovagal syncope.
Midodrine is reported as an effective treatment for vasovagal syncope.
Two serotonin-specific reuptake inhibitors (SSRIs) are reported as effective for treating vasovagal syncope.
Beta blockers are reported to be ineffective and should not be used for treating vasovagal syncope.
Atomoxetine is described as an investigational treatment for vasovagal syncope with efficacy not yet established.
Pacemakers and cardiac ablation are reserved as last-line treatments for the rare patient with vasovagal syncope who fails conservative therapy.
Advice on salt and fluid intake and physical maneuvers form the first-line, non-pharmacologic treatment of vasovagal syncope.
Quality of life is reduced in patients with vasovagal syncope and is accompanied by anxiety, though it improves with care.
Injuries related to fainting episodes are common in vasovagal syncope, but serious injuries are rare, and most patients eventually stop fainting over time.
Beta blockers are not recommended for treating vasovagal syncope because they lack demonstrated benefit.
Atomoxetine is currently under investigation as a potential treatment for vasovagal syncope.
Pacemakers and catheter ablation should be reserved as last-resort treatments for the rare, severely afflicted patient who fails to respond to more conservative therapies.
Reduced quality of life in vasovagal syncope patients is accompanied by anxiety, which improves with clinical care.
Reported prevalence of peripheral nervous system (PNS) manifestations in Sjögren's disease varies widely across studies, from 8% to 60%.
PNS manifestations of Sjögren's disease are diagnosed at a mean age of 59 years and often precede the formal SjD diagnosis, in up to 90% of affected patients.
Autonomic nervous system impairment occurs in up to 50% of patients with Sjögren's disease, ranging from mild to severe autonomic failure.
Mononeuropathies (trigeminal neuralgia, trigeminal neuropathy, facial neuropathy, upper-extremity neuropathies) occur in 12% to 50% of patients with SjD.
Polyneuropathies (large fiber, small fiber, demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy, ganglionopathy, vasculitic neuropathy) have a published prevalence of 10% to 20% in SjD.
An estimated 30% to 40% of patients with Sjögren's disease test negative for the anti-SSA autoantibody, so a negative test does not exclude the diagnosis.
For trigeminal neuralgia in SjD, carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine is recommended as first-line treatment.
Second-line or adjunct treatments for trigeminal neuralgia/neuropathy in SjD may include gabapentin, pregabalin, baclofen, lamotrigine, lacosamide, or phenytoin.
For SjD-related facial neuropathy, a short course of glucocorticoids (at least 10 days) is recommended, with consideration of adding valacyclovir.
Rituximab is recommended as first-line treatment for vasculitic neuropathy in SjD because it carries a lower risk of adverse events than cyclophosphamide.
For heart rate control in SjD-associated autonomic dysfunction with prominent heart rate variability, non-selective beta blockers or ivabradine (an HCN channel blocker) are recommended.
For orthostatic tachycardia with low blood pressure in SjD, vasopressors (midodrine, droxidopa) or fluid expansion (fludrocortisone, IV saline) are recommended.
Pyridostigmine may be useful for stabilizing heart rate and blood pressure in individuals with orthostatic tachycardia related to SjD.

The recommendation on IVIG for nonvasculitic large fiber polyneuropathy received the lowest consensus agreement (79%) of all guideline votes, with concerns raised about cost, side effects, and evidence strength.
A skin biopsy assessing sweat gland nerve fiber density may aid in diagnosing autonomic small fiber neuropathy in patients with SjD.

Two late-phase clinical trials showed positive results for B cell-targeted therapies in Sjögren's disease: ianalumab (anti-BAFF receptor antibody) demonstrated Phase 3 efficacy, and telitacicept met its primary endpoints.
Ganglionopathy in SjD can cause profound ataxia that is severe, rapidly progressing, and disabling if left untreated, justifying a strong treatment recommendation.

At three months, participants receiving mindfulness plus education alongside medication withdrawal had fewer headache days than the control (medication withdrawal alone) group, with a significant time-by-group interaction.
A significantly greater proportion of the intervention group achieved a ≥50% reduction in headache frequency at three months compared to control.
At 12 months, significantly more participants in the intervention group achieved a ≥50% headache frequency reduction than controls.
Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy showed no effect on headache frequency at four months compared to usual care.
Behavioural sleep modification training significantly reduced mean headache frequency at six weeks compared to sham control.
Following behavioural sleep modification, some participants reverted from chronic to episodic migraine whereas none of the control group did so, a statistically significant difference.
At two weeks, the control group showed a greater reduction in headache frequency than the CBT-insomnia group, with no significant difference in odds of headache.
At six weeks, CBT for insomnia reduced the odds of having a headache compared to control, though this did not meet the trial's pre-specified corrected significance threshold.
An educational and self-management support intervention had no significant effect on headache impact (HIT-6) at 12 months, with confidence intervals excluding the pre-specified worthwhile difference.
Mindfulness plus education showed improved quality-of-life (MSQ) and disability (MIDAS) scores at 12 months only, with no differences at intermediate timepoints on HIT-6 or WHODAS-12.
A significantly greater proportion of the intervention group achieved a clinically meaningful (≥6 point) improvement in HIT-6 at 12 months compared to control.
Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy significantly reduced headache-related disability (MIDAS) despite no effect on headache frequency, with fewer participants reporting severe disability.
Mindfulness-based cognitive therapy showed no significant difference on the Headache Disability Inventory.
CBT for insomnia showed no difference in MIDAS or HIT-6 scores at two or six weeks after correcting for baseline, though no statistical analysis was presented.
Coping skills training had no significant effect on pain severity compared to control.
Average migraine attack intensity over 30 days did not differ between mindfulness-based cognitive therapy and usual care at four months.
Behavioural sleep modification training was associated with a significant between-group difference in a composite headache index score reflecting pain intensity.
Coping skills training was associated with a significant improvement in quality of life scores compared to control at seven weeks.
Mindfulness plus education was associated with numerically better quality of life scores at 12 months, but the difference was not statistically significant.
CBT for insomnia showed no significant difference from control in depression (borderline) or anxiety scores at six weeks.
After behavioural sleep modification training, medication overuse ceased entirely in those who reverted to episodic migraine and in most of those who did not.
Mindfulness plus education was associated with significantly lower total medication and NSAID consumption at 12 months compared to control, but not lower triptan use.

Calhoun and Ford (2007) found that behavioural sleep modification training resolved medication overuse in all participants who reverted to episodic migraine and in 60% of those who remained chronic at 12 weeks.
Grazzi et al. (2023) found that at 12 months the intervention group had significantly lower total drug intake and NSAID consumption than controls, but no significant difference in triptan use.
A cited systematic review of global epidemiology found that chronic migraine prevalence is 2.5 to 6.5 times higher in women than in men.

A longitudinal study of over a thousand participants found that nearly 75% of those with chronic migraine at baseline fell below the 15-headache-day diagnostic threshold at least once within 12 months.
Participants just below the diagnostic frequency threshold for chronic migraine were reported to have comparable levels of headache-related disability to those meeting full ICHD-3 criteria.
A 2017 systematic review found no evidence that psychological interventions delivered by a specialist clinician were more effective than those delivered by an allied healthcare professional.
A 2012 trial found that cognitive-behavioural therapy was effective in reducing depression scores in individuals with migraine, though this trial was not specific to chronic migraine.
Depression frequently co-occurs with migraine, as reported in prior literature cited by the review.

In the Underwood et al. (2023a) trial population, which included chronic tension-type headache and episodic migraine alongside chronic migraine, 53% had probable anxiety and 22% had probable depression.
In the Calhoun and Ford (2007) trial, 40% of participants had a formal diagnosis of depression, whereas all Smitherman et al. (2016) participants had comorbid insomnia.
Medication overuse headache prevalence varied widely across the included trials: 100% in Grazzi et al., 74% in Calhoun and Ford, 56% in Underwood et al., and 0% in Smitherman et al.
POTS was diagnosed in 30.3% of non-hospitalised patients compared to only 2.5% of hospitalised patients with post-COVID-19 condition.
Clinically significant depression (PHQ-9 ≥10) was much more prevalent in non-hospitalised patients (53.7%) than reported in other post-COVID-19 studies (~15%) or the general population (~6%).
In multivariable regression, participants with PHQ-9 ≥10 (clinical depression) reported on average 7.11 points lower EQ VAS self-rated health than those with PHQ-9 <10.
Participants with FSS <4 (no clinically significant fatigue) had on average 5.48 points higher EQ VAS self-rated health than those with fatigue.
A higher 6-Minute Walk Test ratio (percent predicted exercise capacity) was strongly positively associated with higher self-rated health (EQ VAS).
Clinically significant dyspnoea (mMRC ≥2) was associated with 6.83 points lower EQ VAS self-rated health.
Each additional self-reported symptom was independently associated with a 0.65-point decrease in EQ VAS self-rated health.
Counterintuitively, having a normal (unimpaired) MoCA score was associated with a 3.30-point lower EQ VAS in the adjusted model.
Greater percentage of sick leave was negatively associated with self-rated health (EQ VAS).
Previously hospitalised patients reported 8.34 points higher self-rated health (EQ VAS) than non-hospitalised patients, adjusting for other factors.
Non-hospitalised patients reported a substantially higher number of persistent symptoms (mean 12) than hospitalised patients (mean 5).

Four distinct recovery cluster profiles were identified using PCA and k-means clustering on PHQ-9, GAD-7, 6MWT, MIP and 1MSTST data, ranging from very severe combined mental/physical impairment (Cluster 1) to mild impairment (Cluster 4).

Cluster 4, with normal physical and mental health values, comprised 34% of the cohort, had a higher proportion of hospitalised participants (57%), and reported higher self-rated health (EQ VAS 63.6) than other clusters, though still below general-population norms.

Hospitalised patients showed lower than predicted dynamic lung function values, indicating restrictive pulmonary impairment, whereas non-hospitalised patients showed more impaired inspiratory muscle strength and dysfunctional breathing patterns.
