Non-hospitalised patients had significantly worse (lower) scores than hospitalised patients on functional status (PCFS), self-rated health (EQ VAS), dyspnoea (mMRC), physical activity (Frändin-Grimby), 6-minute walk test, mental health measures, and fatigue.
POTS, the most common post-COVID-19 dysautonomia phenotype, was particularly prominent within Cluster 1, the group with the most severe combined mental and physical impairment.
Fatigue was one of the most common reported symptoms overall and was strikingly more prevalent in the non-hospitalised group than the hospitalised group.
Pyridostigmine bromide treatment decreased red blood cell acetylcholinesterase activity by 22% from baseline while it increased by 20% in the placebo group.

Postexercise heart rate recovery at 1 minute increased significantly from baseline within the pyridostigmine bromide group after 4 weeks of maximally tolerated dose, but did not change within the placebo group.
The primary endpoint, change in postexercise heart rate recovery at 1 minute, did not differ significantly between the pyridostigmine bromide and placebo groups after 8 weeks.
Resting heart rate and time-domain and frequency-domain measures of heart rate variability did not differ between pyridostigmine and placebo groups after 8 weeks of treatment.
Peak oxygen uptake and other expired gas analysis exercise variables did not differ between pyridostigmine and placebo groups.
The cholinergic side-effects symptom score significantly worsened in subjects treated with pyridostigmine bromide compared with placebo after 4 weeks of maximal tolerated dose.
Noncholinergic (general somatic) symptoms did not differ between the pyridostigmine and placebo groups.
Gastrointestinal complaints were reported more frequently in the pyridostigmine bromide group compared with placebo.
Plasma catecholamine levels (norepinephrine, epinephrine, dopamine) did not change differentially between pyridostigmine and placebo groups from baseline to 1 week after study drug cessation.
Within the pyridostigmine bromide group, the change in RBC acetylcholinesterase activity was not significantly associated with the change in heart rate recovery.
Study drug adherence and the proportion of subjects tolerating the highest dose (60 mg TID) did not differ between the pyridostigmine bromide and placebo groups.

Disease-specific quality of life (Kansas City Cardiomyopathy Questionnaire), heart rate and blood pressure changes, ECG intervals, spirometry, safety labs, and device-detected arrhythmia/pacing did not differ between pyridostigmine and placebo groups.
Reserpine administration induced plantar mechanical allodynia in mice, modeling fibromyalgia pain.
Reserpine administration induced cold allodynia in mice, consistent with fibromyalgia-like sensory hypersensitivity.
Reserpine administration induced mechanical-induced affective-motivational (pain-related emotional) behaviour in mice.
Reserpine administration induced heat thermal hyperalgesia in mice.
Reserpine administration caused loss of muscle strength in mice, modeling fatigue-like symptoms of fibromyalgia.
Reserpine administration induced periorbital mechanical allodynia in mice, relevant to comorbid migraine symptoms in fibromyalgia.
Oral stigmasterol (0.3, 1, and 3 mg/kg) reduced reserpine-induced plantar mechanical allodynia in a time- and dose-dependent manner.
Stigmasterol reduced mechanical-induced affective-motivational (pain-related emotional) behaviour caused by reserpine in a time- and dose-dependent manner.
Stigmasterol at 3 mg/kg orally reduced reserpine-induced cold allodynia.
Stigmasterol at 3 mg/kg orally reduced reserpine-induced heat thermal hyperalgesia.
Stigmasterol at 3 mg/kg orally reduced reserpine-induced periorbital mechanical allodynia, a comorbid migraine-like symptom in this fibromyalgia model, without causing motor impairment.
Stigmasterol at 3 mg/kg orally reduced reserpine-induced loss of muscle strength, a fatigue-like symptom, without causing motor impairment.
Pregabalin (30 mg/kg, orally), an FDA-approved fibromyalgia drug, reduced the nociceptive behaviours caused by reserpine, serving as a positive reference drug.
Sumatriptan (0.6 mg/kg, orally), an anti-migraine drug, reduced the nociceptive behaviours caused by reserpine, serving as a positive reference drug relevant to the migraine-comorbid phenotype.
Sixty-six percent of patients with complex regional pain syndrome reported that headaches, primarily with migraine features, developed or worsened after the onset of their condition.
Twenty-two percent of patients with complex regional pain syndrome developed daily or near-daily headaches after CRPS onset.
Limb pain and hyperalgesia were greater in complex regional pain syndrome patients whose headaches developed or worsened than in those with stable headaches or no headaches.

Photophobia and forehead hyperalgesia were greater on the side ipsilateral to CRPS symptoms than contralateral in patients with stable or worsening headaches, but were symmetrical in headache-free patients.
In patients with recurrent tension-type headaches, photophobia was symmetrical between sides, unlike the ipsilateral pattern seen with migraine-type headaches.
Patients whose headaches worsened after CRPS onset were younger at CRPS onset than those with stable headaches or no headaches, consistent with greater migraine vulnerability at younger ages.
In a subgroup, pain from upper-limb complex regional pain syndrome extended to the ipsilateral dorsal cervical region, an area also implicated as a pain source in migraine.
In a subgroup of patients, complex regional pain syndrome pain spread from the affected upper limb to the ipsilateral dorsal cervical region, a site implicated as a pain source in migraine.

Headaches ipsilateral to complex regional pain syndrome symptoms also recurred in patients with lower limb involvement, suggesting mechanisms beyond simple cervical referral drive the ipsilateral headache association.

The authors propose that shared pathophysiology between migraine and complex regional pain syndrome, including neuroinflammation, central sensitization, and loss of inhibitory pain control, increases susceptibility to ipsilateral cranial symptoms and mutually exacerbates pain in both disorders, potentially forming a positive feedback loop.
MT1 mRNA levels were much higher than MT2 mRNA levels in the trigeminal ganglion of both male and female rats, with a similar expression pattern between sexes.
In the sphenopalatine ganglion of male rats, MT1 mRNA expression was significantly higher than MT2 mRNA expression.
In the hypothalamus (used as positive control), MT1 mRNA levels were significantly higher than MT2 mRNA levels.
MT1 immunoreactivity was detected in the cytoplasm and nuclei of trigeminal ganglion neurons of various sizes and in satellite glial cells, with 55-60% of all TG neurons expressing MT1.
MT2 immunoreactivity was detected mostly in the cytoplasm of medium to large-sized trigeminal ganglion neurons and in Aδ-fibers, with 25-30% of all TG neurons expressing MT2.
There was no significant difference in MT1 or MT2 protein expression between male and female rat TG, but MT1-immunoreactive cell counts were approximately twofold higher than MT2 in both sexes.
MT1 receptors were co-localized with CGRP in the cytoplasm of approximately 10% of small to medium-sized trigeminal ganglion neurons, but not in nerve fibers or glial cells.
MT1 was co-localized with RAMP1, an integral component of the CGRP receptor, in about one-third of medium-sized trigeminal ganglion neurons, but not in Aδ-fibers.
MT2 receptors were co-localized with CGRP in approximately 15% of small to medium-sized trigeminal ganglion neurons, but not in nerve fibers.
MT2 and RAMP1 were co-localized in approximately 25% of medium to large-sized trigeminal ganglion neurons as well as in Aδ-fibers.
MT2 receptor protein was co-expressed with CASPR at the nodes of Ranvier along trigeminal Aδ-fibers, indicating MT2 expression in nodal regions of myelinated trigeminal axons.
Thin MT2-immunoreactive Aδ axons, identified by co-expression of the bowtie-shaped CASPR paranodal pattern, were observed throughout the rat dura mater.
No expression of MT1 was observed in sensory nerve fibers of the rat dura mater.
Both MT1 and MT2 receptors were expressed in sphenopalatine ganglion neurons, with MT1 additionally observed in the cytoplasm and nucleus of SPG satellite glial cells.
MT1 was co-localized with VIP in the cytoplasm of some sphenopalatine ganglion neurons.
MT1 and PACAP showed co-localization in both the cytoplasm and nuclei of numerous sphenopalatine ganglion neurons.
MT2 was co-localized with both VIP and PACAP in the cytoplasm of sphenopalatine ganglion neurons, though no co-localization of MT2 and VIP was seen in nerve fibers.
MT1 was expressed in the cytoplasm and nucleus of dorsal root ganglion neurons as well as in satellite glial cells, showing a similar localization pattern to the trigeminal ganglion.
MT2 immunoreactivity was localized predominantly in the cytoplasm of dorsal root ganglion neurons and in Aδ-fibers.
MT1 immunoreactivity was observed in all layers of the basilar artery, including the adventitia, endothelium, and smooth muscle cells, while MT2 was not detected in cerebral artery walls.
Patients with migraine or cluster headache exhibit low levels of nocturnal melatonin release, reflecting circadian disruption in these primary headache disorders.
Prior clinical studies suggest that administration of melatonin or related melatonergic analogs may be an effective strategy for preventing and treating migraine and cluster headache.
Maximum nocturnal EDA was higher on nights preceding migraine compared to nights preceding non-migraine headache, though the group-level statistical comparison was not significant.
Person-specific machine learning models using nocturnal ANS and sleep features achieved better-than-random classification of next-day migraine for 5 of 9 evaluable participants.

Predictive performance for next-day migraine differed markedly by migraine subtype: most episodic migraine patients (especially those with aura) showed better-than-random performance, while most chronic migraine patients performed below random.
Grouping migraine and non-migraine headache together as a combined 'headache' outcome significantly improved model performance for one participant relative to modeling migraine alone.

In the best-performing next-day migraine model (participant 1041), a 25% decision threshold achieved 100% sensitivity (identifying all migraine days) at the cost of low precision (36%), i.e. a high false-positive rate.
SHAP analysis identified reduced nocturnal sleep time as the most influential feature predicting increased likelihood of next-day migraine for participant 1041.
Greater nocturnal autonomic variability (lower minimum pulse rate, higher SD of respiratory rate, higher SD of pulse rate) was predictive of next-day migraine for participant 1041.
Higher maximum nocturnal EDA was predictive of next-day migraine for participant 1041 according to SHAP analysis.
In the best-performing next-day headache model (participant 1054), a 50% decision threshold balanced sensitivity (75%) and precision (71%), correctly identifying 15 of 20 headache days.
For participant 1054, increased nocturnal sleep time and increased sleep interruptions were among the top SHAP features associated with next-day headache.
A higher minimum nocturnal pulse rate variability was linked to greater next-day headache probability, consistent between participants 1041 and 1054.

For participant 1054, EDA features contributed to the next-day migraine prediction model but not to the next-day headache (combined) model, suggesting EDA may specifically distinguish migraine from non-migraine headache.

GAM analysis showed greater nocturnal PRV fluctuation before migraine nights, with lower PRV during the first 100 minutes of sleep, an increase after approximately 150 minutes, and sustained higher PRV in later sleep phases.
EDA showed greater nocturnal fluctuations before migraine nights, with peaks occurring approximately 120-150 minutes after sleep onset in both highest-performing participants.

The EmbracePlus wearable was generally well tolerated with a mean data efficiency of 86.5%, though two participants reported watchband discomfort (one discontinuing early) and one discontinued due to connectivity issues.
Anxiety was the most common medical comorbidity reported among study participants with migraine.
Group-level LMM analysis showed lower average nocturnal PRV on nights preceding non-migraine headache compared to nights preceding both headache-free days and migraine days.
The first infrazygomatic sphenopalatine ganglion neurocryoablation procedure produced approximately 50% improvement in the patient's headache pain, though headache symptoms persisted.
A second neurocryoablation of the sphenopalatine ganglion increased pain relief to about 75% at two-week follow-up, with complete resolution of sharp/stabbing pain, lacrimation, and nasal discharge.
The 75% pain relief achieved after the second cryoablation persisted at the two-month follow-up appointment.
Following sphenopalatine ganglion neurocryoablation, the patient reported a notable improvement in her ability to sleep in addition to pain relief.
At six-month follow-up the patient continued to experience relief from sharp, stabbing left-sided maxillary pain, but she developed new headache pain affecting her forehead.

Prior repeated percutaneous infrazygomatic sphenopalatine ganglion blocks with bupivacaine and triamcinolone initially gave complete relief lasting 2 weeks and moderate relief lasting 3-4 weeks, but the therapeutic benefit gradually faded with repeated use.
No adverse effects were noted following the CBCT-guided infrazygomatic sphenopalatine ganglion neurocryoablation procedure.

Neurocryoablation disrupts nerve structure and produces Wallerian degeneration while leaving the myelin sheath and endoneurium intact, in contrast to thermal radiofrequency ablation which produces coagulation necrosis and fibrous scar formation.

Cone beam CT (CBCT) guidance provides combined 3-D CT planning and 2-D fluoroscopic monitoring, offering greater geometric accuracy and spatial resolution for head and neck structures and enabling safer trajectory planning and probe placement compared with conventional fluoroscopy alone.
Post-procedure numbness of the upper soft palate, attributed to the local anesthetic, suggested accurate placement of the probe near the sphenopalatine ganglion.

The patient had previously failed multiple pharmacologic and device-based treatments for her headaches, including topiramate, indomethacin, verapamil, gabapentin, nortriptyline, valproate, oxcarbazepine, duloxetine, and an external vagal nerve stimulator.
Initial subcutaneous BoNT-A injections along the pinna, using the method previously described by Boulton, provided no relief for the patient's bilateral red ear syndrome.

A novel multi-nerve BoNT-A injection paradigm targeting the greater occipital, lesser occipital, and greater auricular nerves and the posterior auricular branch of the facial nerve reduced flare duration from three to four hours to under one hour and made flares milder and easier to manage.

Multiple pharmacologic therapies (topiramate, naproxen, indomethacin, colchicine, celecoxib, and topical anesthetics) were largely ineffective for this patient's red ear syndrome, and some were poorly tolerated.
Proposed pathophysiology of red ear syndrome includes central dysfunction of trigeminal-autonomic pathways and peripheral dysfunction of upper cervical nerves, particularly the C3 root.
BoNT-A is proposed to act in red ear syndrome via inhibition of neurotransmitter release, modulation of nociceptive signaling, and reduction of parasympathetic outflow.

Unlike a previously reported case in which BoNT-A reduced headache frequency by approximately 75%, this patient's red ear syndrome episode frequency did not decrease, possibly due to trigger dependence or dosing limitations.

A prior case (Castellanos-Gonzalez et al.) showed BoNT-A improvement lasting up to five months before symptom recurrence; this patient's improvement was similar but relapsed sooner, at approximately four months.

The patient's heat-triggered erythema, burning pain relieved by cooling, and absence of headache align with an erythromelalgia-like presentation rather than the typical trigeminal-autonomic/headache-associated red ear syndrome phenotype.
BoNT-A has been reported elsewhere to improve neurovascular features of rosacea, which the authors note may provide context for its therapeutic use in this red ear syndrome case.

A 50-year-old woman developed an orthostatic (posture-dependent) headache following core-strengthening exercise that was initially misdiagnosed as sinusitis, migraine, and perimenopausal syndrome before spontaneous intracranial hypotension (SIH) was diagnosed.
In a prior case series, migraine was the most common initial misdiagnosis given to patients later confirmed to have SIH.
In a cohort of 80 consecutive SIH patients, only a minority reported an identifiable triggering event, and most of these were atraumatic.
Weighted core-strengthening exercise, similar to yoga, Pilates, and weightlifting, is considered a plausible precipitating factor for the patient's spontaneous dural tear and CSF leak.

MRI brain findings supporting the SIH diagnosis included bilateral dural thickening, an enlarged pituitary gland, brainstem sagging, drooping of the corpus callosum, reduced mamillopontine distance, and venous sinus engorgement.
Spinal MRI revealed a small anterior longitudinal epidural collection (SLEC) between T12 and L1, localising the CSF leak responsible for the patient's SIH.
Conservative management, including strict bed rest, hydration, oral caffeine, and analgesia, failed to relieve the patient's SIH symptoms.
A first non-targeted lumbar epidural blood patch with 12 mL of autologous blood produced partial improvement in headache and visual symptoms, but symptoms recurred within days.

A second non-targeted lumbar epidural blood patch with 15 mL of blood, four weeks after the first, led to significant resolution of the patient's SIH symptoms and imaging abnormalities, obviating the need for myelography.
In a cohort of 23 SIH patients treated with EBP, over 40% experienced symptom recurrence after initial relief, and most of these responded successfully to a second EBP.

In a 2014 cohort of nongeriatric patients with chronic subdural haematoma linked to spinal CSF leaks, the majority had unilateral rather than bilateral collections, consistent with the presenting patient's unilateral subdural haematoma.

The patient's headache presentation, lacking the gradual onset, unilateral pulsating pain, and lack of positional dependence typical of migraine, allowed clinicians to exclude migraine as a differential diagnosis in favour of SIH.
Early treatment of SIH is associated with a favourable long-term prognosis, as illustrated by this patient's complete neurological recovery.
GPT-4o produced a differential diagnosis in every case (100% diagnostic yield), higher than physicians (81.9%) and allied professionals (84.5%) assessing the same syncope referral letters.
GPT-4o's differential diagnosis correctly included the final adjudicated diagnosis in 75.9% of cases, compared with 48.6% for physicians and 36.7% for allied professionals.
GPT-4o had a negative Diagnostic Precision Score, reflecting overinclusive differential diagnoses, whereas physicians and allied professionals had positive scores.
Physicians achieved a significantly higher Diagnostic Precision Score than both allied professionals and GPT-4o.
The difference in Diagnostic Precision Score between allied professionals and GPT-4o did not reach statistical significance.
Internists and geriatricians individually achieved significantly higher Diagnostic Precision Scores than GPT-4o.
GPT-4o assigned a cardiac diagnosis in 12.9% of referral letters, of which only one matched the final diagnosis; the rest were ultimately reflex syncope, orthostatic hypotension, or no diagnosis.
Allied professionals assigned a cardiac diagnosis in 23.4% of referral letters, with 11 concordant with the final diagnosis.
Physicians assigned a cardiac diagnosis in 14.9% of referral letters, with 16 concordant with the final diagnosis.

The expert-committee adjudicated final diagnosis distribution was reflex syncope in 46.2%, unexplained syncope in 24.0%, orthostatic hypotension in 20.3%, cardiac syncope in 7.4%, and psychogenic pseudosyncope in 1.8% of cases.
The number of clarifying questions GPT-4o generated was not significantly associated with diagnostic certainty.
When medical professionals reached an accurate diagnosis, they suggested significantly fewer additional diagnostic tests.
An accurate diagnosis by GPT-4o was not associated with suggesting fewer diagnostic tests.

GPT-4o predominantly recommended specialist-level tests (tilt-table testing, implantable loop recorder, Holter monitoring) and, unlike medical professionals, also suggested specific therapeutic interventions such as counterpressure maneuvers, increased fluid intake, and patient education.
Medical professionals most frequently recommended pre-referral history-taking, 12-lead ECG, and Holter monitoring as diagnostic tests.
GP referral letters for syncope were highly variable in length, and the syncope-specific historical content made up less than half of the total letter length on average.

High-risk syncope features per ESC risk stratification were identifiable in about a quarter of referral letters, while over 40% had only a single high-minor risk feature without structural heart disease.

Nearly a third of patients referred for syncope were on antihypertensive medication prior to referral, most commonly using more than one agent, and no referral letters documented medication review or adjustment.
GPT-4o's overall inclusion rate for syncope diagnosis was consistent with prior literature reporting AI accuracy up to 85% in detecting syncope, though it still missed most cardiac causes.

A 9-year-old girl with classic orthostatic headache and normal brain/spine imaging (occult SIH) had complete and sustained resolution of headache after a high-volume (~15 cc) empiric epidural blood patch.
Patients with spontaneous intracranial hypotension are frequently misdiagnosed initially as having migraines, meningitis, or a psychogenic disorder.
In a small pediatric SIH case series (n=4), most patients (3 of 4) had a pre-existing history of migraines.
A meta-analysis of 38 articles including 2078 SIH patients (ages 2-88) found that CSF leakage was visible on brain MRI in only 19% of patients.
Low CSF opening pressure is reported in a wide range (34-93%) of SIH cases, indicating it is not consistently present.
Advanced imaging modalities (CT myelography, spinal MRI, radionuclide cisternography, MR myelography, digital subtraction myelography) detect extradural CSF leak in 48-76% of SIH cases.
In an adult case series, 44.6% of patients with classic SIH symptoms showed no CSF leakage on imaging, meeting criteria for occult SIH.

Among adults with occult SIH treated with empiric EBP, the route of administration affected outcomes: lumbar EBP frequently required repeat treatments, whereas thoracic EBP achieved resolution in all treated patients.
In a 2023 adult cohort, 40% of patients with clinically suspected SIH had no abnormalities on brain and spine imaging, consistent with occult SIH.
Empiric EBP in adult occult SIH patients led to symptom improvement in the majority, with a substantial proportion achieving complete remission by 3 months.
In a pediatric SIH case series (n=24), EBP led to permanent symptom resolution in about a third of patients, while over half had only temporary improvement with recurrence.
In children with lymphatic malformations and CSF-lymphatic fistulas, EBP was often unsuccessful, with most patients requiring surgery or embolization instead.
A pediatric SIH patient presenting with headache, ataxia, and hearing loss had complete resolution of headache and ataxia after EBP, but no improvement in hearing.
A review of 12 pediatric SIH patients whose CSF leaks were localized with advanced myelographic imaging found that nearly all achieved near-complete or complete symptom resolution after treatment.
ICHD-3 diagnostic criteria for SIH require an orthostatic headache plus either low CSF pressure (<60 mm) or imaging evidence of CSF leakage.
The pathophysiology of SIH is attributed to spontaneous spinal CSF leaks reducing intracranial CSF volume and pressure, causing compensatory venous engorgement and brain sagging.
The authors hypothesize that higher-volume epidural blood patches may improve efficacy in occult SIH by coating a broader area of dura and tamponading an unlocalized leak.

A single 20-minute session of yoga-based visual respiratory biofeedback (alternate nostril yogic breathing) significantly increased spatial working memory (Corsi span) in migraine patients compared to a control group who watched a neutral documentary.
Both the experimental and control groups showed a significant increase in Corsi total score after the intervention, with no significant difference between groups in the group-by-time interaction.

The experimental group demonstrated significantly greater improvement in interoceptive accuracy, measured by the Heartbeat Counting Task, compared to the control group after the yoga-based visual respiratory biofeedback session.
Migraine was significantly more prevalent among adult FMF patients with coexisting celiac disease than among FMF patients without celiac disease.
Fibromyalgia was significantly more common among FMF patients with coexisting celiac disease than among FMF patients without celiac disease.
Autoimmune thyroid disease and overall thyroid dysfunction were significantly more frequent in FMF patients with celiac disease than in FMF patients without celiac disease.
Diabetes mellitus was significantly more prevalent in FMF patients with coexisting celiac disease than in FMF patients without celiac disease.
Depression was significantly more common in FMF patients with coexisting celiac disease than in FMF patients without celiac disease.
Serum amyloid A positivity at any time was significantly higher in FMF patients with celiac disease than in FMF patients without celiac disease, suggesting an enhanced inflammatory burden.

FMF patients with coexisting celiac disease had significantly more emergency department admissions for abdominal pain and a higher incidence of peritonitis than FMF patients without celiac disease, without a corresponding increase in surgical interventions.
Rates of acute appendicitis and emergency abdominal surgery did not differ significantly between FMF patients with and without celiac disease.
Joint involvement did not differ significantly between FMF patients with and without coexisting celiac disease.

Use of compressed (coated, film-compressed) colchicine formulations was significantly more common among FMF patients with coexisting celiac disease, potentially reflecting greater colchicine intolerance or resistance in this subgroup.
Methotrexate, hydroxychloroquine, and methylprednisolone were prescribed significantly more frequently in FMF patients with coexisting celiac disease than in FMF patients without celiac disease.
Anakinra use showed a borderline, non-statistically-significant trend toward higher use in FMF patients with coexisting celiac disease.
Participants with chronic pain conditions (nociceptive and nociplastic) reported greater perceived brightness in response to experimental visual stimulation compared with pain-free controls.
Higher self-reported fibromyalgia symptom severity predicted a lack of analgesic response to arthroplasty (hip osteoarthritis) and hysterectomy (chronic pelvic pain) surgery.
Increased visual sensitivity independently predicted nonresponsiveness to surgery among osteoarthritis and chronic pelvic pain patients, used as a model for nociplastic pain.
Experimental pressure pain sensitivity did not independently predict nonresponsiveness to surgery, unlike visual sensitivity.
Visual sensitivity and fibromyalgia symptom severity together explained more variance in surgical responder status than either measure alone.
Elderly patients were more likely than younger age groups to receive diagnoses of tension-type headache, other primary headaches, secondary headache disorders, or probable headache diagnoses.
Among migraine patients, chronic migraine was significantly more common in the elderly group compared to other age groups.
Migraine with aura occurred slightly more often in younger individuals compared to older patients.
Older migraine patients reported longer disease duration than younger patients.
Older migraine patients experienced longer migraine attack duration than younger patients.
Older migraine patients reported fewer accompanying symptoms (less autonomic impairment) during attacks than younger patients.
A relevant proportion of elderly headache patients showed excessive/overuse of acute headache medication.
Fatigue was reported more frequently in older headache/migraine patients than in younger patients.
Idiopathic Intracranial Hypertension typically presents with bilateral, pressing or pulsatile headache that resembles migraine or tension-type headache.
Spontaneous Intracranial Hypotension is characteristically associated with orthostatic headache.
SIH can also present atypically with non-orthostatic headache, thunderclap-onset headache, or chronic daily headache rather than the classic orthostatic pattern.
IIH and SIH frequently coexist with medication-overuse headache, which further blurs diagnostic boundaries between these conditions.
Approximately 30% of patients with idiopathic Normal Pressure Hydrocephalus may present with dull, holocranic headache, a feature historically underrecognized in this condition.
Overlapping headache phenotypes can occur across these CSF dynamic disorders, including orthostatic headache following ventriculoperitoneal shunt overdrainage in patients with iNPH.
Rebound intracranial hypertension can occur following epidural blood patch treatment for SIH, illustrating phenotype overlap with IIH-type headache.
Greater attachment-related anxiety toward mothers was positively correlated with greater somatic symptom severity in pediatric migraine patients.
Greater attachment-related avoidance toward mothers was positively correlated with greater somatic symptom severity.
Greater attachment-related anxiety toward fathers was positively correlated with greater somatic symptom severity.
Greater attachment-related avoidance toward fathers was positively correlated with greater somatic symptom severity.
Resting vagally mediated HRV (RMSSD) was not significantly correlated with somatic symptom severity.
Higher attachment-related avoidance toward fathers was associated with lower resting vagally mediated HRV (RMSSD).
In a multiple regression model, attachment-related anxiety toward mothers independently predicted higher somatic symptom scores.
In the same regression model, attachment-related avoidance toward mothers independently predicted higher somatic symptom scores.
Gender was not a significant independent predictor of somatic symptom severity in the maternal attachment regression model.
In the paternal attachment regression model, attachment-related avoidance toward fathers was a significant independent predictor of higher somatic symptom scores.
Attachment-related anxiety toward fathers showed a non-significant trend as a predictor of somatic symptom severity.
Resting RMSSD did not significantly predict somatic symptom severity in a regression model including BMI and gender.
BMI did not significantly predict somatic symptom severity.
Female gender was associated with significantly higher somatic symptom severity scores compared to male gender in the regression model including RMSSD and BMI.
A mediation model showed a significant indirect effect whereby lower resting vmHRV was linked to higher somatic symptom severity through increased attachment avoidance to fathers.
In the mediation model's first path, lower resting RMSSD was significantly associated with higher attachment avoidance to fathers.
In the mediation model's second path, greater attachment avoidance to fathers was significantly associated with higher somatic symptom (CSI-24) scores.
The direct effect of resting RMSSD on somatic symptom severity, independent of the attachment avoidance to father mediator, was not statistically significant.
The overall total effect of resting RMSSD on somatic symptom severity (combining direct and indirect paths) was not statistically significant.

In a large population-based cohort of knee osteoarthritis patients, higher stool Streptococcus abundance was significantly associated with greater knee pain severity and knee inflammation, a link that was replicated in an independent cohort.

A systematic review found that migraine patients, compared to controls, have reduced gut microbial species richness and evenness and a distinct bacterial composition, suggesting dysbiosis that may reduce gut barrier function and increase intestinal permeability.

A systematic review reported a pro-inflammatory cytokine profile in irritable bowel syndrome associated with increased Bacteroidetes and decreased Firmicutes abundance, supporting a role for gut microbiota in visceral pain.

Systematic reviews highlight frequent co-occurrence of irritable bowel syndrome and fibromyalgia, sharing reduced abundance of Bifidobacteriaceae and Ruminococcaceae, underscoring overlap between gut dysbiosis, inflammation, and chronic pain.

A systematic review with meta-analyses found decreased gut microbiome diversity (fewer observed species, lower Shannon index, lower phylogenetic diversity) in chronic pain patients versus pain-free controls, with lower Lachnospiraceae, Faecalibacterium, Roseburia, F. prausnitzii, and O. splanchnicus, and higher Eggerthella.

A systematic review found reduced gut microbiome diversity in chronic insomnia patients, with lower Faecalibacterium and Lachnospira and higher Actinobacteria, Streptococcus, Clostridium, Blautia, and Holdemanella; insomnia severity correlated negatively with Faecalibacterium/Lachnospira and positively with Blautia.

People with periodontitis have a higher risk of developing fibromyalgia, and conversely fibromyalgia patients without prior periodontitis have an increased risk of subsequently developing periodontitis, indicating a bidirectional association.

An observational study found low self-reported oral health scores correlated with higher pain scores in women with migraine, abdominal, and body pain, with pain and chronic pain presence associated with higher abundance of oral pathobionts including Gardnerella, Lancefieldella, and Mycoplasma salivarius.

A systematic review found that synbiotics and probiotics consistently reduced painkiller consumption (excluding triptans) and improved migraine frequency in migraine patients, with synbiotics also reducing migraine pain severity in both adults and children.
In individuals with irritable bowel syndrome, probiotics and synbiotics demonstrated modest but consistent reductions in abdominal pain and overall symptom severity.
Mendelian randomization analyses suggested potential causal associations between gut microbiota composition and intervertebral disc degeneration, low back pain, and sciatica.

A prospective cohort study of 141 older patients with lumbar degenerative disorders found periodontitis severity was associated with higher incidence of intervertebral disc degeneration, endplate changes, and worse clinical outcomes, suggesting a mouth-gut-disc axis.

A population-based study in the United States found a significant link between chronic pain and tooth loss, independent of ethnicity, lifestyle determinants, and immune-mediated inflammatory diseases such as rheumatoid arthritis.

Case-control studies revealed that depression and anxiety alter the oral microbiome, increasing taxa like Neisseria species and Prevotella nigrescens while decreasing diversity, promoting periodontitis and contributing to systemic inflammation via the microbiota-gut-brain axis.

The gut microbiome composition of proton pump inhibitor users differs profoundly from non-users, mainly due to a strong increase in Lactobacilli abundance driven by translocation of oral Streptococcus species.

Proton pump inhibitors can cause hypomagnesemia, particularly with higher doses or prolonged use, of particular concern in chronic pain patients frequently exposed to polypharmacy affecting electrolyte balance.

Polypharmacy (concurrent use of ≥5 medications) is highly prevalent among people with chronic pain, reported by 71.4% of Canadians and 89.5% of Germans, with up to 26% and 49% respectively reporting excessive polypharmacy (≥10 medications).
Meta-analyses indicate that approximately 40% of chronic pain patients experience clinically significant depression and anxiety.
Meta-analyses confirm that overweight and obesity are positively associated with low back pain and knee osteoarthritis, with chronic pain prevalence higher in those with higher BMI.
A meta-analysis concluded that altered dietary patterns and specific nutrient intake may have analgesic properties for patients with persistent pain (evidence level 1a).

Studies demonstrated analgesic effects of a low-FODMAP diet on abdominal pain in IBS patients; however, a systematic review reported that this diet induces gut microbiota changes that may be detrimental.
Mendelian randomization analyses suggest potential causal associations between gut microbiota composition and intervertebral disc degeneration, low back pain, and sciatica.

In post-menopausal women with chronic insomnia, gut microbiome composition differs between objective insomnia (higher Coriobacteriaceae including Collinsella and Adlercreutzia, plus Erysipelotrichaceae, Clostridium, and Pediococcus) and paradoxical insomnia (characterized by Bacteroides, Staphylococcus, Carnobacterium, Pseudomonas, and Odoribacter).
In older adults, gut microbiota richness shows a robust positive association with objective sleep quality, independent of subjective sleep quality, demographics, lifestyle, and health covariates.

Bacteroidetes, Ruminococcus, and Veillonella, linked to short-chain fatty acid production and anti-inflammatory potential, are associated with better objective sleep quality in older adults, whereas Collinsella and Holdemania are associated with poorer subjective sleep quality.
Rheumatoid arthritis is associated with tooth loss and periodontitis.

In a case-control study of individuals with irritable bowel syndrome, obese participants had the highest pain responses to a test solution, associated with differences in specific bacterial genera and families.

Case-control studies found that depression and anxiety alter the oral microbiome, increasing taxa like Neisseria species and Prevotella nigrescens while decreasing diversity, promoting periodontitis and contributing to systemic inflammation via the microbiota-gut-brain axis.

Proton pump inhibitors can cause hypomagnesemia, particularly with higher doses or prolonged use, which is concerning given frequent polypharmacy affecting electrolyte balance in chronic pain patients.
Nonsteroidal anti-inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), frequently used by patients with chronic pain, affect gut microbiome composition.

Polypharmacy (≥5 medications) is highly prevalent among people with chronic pain, reported by 71.4% of Canadians and 89.5% of Germans, with up to 26% and 49% respectively reporting excessive polypharmacy (≥10 medications).
Receiving conservative treatment for chronic pain, such as physical or psychological pain therapy, is related to lower chances of excessive polypharmacy.

Polypharmacy involving multiple centrally-acting drugs is associated with worse pain control, whereas for patients with daily pain and anxiety, pain was best reduced with one medication or non-opioid/non-benzodiazepine combinations such as gabapentinoids or serotonin-noradrenaline reuptake inhibitors.

The gut microbiome can modulate the metabolism of psychotropic drugs such as duloxetine, which binds to several microbial metabolic enzymes, alters microbial metabolite secretion, and is bioaccumulated within bacterial cells without chemical modification.
Melatonin appears beneficial to gut health, exerting anti-inflammatory and potentially protective effects.

A systematic review found that both synbiotics and probiotics consistently reduced painkiller consumption (excluding triptan use) in people with migraine, improved migraine frequency, and synbiotics reduced migraine pain severity in both adults and pediatric patients.
In individuals with irritable bowel syndrome, probiotics and synbiotics demonstrated modest but consistent reductions in abdominal pain and overall symptom severity.
A meta-analysis concluded that altered dietary patterns and altered specific nutrient intake may have analgesic properties for patients with persistent pain (evidence level 1a).
A systematic review concluded that plant-based diets might have analgesic effects for people with chronic pain.

A low-FODMAP diet demonstrated analgesic effects on abdominal pain in patients with irritable bowel syndrome, but a systematic review reported that this diet induces gut microbiota changes that may be detrimental.
Meta-analyses confirm that overweight and obesity are positively associated with low back pain and knee osteoarthritis, with chronic pain being more prevalent in those with higher body mass index.
In people with chronic low back pain, pain intensity and disability show dose-response relationships to body mass index, waist circumference, percent fat, and fat mass.
A pro-inflammatory diet is associated with features of central sensitization in patients with chronic low back pain.
A preclinical study suggests that the gut microbiome regulates stress responsiveness in a circadian manner by influencing the hypothalamus-pituitary-adrenal axis.
45% (44/97) of patients with primary Sjögren disease also met diagnostic criteria for fibromyalgia.
Among the pSjD patients with concomitant FM, 43 of the 44 were female, indicating strong female predominance in the overlap group.
Patients with concomitant fibromyalgia had significantly higher ESSDAI central-nervous-system domain scores than those without fibromyalgia.
The overall ESSDAI disease activity score did not differ significantly between pSjD patients with and without fibromyalgia.

No statistically significant correlation was found between fibromyalgia diagnosis and the presence of neurophysiological abnormalities (polyneuropathy subtypes or myogenic muscle injury) in pSjD patients.
Folic acid concentration trended higher in fibromyalgia-positive pSjD patients versus FM-free patients, though the difference did not reach statistical significance.
Complement C3c levels trended lower in fibromyalgia-positive pSjD patients versus FM-free patients, though the difference did not reach statistical significance.
ESSPRI total score showed a significant positive correlation with concomitant fibromyalgia diagnosis in pSjD patients.
ESSPRI fatigue subscore showed a significant positive correlation with concomitant fibromyalgia diagnosis in pSjD patients.
ESSPRI-based neuropathic pain score showed a significant positive correlation with concomitant fibromyalgia diagnosis in pSjD patients.
SF-36 vitality score showed a significant negative correlation with concomitant fibromyalgia diagnosis in pSjD patients.
SF-36 physical functioning score showed a significant negative correlation with concomitant fibromyalgia diagnosis in pSjD patients.
SF-36 total score showed a strong negative correlation with concomitant fibromyalgia diagnosis in pSjD patients, and was proposed as a useful screening indicator.
No significant correlation was found between presence of SjD-associated antibodies and co-occurrence of fibromyalgia with pSjD, suggesting a non-immune mechanism may underlie the association.
No statistically significant correlation was found between concomitant fibromyalgia diagnosis and patient age, pSjD disease duration, or stressful life events measured with the Holmes-Rahe scale.

A cited study reported that a specific OAS1 defect confers interferon-γ resistance in Sjögren disease patients, leading to elevated IFN-γ and increased risk of lymphoma, neuropathy, and severe fatigue.

The kynurenine metabolic pathway, stimulated by elevated interferon-γ, is proposed to shift tryptophan catabolism away from serotonin synthesis and contribute to neuropsychiatric symptoms in Sjögren disease.
An imbalance in microglial M1 (pro-inflammatory) versus M2 (anti-inflammatory) polarization is proposed as a pathomechanism contributing to nociplastic pain, including fibromyalgia.
A previously published retrospective study found SjD-associated antibodies present in one third of tested fibromyalgia patients.

Intravenous lidocaine infusions (2–7.5 mg per infusion) showed delayed therapeutic effect in fibromyalgia, often not apparent until after 6–8 monthly infusions, based on the authors' clinical experience.
Imbalance between pro-inflammatory M1 and anti-inflammatory M2 microglial activation states is proposed as a shared mechanism underlying nociplastic pain, including fibromyalgia.

Elevated interferon gamma is proposed to stimulate the kynurenine metabolic pathway, shifting tryptophan catabolism away from serotonin synthesis and contributing to neuropsychiatric symptoms in Sjögren disease.

A defect in OAS1 has been reported to cause resistance to interferon gamma in Sjögren disease patients, leading to elevated IFN-γ concentrations and increased risk of lymphoma, neuropathy, and severe fatigue.

Intravenous lidocaine infusions (2-7.5 mg per infusion) show delayed but promising anti-inflammatory effects in treatment-resistant fibromyalgia, with benefit often not apparent until after 6-8 monthly infusions.

Minocycline, naltrexone, infliximab, and dextromethorphan have been suggested in the literature as potentially correcting microglial M1/M2 imbalance in nociplastic pain, though none are currently part of routine fibromyalgia management.

A prior study by Applbaum et al. found a higher prevalence of novel, early-stage autoantibodies among fibromyalgia patients who later developed primary Sjögren disease, contrasting with the present study's lack of antibody-FM correlation.

A 2023 study by Sambataro et al. demonstrated that immunization (autoantibody positivity) is not uncommon among fibromyalgia patients, challenging the traditional view of FM as an immunologically silent condition.
Among the 44 pSjD patients who met fibromyalgia diagnostic criteria, all but one were female, indicating a strong female predominance of comorbid FM in this cohort.
Rats exposed to prenatal LPS had a significantly lower baseline hind-paw mechanical withdrawal threshold than control rats, indicating baseline mechanical allodynia.
Acute LPS administration alone did not change hind-paw mechanical thresholds 3 hours post-injection compared to baseline or to controls.
A single nitroglycerin injection progressively decreased hind-paw mechanical thresholds over 1-3 hours in control rats, modeling episodic migraine allodynia.
Prenatal LPS exposure aggravated chronic NTG-induced mechanical allodynia, with pre- and post-injection thresholds declining progressively across five injections to lower values than controls.
Acute LPS administration also aggravated chronic NTG-induced mechanical allodynia, with pre-injection thresholds becoming significantly lower than controls by the third injection.
By day 9 of chronic NTG administration, prenatal LPS rats spent significantly less time in the light chamber than controls, indicating more pronounced photophobia.
Acute LPS administration did not significantly change photophobic behavior compared to controls in the NTG migraine model.
Acute LPS administration significantly increased meningeal mast cell degranulation compared to control rats.
Prenatal LPS exposure also significantly increased meningeal mast cell degranulation in adult offspring compared to controls.
In the acute LPS group, chronic NTG administration significantly raised plasma CGRP levels relative to baseline.
In the control group, plasma CGRP showed only a non-significant upward trend after chronic NTG administration.
Serotonin application significantly increased the firing rate of trigeminal afferent action potentials in control hemiskull preparations.
Acute LPS pretreatment markedly amplified the peak serotonin-evoked trigeminal afferent firing compared to controls.
Normalized serotonin-evoked increase in trigeminal afferent activity was significantly greater in acute LPS rats than controls.
Normalized serotonin-evoked increase in trigeminal afferent activity was also significantly greater in prenatal LPS rats than controls.
LPS incubation of cultured trigeminal ganglion neurons significantly increased the proportion of neurons responding to serotonin.
LPS incubation did not change the proportion of trigeminal ganglion neurons responding to capsaicin.
LPS incubation increased the mean amplitude of serotonin-evoked calcium transients in cultured trigeminal ganglion neurons.
LPS incubation increased the mean amplitude of capsaicin-evoked calcium transients in cultured trigeminal ganglion neurons.

LPS incubation did not affect the non-specific KCl-evoked calcium response amplitude, indicating the LPS effect was selective for serotonin/capsaicin signaling rather than general neuronal excitability.
LPS incubation increased the number of trigeminal ganglion neurons co-responsive to both serotonin and capsaicin.
LPS incubation nearly halved the proportion of trigeminal ganglion neurons non-responsive to either serotonin or capsaicin, consistent with broad sensitization.

Nitroglycerin injection itself did not significantly affect rearing counts or chamber transitions in any of the experimental groups, indicating that photophobia results were not confounded by generalized changes in locomotion.
S1 latency of the cutaneous silent period was significantly longer in pSjD patients than in healthy controls.
S2 latency of the cutaneous silent period was significantly longer in pSjD patients than in healthy controls.
CSP duration was significantly longer (prolonged) in pSjD patients compared to healthy controls, reflecting small A-delta fiber dysfunction.
Using CSP abnormalities together with neuropathic symptoms and normal routine nerve conduction studies, small A-delta fiber neuropathy was diagnosed in 38% (41/109) of pSjD patients.
No statistically significant differences were found in amplitude or conduction velocity of motor and sensory median nerve fibers between pSjD and healthy control groups.
A significant difference was noted between pSjD and HC groups in median nerve motor latency (MNML) and F-wave latency.
GEE model analysis showed a significant association between older age and increased S2 latency and CSP duration.
The presence of anti-PM Scl-75 antibody was significantly associated with S2 latency in pSjD patients after FDR correction.
A trend was observed between complement C3c concentration and S1 latency in pSjD patients.
A trend was observed between anti-PM Scl-75 antibody and CSP duration.
Fibrinogen concentrations tended to correlate with increased S1 and S2 latency, but this association was not statistically significant.
The presence of anti-Ro52, anti-SSB/La, PM/Scl-75, and DFS70 antibodies was associated with reduced CSP duration, although this did not reach statistical significance.
No relationship was observed between the duration of pSjD and CSP parameters, aligning with prior research by Gono et al.

No obvious relationship was found between B-cell activation/inflammatory serologic markers (ANA, anti-SSA, anti-SSB) and the presence of small fiber neuropathy without ataxia, consistent with Sène et al.'s findings but contrasting with Font et al.'s proposed ANA/anti-Ro association.
The pSjD population reported moderate-intensity neuropathic pain on average.
Unlike some prior reports, this cohort did not observe an association between cryoglobulins and sensory neuropathy in pSjD.

The 38% prevalence of small A-delta fiber neuropathy found via CSP markedly exceeds the ~9.2% prevalence previously reported using QST, skin biopsy, and laser-evoked potentials, though it is more consistent with a recent report by Mori et al.
Linkage analysis in the consanguineous OI family mapped a candidate disease locus to chromosome 4 with a suggestive LOD score of 1.7, encompassing the SEC24D gene.

Sequencing of the SEC24D 5'UTR/promoter region identified a novel homozygous variant (c.-167C>T) segregating with disease in the three affected siblings, with unaffected relatives being heterozygous carriers or non-carriers.
RT-qPCR of RNA from patient-derived fibroblasts showed SEC24D mRNA expression comparable to matched controls, despite the pathogenic 5'UTR variant.

Western blotting revealed markedly reduced SEC24D protein levels in the proband's fibroblasts compared to four control fibroblast lines, despite normal mRNA levels, indicating a post-transcriptional/translational defect.

The c.-167C>T variant creates a novel upstream AUG codon within a moderately conserved Kozak consensus sequence, positioned in-frame and 56 amino acids upstream of the canonical SEC24D start codon, predicted to produce an elongated N-terminal protein isoform.

In vitro transcription-translation assays using SEC24D expression vectors showed markedly reduced protein production from the mutant (c.-167C>T) construct compared to the wildtype construct, despite the mutant protein being predicted to be slightly larger.

Co-transfection of HEK293T cells expressing the mutant SEC24D (c.-167C>T) vector with antisense oligonucleotides (ASOs) designed to block ribosomal recognition of the novel upstream AUG increased SEC24D protein production, with ASO2 producing a statistically significant increase, while having no effect on the wildtype vector.

Unlike a previously reported IFITM5 5'UTR variant that produces an elongated, apparently stable protein causing dominant OI, the SEC24D 5'UTR variant identified here leads to instability or degradation of the resulting protein despite a shared upstream-AUG mechanism.

During peer review, an identical SEC24D c.-167C>T variant was reported in compound heterozygous state with a frameshift variant in a fetus with osteogenesis imperfecta presenting broad fontanels, low-set ears, and mild hypertelorism, further supporting pathogenicity of this variant.

The three affected siblings presented with a severe OI phenotype including prenatal fractures, over 50 fractures by adulthood, osteopenia/osteoporosis, short stature, limb deformities, pectus deformity, and wheelchair dependence, alongside mild craniofacial features (macrocephaly, frontal bossing, triangular face, dentinogenesis imperfecta, high-pitched voice) overlapping with Cole-Carpenter syndrome type 2.

Prior targeted sequencing of 18 known OI-associated genes and whole exome sequencing failed to identify a pathogenic variant in the affected proband, prompting linkage analysis to locate the disease locus.
Over a third of aging Veterans with chronic low back pain reported nociplastic pain features severe enough to meet 2016 ACR fibromyalgia diagnostic screening criteria.
Nociplastic feature severity and prevalence of meeting fibromyalgia screening criteria were significantly higher in younger (50-64 years) versus older (65+ years) Veterans with chronic low back pain.
Self-reported physical function among aging Veterans with chronic low back pain was substantially below population norms, roughly two standard deviations lower.
Psychological function in this population was closer to the general population average than physical function.
In multivariable regression adjusting for sociodemographic and clinical factors, higher fibromyalgia severity (nociplastic) scores were significantly associated with poorer physical function.
Higher fibromyalgia severity (nociplastic) scores were significantly associated with poorer psychological function after adjustment for covariates.
Higher BMI was independently associated with poorer physical function in the adjusted regression model, alongside pain intensity, comorbidity burden, female gender, and prior back surgery.
Employment status other than full/part-time employment, along with nociplastic features and higher pain intensity, was significantly associated with poorer psychological function.

The strength of association between nociplastic features and poorer overall function did not significantly differ between younger and older age groups, indicating the relationship holds regardless of age.

Nearly half of Veterans with chronic low back pain reported back pain with likely or possible neuropathic features on the PainDETECT questionnaire, indicating overlap of neuropathic and nociplastic mechanisms.

Despite being recruited on the basis of a single site of pain (low back), Veterans reported pain at multiple discrete body sites on average, suggesting the presence of multiple chronic overlapping pain conditions.
A minority of Veterans with chronic low back pain used prescribed opioids specifically for back pain, with a smaller subset using them long-term.
Comorbidities were common among aging Veterans with chronic low back pain, with hypertension and arthritis being the most frequently reported.
Prior small studies of older Veterans found lower fibromyalgia screening prevalence than the current study, which the authors attribute to a relatively younger sample mean age.

A prior longitudinal study found that recognition of nociplastic/fibromyalgia features was delayed by a mean of seven years, during which patients received potentially ineffective peripherally-directed treatments.
Noninvasive transmucosal SPG stimulation reduced numeric rating scale pain scores from baseline through one month to individual follow-up in all four facial pain patients.
Visual analog scale pain scores decreased from baseline to one month and were sustained at follow-up in the case series.
The MPQ present pain index decreased from baseline to one month, with a slight rebound at longer follow-up.
Quality of life physical functioning scores on SF-36 improved substantially from baseline through follow-up after SPG stimulation.
In the literature review, implanted SPG stimulation for chronic cluster headache produced ≥50% reduction in attack frequency in 35% to 45% of patients over long-term follow-up.
Alleviation in headache disability and improvement in quality of life with implanted SPG stimulation were sustained up to 24 months according to the reviewed literature.
The reviewed literature indicated that efficacy of SPG stimulation therapy critically depends on accurate electrode placement.
The literature review found that noninvasive intranasal SPG stimulation also showed durable benefits in refractory primary headaches.
MPQ present pain index scores decreased from baseline to one month and remained reduced at individual follow-up in the case series of four patients with refractory facial pain.
SF-36 pain scores improved from baseline to one month and were partially sustained at follow-up in the case series of four patients treated with noninvasive SPG stimulation.
SF-36 vitality scores increased from baseline through one month and continued improving at individual follow-up in the four-patient case series.
Vitality scores on the SF-36 quality-of-life questionnaire improved from baseline through one month to individual follow-up in the case series.
The required frequency of noninvasive SPG stimulation sessions decreased over time as pain relief and quality-of-life improvements were sustained in all four cases.
Noninvasive SPG stimulation may serve as a bridging or test therapy for patients who may eventually require permanent implanted SPG stimulation.
The authors suggest noninvasive, nonpermanent SPG stimulation could be explored for other craniofacial pain disorders, including migraine and tension-type headache.

Published case reports describe sphenopalatine ganglion (SPG) block use across a range of orofacial pain and headache disorders, including trigeminal neuralgia/neuropathies, burning mouth syndrome, non-specified facial pain, autonomic cephalalgias, tension-type headache, and acute cephalalgias.
Case reports describe use of SPG block for COVID-related headache, alongside other headache and orofacial pain conditions.
Across the reviewed case reports, the most common SPG block technique was intranasal application via cotton tip applicators, with lidocaine 2-10% being the most frequently used anesthetic agent.
Neurogenic pain conditions (e.g., trigeminal neuralgia/neuropathies) and migraine showed superior therapeutic responses to SPG block compared with other orofacial pain diagnoses reported.
Most case reports documented pain relief following SPG block, but long-term outcome data were not available in the literature reviewed.
The authors conclude that SPG block appears effective and safe for orofacial pain and headache disorders, though higher-level evidence is still needed to confirm this.
SPG block was reported as a treatment approach for COVID-related headache in case reports.
SPG block was also reported for use in acute cephalalgias.
The most frequently used SPG block technique across the reviewed reports was intranasal application using cotton tip applicators.
Lidocaine at concentrations of 2-10% was the most commonly used anesthetic agent for SPG block in the reviewed case reports.
Neurogenic pain conditions and migraine showed superior therapeutic response to SPG block compared to other diagnostic categories reviewed.
Most case reports documented symptomatic relief with SPG block, but no long-term outcome data were available.
SPG block was found to be effective and safe overall across the reviewed reports, though higher-level evidence is still needed.
Interictal serum DBH activity, the enzyme that converts dopamine to norepinephrine, was significantly lower in TTH patients than in healthy controls.
Plasma norepinephrine measured by HPLC was substantially lower in TTH patients than in healthy controls.
Epinephrine concentrations were reduced in TTH and negatively correlated with headache severity.
Dopamine levels were positively correlated with headache duration, suggesting progressive catecholaminergic alterations over time.
In TTH patients, an attenuated plasma NE rise during a stress task correlated with delayed or impaired recovery from stress-induced pain.
TTH patients showed stable cortisol during stress rather than the expected circadian decline seen in controls and migraine patients, suggesting HPA axis dysregulation.
Pediatric TTH patients showed a non-significant trend toward lower plasma neuropeptide Y, an indirect marker of NE co-release, compared with healthy controls.
One small study found no significant differences in NE or other amines in chronic TTH, but it was underpowered and mainly designed for migraine.
Amitriptyline, but not citalopram or placebo, produced a significant reduction in headache area-under-the-curve, despite both drugs reducing platelet serotonin.
No correlation was found between platelet serotonin levels and headache severity reduction, suggesting 5-HT reuptake inhibition is not amitriptyline's primary analgesic mechanism.
Baseline β-endorphin levels, an indirect marker of noradrenergic-opioidergic function, were significantly lower in TTH patients than in healthy controls.
Clonidine, an α2-adrenergic agonist, failed to raise β-endorphin levels in TTH patients, indicating a blunted adrenergic-opioidergic response.
Unlike TTH patients, migraine patients showed a moderate β-endorphin response to clonidine, suggesting partial preservation of adrenergic function in migraine.
TTH patients with higher baseline plasma MHPG, a marker of NE turnover, showed a significantly greater response to tizanidine, with MHPG declining after treatment in responders.
Serum free fatty acid levels were higher in tizanidine responders at baseline and decreased after treatment, indicating increased beta-adrenergic and reduced α2-adrenergic drive in TTH.
Acupuncture significantly reduced urinary epinephrine and norepinephrine excretion compared with control, suggesting modulation of sympathetic overactivity.
Biofeedback treatment did not alter plasma NE or sympathetic activity indices, nor did it improve TTH symptoms.
Changes in ES2 duration following noradrenergic drug treatment did not correlate with changes in headache frequency or intensity in CTTH patients.

Gobel et al. found that amitriptyline produced no significant change in ES2 duration, contingent negative variation amplitude, or pericranial EMG activity, with only a non-significant trend toward ES2 prolongation.

In a double-blind RCT of 53 CTTH patients, six weeks of amitriptyline 75 mg significantly reduced monthly headache days and episode duration and reduced pain sensitivity to experimental pain compared with placebo.
Tizanidine prolonged ES2 duration of the temporalis muscle under lower-intensity sensory stimulation but had no effect at higher stimulation intensity in TTH patients.

Folgelholm et al. found that tizanidine administration did not significantly change trapezius muscle EMG activity and this did not correlate with clinical improvement, suggesting a central rather than peripheral myogenic mechanism.
TTH patients showed impaired habituation of the sympathetic skin response, indicating dysfunction in central autonomic regulation and processing.

Resting heart rate, a marker of sympathetic tone, was significantly lower in episodic TTH compared with chronic TTH and controls, while heart rate recovery (parasympathetic activity) was similar across groups.
In a small pediatric study, pupillary response to phenylephrine did not differ significantly between TTH patients and healthy controls.
A study of personality dimensions linked to aminergic neurochemical domains found no significant differences between TTH patients and controls.

In patients with chronic TTH and comorbid anxiety and/or depression, low-dose amitriptyline (10 mg) significantly reduced headache frequency, depression, anxiety, insomnia and psychosomatic complaints.

Amitriptyline 25 mg twice daily significantly reduced headache frequency, severity and analgesic consumption in patients with TTH and Parkinson's disease, independently of mood or depression score changes.
Cerbo et al. found amitriptyline significantly reduced headache frequency, duration and acute medication consumption in chronic TTH, but these effects were not observed in episodic TTH.
In episodic TTH, amitriptyline did not show a sustained advantage over fluoxetine in reducing headache frequency and intensity.

Tricyclic antidepressants (amitriptyline up to 100 mg/day or nortriptyline up to 75 mg/day) yielded significant reductions in headache frequency, severity, analgesic use and disability in chronic TTH, with combined TCA and stress management more likely than either monotherapy to achieve ≥50% reduction in headache index.
Amitriptyline (50 mg) reduced headache attacks more than citalopram (20 mg) in patients with comorbid depression, migraine and TTH; citalopram non-responders improved when amitriptyline was added.
Amitriptyline produced a greater reduction in headache AUC (30%) than citalopram (12%) or placebo (10%), and also significantly reduced headache duration, frequency and acute medication consumption.
Amitriptyline was found superior to fluoxetine (20 mg) specifically in chronic TTH, per discussion synthesis of comparative trial results.

Amitriptyline (25 mg) produced significantly greater reductions in headache index and acute medication use than sertraline (50 mg), with 70.3% vs 44.4% of patients achieving ≥50% headache index reduction.
Both amitriptyline and ritanserin (an indirect noradrenergic booster via 5-HT2C antagonism) improved headache outcomes, without a statistically significant difference between them.
Amitriptyline compared favourably to buspirone, a partial 5-HT1A agonist with no NE reuptake effect, leading to significantly greater reduction in analgesic use and more favourable patient ratings.

Saper et al. found that tizanidine hydrochloride (mean dose 18 mg) significantly reduced headache frequency, severity and duration over 12 weeks, though the study mixed chronic daily headache subtypes without stratified analysis, limiting CTTH-specific generalizability.

Adjunctive tizanidine (4 mg/day) combined with amitriptyline (20 mg/day) produced significantly greater reductions in headache frequency, intensity and duration than amitriptyline alone after one month, but the between-group difference was no longer significant by 3 months.
In a larger RCT, modified-release tizanidine at 6 mg or 12 mg per day did not demonstrate significant clinical superiority over placebo in chronic TTH management.

Low-dose mirtazapine (4.5 mg/day) alone or combined with ibuprofen (400 mg/day) did not reduce headache AUC compared with placebo, though combination therapy was well tolerated with more drowsiness and weight gain.
Higher-dose mirtazapine (30 mg/day) reduced the headache AUC by 34% compared to placebo in chronic TTH patients, a statistically significant prophylactic effect.

Mirtazapine (30 mg/day) and amitriptyline (25 mg/day) both improved headache frequency and intensity in chronic TTH with no significant difference between groups, but mirtazapine produced greater subjective improvement and significantly fewer adverse effects.
In an open-label retrospective study, venlafaxine XR (150 mg/day) significantly reduced mean monthly headaches from 24 to 15.2, with efficacy independent of comorbid depression or anxiety.
An open-label retrospective study found that venlafaxine XR significantly reduced mean monthly headache frequency in patients with chronic tension-type headache.
A randomized placebo-controlled trial found venlafaxine XR significantly reduced headache days in chronic and episodic TTH patients without comorbid depression or anxiety.

Both mianserin and clomipramine significantly reduced VAS pain scores compared with placebo in chronic TTH, though the proportion achieving ≥50% pain reduction did not differ significantly due to a strong placebo effect.
Mianserin significantly reduced headache intensity and frequency in TTH, while clonidine at 0.150 mg/day showed no comparable therapeutic effect.
Clonidine at 0.150 mg/day did not produce a significant reduction in headache intensity or frequency in TTH patients, unlike mianserin.
Mianserin showed similar efficacy to fluvoxamine, a selective serotonin reuptake inhibitor, in reducing headache frequency, severity and analgesic use in TTH.

Maprotiline, a potent norepinephrine transporter inhibitor, produced statistically significant improvements in headache outcomes in CTTH, with only mild non-significant improvement in depressive symptoms, suggesting a noradrenergic-mediated analgesic effect independent of antidepressant action.
Imipramine significantly reduced headache severity compared with transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) in chronic TTH patients.
Desipramine, an SNRI, and fluoxetine, an SSRI, produced comparable improvements in pain, mood, and quality of life in chronic TTH.
Paroxetine, an SSRI with weak norepinephrine transporter inhibition, showed limited and non-significant efficacy in chronic TTH patients refractory to amitriptyline.

The review notes that NE-induced stress does not trigger headaches in healthy individuals, supporting the idea that TTH involves chronic noradrenergic dysregulation rather than acute stress-induced NE surges.
A study of adult migraine patients found significantly reduced REM sleep compared to controls, consistent with earlier findings.
Decreased sleep efficiency in migraine patients was the most consistently reported PSG finding, seen in 4 of 8 studies, sometimes accompanied by increased time in bed.
Four of six adult migraine studies reporting number of awakenings identified a significant increase compared to controls, suggesting sleep fragmentation.
Of only three adult migraine studies reporting wake after sleep onset (WASO), one identified a significant increase compared to controls.

In a study of 25 migraine without aura patients, N1 percentage was significantly increased while N3 percentage was significantly decreased compared to controls, suggesting a shift toward lighter, less restorative sleep.
In contrast to other reports, two studies by Engstrom and colleagues found a significant increase in N3 (slow wave) sleep in migraine patients, contradicting the N3 reduction reported elsewhere.

Sleep-related migraine (SM) patients showed significantly elevated N1 versus controls, while non-sleep-related migraine (NSM) patients showed significantly elevated N3 versus both controls and SM patients, indicating subtype-specific sleep architecture differences.
A population-based study with lower average migraine attack frequency found no significant sleep architecture changes compared to controls, unlike tertiary-centre studies.
Total sleep time was found to be significantly reduced in three of four paediatric migraine studies reporting this measure.
Both paediatric migraine studies reporting number of awakenings found a significant elevation compared to controls.
Wake after sleep onset was significantly elevated in one paediatric migraine study, suggesting overlooked sleep fragmentation.
One paediatric migraine study found a significant increase in sleep stage transition index versus controls, further indicating sleep fragmentation.
Periodic limb movements were found to be elevated in two paediatric migraine studies, potentially contributing to sleep fragmentation.
Increased bruxism during sleep was noted in one paediatric migraine study.
In cluster headache bout, sleep onset latency has been shown to be elevated and sleep efficiency reduced compared to controls.
REM architecture may be altered in cluster headache, with elevated REM latency and decreased REM sleep noted compared to controls.
Two cluster headache studies identified an increase in N1 sleep during the cluster bout, especially on nights with headache.
No significant differences in objective actigraphy sleep architecture were noted in chronic migraine patients, despite significant disruption reported via subjective measures in the same cohort.
A rest-activity actigraphy study found increased area under the curve during sleep (indicating elevated movement/fragmentation) and reduced inter-day stability in chronic migraine patients.
An elevated fraction of sleep over daytime, supporting increased napping, was found in chronic migraine patients compared to controls.
Longer daytime nap duration was associated with decreased sleep efficiency the following night in chronic migraine patients, potentially contributing to poor sleep quality and inter-day variability.
A trend towards elevated wake after sleep onset was seen in paediatric migraine on actigraphy, consistent with prior PSG findings, but did not reach statistical significance.
Two actigraphy studies in cluster headache identified increased time in bed in patients compared to controls, potentially indicating a perceived increase in sleep need.
Consistent with PSG findings, actigraphy-assessed sleep onset latency was elevated in cluster headache patients both during bout and in remission.

Conflicting evidence exists for arousal index in migraine, with some studies reporting an increase and others a decrease compared to controls, and one study finding a reduction specifically during REM sleep.

CAP rate alterations are evident in migraine compared to controls, with two studies showing a reduction and a third showing an increase, and no concordant phenotype across CAP A1, A2, and A3 subtypes.

Delta-bursts (A1-like microstructure) were significantly reduced specifically in sleep-related migraine patients across two studies, whereas non-sleep-related migraine patients showed reduced fast arousals instead, indicating a need for subtype stratification.

A single actigraphy study found no significant sleep architecture differences in chronic migraine patients compared to controls, despite significant disruption reported via subjective measures in the same cohort.
A second actigraphy study found an increase in area under the curve during sleep in chronic migraine patients, indicating elevated movement and potential sleep fragmentation.
The same rest-activity study identified reduced inter-day stability in chronic migraine patients, indicating disrupted habitual sleep-wake regularity.
Chronic migraine patients showed an elevated fraction of sleep over daytime, consistent with increased napping compared to controls.
Longer nap duration was associated with decreased sleep efficiency the following night, potentially contributing to poor sleep quality among chronic migraine patients.
Two paediatric actigraphy studies identified a tendency towards elevated sleep onset latency in migraine, contradicting some polysomnography findings.
A trend towards elevated wake after sleep onset was observed in paediatric migraine versus controls, consistent with prior polysomnography findings, but did not reach statistical significance.
Two actigraphy studies in cluster headache identified increased time in bed in patients compared to controls, potentially indicating a perceived increase in sleep need.
Sleep onset latency was found to be elevated in cluster headache patients both during bout and in remission, consistent with polysomnography findings.
Evidence on arousal index in migraine is conflicting, with some studies reporting an increase and others a decrease compared to controls.
One study identified a significant reduction in arousal index specifically during REM sleep among migraine patients.
Two studies identified a reduction in CAP rate in adult migraine patients compared to controls, while a third study reported the opposite finding.
CAP phase distribution findings in migraine are heterogeneous, with one study finding reduced A1 concomitant with increased A2/A3, while another reported reduced A2 and A3.

Delta-bursts (A1-like activity) were significantly reduced only in sleep-related migraine patients, while non-sleep-related migraine patients showed reduced fast arousals instead, indicating a need for patient stratification.
A single paediatric study found a significant decrease in CAP rate driven by a decrease in A1 index, while the relative proportion of A2 and A3 phases was elevated.
One paediatric study identified an increase in arousal index indicating elevated fast arousals, while arousal index during REM sleep was found to be decreased in another study.
A study of paediatric migraine patients found a significant increase in sleep spindle amplitude alongside a decrease in the frequency of fast spindles.

Arousal index was found to be reduced in cluster headache patients in a single study, and in a subset with chronic cluster headache or on nights with headache attack in a second study, but not in episodic cluster patients.
In a preclinical migraine model, nitroglycerin provocation reduced sleep time and increased sleep onset latency in the 6 hours following administration.
