Lillo Vizin et al. found no significant sleep architecture changes in the same acute nitroglycerin model, nor following chronic nitroglycerin exposure, or in dural inflammation and restraint-stress/umbellone priming models using immobility-defined sleep.

A population-based study with lower average migraine attack frequency (over half with less than one attack per month) failed to identify any significant sleep architecture changes compared to controls.
Diary-assessed low sleep efficiency (<90%) was significantly associated with a higher risk of migraine occurrence on the following day.
Actigraphy-assessed sleep efficiency showed a similar pattern of association with subsequent-day migraine risk, but the confidence interval overlapped 0.
Short sleep duration (<6.5 hours), whether on one night or two consecutive nights, was not found to be a significant predictor of headache occurrence the following day(s).
Sleep duration showed a small but significant increase following migraine attack occurrence.

In paediatric migraine patients, motor activity index was significantly reduced on nights preceding, during and following a migraine attack compared to the headache-free interval, indicating decreased arousability around attacks.
Elevated noradrenaline has been shown to precede transitions from NREM to wake and microarousals, implicating brainstem wake-promoting systems in sleep fragmentation relevant to migraine.
Altered locus coeruleus functional connectivity has been noted in patients with comorbid migraine and insomnia.

Cortical spreading depression, the physiological correlate of migraine aura, is increased following sleep deprivation in animal models, and its occurrence can result in elevated NREM and reduced REM sleep.
Resting state EEG complexity has been shown to differ from controls in the interictal phase but not in the preictal phase of migraine.
Impaired habituation to sensory stimuli in migraine patients has been shown to improve prior to an attack.

Migraine prophylactic medications including propranolol and amitriptyline have known effects on sleep, particularly REM sleep, which may confound polysomnography findings when continued medication use is not reported.
Estimation of sleep time based on mobile phone use suggested that deviation from normal sleep and interrupted sleep increase subsequent headache risk.
Across the broader pain field, sleep fragmentation, rather than sleep deprivation, is suggested to increase spontaneous pain and reduce pain inhibition.
Cluster headache patients who report sleep as an attack trigger tend to report worse subjective sleep quality than those for whom sleep is not a trigger.

44% of MSA participants with recent pain reported painful injuries or bruises due to falls.

Digestive problems were independently associated with higher odds of painful cold hands and feet in MSA.

Frequent falls showed a very strong independent association with painful injuries or bruises in MSA.

Musculoskeletal pain occurred at a similar rate in MSA and healthy controls, unlike other pain domains.

GLP-1RA use was associated with significantly lower odds of pain-related diagnostic codes in fibromyalgia patients.
GLP-1RA use was associated with significantly lower odds of fatigue-related diagnostic codes in fibromyalgia patients.
There was no significant difference in disability-related diagnostic codes between GLP-1RA users and non-users with fibromyalgia.
Body mass index remained higher in fibromyalgia patients using GLP-1RA compared with matched non-users, likely reflecting confounding by indication.
Haemoglobin A1c remained higher in fibromyalgia patients using GLP-1RA compared with matched non-users after five-year follow-up.

MOH patients were older (median 34 years) compared with non-MOH primary headache patients (median 28 years).

Insomnia was significantly more frequent among MOH patients than non-MOH patients.
Musculoskeletal pain or fibromyalgia was significantly more frequent among MOH patients than non-MOH patients.

Diagnoses made by previous physicians matched those of headache specialists in only 43.8% of 146 patients with definitive specialist diagnoses.
Agreement between previous physicians' and specialists' diagnoses, excluding undiagnosed patients, was only fair (kappa = 0.38).
Nearly half of patients with a definitive specialist diagnosis had received no specific primary headache diagnosis from their previous physician.
Among the five diagnostic categories, migraine had the lowest accuracy rate and specificity when comparing previous physicians' diagnoses to specialist diagnoses.
The most frequent misdiagnosis pattern among patients with specific prior diagnoses was migraine being mistaken for tension-type headache and vice versa.
A sensitivity analysis that double-counted patients with two or more headache types produced similar results, with overall diagnostic accuracy of 40.6% and kappa of 0.31.

In multivariable logistic regression, diagnoses made by internal medicine physicians were significantly less likely to be concordant with headache specialists' diagnoses compared with specialist departments.
No significant association was found between institution type (clinic vs hospital) and diagnostic accuracy in the multivariable model.

When patients referred from neurology, neurosurgery, pain management, and headache departments were excluded (i.e., only 'nonspecialist' referrers considered), diagnostic accuracy was lower and most patients remained undiagnosed at the previous institution.
In the nonspecialist subgroup, migraine again had the lowest accuracy and specificity among the five headache categories.
Migraine was by far the most common definitive diagnosis made by headache specialists in this referred population, accounting for over three-quarters of patients.

Non-invasive transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation devices applied to the ear or neck have received regulatory approval in the US and other countries for managing several conditions including migraine, obesity, and chronic pain.
Early clinical studies of transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation reported encouraging results for treating migraine, alongside rheumatoid arthritis and lupus.
Early clinical studies of transcutaneous vagus nerve stimulation reported encouraging results for treating chronic fatigue syndrome.

A PRISMA-compliant meta-analysis of 36 human studies including 780 VNS-treated participants found no significant reduction in the cytokines TNF-α or IL-6 after short- or long-term vagus nerve stimulation, with small, non-significant effect sizes overall.
Within the same meta-analysis, significant reductions in CRP after VNS occurred only in a small subgroup of long-term studies involving patients with acute inflammation.

In the cholinergic anti-inflammatory pathway, acetylcholine released from cholinergic T cells via the splenic nerve binds α7 nicotinic acetylcholine receptors on macrophages, inhibiting release of pro-inflammatory cytokines such as TNF-α, IL-1β, and IL-6.
Among consistent triptan users, 85% never switched medications, while 9% switched once, 3% switched twice, and 3% switched three or more times within a two-year period.
Younger patients were more likely to switch triptan medications than older patients.
A prior diagnosis of fibromyalgia was identified as a clinical risk factor for switching triptan medications twice within the follow-up period.
Use of gastro-oesophageal reflux medications was associated with switching triptan medications twice within the follow-up period.
A history of oral cavity disorders was associated with switching triptan medications three or more times.
A history of intestinal disorders was associated with switching triptan medications three or more times.
Prior intestinal disorders were associated with switching triptan medications three or more times.
Prior gynecological diagnoses were associated with switching triptan medications three or more times.
A genome-wide association study found no single nucleotide polymorphisms significantly associated with triptan switching behavior in this cohort.
A supplementary analysis of previously reported SNPs associated with migraine susceptibility and triptan response found no significant genetic associations with triptan switching in this cohort.
Heart rate variability features extracted from nocturnal wearable BVP signals during the prodrome phase could be used with machine learning to predict upcoming migraine attacks.
HRV changes during the migraine prodrome phase showed significant individual variability across participants, complicating development of a generalized prediction model.
A single GON block with triamcinolone and lidocaine reduced migraine attack frequency in the four weeks after injection compared with placebo in an RCT of episodic migraine patients.
The same RCT found no significant difference between GON block (triamcinolone/lidocaine) and placebo in migraine duration or severity.
Bilateral GON blocks given weekly for three weeks reduced episodic migraine frequency at two months follow-up.
As acute treatment, bupivacaine GON blocks provided pain freedom in up to 31% of migraine patients compared with placebo, and were as effective as intravenous metoclopramide and NSAIDs.
An RCT comparing bupivacaine GON block to intravenous metoclopramide for acute headache treatment in the emergency department found the two treatments equivalent.
Combined supraorbital and greater occipital nerve blocks were superior to supraorbital nerve blocks alone for acute migraine management.
In patients with acute migraine aura, bupivacaine GON blocks completely resolved aura in half of patients with no recurrence over the following week.
In chronic migraine, addition of triamcinolone to bupivacaine GON block did not show additional significant benefit over bupivacaine alone for short-term preventive treatment.
Weekly bupivacaine GON blocks for four weeks significantly reduced headache frequency and pain, with benefit lasting up to three months of follow-up.
Triamcinolone and lidocaine GON blocks reduced pain severity, attack frequency, and analgesic use for up to two months after the intervention in another RCT.

A multi-nerve block approach (GON with LON, STN, SON, and ATN blocks using methylprednisolone and lidocaine/bupivacaine) reduced headache attack frequency in up to two-thirds of chronic migraine patients in open-label and prospective non-randomised UK cohorts.
In chronic migraine patients who respond to GON blocks, adding prophylactic medication did not show further improvement beyond the GON block alone.
In an RCT, monthly GON blocks were more effective than topiramate monotherapy in reducing monthly migraine days, supporting use in medication-refractory patients.

In chronic migraine with medication overuse headache, GON blocks provided better outcomes than standard detoxification (medication withdrawal alone), and a further RCT of triamcinolone GON block plus withdrawal confirmed better outcomes than withdrawal alone.

Dilli et al. found that active (corticosteroid-containing) and placebo GON block arms were equally effective and well tolerated, illustrating the difficulty of proving added corticosteroid benefit given methodological RCT limitations.
In episodic cluster headache, methylprednisolone and lidocaine GON blocks significantly reduced weekly attack frequency at four weeks post-injection compared with placebo.
In a large observational cohort, 78 patients with SUNCT/SUNA received unilateral or bilateral GON blocks; 37% (29/78) reported headache improvement lasting a mean of 38.4 ± 34.7 days.
An RCT of cervicogenic headache patients found that occipital nerve blockade significantly relieved cervicogenic headache and associated symptoms at two weeks post-injection.
Repetitive GON blocks resulted in prolonged pain relief lasting up to six months in patients with cervicogenic headache.
RCTs of post dural puncture headache have consistently shown that GON blocks significantly improve pain scores up to 24 hours post-block compared with standard treatment alone.

In post dural puncture headache after caesarean section under spinal anaesthesia, dexamethasone and lidocaine delivered to suboccipital muscles significantly improved pain scores at 24 hours compared with placebo.

A systematic review of GON blocks found the most common side effects were pain at injection site, dizziness, and nausea, with rare irreversible adverse effects including avascular necrosis of the hip (causality not established) and persistent alopecia.
A meta-analysis comparing local anaesthetic-only nerve blocks to placebo found no significant difference in adverse events.

Local anesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST), most notably after bupivacaine use, is a rare but potentially life-threatening complication with incidence estimated between 0.27 and 1.8 per 1000 peripheral nerve blocks.

An RCT comparing occipital nerve block to acetaminophen and caffeine for headache in pregnancy found no difference in birth weight or mode of delivery, though the nerve block led to a lower pain rating within one hour.

Peripheral nerve blocks are proposed to reduce nociceptive input into the trigeminocervical complex, modulating central descending inhibitory pain pathways to abort acute headache attacks or shorten bout duration, with local anaesthetics acting via reversible sodium channel blockade of C- and Aδ nerve fibres.
A randomized controlled trial found that occipital nerve blockade significantly relieved cervicogenic headache and associated symptoms two weeks after injection.

A RCT in patients with occipital neuralgia and cervicogenic headache found significant reductions in headache days and analgesic use after ultrasound-guided GON blocks at the C2 level compared with baseline.
A cohort study found that GON blocks delivered via a sub-compartmental injection technique produced longer-lasting headache relief in cervicogenic headache patients.
A RCT in cervicogenic headache patients found improvement with both GON blocks and cervical level 2/3 nerve blocks.
Repetitive GON blocks resulted in prolonged pain relief lasting up to six months in patients with cervicogenic headache.
Multiple RCTs of post dural puncture headache consistently showed that GON blocks significantly improved pain scores up to 24 hours post-block compared with standard treatment alone.

In patients with post dural puncture headache after caesarean section under spinal anaesthesia, a RCT showed that dexamethasone and lidocaine delivered to the suboccipital muscles significantly improved pain scores at 24 hours compared with placebo.
A cohort study in patients after spinal anaesthesia supported prior findings, showing improvement in pain scores at 24 hours after a GON block.

Case reports and small case series suggest a role for GON blocks in managing spontaneous intracranial hypotension, subarachnoid haemorrhage, and post-traumatic headache, though evidence remains limited.
Peripheral nerve blocks are generally safe and well-tolerated, with the most common side effects being pain at the injection site, dizziness, and nausea.
A systematic review of GON blocks found the only irreversible adverse effects to be avascular necrosis of the hip (causality not established) and very rare persistent alopecia.
A meta-analysis comparing local anaesthetic-only nerve blocks to placebo found no significant difference in adverse events between groups.

The incidence of local anaesthetic systemic toxicity (LAST) associated with peripheral nerve blocks has been estimated in reviews of case reports and registries to range from 0.27 to 1.8 per 1000 peripheral nerve blocks.

A RCT comparing occipital nerve block to acetaminophen and caffeine for headache in pregnancy found no difference in birth weight or mode of delivery, while the nerve block led to a lower pain rating within one hour.
Local effects of corticosteroid injection used in nerve blocks can include alopecia, atrophy, and hypopigmentation.
Systemic effects of corticosteroids used in nerve blocks can include hyperglycaemia in patients with diabetes, candidiasis, and Cushing's disease.
Methylprednisolone may have an enhanced safety profile compared with other corticosteroids, as no irreversible adverse effects were reported with its use in a systematic review.
Migraine patients had the lowest mean mechanical detection threshold on the face compared with healthy controls, TMD, and TMD+migraine groups, indicating greater facial mechanical sensitivity.
The TMD+migraine+fibromyalgia group had the numerically lowest mechanical detection threshold on the hand, though this was not reported as statistically significant.

Migraine patients had the lowest pressure pain threshold on the face compared with healthy controls, who showed the highest facial PPT, with significant differences also seen versus TMD+migraine and TMD+migraine+fibromyalgia groups.
The TMD+migraine+fibromyalgia group had the numerically lowest pressure pain threshold on the hand, but no significant differences were observed across all five groups for this measure.

During serial (repeated) pinprick stimulation, the TMD+migraine+fibromyalgia group reported the highest pain scores while healthy controls reported the lowest, with significant differences emerging only for serial, not single, stimulation.
Mean wind-up ratio did not differ significantly across the five study groups (control, TMD, migraine, TMD+migraine, TMD+migraine+fibromyalgia).
During the CPM test, healthy controls reported significantly higher pain scores than all four patient groups for both single and serial stimulation.

For serial stimulation, healthy controls showed the lowest (most negative, i.e., most effective) CPM magnitude, significantly different from migraine, TMD+migraine, and TMD+migraine+fibromyalgia groups, indicating impaired pain inhibition in the patient groups.
With single stimulation, the percentage CPM effect (pain inhibition efficiency) was significantly higher in healthy individuals than in all patient groups.
With serial stimulation, all patient groups except TMD-only showed a lower percentage CPM effect than controls, and TMD differed significantly from TMD+migraine.
The proportion of participants showing an efficient CPM response (at least 29% pain inhibition) was highest among healthy controls and lowest in the TMD+migraine+fibromyalgia group.

The number of pain comorbidities (TMD, TMD+migraine, TMD+migraine+fibromyalgia) was significantly negatively correlated with CPM effect during single stimulation, indicating that more comorbid pain conditions were associated with poorer pain inhibition.
A similar significant negative correlation between number of comorbidities and CPM effect was found during serial stimulation.

Distribution of pain modulation profile (PMP) classification (double pro-nociception, inhibitory pro-nociception, facilitatory pro-nociception, antinociception) differed significantly among the five groups during serial stimulation but not during single stimulation.

In the TMD-only group, CPM in the non-trigeminal (hand) area was not significantly different from healthy controls, consistent with most prior literature supporting intact endogenous pain modulation in TMD patients outside the trigeminal region.
TMD-only patients showed a lower CPM effect than pain-free controls specifically with single stimulation, though not with serial stimulation.
Among the case groups, the TMD+migraine+fibromyalgia group reported the highest mean clinical pain score.

Among surveyed physicians, 30% preferred implantable cardiac monitor as the initial test for unexplained syncope in older patients, 8% preferred tilt table testing, and 62% said their choice would depend on the clinical scenario.
North American electrophysiologists were significantly more likely than European electrophysiologists to prefer ICM as the first diagnostic test for unexplained syncope.
Physician sex was not significantly associated with preference for ICM, tilt table testing, or no preference in syncope diagnostic strategy.
There was a non-significant trend toward younger physicians favoring ICM and older physicians more often having no clear preference for the initial syncope test.

The most influential factor in physicians' choice of syncope diagnostic test was the eventual likelihood of obtaining a diagnosis, ranked as the single most important factor by nearly half of respondents.
The top-tier factors influencing test choice were likelihood of obtaining a diagnosis, time to diagnosis, and risk of missing a diagnosis with tilt table testing.
Test familiarity, local availability, and cost were ranked as the least important factors in physicians' selection of a syncope diagnostic test.
Physicians reported significantly greater concern about missing a diagnosis with tilt table testing than with implantable cardiac monitoring.

Physician follow-up decisions differed markedly depending on which test was inconclusive: a negative tilt table test prompted escalation to ICM, while an inconclusive ICM prompted watchful waiting rather than tilt testing.
Under a tilt-table-testing strategy, physicians were most concerned about missing heart block, supraventricular and ventricular tachycardia, sick sinus syndrome, vasovagal syncope, and epilepsy.
Under an ICM-based strategy, physicians' main concerns were missing hypotensive causes of syncope or reaching no diagnosis at all.
Regional availability of tilt table testing and implantable cardiac monitoring differed, with all European sites offering both modalities compared to a lower proportion in North America.
Published diagnostic yield data cited by the authors indicate tilt table testing produces a diagnosis much faster than ICM, despite physicians favoring ICM.
Background literature cited in the study indicates that even after thorough initial evaluation, the cause of syncope remains unexplained in a substantial minority of older patients.
A pragmatic randomized controlled trial (STUTTER) is underway comparing head-up tilt table testing versus ICM as the initial diagnostic strategy in older adults with unexplained syncope.
Among pregnant women with migraine, hypertension was significantly more prevalent in those who developed pre-eclampsia compared to those who did not.
Heart disease was more prevalent among migraine patients who developed pre-eclampsia than those who did not.
Diabetes prevalence was significantly higher among migraine patients who developed pre-eclampsia.
Hypothyroidism showed the strongest association with pre-eclampsia among migraine patients, with higher prevalence in those who developed pre-eclampsia.
Placental anomalies detected on ultrasound were significantly more prevalent among migraine patients who developed pre-eclampsia.
Fibromyalgia showed a marginal but statistically significant association with pre-eclampsia among pregnant women with migraine.
Cigarette use was significantly higher among migraine patients who developed pre-eclampsia compared to those who did not.
History of headache during menstrual periods was significantly associated with development of pre-eclampsia among migraine patients, suggesting hormonal and vascular susceptibility.
Asthma/allergy and pre-pregnancy depression did not differ significantly between migraine patients with and without pre-eclampsia.
In the adjusted binary logistic regression model, migraine, hypertension, hypothyroidism, placental anomaly and cigarette use were significant predictors of pre-eclampsia.

In the adjusted logistic regression model, cigarette use showed a negative standardized coefficient, paradoxically suggesting reduced pregnancy complications with smoking during migraine, unlike the other predictors.
The binary logistic regression model explained only a modest proportion of variance in pre-eclampsia risk, though predictors remained statistically significant.
Among pregnant women with migraine in this cohort, 12.76% were affected by pre-eclampsia.
The majority of women in the cohort reported that their migraine symptoms decreased during pregnancy.
The authors propose that migraine and pre-eclampsia share an endothelial dysfunction pathway, providing mechanistic plausibility for the observed statistical association.
In the Chinese CHRIS registry, cluster headache showed strong male predominance with a female-to-male ratio of 1:3.94.
Female CH patients had significantly lower BMI than male CH patients.
Female CH patients had a significantly younger median age at onset than male patients.
Chronic CH was numerically more common among female participants than male, though the difference did not reach statistical significance in the table test.
Migraine comorbidity was significantly more prevalent among female than male CH patients.
No significant sex difference was observed in positive family history of migraine among CH patients.
No significant sex difference was found in family history of cluster headache.
Female CH patients reported conjunctival injection, rhinorrhea, and facial sweating less often than male patients during attacks.
Female CH patients had higher rates of upper eyelid edema and ptosis/miosis than male patients.
Nausea, a migraine-associated symptom, was significantly more frequent in female than male CH patients.
Vomiting and post-attack debilitation were significantly more common in female than male CH patients.
Photophobia, diarrhea, and osmophobia were significantly more prevalent among female than male CH patients.
Restlessness/agitation during attacks was equally common in both sexes.
Female CH patients reported alcohol and cigarette use as attack triggers far less often than males, but emotional triggers more often.
Emotional strain/distress was a more common trigger of attacks among female CH patients, ranking second most common in females versus fifth in males.
A subset of female CH patients identified menstruation as an attack trigger.
Current smoking and alcohol consumption were significantly less common among female than male CH patients.
Female CH patients had significantly higher depression (PHQ-9) scores and severity than male patients.
Female CH patients had significantly higher anxiety (GAD-7) scores and severity distribution than male patients.
No significant sex difference was found in reported suicidal thoughts among CH patients.
Female CH patients used oral rizatriptan for acute treatment significantly more often than male patients.
Headache severity measured by the visual analogue scale (VAS) did not differ significantly between female and male CH patients.
No significant sex difference was found in headache laterality, with right-sided attacks predominating in both sexes.
No significant sex difference was observed in the overall presence of diurnal (circadian) rhythmicity of attacks.
No significant sex difference was found in the seasonal rhythmicity of cluster headache attacks or their monthly distribution.
Tearing (lacrimation), the most common cranial autonomic symptom, occurred at nearly identical frequency in both sexes.
Restlessness or agitation, the most common accompanying symptom in male participants, occurred at a similar frequency in females.
Phonophobia frequency did not differ significantly between female and male CH patients.
Hyperpathia frequency did not differ significantly between female and male CH patients.
Aggravation of headache by physical activity did not differ significantly between sexes.
Insomnia, the most commonly reported trigger of CH attacks, showed no significant sex difference in prevalence.
Temperature variation as a trigger for CH attacks showed comparable rates between sexes.
Fatigue as a trigger for CH attacks was reported at similar rates in both sexes.
Nearly one-tenth of female CH patients identified menstruation as a trigger for their attacks, a factor not applicable to male patients.
Sleep, the most frequently reported mitigating factor for CH attacks, showed no significant sex difference.
Massage as a mitigating factor for CH attacks did not differ significantly between sexes.
Cold compress use as a mitigating factor for CH attacks showed no significant sex difference.
Hot compress use as a mitigating factor for CH attacks showed no significant sex difference.
Sport/physical activity as a mitigating factor for CH attacks showed no significant sex difference, though there was a non-significant trend toward higher use by males.
Suicidal thoughts related to CH did not differ significantly between female and male patients.
Family history of migraine did not differ significantly between female and male CH patients.
Family history of cluster headache did not differ significantly between female and male patients.
A U.S. study found that patients with cluster headache incurred significantly higher total direct healthcare costs than non-headache controls.
A large Swedish cohort study reported significantly higher sickness absence rates among people with cluster headache compared with healthy controls.
Western studies show a time-related increase in the female-to-male ratio of cluster headache, from about 1:7.2 in 1980s Italy to about 1:1.35 in 2010s United States.
Eastern studies similarly show a rising female-to-male ratio of cluster headache over time, from 1:7 in 2013 to 1:4.63 in 2022 and 1:4.33 in 2024.
Several U.S. studies have reported a bimodal age-at-onset distribution among female cluster headache patients.
Two Italian studies suggested that genetic factors contribute to earlier onset in female familial cluster headache and greater susceptibility to migraine-associated symptoms in female patients.
A Danish study observed that the peak timing of cluster headache attacks in women was delayed by about one hour compared with men.
Data from a U.S. national integrated healthcare system showed higher prevalence of comorbid depression and PTSD among women with cluster headache compared with men.

Existing Asian studies have found only minor sex differences in cluster headache, mainly in attack duration, unhealthy lifestyle, and associated symptoms, contrasting with more pronounced sex differences reported in Western populations.
In Western studies, male cluster headache patients had higher BMI than healthy controls, whereas female patients showed the opposite trend.
An Italian study proposed that hormonal changes around menopause may exacerbate cluster headache symptoms and contribute to progression toward chronic cluster headache in women.
Proposed mechanisms linking cluster headache and migraine comorbidity include the shared trigeminovascular pathway, overlapping activated brain regions, and central sensitization.
A large U.S. study found that female cluster headache patients not only had earlier onset but may also show a second incidence peak after age 50.
An Italian study found that female patients with familial cluster headache had significantly earlier onset than those with non-familial cases, suggesting a more prominent genetic role in females.

A Korean multicenter cohort study found that cluster headache patients with migraine comorbidity had higher risk of anxiety and depression, and that female patients more frequently had migraine comorbidity than males.
An Italian study revealed stress-related cortisol changes in female patients, suggesting that neurosteroid fluctuations may influence the natural course of migraine and cluster headache.
A study from Taiwan found that female cluster headache patients were more prone to emotional fluctuations and sleep disturbances before attacks.
A 2023 meta-GWAS implied that smoking may be a pathogenic risk factor for cluster headache.
Chronic cluster headache prevalence trended higher in female than male participants (4.10% vs 1.98%), though the overall difference in CH type by sex did not reach statistical significance.

The prevalence of current smoking among female CH patients was 2.7 times higher than in the general Chinese female population, suggesting smoking may be a coping mechanism rather than a primary CH trigger.
Some studies propose that cadmium in tobacco smoke may promote cluster headache onset via toxic effects on the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, though this mechanism remains unconfirmed.

A 2023 meta-GWAS suggested smoking may be a pathogenic risk factor for cluster headache, whereas a 2025 meta-analysis found no significant association, indicating conflicting evidence on smoking's causal role.

A Korean multicenter cohort study found that CH patients with migraine comorbidity had higher risks of anxiety and depression, and female patients more frequently exhibited migraine comorbidity than male patients.

An Italian study reported stress-related cortisol changes in female cluster headache patients, suggesting fluctuations in neurosteroids may influence the natural course of migraine and cluster headache.
A Taiwanese study found that female cluster headache patients were more prone to emotional fluctuations and sleep disturbances prior to attacks compared to male patients.
No significant sex differences were observed in mitigating factors for CH attacks, including massage, cold compress, hot compress, and physical activity.
Sleep was the most frequently reported mitigating factor for CH attacks, with no significant sex difference in its use.
Insomnia and temperature variations were the most commonly reported triggers of CH attacks with similar prevalence between sexes.
Menstruation was identified as a trigger for cluster headache attacks by 9.84% of female participants.
Overall use of acute treatment during prior bouts did not differ significantly between male and female CH patients.

Triptans were the most frequently used acute therapy in both sexes with no significant difference in overall use, and lidocaine nasal drops were the least used option in both sexes with no significant sex difference.
Pure oxygen therapy was the most effective acute intervention for cluster headache, with comparable efficacy reported by female and male participants.
Only 15.75% of participants overall reported receiving transitional or preventive therapy for cluster headache, reflecting low utilization of standardized preventive protocols in China.
No significant sex difference was found in suicidal thoughts among cluster headache patients despite female patients having higher depression scores overall.
Female participants did not show a higher prevalence of a positive family history of migraine or cluster headache compared to male participants.
Prior Western studies indicate female CH patients have earlier age of onset and a second peak incidence after age 50, unlike male patients.

An Italian study found that female patients with familial cluster headache experienced significantly earlier onset than those with non-familial cases, suggesting a more prominent genetic role in females.

In Western studies, male CH patients had significantly higher mean BMI than healthy controls whereas female CH patients showed the opposite trend, a pattern not fully replicated in this Chinese cohort due to hospital-based selection bias.
Female participants demonstrated significantly higher educational attainment than male participants, particularly at the university or higher level, contrasting with the study team's previous report.
The female-to-male ratio of cluster headache patients in China increased over time from 1:7 in 2013 to 1:4.33 in 2024 and to 1:3.94 in the present study, mirroring trends seen in Western populations.
Benign paroxysmal vertigo of childhood (BPVC) was the most common etiology, diagnosed in 12 of 40 patients (30%).
Psychogenic vertigo was the second most common diagnosis, occurring in 5 patients (12.5%), of whom 3 were female (60%) and 2 were male (40%).
All 3 patients diagnosed with migraine-associated vertigo had a family history of migraine.
Three patients with vertigo of otherwise undetermined cause were diagnosed with epileptic vertigo based on abnormal EEG findings, and antiepileptic treatment was initiated.
Of the 3 patients with epileptic vertigo, 2 (66.6%) had a family history of epilepsy while 1 (33.3%) did not.
A patient diagnosed with vestibuloneuritis was treated with methylprednisolone (1 mg/kg, tapered over 10 days) and showed significant clinical improvement.
One month after steroid treatment, the vestibuloneuritis patient experienced a mild relapse that resolved within 3 days after treatment with piracetam alone.
Five patients (12.5%) were diagnosed with vertigo attributed to vitamin B12 deficiency, defined as serum B12 ≤200 pg/mL.
All 5 patients with B12-deficiency-associated vertigo had significant symptom relief after sublingual methylcobalamin replacement therapy.
Iron deficiency anemia (hemoglobin ≤10 g/dL) was identified in 4 patients (10%) as a cause of vertigo.
Vertigo symptoms improved in patients with iron and B12 deficiency after vitamin/iron replacement therapy was initiated.
Four patients (10%) had vertigo attributed to orthostatic hypotension.
For orthostatic-hypotension-related vertigo, avoiding sudden movements and rising slowly from bed were recommended as treatment.
A 17-year-old male patient with traumatic vertigo was found to have an intracranial subdural hematoma with midline structure shift on cranial MRI and required emergency surgery.
Two patients developed vertigo attributed to infectious cerebellitis following chickenpox infection one week earlier, with symptoms resolving without treatment.
The BPVC rate in this cohort (30%) was lower than the 39% reported by Batu et al. in a study of 100 pediatric vertigo patients, attributed to a more diverse etiology mix in this study.

A previously reported correlation exists between BPVC and increased likelihood of developing migraine at later ages, though the present study lacked sufficient follow-up to evaluate this relationship.
Headaches often accompany both migraine-related vertigo and psychogenic vertigo, complicating differential diagnosis between the two.
The pathogenesis of BPVC is not clearly established but is hypothesized to involve pathology in the vestibular nucleus and vestibulocerebellar pathways.

According to ICD-3 criteria, childhood syndromes associated with migraine include gastrointestinal disturbance recurrence, cyclic vomiting syndrome, abdominal migraine, benign paroxysmal vertigo, and benign paroxysmal torticollis.
24-hour RMSSD was significantly lower in adolescents with disorders of gut-brain interaction compared with healthy controls.
Log-transformed 24-hour low frequency (lf) HRV was significantly lower in the DGBI group than healthy controls.
Log-transformed 24-hour high frequency (hf) HRV, a marker of vagal modulation, was significantly lower in the DGBI group than healthy controls.
When HRV parameters were separately analyzed by daytime and nighttime periods, they remained significantly lower in the DGBI group than in healthy controls.
The DGBI group showed a blunted nocturnal rise in RMSSD compared with healthy controls, though the nocturnal increase was still statistically significant within the DGBI group.

Psychological measures (catastrophizing, anxiety, depression, trauma) showed no significant differences between the DGBI and healthy control groups, consistent with the DGBI cohort being actively managed.
In the DGBI group, 24-hour RMSSD was inversely correlated with child-reported pain catastrophizing.
In the DGBI group, 24-hour RMSSD was inversely correlated with RCADS-measured depression.
In the DGBI group, 24-hour RMSSD was inversely correlated with TSCC-measured post-traumatic stress symptoms.
Parental pain catastrophizing was inversely correlated with the adolescent's 24-hour hf HRV, with a weaker correlation during daytime.
The inverse correlation between parental catastrophizing and the adolescent's hf HRV was stronger at nighttime than during the day, as was the correlation with nighttime RMSSD.
In the DGBI group, 24-hour RMSSD and hf HRV were inversely correlated with functional disability, and this correlation differed significantly from healthy controls.
The inverse correlation of hf HRV/RMSSD with functional disability was weaker during the day than over 24 hours, while the nighttime correlation was similar to the 24-hour value.
Parent-reported and child-reported pain catastrophizing scores were only mildly correlated with each other.
Child depression scores correlated better with child-reported catastrophizing than with parent-reported catastrophizing.
Child depression scores were not significantly correlated with parent-reported pain catastrophizing.
Functional disability was strongly correlated with child depression scores.
Functional disability showed only a moderate, non-significant correlation with parent-reported pain catastrophizing.
Functional disability showed no correlation at all with child-reported pain catastrophizing.
During the third week of illness the patient developed orthostatic hypotension with a blunted heart-rate response, attributed to encephalitis-related autonomic dysfunction.
CSF testing was positive for anti-GAD65 antibodies by qualitative immunoblot, establishing the diagnosis of anti-GAD autoimmune encephalitis.
Neurological syndromes associated with GAD autoimmunity show a marked female predominance, with women comprising over 80% of affected individuals across the primary phenotypes.

GAD-specific CD4+ T cell populations have been shown to induce severe encephalomyelitis in murine models independently of other effector cells, implicating T cell-mediated rather than purely antibody-mediated pathology.
Repeat lumbar puncture demonstrated elevated CSF protein with mild lymphocytic pleocytosis, consistent with a sustained CNS inflammatory process.
The patient had markedly elevated CSF opening pressure with bilateral papilledema, indicating intracranial hypertension, an atypical but reported feature of autoimmune encephalitis.
High-dose intravenous methylprednisolone followed by oral prednisone led to marked clinical improvement in the patient's neuropsychiatric symptoms.
Rituximab maintenance therapy was associated with sustained remission, with the patient seizure-free and cognitively intact without further relapse at 18-month follow-up.

Intravenous sodium valproate produced marked improvement in abdominal pain, hiccups, and disorganized speech, interpreted as atypical seizure equivalents; residual staring/unresponsiveness episodes resolved after adding levetiracetam.
Relapse rates in autoimmune encephalitis have been reported to range between 12% and 35% in the literature.

In the largest reported series of GAD-65 antibody-associated encephalitis (73 patients), limbic encephalitis was the predominant presentation, with mesial temporal lobe involvement observed in 68% of cases.

Despite immunotherapy, 82.8% of patients in this GAD-65 encephalitis series experienced persistent neurological symptoms such as seizures and cognitive impairment, while mortality remained relatively low at 5.7%.

In a pediatric cohort with anti-GAD antibody-positive encephalitis/encephalopathy, language difficulties and ataxia were more common initial symptoms in patients with high antibody titers, but no significant correlation was found between antibody titer and disease severity or clinical outcomes.

MRI in GAD-associated encephalitis can be normal, as in this patient, but abnormal hippocampal signals, cortical/subcortical T2 hyperintensities, and parenchymal atrophy have been reported in 26%, 37%, and 47% of cases respectively in prior literature.
Symptom onset occurred a few weeks after COVID-19 vaccination, a temporal association noted by the authors though causality with anti-GAD encephalitis remains unproven.
Post-exertional malaise (PEM) is recognized as one of the most frequent manifestations of long covid, present in approximately 80% of affected patients.
The peripheral physiological adaptations observed in long covid patients cannot be fully explained by physical inactivity/deconditioning alone.
Invasive cardiopulmonary exercise testing shows long covid patients commonly exhibit preload failure with insufficient cardiac filling.

Studies of cardiopulmonary structure and function reveal cardiovascular alterations in long covid, including myocardial scarring, inflammatory changes, and residual myocardial alterations in a subset of patients.

The authors argue that although some cardiac volume reductions may indicate deconditioning, preload failure and inflammation-mediated scarring are not typical of deconditioning, so deconditioning alone cannot explain cardiac alterations in all long covid patients.
Mitochondrial dysfunction, including deranged mitochondria, has been demonstrated in multiple tissues of long covid patients.
Accumulating evidence shows endothelial damage and dysfunction in long covid patients, who may exhibit leaky vessels or impaired vasomechanical regulation.
Endothelial dysfunction and impaired mitochondrial function may both contribute to poor oxygen extraction observed in long covid patients.
The authors recommend targeted pharmacotherapy for PEM and POTS, including low-dose naltrexone, beta-blockers, or pyridostigmine, to reduce symptom burden.

Heart-rate pacing guided by the first ventilatory threshold allows patients to stay within their individual energy envelope, minimizing PEM exacerbations while supporting gradual, safe reconditioning.
Traditional graded exercise therapy remains contraindicated for patients with PEM, in contrast to personalized, data-driven pacing approaches.
Wearable heart rate monitors may be a practical method for tracking patient activity levels, though they may not be feasible in less-resourced settings.
PEM is the core symptom and key diagnostic aspect of the Canadian Consensus Criteria for ME/CFS and can be diagnosed using the DePaul Symptom Questionnaire.

Healthcare providers are advised to systematically screen for long covid aetiology, exclude other pathologies, and quantify POTS and PEM severity, for example via the functional capacity questionnaire.
Extended periods of daytime lying or bed rest, though initially seeming beneficial, can induce cardiovascular and skeletal muscle deconditioning.

Migraine incidence in 2022 showed marked female predominance, peaking at 7.5 cases per 1,000 among women aged 18–24 versus 2.3 per 1,000 in men of the same age group, with women consistently having higher incidence across all age groups.

Observed point prevalence of migraine in the CHS-insured population was lower than expected from global reference rates across nearly all age groups, peaking at 10 per 1,000 in the 30-39 age group versus roughly double that internationally, suggesting underdiagnosis.
Anxiety was significantly more common in patients with migraine than in matched controls (24.6% vs 14.1%), corresponding to an odds ratio of 2.02.
Depression was significantly more common in patients with migraine than in matched controls (18.6% vs 11.5%), corresponding to an odds ratio of 1.81.
Low back pain was reported by 78.7% of patients with migraine compared with 58.4% of controls, corresponding to an odds ratio of 2.67.
Fibromyalgia was more prevalent among patients with migraine than controls (1.5% vs 0.6%), corresponding to an odds ratio of 2.42.
Endometriosis, a visceral pain disorder, was nearly twice as common among patients with migraine as controls (2.1% vs 1.1%), OR 1.86.
Hypertension was more prevalent among patients with migraine than controls (25.2% vs 19.6%), OR 1.64.
Dyslipidemia was more prevalent among patients with migraine than controls (36.1% vs 27.7%), OR 1.69.
The odds of cerebrovascular disease/stroke were higher in patients with migraine than controls (0.8% vs 0.5%), OR 1.67, consistent with prior meta-analyses linking migraine to stroke risk.
Diabetes mellitus was less common among patients with migraine than controls (1.9% vs 2.1%), OR 0.91, an inverse association consistent with some but not all prior epidemiologic reports.

Preventive migraine treatment use was strikingly low: 9.6% of patients diagnosed by 2018 had ever used a prophylactic medication versus 8.8% of those diagnosed by 2022, with active yearly use of only 2.2% in 2018 and 2.5% in 2022.
Migraine-specific preventives were rarely used; by 2022, CGRP monoclonal antibodies were used by only 0.1% of patients with migraine, and gepants were used by only a few individuals.
Use of angiotensin receptor blockers as migraine preventives doubled from 0.2% to 0.4% between 2018 and 2022.

Preventive treatment use increased in younger age groups between 2018 and 2022 (highest increase of 27% in the 25-34 group) but decreased in older groups (7% decrease in 65-74, 29% decrease in those over 75), and was nearly absent in patients aged 65 or older.
Patients with migraine were younger and predominantly female, and more likely to belong to higher socioeconomic score categories than controls (34.4% vs 29.6%).
Across 39 within-subject fMRI experiments in chronic primary pain patients, a conjunction meta-analysis found robust activation of the dorsal anterior insula during provoked/experimental pain.
Using cluster- and voxel-level corrections, the meta-analysis found consistent activity in the mid-cingulate gyrus, implicating it in pain processing in chronic primary pain.
Cluster- and voxel-level corrected analyses showed consistent activity in the medial frontal gyrus during provoked pain in chronic primary pain patients.

Among 662 abdominal migraine patients, 629 (95%) were pediatric and 33 (5%) were adults.
Female-to-male ratio for abdominal migraine was approximately 1.60:1 overall, with a 2:1 ratio in adults and 1.57:1 in pediatric patients.
Pediatric patients had a median age of onset of 4.20 years and a median diagnostic delay of 3.10 years.
Adult abdominal migraine patients had a median diagnostic delay of 4.00 years, with the longest delay reaching 58 years.
46.83% of abdominal migraine patients had a personal and/or family history of migraine, rising to 82% in the adult subgroup, both far exceeding the general population migraine prevalence of 11.6%.
Among documented cases, colicky pain (40%) and dull pain (32.7%) were the most common pain qualities reported in abdominal migraine.
The most frequently reported pain locations in abdominal migraine were periumbilical (43.3%) and midline (23.6%).
The majority (83.2%) of patients with documented pain severity experienced moderate to severe abdominal pain.
Median episode duration was 13.30 hours, with 75.3% lasting 2-72 hours (ICHD-3 criterion range), 24.1% shorter than 2 hours, and 0.6% exceeding 72 hours.
Among 448 patients with documented accompanying symptoms, nausea (66.1%), vomiting (53.6%), headache (47.1%), pallor (31.9%), and loss of appetite (24.3%) were the most common.
Headache prevalence (47.1%) was significantly higher than anorexia (24.4%) or pallor (32.1%) among accompanying symptoms.

Prodromal/aura symptoms occurred in 26 patients, with pediatric patients showing mood disturbances (depression/irritability) in 60.0% of cases and adult patients exhibiting diverse somatosensory phenomena.
In an observational study of 44 pediatric abdominal migraine patients, 50% remained attack-free during summer, suggesting a temperature-related alleviating effect.

A prospective observational study of 28 children with abdominal migraine found 96.4% exhibited significantly altered visual evoked potential (VEP) responses to red and white flash stimuli during the interictal period compared to healthy controls.
Delayed gastric emptying was observed in 18 pediatric abdominal migraine patients, and EEG showed increased slow-wave activity in 4 children.
Triptans showed an overall response rate of 98.04% (50/51 patients) for acute treatment of abdominal migraine.
NSAIDs showed an overall response rate of 62.5% (5/8 patients) for acute treatment of abdominal migraine.
Anticonvulsants, notably topiramate, yielded a prophylactic response rate of 95.0% (19/20 patients) in abdominal migraine.
Beta-blockers achieved a 100% (12/12 patients) prophylactic response rate for abdominal migraine.
Antihistamines achieved a 92.8% (64/69 patients) prophylactic response rate for abdominal migraine.
Case reports suggest that CGRP-targeted agents may have therapeutic potential in abdominal migraine.

Abdominal migraine symptoms resolved in 5 pediatric patients between ages 10-18, while 7 patients developed migraine headaches in adulthood, suggesting AM may be an early manifestation of the migraine life cycle.
Anxiety and depression were predominantly observed in adult abdominal migraine patients, whereas motion sickness and allergic history were more frequently reported in pediatric cases.

An adult female patient with abdominal migraine experienced marked symptom alleviation during pregnancy, consistent with known remission of classical migraine during gestation attributed to hormonal changes.
Hereditary alpha-tryptasemia (HαT), caused by increased TPSAB1 gene copy number, is more prevalent among SM patients than in the general population.
HαT prevalence is particularly high among patients with bone marrow mastocytosis (BMM), a subset of SM without skin lesions.
HαT is associated with more severe symptoms of mast cell activation in patients with SM and in those with certain allergies.
A follow-up study found that the frequency of anaphylactic episodes in SM patients was identical regardless of HαT status, contrasting with reports that HαT increases severity.
Total tryptase per mast cell may be slightly higher in HαT-positive SM patients, but histamine and PGD2 levels are not increased compared to HαT-negative or healthy individuals.
KIT D816V is detectable in the vast majority of adult SM patients, with prevalence ≥90% in typical indolent SM (ISM) and smoldering SM (SSM).
KIT D816V confers resistance to imatinib, the most prevalent KIT mutation seen in both children and adults with mastocytosis.
The clinical aggressiveness of SM does not correlate with the presence of KIT D816V or other KIT mutations in adults.
In children, about half of cutaneous mastocytosis cases with a KIT mutation carry KIT D816V, with the remainder harboring other KIT mutations often located in exons 8 and 9.

Midostaurin is a multi-targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitor that blocks KIT D816V, suppresses growth of KIT-transformed mast cells, and inhibits IgE-dependent mediator release from mast cells and basophils, partly via SYK inhibition.
Avapritinib is described as a more selective and more potent inhibitor of KIT D816V compared to midostaurin.
Avapritinib can induce complete or near-complete hematologic remission in roughly 20-30% of patients with smoldering or advanced systemic mastocytosis.

The recommended starting dose of avapritinib for non-advanced SM (25 mg/day) is substantially lower than for advanced SM (200 mg/day), and adverse effects from wild-type KIT inhibition are usually not seen at the lower dose.
Avapritinib blocks IgE-dependent histamine release in basophils obtained from SM patients but has no such effect in basophils from healthy donors.

In a multicenter study, a serum tryptase level below 90 ng/mL combined with bone marrow mast cell infiltration below 15% predicted hypersensitivity reactions, particularly to Hymenoptera venom, in SM patients.
Patients with bone marrow mastocytosis (BMM), a SM subset with low neoplastic mast cell burden and no skin lesions, frequently experience severe anaphylactic reactions, often to Hymenoptera venom.
KIT D816V promotes the oncogenic machinery driving mast cell expansion but may actually decrease IgE-dependent mediator releasability, as shown in the ROSA human mast cell line.
Stem cell factor (SCF), the ligand for KIT, promotes mast cell activation and mediator release in addition to its role in mast cell growth and survival.
Interleukin-3 (IL-3) is a major regulator of growth, differentiation and function of human basophils, but has little or no effect on normal mature human mast cells.
Clonal, KIT-mutated basophils are part of the malignant hematopoietic clone especially in smoldering SM and advanced SM.
The suppressive effect of midostaurin on IgE-dependent histamine release was confirmed ex vivo in basophils obtained from SM patients being treated with the drug.
Imatinib and masitinib can eliminate normal (non-clonal) mast cells and some mutant KIT forms, but cannot eliminate KIT D816V-positive mast cells because this mutation confers drug resistance.
Midostaurin and avapritinib, the two KIT-D816V-targeting TKIs used in clinical practice for SM, produce rapid improvement in mediator-related symptoms and quality of life.

Vestibular migraine diagnosis was strongly associated with reporting spontaneous vertigo episodes.
Vestibular migraine diagnosis was associated with reporting frequent nausea/vomiting, with a moderate effect size.

Logistic regression showed persistent postural-perceptual dizziness (PPPD) was unexpectedly and strongly negatively associated with visual-induced vertigo, despite visual dependence typically being a hallmark PPPD trigger.
Vestibular neuritis was associated with the lowest frequency of autonomic symptoms among the vestibular diagnoses examined in the registry regression models.
A meta-analysis found pooled prevalence of at least one premonitory symptom in migraine of 29% in population-based studies versus 66% in clinic-based studies.
Recent prospective studies report premonitory symptom prevalence between 77% and 88% in migraine, higher than the wide historical range of 9-88%.

In a large multicentre clinic-based study, only 21.5% of migraine patients reported at least one premonitory symptom, most commonly neck stiffness, dizziness, yawning and drowsiness, more common in migraine with aura.
Premonitory symptoms of migraine have been documented by parental report in children as young as 18 months, as well as in adolescents and adults.

A cross-sectional study found significant overlap between perceived migraine triggers and premonitory symptoms, including bright light with premonitory photophobia, loud noise with premonitory phonophobia, and sleep disturbance with premonitory tiredness.

Analysis of screening data from the PRODROME trial found that identifiable premonitory symptoms (light sensitivity, fatigue, neck pain, sound sensitivity, difficulty concentrating, dizziness) were followed by headache within 1-6 hours in 81.5% of events.

PET imaging in 8 migraine patients showed significantly increased cerebral blood flow in the hypothalamus, thalamus, cingulate cortex, and dorsolateral pons during the premonitory phase of NTG-triggered attacks.

A double-blind placebo-controlled ASL-MRI study in 21 migraine patients found increased perfusion in the hypothalamus, thalamus, basal ganglia, and limbic cortex during the premonitory phase after correcting for NTG vascular effects.

A crossover fMRI study in 25 migraine patients found increased positive connectivity between bilateral thalami and praecuneus/cuneus, and a shift from positive to negative connectivity between pons and limbic lobe during the premonitory phase.
Intranasal ammonia stimulation during the interictal period elicited increased neuronal activity in the spinal trigeminal nucleus preceding migraine onset, reflected by elevated BOLD signal.

In one patient scanned daily for 30 days, intranasal ammonia provoked heightened hypothalamic activation preictally, with altered hypothalamus connectivity to the spinal trigeminal nucleus and dorsal rostral pons the day before headache onset.

A cohort of seven episodic migraine patients showed hypothalamic activation as early as two days prior to headache onset during trigemino-nociceptive, olfactory, and visual stimulation with serial fMRI.

A study comparing preictal, postictal, and interictal migraine patients with healthy controls found increased infraslow oscillatory activity in the hypothalamus and brainstem immediately prior to a migraine attack.
In a small longitudinal fMRI study, variability in the dorsal pons and spinal trigeminal nucleus increased markedly within 24 hours prior to migraine onset.

A longitudinal intra-individual fMRI study of 12 migraine patients across 82 sessions found cyclical connectivity changes in sensory, limbic and salience networks that increased over the interictal period, peaked before headache onset, and returned to baseline during headache.

An fMRI study of orofacial nociceptive stimulation in 31 migraine patients versus 31 healthy controls found reduced pain sensitivity and increased spinal trigeminal nucleus activation within 24 hours before headache onset, with reduced connectivity to the rostral ventral medulla.

DTI showed increased mean diffusivity in spinal trigeminal nucleus, pons, PAG and cuneiform nucleus interictally in migraine patients, which normalized within 24 hours before an attack then rose again over the following three days; fractional anisotropy in the medial lemniscus/ventral trigeminal thalamic tract was elevated versus controls throughout the cycle.

Using pCASL, reduced blood flow in the lateral hypothalamus was observed within 24 hours before migraine headache onset, along with decreased functional connectivity between the hypothalamus and PAG, dorsal pons, rostral ventromedial medulla, and cingulate cortex.

In a rodent model, administration of a KOR agonist increased urination and water consumption without inducing yawning or allodynia, suggesting hypothalamic dynorphin-KOR signalling can promote polyuria and thirst symptoms reported in the migraine premonitory phase.

Pharmacological modulation of serotonin, PACAP, and dopamine signalling in the ventral tegmental area altered trigeminal cervical complex neuronal responses and lowered circulating glucose, suggesting homeostatic/reward network interaction with sensory pathways during the premonitory phase.
Danish and Taiwanese cohorts found 85-90% of cluster headache patients experience pre-cluster symptoms before a bout, while a Chinese study reported only 20.8% prevalence.

A study found reduced seasonal variation in peripheral CLOCK gene expression in individuals with cluster headache, both during and outside bouts, compared with healthy controls, supporting circadian clock dysfunction in CH pathophysiology.
Danish and Taiwanese cohort studies found that 85-90% of cluster headache patients report pre-cluster symptoms before the onset of a new cluster bout.
A Chinese study reported a much lower pre-cluster symptom prevalence of 20.8%, contrasting with Western cohort estimates.

Cluster headache bouts show seasonal/circannual rhythmicity, leading to the hypothesis that dysfunction of the hypothalamic suprachiasmatic nucleus (master circadian clock) contributes to the pre-cluster phase.
Blau and Engel first described pre-attack warning symptoms in cluster headache in 1998, reporting that 61% of patients experienced warning signs before an attack.

Shadow pain and cranial autonomic symptoms typically appear about 10 minutes before pain onset in cluster headache, while cognitive and homeostatic symptoms occur earlier, 20-60 minutes before the attack.

In a Danish observational study of 80 cluster headache patients, 83.3% reported pre-attack symptoms, with shadow pain specifically associated with male sex and episodic (vs chronic) CH but no other sex/subtype associations found.

A study of 164 patients with episodic and chronic cluster headache found that 85% reported identifiable premonitory symptoms, with higher prevalence among patients using high-flow oxygen for acute treatment.
A higher number of reported attack triggers and a personal history of smoking were associated with increased likelihood of reporting pre-attack symptoms in cluster headache.

Alcohol consumption is the most frequently reported trigger of cluster headache attacks, identified by more than 50% of patients, with red wine more strongly associated with attack provocation than other alcoholic beverages.
Up to 90% of cluster headache patients report a history of first- or second-hand tobacco exposure, though its role as a direct trigger of attacks remains poorly defined.
Genetic studies have reported mutations in core circadian clock genes, including CLOCK, PER3, and CRY, in patients with cluster headache.
A recent study found reduced seasonal variation in peripheral CLOCK gene expression in individuals with cluster headache, both during and outside of bouts, compared with healthy controls.
A study found reduced seasonal variation in peripheral CLOCK gene expression, both during and outside of cluster bouts, in cluster headache patients compared with healthy controls.

Biochemical studies have not found consistent abnormalities in hypothalamic-regulated hormones such as cortisol, thyroid-stimulating hormone, melatonin, or follicle-stimulating hormone in cluster headache patients.

A longitudinal resting-state fMRI study found reduced hypothalamic functional connectivity with the medial frontal gyrus and occipital cuneus during out-of-bout phases of cluster headache compared with healthy controls, with even greater reductions during active bouts.

Chou et al. demonstrated persistent dysfunction across several large-scale brain networks, including the default mode, frontal, salience, and somatosensory systems, during out-of-bout states in cluster headache.

A diffusion tensor imaging study revealed chronic microstructural white matter changes in tracts such as the corpus callosum and cingulum in cluster headache patients, indicating long-term remodeling beyond symptomatic phases.
Voxel-based morphometry studies comparing in-bout versus out-of-bout phases, and CH patients versus healthy controls, generally found no significant alterations in hypothalamic volume.

Giorgio et al. found decreased frontal grey matter and increased cerebellar and occipital volume in cluster headache patients, suggesting widespread structural changes beyond traditional pain-processing networks.
In a crossover trial of 24 participants, nitroglycerin infusion triggered cluster attacks in 76% of participants compared with 4% during placebo infusion.

In a randomized crossover trial of 32 CH patients, CGRP infusion induced cluster attacks in 89% of participants with active episodic CH and 50% of those with chronic CH, but not in any participant in remission, and no premonitory symptoms were reported.
In a crossover trial of 14 participants with active episodic CH, PACAP infusion induced cluster-like attacks in 43% and VIP infusion in 36%, compared with only 0-20% of participants in remission.

González-Martínez et al. directly compared symptom prevalence preceding headache attacks in migraine and cluster headache, finding a similar overall prevalence of pre-attack symptoms in CH (85%) and premonitory symptoms in migraine (84%), with no significant difference in an adjusted regression model.

'Shadow' pain and lateralized cranial autonomic symptoms occur in approximately 70-80% of cluster headache pre-attack/pre-cluster phases, compared to about 40% of premonitory phase occurrences in migraine.

CGRP appears to play a role in cluster headache, as CGRP infusion can trigger attacks, galcanezumab reduces attack frequency, and preventives such as corticosteroids and verapamil influence CGRP levels.

In the phase 3 randomized double-blind placebo-controlled PRODROME trial (n=518), ubrogepant taken during the migraine premonitory phase resulted in 46% of qualifying events not progressing to moderate/severe headache within 24 hours, compared with 29% for placebo, with similar benefits at 48 hours.

Ubrogepant significantly resolved common premonitory symptoms such as photophobia, phonophobia, neck pain, fatigue, dizziness, and cognitive difficulties, with effects appearing as early as 1-4 hours post-dose and lasting up to 48 hours.

Both topiramate and flunarizine significantly improved non-headache features, including premonitory symptoms, across the premonitory, headache, and resolution phases after eight weeks of treatment in patients with episodic migraine, with no significant difference between the two drugs.

An open-label observational cohort study using daily headache diaries found that three months of galcanezumab treatment reduced the incidence of premonitory symptoms followed by headache by 48% in responders versus 25% in non-responders, and by 50% in super-responders versus 12% in super non-responders.

A small open-label study by Luciani and colleagues indicated that naratriptan 2.5 mg taken during the premonitory phase may reduce headache occurrence when patients anticipated an impending migraine attack.

Studies reviewed by Becker and by Karsan & Goadsby have shown potential benefit of anti-dopaminergic drugs such as flunarizine, prochlorperazine, haloperidol, droperidol, and domperidone given during the migraine premonitory phase.

A Taiwanese study of 168 patients found that cluster headache patients presenting with sleep disturbances or any cranial autonomic symptom during the pre-cluster phase showed a better response to verapamil as a preventive treatment.

The trial's sample size of 170 patients was calculated to detect a 3.5 moderate/severe headache day per month difference between onabotulinumtoxinA and placebo arms with 80% power, based on a pilot-study SD of 7 for change in headache days per week and assuming 25% dropout.
Recently published real-world data on repeated onabotulinumtoxinA sphenopalatine ganglion treatments reported favorable safety and efficacy in an open-label setting.

A compiled safety dataset of previously reported adverse events to sphenopalatine ganglion injections included 93 patients, of whom 59 experienced adverse events, used to define expected adverse events for this trial.
Population-based studies show chronic migraine has a prevalence of 1.4-2.2%.
Migraine is listed by the World Health Organization as the sixth most disabling disorder and is the first cause of disability among individuals under 50 years of age.
Neurological involvement in Sjögren's disease (neuro-SjD) has been reported by up to 20% of patients in prior literature, representing a relevant extra-glandular manifestation.
All 4050 surveyed Sjögren's disease patients reported experiencing at least one neurological symptom, with each symptom rated as having a medium-to-severe impact in at least half of patients.
Only 21.6% of symptomatic patients received a formal diagnosis of neuro-SjD, most often made by a neurologist.
Among patients diagnosed with neuro-SjD, only 21% received pharmacological therapies for their neurological symptoms.
Of the neuro-SjD patients who received pharmacological treatment, only 23% reported significant or complete symptom improvement.
Overall satisfaction with neuro-SjD care was poor, with half of respondents feeling that healthcare providers underestimated their neurological symptoms.
Simulated rebreathing (high CO2 + low O2) significantly increased standing systolic blood pressure compared to room air in patients with neurogenic orthostatic hypotension.
Simulated rebreathing significantly increased standing stroke volume compared to room air in patients with nOH.
Simulated rebreathing significantly increased standing cardiac output compared to room air in patients with nOH.
Simulated rebreathing significantly increased middle cerebral artery velocity while standing compared to room air in patients with nOH.
Standing heart rate did not differ significantly between room air and simulated rebreathing.
Standing systemic vascular resistance did not differ significantly between room air and simulated rebreathing.
Simulated rebreathing significantly reduced cumulative hypotensive standing time compared to room air.

The proportion of patients meeting systolic blood pressure criteria for orthostatic hypotension after 3 minutes of standing trended lower with simulated rebreathing versus room air but did not reach significance.
End-tidal oxygen was, as expected, substantially reduced during simulated rebreathing compared to +CO2 alone, confirming the intended hypoxic-hypercapnic gas manipulation.
Hemodynamic responses (blood pressure, stroke volume, cardiac output, heart rate, systemic vascular resistance, MCAv) did not differ significantly between simulated rebreathing and +CO2 alone.
Ventilation did not differ significantly between simulated rebreathing and +CO2 alone.
End-tidal CO2 levels did not differ significantly between simulated rebreathing and +CO2 alone.
Hypotensive standing time did not differ significantly between simulated rebreathing and +CO2 alone, indicating equal pressor efficacy.
The proportion of patients meeting orthostatic hypotension diagnostic criteria did not differ significantly between simulated rebreathing and +CO2 alone.

Simulated rebreathing was significantly less tolerable than +CO2 alone, with only 20% of patients completing the full 5-minute protocol versus 90% for +CO2 alone, primarily due to dyspnea from low inspired oxygen rather than orthostatic symptoms.

CB1 receptors are localized predominantly to trigeminal ganglion neuronal somata and Aδ-fibers, colocalizing with CGRP and RAMP1, while CB2 receptors are mainly found on satellite glial cells with minimal colocalization with CGRP-positive neurons.

CB1 agonism alone has limited effect on CGRP release under basal conditions, but becomes effective at suppressing CGRP release once TRPV1 activity is pharmacologically suppressed, indicating state-dependent CB1-TRPV1 crosstalk.

CB1 activation reduces Aδ- and C-fiber-evoked firing of trigeminocervical complex neurons and attenuates dural-evoked responses in the ventrolateral periaqueductal gray, consistent with recruitment of PAG-RVM inhibitory circuits.

Activity-dependent synthesis of AEA and 2-AG in the PAG activates presynaptic CB1 receptors to suppress GABA and glutamate release, shifting RVM circuitry toward OFF-cell-mediated inhibition and away from ON-cell facilitation.

In chronic headache states, reduced endocannabinoid tone diminishes both trigeminovascular and descending inhibitory control, while CB2 receptors become upregulated in microglia and immune cells to dampen neuroinflammatory signaling.

Methanandamide suppresses nitroglycerin-evoked CGRP release from plasma, trigeminal ganglion, brainstem, and meninges, an effect blocked by CB1 antagonists but not TRPV1 or CB2 antagonists (except in mast cells).

Peripherally restricted FAAH inhibition with URB937 reduces both acute and chronic NTG-induced hypersensitivity, decreases CGRP and substance P release, and lowers pro-inflammatory cytokine production in the trigeminal ganglion and brainstem, in a CB1-dependent manner.

Dual FAAH/MAGL inhibition with JZL195 reduces NTG-induced orofacial hyperalgesia, serum CGRP, and pro-inflammatory transcripts in the trigeminal ganglion and cervical spinal cord, effects abolished by CB1 antagonism.

In NTG-treated animals, AEA attenuates trigeminal sensitization by reducing TRPV1 activity and suppressing nNOS, NF-κB, and COX-2 expression in the C1/C2 dorsal horns, limiting inflammation-mediated central sensitization.
AEA suppresses the NTG-induced increase in serotonin transporter (5-HTT) expression, suggesting endocannabinoids can modulate headache via interaction with serotonergic pathways.

NTG-induced migraine-like states engage the kynurenine pathway, shifting tryptophan metabolism toward kynurenine derivatives that promote NMDA-receptor-dependent excitatory signaling; endocannabinoid signaling intersects with this pathway via AEA-modulated kynurenine metabolism.
CB1 receptor activation in rat neocortical slices reduces the incidence and propagation of cortical spreading depression, indicating cannabinoid signaling raises the threshold for aura initiation.
In a KCl-evoked CSD animal model, MAGL and ABHD6 expression was increased in the PAG, and inhibition of either enzyme prevented or reversed periorbital allodynia.
Endocannabinoids such as AEA and NADA increase meningeal blood flow and stimulate CGRP release through TRPV1 activation, effects prevented by TRPV1 antagonists or CGRP receptor blockers.
Observational studies in cluster headache patients show mixed responses to cannabis use, ranging from reported relief to no benefit or symptom worsening.

A salivary lipid profiling study found that patients with chronic tension-type headache exhibit altered endocannabinoid signatures, with particular dysregulation of 2-AG levels, suggesting impaired endocannabinoid-mediated pain control.

In the CHIMERA closed-head injury model of post-traumatic headache, selective MAGL inhibition reduces periorbital allodynia, decreases CGRP expression in trigeminal pathways, and suppresses microglial and astrocytic activation.

In the controlled cortical impact TBI model, cortical AEA and related fatty acid ethanolamides are reduced alongside persistent allodynia and glial activation, accompanied by upregulation of FAAH and MAGL.
Positron emission tomography imaging confirmed central FAAH occupancy with the FAAH inhibitor PF-04457845 in humans, supporting clinical feasibility of ECS-targeted drug development.

In an observational study of patients with chronic migraine and medication-overuse headache, the synthetic cannabinoid nabilone reduced headache intensity and analgesic consumption more effectively than ibuprofen.

A separate pilot trial found that nabilone decreased medication intake, improved quality of life, and reduced pain intensity in patients with medication-overuse headache, though the study was small and open-label/crossover in design.

Estradiol downregulates FAAH through estrogen receptor-dependent signaling, elevating anandamide and altering CB1/CB2 receptor activity, linking hormonal fluctuations to headache vulnerability and cannabinoid treatment responsiveness.

Female rodents exhibit reduced AEA levels associated with elevated FAAH activity and enhanced trigeminal sensitivity compared with males following nitroglycerin exposure, indicating a sex difference in endocannabinoid tone disruption.
In trigeminovascular and meningeal activation models, females display greater mast cell activation and more pronounced microglial cytokine responses than males.
Cortical spreading depression models demonstrate robust sex differences in cortical excitability, with females exhibiting lower CSD thresholds and increased susceptibility compared with males.

Observational cohorts and real-time symptom tracking studies reveal that women often report greater therapeutic benefit from cannabis-based headache treatments but also experience higher rates of adverse effects than men.
Migraine becomes two- to four-times more common in women than men after puberty, coinciding with reproductive hormonal fluctuations that also modulate endocannabinoid signaling.
Current conventional cigarette use was independently associated with higher odds of self-reported frequent headache compared to never smokers.
Former conventional cigarette use was also independently associated with higher odds of self-reported frequent headache compared to never smokers.

Current heated tobacco product (HTP) use was significantly associated with higher odds of self-reported frequent headache compared to never users, though the association was weaker than for cigarettes.
Former HTP use was not significantly associated with self-reported frequent headache in the main multiple-imputation model.
Younger age was independently associated with higher odds of self-reported frequent headache.
Female sex was strongly and independently associated with higher odds of self-reported frequent headache.
Comorbid dyslipidemia was independently associated with higher odds of self-reported frequent headache.
Comorbid depression was independently associated with higher odds of self-reported frequent headache.
