Comorbid sleep disorder was the strongest independent factor associated with higher odds of self-reported frequent headache.
Daily coffee consumption was independently associated with slightly higher odds of self-reported frequent headache.
Daily consumption of caffeinated soft drinks was independently associated with higher odds of self-reported frequent headache.
Alcohol consumption more than twice a week was negatively (inversely) associated with self-reported frequent headache.
The magnitude of association with self-reported frequent headache was significantly greater for current conventional cigarette use than for current HTP use.

In a sensitivity analysis using list-wise deletion (rather than multiple imputation), both current and former HTP use were significantly associated with self-reported frequent headache, unlike the null result for former use in the main model.
Overall, 25.5% of the 23,228 study participants reported experiencing headaches 'occasionally' or 'frequently' in the past year, meeting the study's definition of self-reported frequent headache.

Fatigue severity (measured by FACIT-F) was significantly greater in both primary and associated Sjögren's disease compared with systemic autoimmune rheumatic diseases without Sjögren's disease, with no difference between the two Sjögren's groups.
Patients with primary Sjögren's disease reported higher ESSPRI fatigue scores than those with associated Sjögren's disease.
Patients with primary Sjögren's disease reported higher ESSPRI dryness scores than those with associated Sjögren's disease.
Pain was independently associated with fatigue severity in patients with primary Sjögren's disease in multivariate analysis.
Pain was independently associated with fatigue severity in patients with associated Sjögren's disease in multivariate analysis.
Dryness was independently associated with fatigue severity in patients with primary Sjögren's disease in multivariate analysis.

In patients with primary Sjögren's disease, presence of arthritis was independently and negatively associated with FACIT-F fatigue score (i.e., associated with worse/more severe fatigue) in multivariate analysis.
In patients with associated Sjögren's disease, C-reactive protein was independently associated with fatigue severity in multivariate analysis, a link not seen in primary Sjögren's disease.
Fatigue was not significantly associated with systemic disease activity as measured by ESSDAI in patients with primary Sjögren's disease.
Women who later received a long COVID diagnosis had significantly higher odds of a pre-pandemic (2019) asthma diagnosis compared with matched controls.
Men who later received a long COVID diagnosis had significantly higher odds of a pre-pandemic (2019) asthma diagnosis compared with matched controls.
In the 12 months before long COVID diagnosis, females had markedly higher odds of an asthma diagnosis compared with matched controls.
In the 12 months before long COVID diagnosis, males had markedly higher odds of an asthma diagnosis compared with matched controls.
Six months after long COVID diagnosis, females continued to show elevated odds of an asthma diagnosis compared with matched controls.
Six months after long COVID diagnosis, males continued to show elevated odds of an asthma diagnosis compared with matched controls.
Long COVID cases identified via U09.9 diagnosis in the Stockholm cohort were predominantly female, comprising 69.1% of cases, with a median age of 47 years.

Long COVID patients showed higher prevalence of all six investigated respiratory diagnoses (upper respiratory infection, bronchitis, asthma, cough, dyspnea, other breathing abnormalities) than matched controls both before and after the pandemic.

In the pre-pandemic year 2019, individuals who later developed long COVID had higher odds of acute upper respiratory tract infection, asthma, and bronchitis than matched controls, in both men and women.
Across diagnoses, odds ratios were generally highest in the 12 months preceding long COVID diagnosis, with this temporal pattern most pronounced for bronchitis.
Unlike most other respiratory diagnoses, asthma odds remained approximately doubled in long COVID patients relative to controls at 6 months after diagnosis.
Dyspnea diagnoses remained substantially elevated in long COVID patients relative to controls at 6 months after long COVID diagnosis.

Elevated odds of asthma diagnosis were already present in the year preceding long COVID diagnosis, suggesting the association is unlikely to be explained solely by increased diagnostic attention after long COVID onset.
Long COVID cases had higher prevalence than controls of asthma diagnosed under specific ICD-10 subcodes: non-allergic, mixed, unspecified asthma, and status asthmaticus.
Nociplastic pain, characterized by altered central and peripheral pain sensory processing, is present in more than one-third of patients seeking evaluation for hip or knee arthritis.
Patients with nociplastic pain undergoing hip or knee arthroplasty experience less pain relief and functional improvement after surgery compared to those without nociplastic pain.
Patients with nociplastic pain undergoing arthroplasty show increased postoperative opioid use compared to patients without nociplastic pain.
Many patients exhibiting nociplastic pain features do not carry a formal diagnosis of fibromyalgia or another recognized nociplastic pain syndrome.
GammaCore, a handheld transcutaneous cervical vagus nerve stimulation device, received FDA clearance in 2015 for the acute treatment of migraine and episodic cluster headache.
GammaCore subsequently received FDA clearance for preventive treatment of migraine in adults and adolescents and, in 2021, for hemicrania continua and paroxysmal hemicrania in adults.

In healthy humans, fMRI shows that tcVNS (the migraine/cluster-headache device) activates the ipsilateral nucleus tractus solitarius and bilateral insula, thalamus, anterior cingulate cortex, and dorsolateral prefrontal cortex.

The TEA device (Transtimulation Research) is an FDA-cleared taVNS system, with bilateral electrode pads placed on the auricular cymba concha, indicated for relieving functional abdominal pain associated with irritable bowel syndrome.
The IB-Stim paVNS device (NeurAxis) received FDA De Novo clearance in 2018 for functional abdominal pain associated with IBS, and in 2025 was cleared for pediatric patients 8 years and older.
DyAnsys' First Relief paVNS device received FDA 510(k) clearance for abdominal pain associated with IBS.

Across human studies, VNS commonly reduces heart rate and increases heart rate variability in within-subject comparisons (during vs. pre-stimulation), but active-vs-sham/control between-group comparisons often fail to replicate these autonomic benefits.

VNS enhances baroreflex sensitivity and can reset the baroreflex set-point to a lower pressure via NTS-mediated inhibition of the rostral ventrolateral medulla, producing vasodilation and blood pressure reduction.
taVNS was reported to significantly inhibit the salivary cortisol response during acute mental stress.
VNS disrupts respiratory sinus arrhythmia, blunting the normal coupling between respiratory and cardiac cycles, with a significant decrease in RSA magnitude during vagal stimulation.
By increasing vagal efferent drive, VNS may enhance gastric emptying and peristalsis and improve digestive efficiency, offering potential benefit for gastroparesis and constipation.
At 8 weeks, PRISM-CBT showed no significant difference from usual care on the primary outcome, the FIQR global impact score.
By 12 months, PRISM-CBT participants showed a greater improvement in FIQR global impact score compared with usual care.
PRISM-CBT showed a greater improvement in FIQR global impact score compared with standard CBT.
PRISM-CBT reduced BPI pain interference compared with usual care at 8 weeks.
PRISM-CBT reduced BPI pain interference compared with usual care at 6 months, sustaining the 8-week benefit.
At 12 months, PRISM-CBT produced a 1.42-point greater reduction in BPI pain interference compared with usual care.
At 8 weeks, PRISM-CBT reduced BPI pain interference by 0.98 points more than standard CBT.
At 6 months, PRISM-CBT reduced BPI pain interference by 0.63 points more than standard CBT.
At 12 months, PRISM-CBT reduced BPI pain interference by 1.92 points more than standard CBT, the largest and most significant between-group difference reported.
At 6 months, PRISM-CBT produced a 0.56-point greater improvement in BPI pain severity compared with usual care.
PRISM-CBT produced a significantly greater improvement in BPI pain severity than standard CBT at 12 months.
Fibromyalgia participants reported higher mean pain intensity than chronic headache participants.
In chronic headache, Brief Pain Inventory pain intensity correlated significantly with interference in general activity.
In chronic headache, pain intensity correlated strongly with mood impairment.
In chronic headache, pain intensity correlated with pain self-efficacy scores.
In chronic headache, motor symptoms were strongly associated with rumination on the Pain Catastrophising Scale.
In chronic headache, sensory deficits were associated with rumination on the Pain Catastrophising Scale.
Participants with fibromyalgia reported higher mean pain intensity than those with chronic headache.
In fibromyalgia, pain intensity was positively correlated with total pain catastrophising scores.
In fibromyalgia, pain intensity was strongly correlated with feelings of helplessness on the PCS.
In fibromyalgia, higher pain intensity was strongly correlated with greater interference with daily life.
Mental health scores were negatively associated with pain in fibromyalgia patients, an association not seen in the headache group.
Fibromyalgia showed higher pain intensity and stronger correlations with psychological dysfunction compared to chronic headache, which showed more selective associations with mood and rumination.

Co-administration of the peripherally restricted cannabinoid agonist PrNMI with the initial pH 6.0 supradural injection prevented both the acute allodynia and the latent (pH 7.0-induced) periorbital allodynia seen in vehicle-treated mice.

Co-administration of the peripherally restricted CB1R inverse agonist 18A with PrNMI abolished PrNMI's analgesic effect, indicating peripheral CB1R activation is required for PrNMI-mediated prevention of allodynia.
Co-administration of the selective CB2R inverse agonist SR144528 with PrNMI also abolished PrNMI's analgesic effect, indicating a contribution of CB2R activation to PrNMI's antinociceptive action.
The selective CB2R agonist RNB61, when co-administered with the pH 6.0 injection, did not prevent either the acute allodynia or the latent sensitization-induced allodynia, unlike PrNMI.

When administered as a post-treatment co-administered with the second (pH 7.0) supradural injection, PrNMI failed to alleviate the latent sensitization-induced allodynia, unlike its efficacy as a pre-treatment.
Fluorogold back-labeling of the dura identified an average of ~2 dural afferent trigeminal ganglion neurons per ganglion, all of small or medium soma size with none of large size.
A slight majority (52.9%) of fluorogold-positive dural afferent trigeminal ganglion neurons bound IB4, a marker predominantly labeling non-peptidergic nociceptors.
IB4-positive dural afferent neurons were significantly smaller in soma size than IB4-negative dural afferent neurons.

Electrophysiological profiling of fluorogold-positive dural afferents distinguished Aδ-type from C-type neurons by presence/absence of a hyperpolarization-induced voltage sag, and Aδ-type neurons had significantly larger soma size than C-type neurons.

Fluorogold-positive dural afferent neurons from pH 6.0-treated (sensitized) mice showed no significant differences in resting membrane potential or evoked action potential parameters compared to those from pH 7.4-treated (control) mice.

The magnitude of pH 6.0-induced depolarization, attributed to ASIC activation, was significantly greater in dural afferent neurons from pH 6.0-treated (sensitized) mice than from pH 7.4-treated control mice.

In dural afferent neurons from naive (pH 7.4-treated) mice, bath-applied PrNMI significantly and reversibly suppressed acid (pH 6.0)-evoked depolarizing potentials, consistent with CB1R-dependent inhibition of ASIC currents.

In dural afferent neurons from sensitized (pH 6.0-treated) mice, bath-applied PrNMI failed to decrease acid-evoked depolarizing potentials, in contrast to its effect in naive neurons, indicating loss of cannabinoid efficacy after sensitization.

Bath-applied RNB61 failed to attenuate acid-evoked depolarizing responses in dural afferent neurons from either naive or sensitized mice, indicating a lack of functional CB2R-mediated modulation of ASIC currents in these neurons.

The authors interpret RNB61's ineffectiveness as indicating a likely absence of functional CB2R directly on control and sensitized dural trigeminal ganglion neurons, implying CB2R contributions to PrNMI analgesia occur via non-neuronal (immune/glial) cells rather than direct neuronal ASIC modulation.
Rural Veterans with chronic overlapping pain conditions (COPCs) were more likely than urban Veterans to receive a primary care visit coded for their COPC.
Rural Veterans with COPCs had significantly lower rates of specialty care visits for their pain condition than urban Veterans.
Rural Veterans with COPCs had fewer mean specialty care visits for their condition compared to urban Veterans.
In multivariable regression adjusting for demographics and comorbidities, rural residence was independently associated with a lower likelihood of receiving specialty care for a COPC.
Veterans whose primary care site was a rural clinic had the lowest adjusted likelihood of receiving specialty care for their COPC, compared to those at urban clinics or medical centers.
Veterans whose primary care was based at a rural clinic were more likely to be seen for their COPC in primary care compared to those at urban clinics or medical centers.
Mean specialty care visits for COPCs increased progressively from rural clinics to urban clinics to large VA medical centers.
Among Veterans with COPCs, migraine patients most commonly received specialty care in neurology.
Among Veterans with COPCs, IBS patients most commonly received specialty care in gastroenterology.
Veterans with fibromyalgia were treated across a broader range of specialty clinics rather than one dominant specialty, including pain clinic, rheumatology, and mental health.
Just over a third of all Veterans with a chronic overlapping pain condition received specialty care for that condition during the study period.
Psychiatric and sleep disorder comorbidities were highly prevalent among Veterans with chronic overlapping pain conditions, with sleep disorders, depressive disorders, and PTSD being the most common.

Compared to a musculoskeletal pain comparator cohort, Veterans with COPCs had lower overall primary care rates but substantially higher overall specialty care rates, although the same rural/urban utilization disparities were present in both cohorts.
Systemic mastocytosis is a clonal mast cell disease driven by the KIT D816V mutation in more than 95% of cases.

In the primary PIONEER trial, avapritinib plus best supportive care significantly improved symptoms, mast cell burden biomarkers, and quality of life compared with placebo at 24 weeks in patients with indolent systemic mastocytosis.
Overall, 13 of 212 (6.1%) patients enrolled in PIONEER experienced anaphylaxis during the screening or treatment period, with a higher rate in the avapritinib arm than placebo.
Restricted to the 24-week interventional treatment period only, anaphylaxis occurred in 4/141 (2.8%) avapritinib-treated patients versus 3/71 (4.2%) placebo-treated patients.
Among the 13 ISM patients who experienced anaphylaxis in PIONEER, the large majority were female.
Basal serum tryptase levels varied widely among the 13 ISM patients with anaphylaxis, ranging from near-normal to markedly elevated values.
Most patients with ISM and anaphylaxis had a detectable KIT D816V mutation, with allele burden varying widely across patients.

Anaphylaxis triggers among the 13 patients were heterogeneous, including foods, medications, Hymenoptera venom, stress, and temperature changes, with 4 patients having at least one event of unknown trigger.

Five of the 13 patients with anaphylaxis had received omalizumab prior to randomization and continued it throughout the treatment period; one patient discontinued omalizumab after developing acute allergic symptoms following a single dose.
About one-third of patients with a history of anaphylaxis experienced multiple anaphylaxis events during the screening and/or treatment periods.

Among avapritinib-treated patients with a history of anaphylaxis, most had investigator-assessed improvement in quality of life during treatment, with reduced medication/hospital use and increased physical functioning.
Among placebo-treated patients with a history of anaphylaxis, most reported mild improvement or no improvement in quality of life during the study.
A meta-analysis found migraine prevalence 52% higher in people with epilepsy than those without, and epilepsy prevalence 79% higher in people with migraine than in non-migraine individuals.
A retrospective Icelandic study found children under 16 with epilepsy had almost a fourfold increased risk of migraine with aura compared to healthy controls.

FHM1-associated CACNA1A gain-of-function mutations enhance calcium influx and glutamate release, lowering the threshold for cortical spreading depression and, in severe cases, triggering epileptiform discharges.

FHM2 loss-of-function mutations in ATP1A2 impair astrocytic clearance of extracellular potassium and glutamate, increasing neuronal network excitability and susceptibility to CSD and epileptiform activity.

FHM3 gain-of-function SCN1A mutations accelerate recovery from fast inactivation of Nav1.1 channels, increasing excitability and promoting CSD propagation, linking FHM3 to both focal and generalized seizures.

PRRT2 loss-of-function frameshift mutations remove negative regulation of SNARE-mediated vesicle fusion and sodium channels, causing neuronal hyperexcitability and linking PRRT2 to both migraine and epilepsy.
The risk of major depressive disorder is 2-4 times greater in individuals with migraine than in the general population, and the relationship is bidirectional.
Genetic risk score analyses found a significant genetic correlation (rG = 0.32) between migraine and MDD, consistent with shared heritability estimated at ~20% of variance.
A GWAS revealed 14 genetic loci shared between migraine and MDD and 36 loci shared between migraine and schizophrenia.

CNR1 (cannabinoid receptor 1) knockout mice show depression-like behaviors after stress, and CNR1 is also associated with migraine risk, implicating the endocannabinoid system in shared serotonergic dysregulation.
Polymorphisms in DRD2 are associated with comorbid risk for migraine with aura, MDD, and anxiety disorders.
Large-scale prospective studies found insomnia increases the risk of new-onset migraine 11 years later by 40%.
Migraine patients have a doubled risk of developing insomnia after 11 years, with risk increasing with headache frequency, independent of anxiety and depression.
A meta-analysis reported a pooled RLS prevalence of 17.0% in migraine patients versus 7.0% in controls.
Migraine patients, especially those with aura, have a significantly increased risk of ischemic stroke (risk ratio ~2.0), most pronounced among young women, smokers, and oral contraceptive users.
A GWAS identified PHACTR1 as a shared genetic risk locus for migraine, coronary artery disease, and cervical artery dissection.
A Mendelian randomization study confirmed a genetic causal association between migraine and stroke, identifying KCNK5, PLXNB1, and MDK as potential shared drug target genes.
PFO closure has been shown to effectively reduce migraine attack frequency or headache days, particularly in migraine with aura.
Cohort studies show migraine odds are 40-80% higher in IBS patients, and cumulative IBS incidence among migraine patients is more than twice that of the general population.
A meta-analysis of five studies found H. pylori infection prevalence of ~45% in migraine patients, significantly higher than 33% in healthy controls.
A large prospective study found that insomnia increases the risk of new-onset migraine 11 years later by 40%.
Migraine patients have a roughly doubled risk of developing insomnia over 11 years, with risk rising with headache frequency.
A meta-analysis found the pooled prevalence of restless leg syndrome to be higher in migraine patients than in controls.
Some studies found much higher migraine incidence in narcolepsy patients than controls, while other controlled studies found no significant association, making this comorbidity controversial.
The dopamine receptor agonist pramipexole reduced both RLS symptoms and migraine frequency in patients with both conditions.
A clinical trial of the dual orexin receptor antagonist filorexant failed to show significant efficacy for migraine prevention.

A retrospective study found anti-CGRP monoclonal antibody treatment significantly improved RLS symptoms, central sensitization, and headache-related disability in patients with comorbid migraine and RLS.
Multiple GWAS have found genetic variants in MEIS1, LGR6, VSTM2L, and CCDC141 associated with increased risk of RLS in migraine patients.
A GWAS in a Han Chinese population identified HDAC9 rs1178326 among loci significantly associated with the comorbidity of insomnia and migraine.
In a mouse model, cortical spreading depression led to closure of the perivascular space and transient impairment of glymphatic flow.
Migraine patients, especially those with aura, have an approximately twofold increased risk of ischemic stroke, particularly among young women, smokers, and oral contraceptive users.
Migraine with aura is linked to increased risk of myocardial infarction, angina, and cardiovascular mortality.
Large cohort studies identified migraine as associated with increased risks of atrial fibrillation/flutter and venous thromboembolism.
Migraine patients show reduced numbers and impaired function of circulating endothelial progenitor cells, indicating compromised vascular repair capacity.
Women with migraine with aura show significantly elevated levels of endothelial microparticles, a marker of endothelial dysfunction.
A GWAS identified PHACTR1 as a shared risk locus for migraine, coronary artery disease, and cervical artery dissection.
A polymorphism near the FGF23 gene is associated with migraine and, in men, white matter lesions and subclinical brain infarcts.
A Mendelian randomization study confirmed a genetic causal association between migraine and stroke, identifying KCNK5, PLXNB1, and MDK as potential drug target genes for both.
The prevalence of patent foramen ovale is significantly greater in the migraine-with-aura population than in the general population, providing an anatomical link to cryptogenic stroke.
PFO closure effectively reduces migraine attack frequency or headache days, with the greatest improvement in migraine with aura.
The odds ratio for migraine is 40-80% higher in IBS patients than non-IBS individuals, and IBS cumulative incidence in migraine patients is more than twice that of the general population.
A meta-analysis of five studies found the prevalence of Helicobacter pylori infection significantly higher in migraine patients than in healthy controls.
Another meta-analysis reported an overall odds ratio of 2.8 for the association between Helicobacter pylori infection and migraine, and highlighted potential benefit of eradication therapy.
Gastric emptying time is significantly prolonged both during and between acute migraine attacks, which can affect oral medication absorption.
Migraine patients have altered gut microbiota composition, including decreased beneficial bacteria and enhanced microbial pathways related to tryptophan degradation and glutamate metabolism.
Preliminary clinical trials show probiotic and synbiotic interventions can reduce migraine attack frequency and analgesic use.
Migraine prevalence in MS patients is 2-3 times higher than the general population, and migraine is associated with a 39% increase in risk of new-onset MS.

Cohort studies show migraine patients have a 40-80% higher odds of IBS compared with non-IBS individuals, and IBS cumulative incidence among migraine patients is more than double that of the general population.
A meta-analysis of five studies found H. pylori infection prevalence of approximately 45% among migraine patients compared with 33% in healthy controls.

Another meta-analysis reported an overall odds ratio of 2.8 for the association between H. pylori infection and migraine, and noted potential benefit of eradication therapy for some migraine patients.

Gastric emptying time is significantly prolonged both during and between acute migraine attacks, and comorbidity rates with migraine reach 36.6% in gastroparesis and 68% in functional dyspepsia patients.
Migraine patients show altered gut microbiota composition with decreased beneficial bacteria and enhanced microbial metabolic pathways related to tryptophan degradation and glutamate metabolism.
In animal experiments, antibiotic-induced gut microbiota dysbiosis contributed to chronic migraine-like pain by increasing TNF-α levels, an effect reversible by microbiota restoration.
Preliminary clinical trials showed that probiotic and synbiotic interventions reduced migraine attack frequency and analgesic use.
Non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation (nVNS) improves both migraine and gastroparesis symptoms, underscoring the shared vagal pathway between the two conditions.

Epidemiological studies show migraine prevalence among multiple sclerosis (MS) patients is approximately 2-3 times higher than the general population (OR 1.96-2.60), while migraine is associated with a 39% increased risk of new-onset MS.
Migraine patients present a reduced number of regulatory T cells in peripheral blood, reflecting a proinflammatory state shared with MS.
High-sensitivity C-reactive protein levels are greater in MS patients with comorbid migraine, suggesting more pronounced systemic inflammation in the comorbid group.
MS patients with periaqueductal gray (PAG) lesions have a fourfold increased risk of migraine-like headaches, implicating failure of descending pain inhibition.

Mendelian randomization studies found no causal effect of migraine on MS, but identified shared risk loci within the major histocompatibility complex region (e.g., HCG20, HLA-B) increasing risk for both conditions.
A meta-analysis of over one million individuals demonstrated a mutual bidirectional increase in risk of developing migraine and asthma.
Serum IgE and histamine levels are significantly higher in migraine patients than in controls, with histamine levels significantly greater during headache attacks than during interictal periods.
Family studies revealed migraine patients have a significantly increased risk of developing allergic diseases (OR = 1.83).

Headache prevalence in fibromyalgia patients is high (35-88%), with migraine as the most common type (45-80%), and about one-third of primary headache patients have comorbid fibromyalgia; migraine attack frequency shows a dose-response relationship with fibromyalgia comorbidity risk.
Botulinum toxin A is reported as an effective treatment for patients with chronic migraine comorbid with fibromyalgia.

TMD prevalence among female patients with migraine and chronic migraine (86.8% and 91.3% respectively) was significantly greater than in headache-free controls (33.3%), and migraine is the most common primary headache type among TMD clinic patients (up to 55.3%).

Retrospective clinical studies found CGRP monoclonal antibodies not only treat headache in migraine patients comorbid with fibromyalgia but also significantly reduce FM-related somatic pain and global disability, with FM improvement correlating with reduction in migraine-related disability.
Cerebrospinal fluid from fibromyalgia patients shows decreased levels of serotonin and norepinephrine metabolites, elevated substance P, and altered endocannabinoid levels.

A large meta-analysis found that diabetes mellitus (especially T1DM) is negatively correlated with migraine occurrence, whereas migraine (especially migraine without aura) is positively correlated with incidence of diabetes mellitus.
Higher body mass index is correlated with increased headache attack frequency, severity, and disability in migraine patients, showing a dose-response relationship.

Migraine risk is significantly greater in patients with endometriosis and vice versa, an association especially pronounced in adolescents (OR=4.7), with a linear relationship between migraine severity and probability of endometriosis.

GWAS analyses revealed a significant positive genetic correlation between migraine and T2DM (rG≈0.06-0.07), and Mendelian randomization based on single-cell data identified AP4E1 and HSD17B12 as key genes in migraine-T2DM comorbidity.

Large-scale GWAS and twin studies revealed a significant positive genetic correlation between migraine and endometriosis (rG≈0.27-0.38), originating primarily from shared genetic susceptibility, with multiple trait analyses identifying shared risk loci including NGF and FSHB.
Magnetic resonance spectroscopy studies revealed reduced ATP levels and mitochondrial phosphorylation potential in the brains of migraineurs during the interictal period.

CGRP can modulate insulin secretion and may reduce the risk of developing T2DM, while insulin can induce CGRP release by activating TRPV1 receptors on trigeminal afferents, sensitizing meningeal nociceptors and increasing headache susceptibility.
Preclinical studies show GLP-1 receptor agonists can inhibit neuroinflammation and modulate CGRP release via central receptors, thereby attenuating migraine-like behaviors.

Mice with endometriosis exhibit elevated serum prolactin levels that sensitize trigeminal afferent fibers and increase migraine susceptibility; cabergoline (a dopamine receptor agonist) reversed this sensitization.
Plasma CGRP levels are elevated in obese individuals, and amylin, a peptide structurally similar to CGRP, is elevated in obesity and diabetes with analogs capable of inducing migraine.
Proinflammatory adipokines (e.g., adiponectin, leptin, resistin) released from adipose tissue are significantly elevated in the plasma of patients with both episodic and chronic migraine.

RCTs of supraorbital transcutaneous nerve stimulation (Cefaly device) show modest but meaningful reductions in monthly migraine days and higher responder rates versus sham stimulation, with paraesthesia as the most common but reversible adverse event.

Transcutaneous occipital nerve stimulation shows beneficial effects on headache frequency, particularly with higher-frequency stimulation parameters, though evidence is limited by small samples and carryover effects.

Non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation (gammaCore) shows feasibility and tolerability with notable 2-hour pain freedom in open-label studies and particular responsiveness in menstrual-related migraine, but randomized trials in chronic migraine yield mixed results.

Single-pulse transcranial magnetic stimulation (sTMS) is supported by randomized trials showing significant improvement in 2-hour pain freedom for acute treatment of migraine with aura, with longer-term data showing reduced headache days in episodic and chronic migraine.

Early studies of transcranial direct current stimulation and remote electrical neuromodulation show promising efficacy signals for aborting acute migraine, but larger, longer-term trials are still required.
Long-term data on paraesthesia-free high-frequency (10 kHz) cervical spinal cord stimulation show meaningful benefit for refractory chronic migraine patients who failed prior treatments.

The Vickers et al. (2018) individual patient data meta-analysis of 20,827 patients across 39 trials found acupuncture significantly superior to sham and no-acupuncture controls for chronic pain conditions including chronic headache, with durable effects showing only a 15% reduction in benefit at one-year follow-up.
In a multicentre RCT of 150 acupuncture-naïve patients with episodic migraine without aura, manual acupuncture reduced migraine days more successfully than sham acupuncture.
Zhao et al. (2017) established acupuncture's superiority over both sham acupuncture and topiramate for migraine prevention.
Li et al. (2020) found acupuncture provided benefits over Western medicine treatment for migraine, with fewer side effects.
A systematic review of 8 RCTs by Vázquez-Justes et al. (2022) showed dry needling significantly improves sensory and functional outcomes across multiple headache types, including migraine.
A 2023 systematic review found aerobic exercise combined with medication decreases headache frequency, duration, and intensity in migraine.

Manual therapy demonstrates effectiveness comparable to prophylactic medications (propranolol, topiramate) for migraine prevention, with systematic reviews showing significant improvements in disability, quality of life, and pain outcomes.

A 2024 meta-analysis reported large manual-therapy effect sizes for cervicogenic headache (SMD −2.01) and moderate effects for tension-type headache (SMD −0.86), with variable effects in migraine depending on presence of cervical dysfunction and myofascial trigger points.
A meta-analysis of 11 RCTs demonstrated that CBT reduces headache frequency and MIDAS disability ratings, with particular benefit for chronic and medication-overuse migraine.
A 36-week RCT found that mindfulness-based stress reduction (MBSR) significantly lowered disability, pain catastrophizing, sadness, and pain unpleasantness in migraine patients.
Systematic reviews report that biofeedback produces positive outcomes in anxiety reduction and autonomic regulation among migraine patients.
A 2025 systematic review of 50 adult RCTs found that CBT, relaxation training, and mindfulness each reduced migraine frequency, while behavioral education improved disability outcomes.

A 2020 meta-analysis demonstrated significant reductions in headache frequency, pain intensity, and duration with yoga, with notable effects for tension-type headache and moderate benefits for migraine.

In the CONTAIN RCT of 160 adults with episodic migraine, adding structured yoga to standard medical therapy produced significantly greater reductions in headache frequency (Δ3.53), intensity, HIT-6 scores, MIDAS disability, and pill consumption after 3 months versus standard therapy alone.
RCTs demonstrated that oral traditional Chinese medicine (TCM) formulations significantly outperform controls in vestibular migraine, reducing the frequency and duration of vertigo.
A 2025 systematic review of 50 adult RCTs found that CBT, relaxation training, and mindfulness each reduced migraine frequency, while behavioral education improved disability outcomes.
Integrated behavioral programs combining CBT, biofeedback, and relaxation training produce strong therapeutic results for migraine across age groups.
A 2020 meta-analysis found yoga significantly reduced headache frequency, pain intensity, and attack duration, with moderate benefit specifically for migraine.

In the CONTAIN RCT, 160 adults with episodic migraine randomized to a structured yoga program plus standard therapy had significantly greater reductions in headache frequency, intensity, HIT-6 scores, MIDAS disability, and pill consumption than standard therapy alone after 3 months.

Chinese patent medicines such as Yangxue Qingnao granules and Toutongning capsules are used for migraine prevention with proposed mechanisms of regulating body temperature and enhancing cerebral blood flow.
RCTs found that oral traditional Chinese medicine formulations significantly outperformed controls in reducing the frequency and duration of vertigo in vestibular migraine.
A narrative analysis of 12 clinical studies (2000-2020) found that 11 showed therapeutic benefit of Ayurvedic monotherapy for migraine with no significant side effects.
Across the same 12 studies (2000-2020), 35.2% of patients experienced total symptom relief with Ayurvedic monotherapy for migraine.
An observational study of 406 individuals found that 70.5% experienced significant reductions in migraine frequency and pain severity after a standardized 90-day Ayurvedic program.
Nasya, a nasal therapy with medicated oils used in Panchakarma, is proposed to modulate trigeminal nerve activity and autonomic balance in migraine.
Virechana, a therapeutic purgation procedure in Panchakarma, is proposed to eliminate excess Pitta and address gut-migraine associations.
Shirodhara, an oil-dripping therapy used in Panchakarma, is proposed to calm the mind and modulate cortical excitability in migraine.
Siravyadha, a therapeutic bloodletting procedure, is used for blood-impurity-related migraines and reported dramatic improvements in MIDAS scores.
Bacopa monnieri is reported to have neuroprotective effects and improve cerebral blood flow relevant to migraine.
Withania somnifera (Ashwagandha) is reported to reduce brain inflammation and modulate the HPA axis relevant to migraine.
Zingiber officinale (ginger) has been shown in clinical studies to relieve acute migraine attacks with efficacy comparable to sumatriptan.
Terminalia chebula (Haritaki) possesses antioxidant and neuroprotective properties relevant to migraine.
Curcuma longa (turmeric) reduces inflammation and may block CGRP-related pathways relevant to migraine.
Strength training produced a greater reduction in migraine frequency than high-intensity or moderate-intensity aerobic exercise.
MBSR significantly improved disability, quality of life, pain catastrophizing, and depression compared to an education control, despite similar reductions in migraine days between groups.
Physical therapy is primarily beneficial for cervical musculoskeletal dysfunction, postural abnormalities, and impaired sensorimotor control in migraine patients.
Chronic overlapping pain conditions (COPCs) as a group were associated with increased odds of type 2 diabetes in Veterans, with adjusted odds ratios ranging from 1.23 to 1.64 across eight COPCs.
Migraine was associated with increased odds of type 2 diabetes in Veterans, with the lowest adjusted odds ratio among the eight COPCs examined.
Fibromyalgia showed the strongest association with type 2 diabetes among the eight COPCs examined.
Among Veterans with T2D, those with both COPCs and diabetic peripheral neuropathy (DPN) had the highest odds of reporting high pain levels compared with those with neither condition.
Veterans with T2D who had both COPCs and DPN had higher odds of reporting sleep concerns than those with neither condition.
Veterans with T2D who had both COPCs and DPN had markedly higher odds of major depressive disorder (MDD) than those with neither condition.
Veterans with T2D who had both COPCs and DPN had markedly higher odds of posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) than those with neither condition.

Among Veterans with type 2 diabetes, those with chronic overlapping pain conditions only (no diabetic peripheral neuropathy) had lower odds of having an A1C greater than 8% compared to the reference group.

When chronic overlapping pain conditions co-occur with diabetic peripheral neuropathy in Veterans with type 2 diabetes, they appear to exert an additive negative effect on pain, sleep, and mental health outcomes compared to either condition alone.
The overall chronic pain group reported significantly higher Low Sensory Threshold (LST) scores than healthy controls, with a moderate effect size.
The overall chronic pain group showed significantly higher Ease of Excitation (EOE) scores than healthy controls, with a small-to-moderate effect size.
The overall chronic pain group showed significantly higher Negative Affectivity (NA) than healthy controls.
The overall chronic pain group showed significantly higher Detachment (DE) than healthy controls, a small effect.
The overall chronic pain group showed significantly higher Psychoticism (PSY) than healthy controls, a small effect.
In network analysis of the chronic pain group, Detachment was the most central node (highest closeness, betweenness, and strength) among all temperament/personality dimensions.

In healthy controls, Negative Affectivity (rather than Detachment) was the most central node (highest closeness) of the temperament/personality network, differing from the pattern seen in chronic pain groups.
Patients with chronic headache showed significantly higher LST scores than healthy controls, with a large effect size.
Patients with fibromyalgia showed significantly higher LST scores than healthy controls, with a large effect size.
Patients with comorbid chronic pain conditions (two or more diagnoses) showed the highest LST scores, significantly exceeding both healthy controls and single-condition fibromyalgia patients.
Patients with comorbid chronic pain conditions showed the highest EOE scores, differentiating them from healthy controls and from patients with vulvodynia alone.
Negative Affectivity was elevated relative to healthy controls across all four chronic pain groups (chronic headache, vulvodynia, fibromyalgia, comorbid), with small-to-moderate effect sizes.

Detachment and Psychoticism were highest in patients with comorbid chronic pain conditions, differentiating this COMPLEX group from chronic headache and vulvodynia but not from fibromyalgia, with small effect sizes.
Within the chronic headache subgroup's personality network, Psychoticism showed a high betweenness value, acting as an important bridge node, whereas in vulvodynia PSY betweenness was null.
In the vulvodynia subgroup's personality network, Detachment showed higher betweenness values than in other clinical groups, which had null DE betweenness.

The authors propose that the elevated LST and EOE temperamental traits found in chronic pain groups partially overlap with central sensitization, a core pathophysiological mechanism of nociplastic pain.
Prior literature cited indicates that chronic headache co-occurs in 45%-80% of patients with fibromyalgia.
Prior literature cited indicates that 20%-36% of patients with chronic headache meet diagnostic criteria for fibromyalgia.

A GRU-D recurrent neural network time-series model predicted moderate-to-severe headache on the next calendar day with a held-out test AUC of 0.84, outperforming classical machine learning and the TabPFN foundation model.
The GRU-D model forecasting moderate-to-severe headache within the following three calendar days achieved a held-out test AUC of 0.76.
A decision tree classifier was the best-performing classical machine learning model for next-day headache forecasting, achieving only modest discrimination.
The TabPFN foundation model performed poorly for next-day headache forecasting, close to chance level.
For 3-day forecasting, the decision tree classifier performed near chance level.
For 3-day forecasting, TabPFN achieved modest test-set discrimination despite a higher cross-validated AUC.

When same-day headache presence, intensity, and duration were excluded from the model to prevent conflating attack continuation with true onset prediction, the GRU-D model still performed nearly as well, supporting genuine prodromal signal detection.
When restricted to predicting new-onset moderate-to-severe headache following a headache-free day, the GRU-D model retained good discrimination.

Permutation feature importance analysis of the best-performing GRU-D model identified headache intensity, headache duration, and heart rate during biofeedback sessions as the strongest predictors for next-day headache forecasting.
The best 24-hour GRU-D model showed low sensitivity but very high specificity, meaning it excels at identifying headache-free days but performs poorly at predicting headache days.
The 3-day forecasting model showed a more balanced sensitivity and specificity than the 24-hour model.
Feature selection strategies (ANOVA, mutual information, random forest importance), data scaling, and resampling/balancing methods including forest diffusion did not improve model performance.
A prior headache diary and sleep-data forecasting model in seven individuals with migraine achieved good per-person accuracy but only near-chance user-independent accuracy.
A prior model linking headache diary and weather data achieved moderate predictive performance for headache occurrence.
A pilot study using the same biofeedback setup as the present study achieved a substantially lower test-set AUC than the current larger-sample GRU-D model.
Self-reported stress and headache diary data were previously used to forecast headache with moderate accuracy.

Autonomic nervous system dysfunction in migraine shows a bidirectional pattern, with sympathetic hypoactivity between attacks and sympathetic hyperactivity during attacks, complicating its use as a stable forecasting biomarker.
Autonomic symptoms have been reported not to consistently correlate with migraine attack frequency or severity, limiting their utility as forecasting biomarkers.

The migraine prodrome is described as involving hypothalamic dysregulation, autonomic imbalance, and sensory hypersensitivity, but these processes are neither uniform across patients nor consistently detectable.
More than half of patients with a newly diagnosed autoimmune rheumatic disease had at least one chronic overlapping pain condition (COPC) diagnosed in the surrounding year.
Prior literature cited in the paper reports that Sjögren's disease patients have the highest prevalence of concomitant COPC diagnosis (62%) among common autoimmune rheumatic diseases.
Female sex was associated with a higher likelihood of having a COPC diagnosis compared with male ARD patients.

Across the full cohort, pain medication burden was high in the year following ARD diagnosis, with a mean MQS-IV score of 3.8, a mean of 9.0 distinct pain medications filled, and 2.1 distinct medication categories used.
Nearly half of all ARD patients met criteria for minor polypharmacy, defined as filling five or more distinct pain medications within one year of diagnosis.
Nearly one-third of ARD patients met criteria for severe polypharmacy, filling ten or more distinct pain medications within one year of diagnosis.

Ankylosing spondylitis patients had the highest overall pain medication burden of all ARDs studied, including the highest MQS-IV score, medication count, and category breadth, with over a third meeting severe polypharmacy criteria.

Patients with rheumatoid arthritis and systemic lupus erythematosus showed similarly high pain medication burden, with approximately half meeting minor polypharmacy criteria and nearly a third meeting severe polypharmacy criteria.
Systemic sclerosis patients had the lowest pain medication burden of all ARDs across every measure.

Psoriatic arthritis and Sjögren's disease patients showed intermediate levels of pain medication use relative to the highest-burden (ankylosing spondylitis) and lowest-burden (systemic sclerosis) ARD groups.
Pain medication burden across ARDs rose steadily from 2008 through 2014-2015 and then gradually declined thereafter, a pattern consistent across all polypharmacy metrics.
The mean number of distinct pain medications filled per patient significantly declined after the 2015 national prescribing guideline update compared with before.
The mean number of distinct pain medication categories used per patient decreased significantly after 2015.
Mean MQS-IV scores, reflecting cumulative medication detriment, decreased significantly after the 2015 prescribing guideline update.
The proportions of patients meeting minor and severe polypharmacy criteria both declined modestly after the 2015 prescribing guideline update.
Patients without a diagnosed COPC received substantially fewer pain medications than patients with a COPC.
Patients with migraine, chronic tension-type headache, urologic chronic pelvic pain syndrome, or fibromyalgia received a higher mean number of pain medications than patients with other COPC types.
Unlike most COPC patient groups, whose medication counts fell from before to after 2015, fibromyalgia patients showed an increase in mean and median pain medication counts over the same period.
Among fibromyalgia patients, the mean number of pain medications increased after 2015 within every underlying autoimmune rheumatic disease except ankylosing spondylitis.

Within ankylosing spondylitis, rheumatoid arthritis, and systemic lupus erythematosus, comorbid fibromyalgia was associated with a steeper rise in pain medication use after 2015, diverging from the overall declining trend seen in the broader ARD population.
CGRP has been identified as a key molecular target for trigeminal nerve-associated migraine therapy.
PACAP has been identified as a key molecular target for trigeminal nerve-associated migraine therapy.
The MERTK-Galectin-3 signaling pathway is proposed as an emerging mechanism contributing to cluster headache pathophysiology and peripheral sensitization.
The trigeminal ganglion exhibits robust circadian rhythms, suggesting a link between headache chronobiology and the timing of drug administration (chronotherapy).
Indolent systemic mastocytosis is a clonal mast cell disease primarily driven by the KIT D816V mutation, which avapritinib selectively inhibits.
Long-term avapritinib treatment produced a durable and clinically meaningful reduction in total symptom score over approximately 3 years.
The long-term safety profile of avapritinib remained comparable to that seen in the earlier placebo-controlled portion of the trial.
Most treatment-related adverse events with long-term avapritinib were grade 1-2, with only limited grade 3 or higher events reported.
Edema was the most frequently reported treatment-related adverse event with long-term avapritinib, and was mostly grade 1 in severity.
Discontinuation due to treatment-related adverse events was uncommon, occurring in only 7 of 226 patients (3%) over the long-term follow-up period.
Patients remained on avapritinib treatment for a median duration of 40.0 months, with some patients treated for over five years, indicating durability of long-term use.
The long-term safety profile of avapritinib in the open-label extension was comparable to that observed in the earlier placebo-controlled portion of the trial.
In the open-label extension (part 3), investigators could increase the avapritinib dose up to 50 mg once daily based on clinical judgment and disease burden.

A significantly greater proportion of patients treated with galcanezumab achieved a clinically meaningful reduction in monthly migraine headache days at 3 months compared with the TOMP efficacy subset of topiramate, amitriptyline, and other guideline-recommended oral preventives.
Galcanezumab showed a trend toward greater 3-month responder rate than topiramate, though this comparison was not prespecified for formal testing.
Galcanezumab showed a trend toward a substantially greater 3-month responder rate than amitriptyline, though this comparison was not prespecified for formal testing.
In the earlier TRIUMPH primary analysis, a significantly greater proportion of galcanezumab-treated patients achieved clinically meaningful response at 3 months compared with the broader TOMP group.
Patients initiating galcanezumab had a higher mean number of comorbid conditions at baseline than those initiating TOMP efficacy subset drugs, topiramate, or amitriptyline.
The galcanezumab cohort demonstrated higher interictal migraine burden at baseline compared with the TOMP cohort as measured by the MIBS-4 total score.

The galcanezumab and topiramate cohorts showed the highest baseline migraine-related disability and quality-of-life burden among the treatment cohorts, as measured by MSQ Role Function-Restrictive domain and MIDAS scores.

In the cited HER-MES randomized trial, erenumab showed more favorable tolerability and efficacy compared with topiramate, with higher treatment persistence and a significantly greater proportion achieving a ≥50% reduction in monthly migraine days.

A cited indirect meta-analysis found comparable efficacy between CGRP monoclonal antibodies (erenumab, galcanezumab, fremanezumab, eptinezumab) and topiramate, but only topiramate doses of ≥100 mg effectively reduced monthly migraine days compared with placebo, doses often not achieved in clinical practice.

Propensity score models for lomerizine and propranolol produced inconsistent, unbalanced results likely due to inadequate sample size, precluding meaningful comparisons with galcanezumab; these drugs were excluded from further analysis.
Most patients across the migraine treatment cohorts were female, reflecting the known female predominance of migraine.
The pooled random-effects prevalence of chronic pain across 52 general-population studies was 26.99%.
Pooled chronic pain prevalence was significantly higher in females (31.42%) than males (21.63%).
Chronic pain prevalence estimates were similar across geographic regions (South America, Europe, Asia, North America) with no statistically significant difference.
Chronic pain prevalence was significantly higher among adults aged ≥45 years (46.68%) than those aged ≥18 years (24.23%).
Prevalence estimates did not differ significantly between interview-based and questionnaire-based data collection methods.
Chronic pain prevalence did not differ significantly between studies sampling at a national level versus regional/local level.
Pooled chronic pain prevalence did not differ significantly by study risk-of-bias category (low, moderate, high risk).
Leave-one-out sensitivity analysis showed the pooled chronic pain prevalence estimate remained stable, ranging from 27.70% to 29.04%.
A cited study from Benin, West Africa found high prevalence of chronic lower back pain in both urban and rural populations, associated with age, marital status, and employment status.
A separate meta-analysis of African school teachers found a pooled chronic low back pain prevalence of 59%.
A prior analysis combining European and American data found chronic widespread pain prevalence of 8.9% and 10.9%, respectively.

Transesophageal echocardiography with saline bubble study performed late in the hospitalization confirmed a patent foramen ovale causing right-to-left shunting responsible for the patient's platypnea-orthodeoxia syndrome.
The patient exhibited marked positional hypoxemia, with oxygen saturation dropping to as low as 56-60% while seated and recovering to 97% when supine.
Percutaneous transcatheter closure of the patent foramen ovale led to rapid improvement in oxygen saturation, allowing reduction of supplemental oxygen and resolution of positional desaturation.
After PFO closure, the patient reported reduced frequency and intensity of his migraine with aura episodes.
Multiple meta-analyses have shown an increased prevalence of patent foramen ovale among patients with migraine compared to the general population.
The magnitude of right-to-left shunting through a patent foramen ovale is reported to be greater in patients with migraine with aura than those without aura.

Vasoactive substances such as serotonin, released via platelet activation, are hypothesized to bypass pulmonary metabolic filtration through a right-to-left shunt and reach the intracranial circulation, potentially triggering migraine episodes.

A connective tissue disorder has been hypothesized to underlie the co-occurrence of patent foramen ovale and aortic dilation, both of which were present in this patient (aortic root 51 mm, ascending aorta 53 mm).
Dilation of the ascending aorta is proposed to distort cardiac structure and alter interatrial septal position/orientation, increasing right-to-left shunting through a patent foramen ovale.
PFO closure has been shown to be safe and effective long-term in patients over 60 years old, with only a slight increase in atrial fibrillation compared to patients younger than 60.

The patient developed traumatic left peroneal neuropathy and lumbosacral radiculopathy, attributed to compression bandaging used for thrombosis prevention, causing weakness and paresthesia that impaired ambulation.

Extremely low dose norepinephrine infusion (0.17-1.0 μg/min) alleviated acute headache attacks in both patients with refractory chronic cluster headache who had previously failed multiple pharmacologic therapies.
Case 1 showed no improvement despite sufficient trials of pregabalin, the CGRP monoclonal antibody galcanezumab, the CGRP receptor antagonist rimegepant, triptans, and flunarizine.
Case 2 did not respond to preventive treatment with topiramate, gabapentin, or lithium carbonate.

After treatment (norepinephrine infusion plus preventive medications), headache attack frequency and acute medication use decreased, MSQ, MIDAS, HRSD and HAMA scores decreased, and HR-QOL dimension scores increased compared with baseline.
Continuous ECG and blood pressure monitoring showed no arrhythmias, palpitations, chest pain, or other cardiovascular adverse events during norepinephrine infusion in either patient.
Case 1 had one transient blood pressure elevation to 152/94 mmHg during a headache exacerbation, which resolved spontaneously within 10 minutes without requiring dose adjustment.

Transient worsening of headache occurred in Case 1 during treatment, attributed to overly rapid reduction of the norepinephrine infusion rate, suggesting gradual tapering may be needed to avoid rebound headache.
At one-year follow-up, both patients remained attack-free on regular preventive therapy, had returned to normal daily activities, and maintained improved scores on headache-related scales.
Prior literature has reported lower serum norepinephrine levels in cluster headache patients compared with healthy controls, suggesting sympathetic hypofunction contributes to CH pathophysiology.
Vasodilation is proposed as a key pathophysiological feature of cluster headache, primarily mediated through activation of the trigeminal autonomic vascular reflex.

Activation of the trigeminal autonomic vascular reflex triggers secretion of neuropeptides including PACAP-38, acetylcholine, and vasoactive intestinal peptide, which induce vasodilation and sensitize sensory nerve endings during cluster headache attacks.

Norepinephrine is proposed to act on α2-adrenergic receptors in the spinal dorsal horn and trigeminal nucleus caudalis, inhibiting nociceptive transmission through the descending pain modulatory system originating in the locus coeruleus.

Adrenergic receptors expressed on trigeminal sensory neurons may allow norepinephrine to directly modulate neuronal excitability and neuropeptide release, potentially attenuating trigeminal nerve activation in cluster headache.

At discharge, both patients were prescribed maintenance preventive medication regimens (verapamil for both; methylprednisolone and topiramate for Case 1; paroxetine for Case 2) to prevent recurrence of cluster headache.
NTG-induced migraine model rats showed elevated CGRP levels in serum and medulla compared to controls, which were reduced by CX-BZ pretreatment.
CX-BZ pretreatment reduced elevated CGRP levels in serum and medulla of NTG-induced migraine model rats.
NTG-induced migraine model rats exhibited elevated TNF-alpha levels in serum and medulla, which were lowered by CX-BZ pretreatment.
CX-BZ pretreatment significantly reduced writhing frequency, a marker of migraine-like nociceptive behavior, in NTG-induced rats.
CX-BZ pretreatment increased thermal pain thresholds in NTG-induced migraine model rats, indicating reduced hyperalgesia.
Untargeted metabolomic profiling revealed distinct metabolic alterations between the model and CX-BZ-treated groups, mainly involving amino acid metabolism and the TCA cycle.
Targeted metabolomics using UPLC-QQQ-MS confirmed regulation of key metabolites within amino acid metabolism and TCA cycle pathways by CX-BZ treatment.
CX-BZ pretreatment (herb pair combination) reduced migraine-like behaviors and normalized inflammatory and metabolic markers in a dose-related manner across low-, medium-, and high-dose groups.
Targeted metabolomics using UPLC-QQQ-MS validated that CX-BZ treatment regulates key metabolites within amino acid metabolism and the TCA cycle pathways that were altered in the migraine model.

Combined therapy with nebivolol and a perindopril arginine/indapamide/amlodipine fixed-dose combination produced complete and sustained remission of migraine attacks and cranial-autonomic symptoms (rhinorrhea, sneezing, tearing) over 12 months of follow-up.
At age 41 the patient developed persistent mild arterial hypertension (~150/95 mmHg) and resting tachycardia (>90 bpm), coinciding with increased fatigue and more frequent headaches.

During the later phase of chronic sumatriptan use, dosing was consistently followed 30-40 minutes after intake by a transient episode of autonomic arousal and sensory hypersensitivity, including diffuse muscle aching and mild pain to normally non-painful stimuli, resolving over 2-4 hours and never occurring without triptan use.

The patient experienced spontaneous interictal episodes of intense parasympathetic outflow—repetitive sneezing (7-10 in succession) followed by profuse watery rhinorrhea unresponsive to antihistamines or decongestants—occurring independently of headache pain and sometimes preceding migraine onset by 24-48 hours.

The authors propose that nebivolol enhances nitric-oxide bioavailability and attenuates sympathetic overdrive, while perindopril, amlodipine, and indapamide improve endothelial reactivity and decrease oxidative stress, potentially contributing to the observed migraine remission.

Migraine attacks occurred predominantly on Saturdays (3-4 times per month) and both headache and nasal/tearing symptoms often resolved after sleep before treatment, suggesting a circadian/behavioral autonomic resetting pattern that disappeared after therapy.

The headache phenotype (pulsatile quality, photophobia, phonophobia, osmophobia, occasional nausea/vomiting, triptan responsiveness) fulfilled ICHD-3 criteria for migraine without aura, and was distinguishable from hypertensive headache and trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias despite prominent cranial-autonomic features.

The authors note (from cited literature, not tested in this patient) that endothelial nitric oxide synthase (eNOS) and CGRP receptor gene polymorphisms may influence individual response to vascular-targeted migraine therapy.

The stereotyped sneezing-then-rhinorrhea episodes are proposed to reflect an acute trigemino-parasympathetic reflex discharge governed by the sphenopalatine ganglion and superior salivatory nucleus, analogous to experimentally described sphenopalatine ganglion stimulation causing vasodilation and plasma protein extravasation.

A meta-analysis of 3,875 acute ischemic stroke patients found vertebral artery hypoplasia was significantly more prevalent in vertebrobasilar stroke patients than in patients with anterior circulation strokes.

A one-year prospective cohort of 420 vertebrobasilar stroke patients found that vascular configurations such as arterial bending and VA hypoplasia were significantly associated with large-artery atherosclerosis, recurrent stroke/TIA, and mortality.
Only 5.3% of patients with sonographic evidence of subclavian steal syndrome are symptomatic.

Atherosclerosis causes stenosis/occlusion in over 90% of subclavian steal syndrome cases, and the left subclavian artery is affected in more than 80% of cases due to its more acute origin angle promoting turbulent flow.
Vertebral artery obstructions exceeding 50% are associated with an increased risk of stroke.
Vertebral artery dissection is a considerable cause of ischemic stroke in young and middle-aged patients, accounting for 10% to 25% of cases.
Nearly 40% of patients with vertebrobasilar dolichoectasia develop cranial nerve VIII-related disorders, arising from thrombotic-ischemic and/or compressive mechanisms.

An imbalance between metalloproteinase and proteinase activity in arterial wall connective tissue is proposed as a mechanism underlying vertebrobasilar dolichoectasia, causing abnormal vascular remodeling and defective connective tissue formation.

In obstructive sleep apnea, hypoxic episodes trigger a cascade of pro-inflammatory cytokines (IL-1, IL-6, TNF-α, interferon-γ) that damage the vascular endothelium and increase platelet aggregation, contributing to stroke risk.

Treatment of obstructive sleep apnea with CPAP was associated with improvements in migraine, including a reduction in mean attack frequency from 5.8 to 0.1 days per month, along with reduced attack duration, pain intensity, and disability days.
In a propensity-matched retrospective cohort of 196,864 OSA patients and 196,864 non-OSA controls, OSA was associated with a 1.85-fold higher risk of developing incident migraine.

Migraine, particularly migrainous infarction, is linked to increased ischemic stroke risk especially in young women, potentially mediated by inflammatory/endothelial alterations, patent foramen ovale, oral contraceptive use, smoking, and vasoconstrictor medications (triptans, ergot derivatives).
Reversible cerebral vasoconstriction syndrome is characterized by thunderclap headaches, sometimes with vertigo, and multifocal cerebral artery narrowing that typically resolves within three months.
Orthostatic hypotension, arising from dysautonomic dysregulation, is a common cause of dizziness, unsteadiness, vertigo, and syncope and is often associated with postural tachycardia syndrome.
Orthostatic hypotension is defined as a systolic BP drop >20 mmHg and/or diastolic BP drop >10 mmHg within 3 minutes of standing from sitting or during head-up tilt testing.

The combination of aging and extreme nocturnal blood pressure dipping (≥20% drop) has been reported to be associated with cerebrovascular damage and cardiovascular events, though evidence remains limited and its clinical significance is controversial.
The Holter monitor, though the gold standard for diagnosing arrhythmias, fails to provide a diagnosis in more than 90% of syncope-related cases.

Small vessel disease is hypothesized to reflect impaired cerebral autoregulation in the deep white matter, making cerebral perfusion pressure-dependent and sensitive to mild systemic hypotension, producing a vague sense of imbalance not meeting criteria for other vestibular disorders.

Newman-Toker et al. proposed that global blood pressure reductions produce local asymmetries in vestibular blood flow due to congenital or acquired left-right vascular caliber differences, causing vertigo via an ischemic mechanism.
A patient developed neurogenic orthostatic hypotension after resection of a brainstem tumor that caused unilateral damage to the Nucleus of the Solitary Tract.
A second patient presented with afferent baroreflex failure due to a giant vascular tumor compressing the brainstem near the Nucleus of the Solitary Tract.
A third patient with an infiltrating and expanding brainstem tumor exhibited both neurogenic orthostatic hypotension and afferent baroreflex failure simultaneously.
In the fully adjusted Cox model, women with long COVID had more than double the risk of a composite cardiovascular event compared with women without long COVID.
Men with long COVID had a significantly increased risk of a composite cardiovascular event compared with men without long COVID, though the effect was smaller than in women.
Women with long COVID had a more than three-fold increased risk of cardiac arrhythmia compared with women without long COVID.
Men with long COVID had an increased risk of cardiac arrhythmia compared with men without long COVID, though the magnitude was smaller than in women.
Long COVID was associated with a significantly increased risk of coronary artery disease in women.
Long COVID was associated with a significantly increased risk of coronary artery disease in men, similar in magnitude to women.
Long COVID was associated with a modestly, marginally significant increased risk of heart failure in women after adjustment.
Long COVID was not significantly associated with heart failure risk in men after adjustment.
Long COVID was associated with an increased risk of peripheral arterial disease in women but not men.
Long COVID was not significantly associated with peripheral arterial disease in men.
Long COVID showed no statistically significant association with stroke in women.
Long COVID showed no statistically significant association with stroke in men, though a trend toward reduced risk was observed.
Unadjusted cumulative incidence of any cardiovascular event was more than double in women with long COVID and nearly double in men with long COVID compared with their respective unexposed groups.

In a propensity score-matched sensitivity analysis with additional adjustment for prepandemic healthcare use, the association between long COVID and peripheral arterial disease was attenuated and no longer statistically significant, unlike the other outcomes which remained robust.
Between October 2020 and January 2025, 8999 individuals (0.7% of the study population; mean age 41.6 years) received a physician-assigned long COVID diagnosis, with two-thirds being women.
The authors propose that persistent endothelial dysfunction, autonomic dysregulation, and immune-mediated injury underlie the observed cardiovascular complications of long COVID.

The pronounced increase in arrhythmia risk among women with long COVID is discussed as consistent with prior reports of elevated postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome and cardiovascular dysautonomia in long COVID populations.
16.2% of veterans treated for fibromyalgia in the VHA in 2022 experienced CNS-active medication polypharmacy.
13.5% of veterans treated for migraine in the VHA in 2022 experienced CNS-active medication polypharmacy.
8.2% of veterans treated for IBS in the VHA in 2022 experienced CNS-active medication polypharmacy.
In fibromyalgia, rural veterans had a similar mean number of concurrent CNS-active medications compared to urban veterans (2.59 vs 2.63).
In migraine, rural veterans had a similar mean number of concurrent CNS-active medications compared to urban veterans (2.43 vs 2.40).
Among veterans with IBS, rural veterans had a slightly lower mean number of concurrent CNS-active medications (1.75) than urban veterans (1.79).

After adjusting for demographics and medical/psychiatric comorbidities, rural residence was associated with only minimally elevated risk of increased concurrent CNS-active medication count across fibromyalgia, migraine, and IBS.
Veterans receiving primary care from rural clinics versus medical centers showed minimally reduced risk of increased CNS-active medication count across the three conditions.
The study concluded that rural residence does not appear to increase risk of CNS-active medication polypharmacy among veterans with fibromyalgia, migraine, or IBS.

Individuals with chronic pain showed significant cortical thinning in the right lingual gyrus, right parahippocampal gyrus, right fusiform gyrus, and left transverse temporal gyrus compared to healthy controls.

Before adjusting for intracranial volume, chronic pain patients showed reduced grey matter volume in the left parahippocampal gyrus, right lingual gyrus, and bilateral entorhinal cortex, the latter being the only region with bilateral alterations across classic structural metrics.

After adjusting for total intracranial volume, none of the previously significant cortical volumetric reductions (including bilateral entorhinal cortex) remained statistically significant, despite minimal change in effect size magnitude.
No cortical region showed a significant difference in surface area between chronic pain patients and healthy controls.
Chronic pain was associated with widespread, nearly global increases in intrinsic (Gaussian) curvature, affecting 49 cortical regions, 21 of which were bilateral.

Extrinsic (mean) curvature was significantly increased in chronic pain patients in the left lateral orbitofrontal cortex, left temporal pole, and right caudal anterior cingulate cortex, with low inter-study heterogeneity.

No subcortical structure (thalamus, accumbens, caudate, putamen, pallidum, hippocampus, amygdala) showed a significant volumetric difference between chronic pain patients and healthy controls, either before or after ICV adjustment.
After ICV adjustment, the amygdala showed a non-negligible trend toward reduced volume in chronic pain bilaterally, though this did not reach FDR-corrected significance overall.
After ICV adjustment, the right hippocampus showed a non-negligible trend toward reduced volume in chronic pain, though this did not reach FDR-corrected significance overall.
After ICV adjustment, the left cerebellar cortex showed a non-negligible trend toward reduced volume in chronic pain, though this did not reach FDR-corrected significance overall.

Significant cross-study heterogeneity was found in seven cortical region-metric combinations, mostly involving intrinsic curvature (left posterior cingulate, right fusiform, right caudal anterior cingulate, right lingual cortex, left precentral gyrus), plus extrinsic curvature of the superior frontal gyrus and volume of the rostral middle frontal gyrus.

Five subcortical regions showed significant between-study heterogeneity, with the pallidum (bilaterally) showing the widest prediction intervals, along with right cerebellar white matter, left ventral diencephalon, and brain stem.
No structural or curvature-based brain metric, nor any subcortical volume, showed a statistically significant sex difference between men and women with chronic pain.

Across all structural and curvature metrics, every statistically significant chronic-pain-related effect fell in the small effect size range (|g| > 0.2 but < 0.5), with none reaching medium effect size.
Both this IPD meta-analysis and prior aggregate meta-analyses converge on the parahippocampal gyrus, a limbic structure involved in pain modulation, as prominently altered in chronic pain.
Individuals with bipolar disorder had a significantly higher absolute lifetime risk of migraine than those without bipolar disorder, with a larger absolute risk difference in women than men.
Migraine risk was more strongly elevated in bipolar disorder type 2 than type 1 relative to the general population.

The authors note that migraine and epilepsy may precede rather than follow bipolar disorder onset, which may explain differing risk estimates when bipolar disorder was modeled as a time-varying (diagnosis-onward) exposure versus a lifetime exposure.
Individuals with bipolar disorder had a significantly higher absolute lifetime risk of fibromyalgia than those without bipolar disorder, with a much larger effect in women.
Fibromyalgia risk was markedly higher in bipolar disorder type 2 than type 1, and was not statistically significant in men with type 1.
Fibromyalgia and chronic fatigue syndrome were roughly three times more prevalent among people with bipolar disorder than the general population, although the absolute risk of each remained under 1%.
Individuals with bipolar disorder had a significantly higher absolute lifetime risk of chronic fatigue syndrome than those without bipolar disorder.
Chronic fatigue syndrome risk was numerically higher in bipolar disorder type 2 than type 1, though the estimate for men with bipolar I disorder was not statistically significant.
Individuals with bipolar disorder had a significantly higher absolute lifetime risk of irritable bowel syndrome than those without bipolar disorder, more pronounced in women.
Irritable bowel syndrome risk was higher in bipolar disorder type 2 than type 1 relative to the general population, in both sexes.

When bipolar disorder was modeled as a time-varying exposure starting at first diagnosis rather than as a lifetime exposure from birth, risk estimates for fibromyalgia and restless legs syndrome were attenuated compared with the main analysis.
Network meta-analysis estimated a mean difference of -0.81 in weekly attack frequency for galcanezumab 300 mg versus placebo, without reaching statistical significance.
Network meta-analysis estimated a mean difference of -0.17 in weekly attack frequency for eptinezumab 400 mg versus placebo, without statistical significance.
Network meta-analysis estimated a mean difference of +0.71 (numerically favoring placebo) in weekly attack frequency for fremanezumab 675/225 mg, without statistical significance.

Network meta-analysis estimated a mean difference of -1.27 in weekly attack frequency for fremanezumab 900/225 mg versus placebo, the largest numerical reduction observed but not statistically significant.
The pooled dose estimate for galcanezumab across trials showed a mean reduction in weekly cluster headache attack frequency of 0.81 compared to placebo.
The pooled dose estimate for fremanezumab across trials showed a mean reduction in weekly cluster headache attack frequency of 0.27 compared to placebo.
The pooled dose estimate for eptinezumab across trials showed a mean reduction in weekly cluster headache attack frequency of 0.17 compared to placebo.
Combining all agents, pairwise meta-analysis found an overall pooled reduction in weekly cluster headache attack frequency of 0.41 versus placebo.
Subgroup analysis found only minimal change in attack frequency for patients with chronic cluster headache treated with CGRP monoclonal antibodies.
Subgroup analysis found a greater numerical reduction in attack frequency for patients with episodic cluster headache treated with CGRP monoclonal antibodies compared to chronic cluster headache.

Across the pooled network meta-analysis, no CGRP monoclonal antibody achieved a statistically significant reduction in weekly cluster headache attack frequency compared with placebo, despite consistent numerical trends favoring treatment.
Subgroup analysis suggested that CGRP monoclonal antibody efficacy signals were more pronounced in episodic cluster headache than in chronic cluster headache, where change was minimal.
Pooled meta-analysis of three studies found no statistically significant difference in absolute LF power between women with and without vasomotor symptoms.
Pooled meta-analysis of three studies found no statistically significant difference in absolute HF power between women with and without vasomotor symptoms.
Pooled analysis of three studies showed no significant difference in the absolute LF/HF ratio between women with and without vasomotor symptoms.
Pooled analysis found no significant difference in RMSSD between women with and without vasomotor symptoms.
Pooled analysis found no significant difference in SDNN between women with and without vasomotor symptoms.
In an individual study of 45 Japanese peri- and postmenopausal women, LF power was significantly lower in women with vasomotor symptoms compared to those without.
In the same individual study, HF power was also significantly lower in women with vasomotor symptoms, indicating lower cardiac parasympathetic function.
