Menopausal women with vasomotor symptoms had higher mean heart rate and higher systolic and diastolic blood pressure than women without symptoms, suggested to reflect compensatory vascular sympathetic activation for reduced cardiac parasympathetic function.
In an individual study of 36 postmenopausal women, the LF/HF ratio was significantly higher in women with vasomotor symptoms compared to those without, indicating increased sympathetic dominance.
In a 24-hour ambulatory ECG study of 150 postmenopausal women, RMSSD was significantly lower in women with vasomotor symptoms, indicating reduced parasympathetic function.
In the same 24-hour ambulatory study, no association was found between frequency-domain HRV markers (LF and HF power) and the overall frequency or severity of vasomotor symptoms.

The authors note that, based on prior cardiovascular literature, lower LF power and RMSSD have been associated with increased cardiovascular risk, including worse outcomes after myocardial infarction and higher mortality in heart failure cohorts.
Migraine prevalence is roughly twice as high in women as in men, with age-related prevalence peaking between 30 and 50 years old.
Over 2 million Americans have chronic migraine, defined as at least 15 monthly migraine days.
More than one billion people worldwide live with migraine, which is the second leading cause of disability globally.
Chronic migraine affects approximately 0.8% of US adolescents aged 10-19, roughly 450,000 youth.
The prevalence of headaches, including migraine, among US children ages 0-17 is approximately 17%.

Pharmacological, device-based, behavioral, and lifestyle interventions for migraine prevention reduce monthly migraine days (MMD) by an average of 2-3 days, which may be insufficient for patients with chronic migraine (>15 MMD).
Pharmacotherapies targeting the CGRP pathway are recommended as the first-line preventive treatment for migraine.
Migraine shows strong familial aggregation, and polygenic risk scores predict both disease risk and response to pharmacotherapies.
Medication overuse is known to exacerbate migraine headaches.
Long-term exposure to environmental pollution can increase the risk of migraine, depression, anxiety, and cardiovascular disease.
Residential green spaces are associated with lower rates of chronic pain and other noncommunicable diseases, as well as reduced migraine and severe headaches.
Living within 300-500 meters of green space may improve mental health, reduce stress, and increase physical activity.
Self-efficacy, the belief in one's ability to manage and improve health, can reduce headache-related disability and improve adherence to behavioral therapies.

A review of 108 neuroimaging studies found that exposure to natural environments modulates large-scale brain networks (default mode, salience, and attentional networks), shifting neural activity toward reduced stress, restored attention, and emotional regulation.
Biophilic design in healthcare facilities such as hospitals and clinics can improve patient outcomes, including reduced stress, mortality, and hospitalization time.

In mice, repeated stress exposure raises circulating PACAP, which activates MRGPRB2 on dural mast cells and drives TRPV1-dependent sensitization of trigeminal ganglion neurons and headache-like behavior.
Dural PACAP acting on MrgprB2 induces mechanical facial allodynia and migraine-like responses in mice via mast cell degranulation.
Monoclonal antibodies against CGRP are approved for migraine treatment, and prevention of mast cell degranulation is thought to contribute to their therapeutic efficacy.

Mast cell-derived tryptase cleaves PAR2 to enhance substance P release, creating a bidirectional feedback loop between mast cells and nociceptors that sustains neurogenic inflammation and hyperalgesia.

Trigeminal ganglion stimulation evokes degranulation of adjacent dural mast cells, which release histamine, serotonin, and prostaglandin I2 (PGI2), producing TRPV1-dependent sensitization of meningeal nociceptors that contributes to prolonged migraine pain.
Rodent studies show that females exhibit greater thalamic mast cell infiltration than males following painful stimuli, associated with heightened sensitivity to neuropathic and inflammatory pain.
The total number of mast cells in the healthy adult mouse brain is estimated at approximately 300-500, substantially fewer than during development, with numbers declining with age.
In humans, meningeal and perivascular mast cell numbers increase substantially during viral, bacterial, or parasitic infection compared to the low baseline seen in healthy adults.
Sex differences in brain mast cell distribution are reported in both rodents and humans, with males showing higher mast cell numbers, particularly during birth and development.

In an Alzheimer's disease mouse model, mast cells respond to endogenous soluble amyloid-beta with elevated basal hemichannel activity and persistent histamine release via amyloid-beta-induced opening of Panx1 and Cx43 hemichannels, occurring before plaque formation and glial activation.

In a mast cell-deficient mouse model of multiple sclerosis, neutrophil influx into the brain was reduced and was restored after reintroducing mast cells, indicating a role for mast cells in early immune cell recruitment.

Mast cell-derived tryptase activates PAR2 on microglia, triggering release of IL-6, TNF, reactive oxygen species and BDNF via MAPK and NF-κB signaling; inhibiting tryptase release attenuates microglial activation, neuroinflammation, and hippocampal neuronal degeneration in vivo.

Mast cell-deficient mice have increased levels of labile zinc in the hippocampus compared to wild-type mice, with no differences in total zinc in whole brain or other tissues, and show elevated ZnT3 transporter expression in the dentate gyrus mossy fiber layer.

Early life adversity such as maternal separation increases mast cell numbers, chymase levels, and TNF expression in the dura of female mice but not males; adult stress similarly elevates chymase with associated anhedonia, and pretreatment with the mast cell stabilizer ketotifen prevents both the chymase increase and reduced sucrose preference.

Mast cell-deficient KitW-sh/W-sh mice show increased anxiety-like behavior and impaired social behavior, an effect replicated in wild-type mice by central administration of the mast cell stabilizer cromolyn, while cerebral compound 48/80 (a degranulator) increases exploratory and social behavior in wild-type but not mast cell-deficient mice.

Restraint stress-induced mast cell activation and dural vascular permeability increase were absent in NK1R-deficient mice but remained intact in substance P-deficient mice, suggesting NK1R-dependent, substance P-independent mast cell activation via alternative ligands.

Estrogen stimulates mast cells to release histamine, which together with estrogen drives microglial release of PGE2, promoting GnRH signaling important for masculinization; experimentally raising estradiol in neonatal female rats increases preoptic area mast cell numbers and masculinizes behavior, while inhibiting mast cell activity reduces male-typical copulatory behavior.

Tryptase has been shown to increase VCAM-1 expression in brain endothelial cells and can destabilize endothelial tight junction proteins including claudins and occludin through activation of PAR2, contributing to blood-brain barrier disruption.

Mast cell degranulation induced by compound 48/80 produced sex-dependent effects on thalamic neuronal activity in rats, with inhibitory effects in males and excitatory effects in females; these changes were not observed in mast cell-lacking brain regions.

Mast cells and mast cell-associated genes have been identified in lesions, white matter, and CSF of patients with multiple sclerosis, and MS drugs such as dimethyl fumarate, natalizumab, and masitinib are proposed to act partly through mast cell-related mechanisms.

Autopsy studies report numerous tryptase-containing mast cells in proximity to amyloid plaques in several brain regions in Alzheimer's disease, and patients with mastocytosis frequently experience depression and anxiety, though whether this reflects CNS-resident mast cells or peripheral mast cell mediators is unknown.
Baseline mean blood pressure and heart rate were significantly higher in male pithed rats than in female pithed rats.
The methoxamine-induced increase in mean blood pressure was significantly greater in female than in male pithed rats.
Continuous infusion of 5-CT (0.001 μg/kg/min) produced a sustained decrease in mean blood pressure during methoxamine-induced vasoconstriction in both male and female pithed rats.

AS-19 (5-HT7 receptor agonist, 20 μg/kg/min) produced a sustained decrease in mean blood pressure during methoxamine infusion in both male and female rats, consistent with 5-HT7 receptor-mediated vasodilation.

In female rats, pretreatment with the combination of GR127935 (5-HT1B/1D/1F antagonist) plus SB258719 (5-HT7 antagonist) reversed the vasodilator effect of 5-CT, reducing the blood pressure response to a level not significantly different from saline.
Baseline frequency-dependent vasodepressor responses to electrical stimulation of the perivascular CGRPergic outflow did not differ significantly between male and female pithed rats.
In male rats, continuous infusion of 5-CT significantly reduced the vasodepressor responses induced by electrical stimulation of the perivascular sensory CGRPergic outflow.
The 5-HT1B receptor agonist CP-93,129 mimicked the inhibitory effect of 5-CT on electrically induced CGRPergic vasodepressor responses in male rats.
The 5-HT1F receptor agonist LY344864 mimicked the inhibitory effect of 5-CT on electrically induced CGRPergic vasodepressor responses in male rats.
The 5-HT7 receptor agonist AS-19 mimicked the inhibitory effect of 5-CT on electrically induced CGRPergic vasodepressor responses in male rats.

Pretreatment with the 5-HT5A receptor antagonist SB699551 did not alter the inhibitory effect of 5-CT on electrically induced vasodepressor responses in male rats, excluding a role for 5-HT5A receptors.
In female rats, i.v. perfusion of 5-CT and the 5-HT7 agonist AS-19 inhibited the perivascular sensory CGRPergic vasodepressor responses to electrical stimulation.

In female rats, the 5-HT1F agonist LY344864 significantly reduced electrically induced CGRPergic vasodepressor responses, whereas the 5-HT1A agonist 8-OH-DPAT and the 5-HT1B/1D agonist sumatriptan had no effect.

In female rats, the 5-HT1A agonist 8-OH-DPAT and the 5-HT1B/1D agonist sumatriptan did not modify electrically induced CGRPergic vasodepressor responses, excluding a role for 5-HT1A and 5-HT1B/1D receptors.

In female rats, the combination of GR127935 plus SB258719 abolished the 5-CT-induced inhibition of perivascular sensory CGRPergic outflow, whereas the 5-HT5A antagonist SB699551 had no effect, confirming that 5-HT1F and 5-HT7 receptors mediate this inhibition.

AS-19 (5-HT7 agonist) significantly reduced the vasodepressor responses induced by exogenous α-CGRP administration in female rats, indicating a pre- and/or postjunctional site of action for 5-HT7 receptors.
LY344864 (5-HT1F agonist) did not modify vasodepressor responses to exogenous α-CGRP in female rats, indicating that its inhibitory action on CGRPergic outflow is purely prejunctional.

The 5-HT7 receptor-mediated inhibition of CGRPergic vasodilation is purely prejunctional in male rats but pre- and/or postjunctional in female rats, revealing a sex-dependent difference in receptor localization.
The title indicates a report on abnormal genital arousal together with sensory symptoms occurring in patients who have autonomic disorders and additional comorbidities.
Patients with comorbid migraine and fibromyalgia had a significantly higher frequency of chronic migraine than patients with migraine only.
Allodynia was significantly more frequent in patients with comorbid migraine and fibromyalgia than in migraine-only patients.
Monthly migraine days were significantly higher in patients with comorbid fibromyalgia than in migraine-only patients.
HIT-6 total scores (headache impact) were significantly higher in patients with comorbid fibromyalgia than in migraine-only patients.
Depression, anxiety, stress, and DASS-12 total scores were all significantly higher in patients with comorbid migraine and fibromyalgia compared to migraine-only patients.
Fibromyalgia severity (FIQR total score) correlated positively with depression, anxiety, stress, and DASS-12 total scores.
Fibromyalgia severity (FIQR total score) correlated positively with monthly migraine days and HIT-6 total scores.
DASS-12 total score correlated positively with monthly migraine days and HIT-6 total scores.
Fibromyalgia was independently associated with chronic migraine in an adjusted binary logistic regression model.
Longer migraine duration was independently associated with chronic migraine.
Allodynia was independently associated with chronic migraine.
Higher DASS-12 total score (psychological distress) was independently associated with chronic migraine.
Presence of fibromyalgia was independently associated with a higher DASS-12 total score in a multiple linear regression model.
Higher monthly migraine days were independently associated with higher DASS-12 total score.
Higher VAS pain intensity score was independently associated with higher DASS-12 total score.
Higher HIT-6 total score was independently associated with higher DASS-12 total score.
Patients with comorbid migraine and fibromyalgia had a significantly higher BMI than patients with migraine only.
Among patients with comorbid fibromyalgia, the majority had primary fibromyalgia while a minority had secondary fibromyalgia.
In patients with comorbid fibromyalgia, the median FIQR total score and domain scores indicated substantial fibromyalgia-related impact.
Central somatization and elevated glutamate levels are proposed shared pathophysiological mechanisms underlying both fibromyalgia and migraine, based on prior literature.
Anti-CGRP monoclonal antibodies are cited as a treatment targeting pathways shared by migraine and fibromyalgia.
The TRPA1 channel and glutamate receptors are proposed as future therapeutic targets shared by migraine and fibromyalgia.
Obesity in fibromyalgia is associated with greater levels of proinflammatory markers implicated in central sensitization, per cited prior literature.
Meta-analysis of 10 studies found that evening chronotypes had significantly higher odds of reporting chronic pain compared with non-evening chronotypes.
Pooled analysis of 6 studies showed only a nonsignificant trend toward greater pain intensity in evening chronotypes, with substantial heterogeneity.

Qualitative synthesis of the 43 included studies indicated that evening chronotypes were more frequently associated with adverse pain outcomes, including higher pain prevalence, greater intensity, and increased interference.
The association between evening chronotype and worse pain outcomes was particularly consistent in musculoskeletal pain and headache disorders, including migraine.
Some studies reported worse pain outcomes in morning types or bimodal chronotypes rather than evening types, indicating heterogeneity across conditions.
A greater number of painful body sites on the Michigan Body Map was associated with lower odds of treatment response to ERCP in chronic pancreatitis.

A greater number of painful body regions on the Michigan Body Map showed a trend toward lower odds of treatment response to ERCP in chronic pancreatitis, though not statistically significant at conventional threshold.
Higher scores on the Fibromyalgia Survey Questionnaire were associated with lower odds of treatment response to ERCP in chronic pancreatitis.
Higher Generalized Sensory Sensitivity scores were associated with lower odds of treatment response to ERCP in chronic pancreatitis.
Central Sensitization Inventory scores were not associated with treatment response to ERCP in chronic pancreatitis.

Among 53 surveyed chronic pancreatitis patients who underwent technically successful pancreatic ERCP, only 47% reported a treatment response (much or very much improved) on the Patient Global Impression of Change scale.
A systematic review established that autonomic dysfunction is a well-documented feature in migraine patients, supporting ANS modulation as a therapeutic target.
Several investigations found reduced parasympathetic activity among individuals with migraine.
Migraine patients showed significantly elevated resting pulse rate and mean heart rate compared to healthy controls.
Migraine patients exhibited significantly diminished mean R-R interval, SDANN, and RMSSD compared to healthy controls, indicating reduced heart rate variability.
Migraine patients, particularly women and those with migraine with aura, show increased cardiovascular risk including ischemic stroke and myocardial infarction.
Cohort studies identified a higher prevalence of cardiac arrhythmias such as atrial fibrillation among migraine patients, likely a consequence of autonomic dysfunction.
Migraine patients show reduced sympathetic vasomotor activity while supine and hyperresponsive sympathetic vasomotor activity while standing, reflecting postural autonomic dysregulation.
An increased vasoconstrictor index reflects the initial vasoconstriction phase of a migraine attack before transitioning into vasodilation.
Migraine with aura is associated with more pronounced autonomic dysfunction compared to migraine without aura.
The interictal period in migraine is characterized by greater sympathetic impairment, whereas the ictal period shows increased sympathetic responsiveness, suggesting adrenoreceptor hypersensitivity.
Neuropeptides and neurotransmitters including substance P, CGRP, and glutamate participate in propagating pain impulses within the trigeminovascular system during migraine.

A 2022 clinical trial found that repeated use of the Valsalva maneuver at symptom onset improved 'Overall Headache Relief Rate' and 'effectiveness of subsequent use' among participants, although pain scores did not significantly change.
In the clinical trial, some patients reported experiencing headaches after performing the Valsalva maneuver, though overall efficacy for headache relief remained favorable.
Transient modulation of cerebral blood flow dynamics and oxygen delivery by the Valsalva maneuver may relieve migraine symptoms by altering vascular tone and cerebral perfusion.
Preliminary angiographic studies support a role for basal artery wall tone dysregulation, such as in the carotid artery, in migraine pathogenesis.
Non-invasive vagus nerve stimulation significantly reduced migraine or headache days in a clinical trial.
Non-invasive cervical vagus nerve stimulation markedly increased the responder rate (≥50%) for migraine.
Low-frequency non-invasive auricular vagus nerve stimulation significantly reduced headache intensity in migraine.
During phase II of the Valsalva maneuver, an increase in CSF pressure can occasionally induce headaches, as observed in primary headache disorders triggered by the maneuver.
Transient hypoxia during Valsalva maneuver phase II potentially induces neural stimulation patterns that, combined with rapid recovery via deep exhalation, may contribute to migraine relief.
The Valsalva maneuver triggers release of endogenous opioids including endorphins, enkephalins, and dynorphins, particularly during the deep breath preceding phase I and deep exhalation in phase IV.
Release of neurotransmitters such as serotonin and GABA has been observed during the Valsalva maneuver.
Certain headache types such as exertional, cough-induced, or laugh-induced headaches can occasionally be triggered by the Valsalva maneuver, but these are typically localized and short-lived.
12 weeks of Pranayama increased mean RR interval by 4.53% in migraine patients, a greater increase than the 1.7% seen with standard care alone.
SDNN, a time-domain HRV index of overall autonomic variability, increased significantly by 17.42% after 12 weeks of Pranayama in migraine patients.
RMSSD, reflecting parasympathetic/vagal tone, increased by 35% in the Pranayama group compared to an 11.85% increase in the control group.
NN50, a marker of parasympathetic activity, increased by 132.35% in the yoga group while it decreased non-significantly in the control group.
pNN50 increased by 178.35% in the yoga group compared to an 8.44% increase in the control group.
Total power of HRV increased significantly by 24.16% in the yoga group, while the 19% increase in the control group was not significant.
High-frequency normalized units (HFnu), reflecting parasympathetic activity, increased by 30.29% in the yoga group but decreased slightly in the control group.
Low-frequency normalized units (LFnu), reflecting sympathetic activity, decreased by 28.36% in the yoga group, while it increased slightly in the control group.
The LF-HF ratio, an index of sympathovagal balance, decreased by 40% in the yoga group, indicating a shift toward parasympathetic predominance, with no change in controls.
VLF power showed a non-significant increase in the yoga group and a non-significant decrease in the control group after 12 weeks.
Heart rate decreased significantly in both groups, but more prominently in the yoga group (5.26%) than in the control group (2.70%).
Systolic blood pressure decreased by 5.19% in the yoga group after Pranayama, whereas it significantly increased in the control group.
Diastolic blood pressure decreased significantly by 6.71% in the yoga group, whereas the 3.11% decrease in the control group was not significant.
Rate pressure product, an index of myocardial oxygen demand, decreased statistically significantly in both the yoga (10.94%) and control (10.23%) groups.
Mean arterial pressure decreased significantly by 4.99% in the yoga group, compared to a non-significant 1.57% decrease in the control group.
Cardiac output decreased in both groups after 12 weeks but the change did not reach statistical significance in either group.
Total peripheral resistance decreased in the yoga group and increased in the control group, but neither change was statistically significant.
Baroreflex sensitivity increased markedly by 18.44% in the yoga group after Pranayama, while it decreased non-significantly in the control group.
MIDAS scores, reflecting migraine-related disability, decreased by 41.17% in the yoga group compared to only 5% in the control group.
HDRS depression scores decreased significantly in both the yoga and control groups after 12 weeks, with a more substantial reduction in the yoga group.
HIT-6 scores, measuring headache impact on daily life, decreased significantly in both the yoga and control groups after 12 weeks.
Exposure of the rat dura mater to hαCGRP in the Ussing chamber significantly decreased transdural electrical resistance compared with baseline.
hαCGRP applied to one side of the dura mater did not appear on the opposite side but declined rapidly on the donor side, indicating local degradation rather than transdural diffusion.
Unlike hαCGRP, ATP and forskolin did not produce statistically significant changes in transdural electrical resistance in the same Ussing chamber system.
Under reducing conditions, LC-MS proteomic analysis of hemi-skull incubations identified 31 distinct hαCGRP fragments, dominated by hαCGRP1-17 (61%) and hαCGRP1-24 (18%).
Under conditions preserving the disulfide bridge, seven fragments were detected, with hαCGRP13-24, hαCGRP11-37, hαCGRP22-37, and hαCGRP26-34 as the most abundant.
Proteomic analysis identified S17-R18 and K24-N25 as the major proteolytic cleavage sites of αCGRP in the dural preparation, similar to sites reported in plasma.
None of the seven synthesized hαCGRP degradation fragments, applied alone at 10 µM, produced vasodilation in precontracted mesenteric arteries.
hαCGRP11-37 shifted the hαCGRP concentration-response curve rightward in mesenteric arteries while preserving maximal relaxation, indicating weak competitive antagonism.
Schild regression showed hαCGRP11-37 is approximately tenfold less potent as a CGRP receptor antagonist than the reference antagonist hαCGRP8-37 in mesenteric arteries.
Full-length hαCGRP produced robust agonist responses (cAMP accumulation) at both the rat and human CGRP receptors expressed in Cos-7 cells.
None of the three fragments tested (hαCGRP1-17, hαCGRP1-24, hαCGRP11-37) induced cAMP production when applied alone across a 10 pM-10 µM range at either the rat or human CGRP receptor.
hαCGRP1-17 and hαCGRP1-24 at 10 µM did not affect full-length hαCGRP-induced cAMP generation at either the rat or human CGRP receptor, indicating no antagonist activity.
hαCGRP11-37 acted as a weak competitive antagonist at both rat and human CGRP receptors, markedly increasing the EC50 of full-length hαCGRP.
hαCGRP8-37, the reference CGRP receptor antagonist, showed higher potency than hαCGRP11-37 at both rat and human CGRP receptors in the cAMP assay.
The positive control compound 48/80 significantly increased dural mast cell degranulation compared with vehicle, validating the assay.
Neither full-length hαCGRP nor its degradation fragments hαCGRP1-17, hαCGRP1-24, or hαCGRP11-37 produced a statistically significant increase in dural mast cell degranulation compared with vehicle.
None of the seven hαCGRP degradation fragments produced a detectable signal above non-specific binding when tested alone in the CGRP ELISA at high molar equivalents.

N-terminal fragments hαCGRP1-17 and hαCGRP1-24 interfered with CGRP ELISA detection of intact hαCGRP, shifting the standard curve and reducing apparent CGRP detection, at 2.6 nM concentration; the C-terminal fragment hαCGRP11-37 did not affect detection at this concentration.
Increasing concentrations of hαCGRP11-37 progressively reduced the CGRP signal detected by ELISA in samples containing 125 pg/mL hαCGRP, with an IC50 in the low nanomolar range.

A designed decoy fragment, hαCGRP13-34, produced a small but statistically significant potentiation of hαCGRP-induced mesenteric artery relaxation at 300 pM, without significantly altering overall pEC50.

The decoy fragment hαCGRP13-34 did not significantly alter capsaicin-evoked CGRP release in the hemi-skull model, suggesting rapid degradation of the decoy prevented sustained protection of full-length CGRP from proteolysis.

A designed decoy fragment, hαCGRP13-34, produced a small but statistically significant potentiation of hαCGRP-induced relaxation of mesenteric arteries at a CGRP concentration of 300 pM, though overall potency (pEC50) did not differ significantly between conditions.

The designed decoy fragment hαCGRP13-34 caused a small increase in apparent CGRP signal in the ELISA assay at concentrations of 1 nM to 100 nM, but no detectable interference at higher concentrations up to 10 µM.

Vestibular paroxysmia is thought to result from ephaptic discharges in the proximal vestibulocochlear nerve, typically due to neurovascular cross-compression.
A pediatric cohort identified a narrowed internal auditory canal as an associated anatomical phenotype in vestibular paroxysmia, more often seen in adolescents and females.
Isolated epileptic vertigo/dizziness is uncommon, and when duration is documented, very brief episodes (≤30 seconds) are more typical of isolated than non-isolated presentations.

Episodic ataxia type 2, most often caused by CACNA1A variants, produces longer attacks lasting minutes to hours, frequently with interictal gaze-evoked nystagmus and migraine comorbidity, and most genetically confirmed cases begin before age 20.

A therapeutic trial of carbamazepine or oxcarbazepine can be both treatment and diagnostic support for vestibular paroxysmia; pediatric reports describe oxcarbazepine as generally well tolerated.

Recent tertiary care data indicate that anxiety disorders in children typically coexist with, rather than exclude, other diagnosable causes of dizziness.
Susceptibility to motion sickness in children appears to increase from infancy, peak before puberty, and decline thereafter.

More recent tertiary data indicate that anxiety disorders often coexist with, rather than exclude, other dizziness diagnoses in children.
Susceptibility to motion sickness appears to increase from infancy to a prepubertal peak and decline thereafter, though the precise age distribution varies across studies.

In the bipartite projection of the ICHD3 matrix, the highest-weight phenotype pairings (weight=11) were all combinations of different chronic migraine sub-phenotypes, indicating extensive structural overlap among chronic migraine's Boolean-encoded rows.

The second-highest bipartite weight (10) occurred in 1,006 phenotype pairings, all also between chronic migraine sub-phenotypes, further reflecting the high internal redundancy of chronic migraine's criteria encoding.

Among headache characteristics, the strongest bipartite association (weight=416) was between the criteria 'greater than 15 days per month' and 'more than 3 months,' both chronic-migraine duration/frequency criteria.
The second-strongest characteristic association (weight=366) linked 'fully reversible' and 'greater than 2 episodes,' the two criteria that define migraine aura in ICHD3.

The third-highest characteristic association weight (284) belonged to a set of mutual pairings among chronic-migraine duration/frequency criteria ('greater than 15 days per month,' 'greater than 5 episodes,' 'greater than 8 days per month,' 'more than 3 months'), showing these criteria cluster tightly together.
Markov clustering with modularity-optimized parameters (inflation=3.3, expansion=3) applied to the ICHD3 phenotype-characteristic matrix produced 64 distinct clusters.

Migraine (episodic and chronic, with and without aura) forms a single large, tightly unified Markov cluster, whereas trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia subtypes such as paroxysmal hemicrania fragment into many small clusters (e.g., 9 clusters), reflecting stronger criteria-level unification of migraine than of TACs.

New daily persistent headache (NDPH) clusters together with frequent and chronic tension-type headache (cluster 1) because both share the 'unremitting' and 'more than 3 months' characteristics, a criterion that migraine's fixed 4-72h duration excludes, revealing an unexpected structural link between NDPH and TTH rather than migraine.

Nummular headache is entirely disconnected from the rest of the ICHD3 network graph, sharing no characteristics with any other primary headache disorder, consistent with its pathognomonic, highly specific defining criteria.

Despite migraine with aura encompassing multiple distinct aura subtypes (visual, sensory, motor, brainstem, retinal, speech/language), the matrix analysis shows the disorder is unified as a single cluster primarily by the generic criteria of aura reversibility and reproducibility (>2 episodes) rather than by the specific type of aura symptom.

Gaussian elimination (row reduction to RREF) of the ICHD3 matrix shows that 63 characteristics are sufficient as basis vectors to describe all definitive (non-probable) primary headache diagnoses, corresponding to about 19 clinical history-taking questions, defining a 63-dimensional headache vector space.

The 'greater than 8 days per month' criterion in the chronic migraine definition allows headache days with tension-type phenotype (not meeting migrainous criteria) to still be counted toward a chronic migraine diagnosis, structurally linking chronic migraine and tension-type headache criteria more than expected.

Trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia subtypes (paroxysmal hemicrania, SUNCT, hemicrania continua, cluster headache) occupy a loose, fragmented region of the network without a distinct cluster per subtype, because they are unified by a set of interchangeable autonomic features (rhinorrhea, miosis, lacrimation, etc.) rather than one mandatory shared characteristic as in migraine.

Primary stabbing headache and hypnic headache cluster together across multiple Markov cluster groups, likely because both share the criterion of lacking trigeminal autonomic features (e.g., absence of miosis, rhinorrhea), forming a shared continuum in the classification structure.

Slow, deep breathing is proposed to influence autonomic balance and brain state through bottom-up mechanisms including pulmonary stretch receptors, respiratory sinus arrhythmia, and gas exchange, as well as a global respiratory rhythm that synchronizes neuronal populations.

T cells within T cell-monocyte complexes in LCPOTS display a proinflammatory effector-memory and TEMRA phenotype producing IFN-γ and IL-17A, which correlated with symptom severity.
Circulating IL-17A is elevated 1.5- to 3-fold in LCPOTS patients compared with COVID-recovered individuals without POTS.
Circulating IFN-γ is elevated 1.5- to 3-fold in LCPOTS patients compared with COVID-recovered individuals without POTS.
Production of IFN-γ and IL-17A by T cells within T cell-monocyte complexes correlated with the severity of symptoms in LCPOTS patients.
The authors propose that this monocyte-driven immune response contributes to systemic inflammation and impaired cardiovagal regulation, which are hallmark features of LCPOTS.
About 35% of the 428 surgical patients (total hip arthroplasty or hysterectomy) failed to achieve a 50% reduction in worst pain at six months post-surgery.

The authors developed an 11-item data-driven screener, GAUGE, comprising pain across seven body regions plus four symptom items assessing interoception (nausea, numbness/tingling) and exteroception (sensitivity to sound, sensitivity to odors) to predict poor analgesic response to surgery.

GAUGE outperformed the Central Sensitization Inventory, Fibromyalgia Survey Criteria, and PainDETECT for predicting surgical non-response and Patient Global Impression of Change, with an RR of 1.535 and AUC of 0.738.
In an independent validation cohort of 54 total knee arthroplasty patients, GAUGE outperformed the Fibromyalgia Survey Criteria in predicting pain severity at six months post-surgery.

Among 80 patients treated with suzetrigine for headache and facial pain disorders, 67.5% reported improvement on Patient Global Impression of Change, with a statistically significant distribution favoring improvement over no-change or worsening.
The highest rate of improvement with suzetrigine occurred in patients with trigeminal autonomic cephalalgias (83.3%, N=6), though sample size was too small for inferential testing.
The lowest improvement rate with suzetrigine was seen in patients with medication-overuse headache (40.0%, N=5).

In a case with refractory unilateral periauricular pain with cranial allodynia and autonomic features unresponsive to multiple preventives and procedures, addition of suzetrigine to celecoxib produced marked reduction in pain severity and meaningful quality-of-life improvement within two weeks.

In a patient with chronic migraine and superimposed probable medication-overuse headache, suzetrigine used as short-term bridging therapy during a caffeine/analgesic weaning schedule resulted in resolution of headaches within 3 days.

In a case of nocturnal headache resembling hypnic headache, refractory to gabapentin, melatonin, and nortriptyline, a 2-week course of suzetrigine produced approximately 80% improvement in headache severity without adverse effects.
Suzetrigine was generally well tolerated in the headache cohort, with mild side effects (pruritus, lightheadedness, constipation) reported in 15 of 80 patients and no serious adverse events observed.

Suzetrigine selectively blocks the NaV1.8 sodium channel, which is expressed primarily in peripheral sensory neurons, distinguishing it from nonselective sodium channel blockers that also affect cardiac and central nervous system channels.
Plasma CGRP levels are elevated during migraine attacks compared to non-attack periods.
Plasma PACAP levels are elevated during migraine attacks compared to non-attack periods.
Infusion of CGRP alone is sufficient to trigger migraine-like attacks in people with migraine, supporting a causal role.
CRF levels are significantly elevated in the cerebrospinal fluid of patients with chronic migraine and medication-overuse headache.
Restraint stress induces degranulation in approximately 70% of dural mast cells in rats.
Plasma histamine levels may increase during migraine attacks, and histamine infusion has been shown to induce severe migraine attacks in patients.
Despite the link between histamine and migraine, antihistamine treatments have not been successful for migraine.
Antibodies targeting PAR2 prevent cutaneous allodynia induced by supradural CGRP or a TRPA1 agonist, implicating PAR2 in CGRP-dependent and -independent migraine-like pain signaling.
MRGPRX2 shows markedly higher agonist potency for substance P than its mouse ortholog MRGPRB2, with an EC50 of 152 nM versus 54 μM respectively.
MRGPRX2 primarily signals through Gαq, activating the PLC-DAG-IP3 pathway to promote Ca2+ influx and mast cell degranulation, as shown by inhibition with a PLC inhibitor and Ca2+ channel blockers.
MRGPRB2 knockout mice and mast cell-depleted mice showed reduced thermal and mechanical hypersensitivity following hindpaw incision, along with reduced ATF3 expression in DRG neurons.
96% of meningeal mast cells express MRGPRB2 and lie in proximity to sensory nerve fibers, based on MRGPRB2-Cre;ROSA26-tdTomato reporter mice.

CRF induces Ca2+ transients in HEK293 cells expressing MRGPRB2 and in human mast cells; these effects are blocked in MRGPRB2 knockout cells but not by CRF1 or CRF2 receptor antagonists, indicating CRF acts directly via MRGPRB2.

Repeated stress increased the number of spontaneously active trigeminal ganglion neurons in wild-type mice, an effect absent in MRGPRB2 knockout mice; male MRGPRB2 KO mice also did not show stress-induced periorbital hypersensitivity.
Human clinical trials have shown that peripheral NK-1 receptor antagonists are ineffective for the treatment of pain and migraine.

Substance P induces mast cell degranulation via MRGPRX2 in human LAD2 mast cells, causing release of IL-8, CCL2, CCL3, and CCL4 capable of sensitizing peripheral neurons; in MRGPRB2-/- mice, hindpaw SP injection failed to elicit CCL2/CCL3 release and immune cell recruitment.
Dural injection of compound 48/80 and PACAP increased mechanical facial hypersensitivity in wild-type mice, an effect significantly reduced in MRGPRB2 knockout mice.
Dural PACAP application resulted in approximately 30% more degranulated dural mast cells in wild-type mice, an effect completely attenuated in MRGPRB2 knockout mice.

PACAP-induced hypersensitivity was prevented by R-7050, a TNF-α receptor inhibitor, and SB366791, a TRPV1 channel antagonist, confirming that TRPV1 and TNF-α signaling act downstream of MRGPRB2/PACAP activation.
Alcohol withdrawal-induced headache-like behaviors, increased dural TNF-α, and increased activated trigeminal ganglion neurons were absent in MRGPRB2 knockout mice compared to wild type.
Elevated MRGPRX2 expression and increased numbers of activated mast cells are seen in lesional skin of atopic dermatitis, alongside elevated serum substance P.
Celastrol and GE1111, MRGPRX2 antagonists, significantly reduce expression of IL-6 and IL-1B via targeting MRGPRX2, which is proposed as beneficial given elevated IL-6 in migraine.
KHM-45 reduced β-hexosaminidase release from mouse peritoneal mast cells in a dose-dependent manner following C48/80 activation.

EP262, a selective non-competitive MRGPRX2 inverse agonist, dose-dependently inhibited cortistatin-14-induced mast cell degranulation and blocked cytokine/tryptase release in human mast cells and skin tissue, but its phase 2 clinical trial in chronic spontaneous urticaria was terminated due to preclinical toxicology findings.

EVO756, a selective small-molecule MRGPRX2 antagonist, reduced MRGPRX2-mediated mast cell degranulation induced by SP, C48/80, cortistatin-14, and LL-34 in multiple human cell types and inhibited MRGPRX2 activation in human DRG sensory neurons.
PSB-172656 is a selective small-molecule MRGPRX2 antagonist that blocks Gαq and Gαi dissociation and β-arrestin-2 recruitment, with selectivity for MRGPRX2 over other MRGPRX subtypes.

Osthole inhibits the increase in intracellular Ca2+ stimulated by SP and other neuropeptides via MRGPRX2, and acts in an MRGPRB2-dependent manner to reduce post-stroke neuroinflammation, a condition associated with migraine.

This case report describes the first documented co-occurrence of Ménière's disease and red ear syndrome in a single patient.
Treatment with betahistine 24 mg twice daily reduced tinnitus frequency and stopped drop attacks in the patient.
A three-month trial of amitriptyline did not improve the patient's Ménière's-like symptoms.
Vestibular physical therapy sessions worsened the patient's symptoms during and for about 48 hours afterward, with no noticeable long-term benefit.
Migraine is approximately twice as common among patients with Ménière's disease compared to the general population.
During Ménière's disease attacks, increased sympathetic activity and decreased parasympathetic activity on the affected side have been reported, normalizing after the attack.
Red ear syndrome is hypothesized to result from parasympathetic hyperactivity and sympathetic inhibition leading to vasodilation of the ear.
Chronic inflammation involving IL-6, IL-1β, and TNF-α has been proposed to increase vascular permeability in the inner ear in Ménière's disease.
Skin biopsies from red ear syndrome patients have shown superficial perivascular lymphocytic infiltrate, suggestive of increased vascular permeability.

Elevated plasma vasopressin levels have been reported during Ménière's disease attacks, along with increased type-2 vasopressin receptors in the endolymphatic sac and upregulated cAMP activity/sensitivity.
Psychogenic stress has been associated with increases in both vasopressin and cortisol, and the patient's stress noticeably increased symptom frequency and severity.
Electrocochleography testing was consistent with a diagnosis of Ménière's disease/endolymphatic hydrops in the patient's right ear.
Rubbing the patient's right pinna induced erythema within 30 seconds that spread to the cheek within about a minute, confirming red ear syndrome.
The patient's red ear syndrome erythema and pain were relieved by cold packs and over-the-counter NSAIDs (Aleve).
Laboratory workup including CBC, metabolic panel, ESR, ANA, and type II collagen antibody were all normal, providing no evidence of autoimmune etiology in this patient.
Ménière's disease prevalence is estimated at 190 per 100,000 persons, higher in females and those of European descent compared to Asian, African, or Native American populations.
Ménière's disease typically begins unilaterally but may progress to bilateral involvement in up to 45% of cases.
Genetic factors are estimated to contribute to approximately 10% of Ménière's disease cases.

Transcranial direct current stimulation shows moderate effects on migraine according to the reviewed clinical evidence.
Repetitive transcranial magnetic stimulation shows moderate effects on fibromyalgia pain according to the reviewed clinical evidence.
Transcranial direct current stimulation shows moderate effects on fibromyalgia pain according to the reviewed clinical evidence.
Transcutaneous electrical nerve stimulation (TENS) was found effective only for acute back pain and not for chronic pain conditions.
Cranial electrical stimulation, neurofeedback, and systolic extinction training show promising but more limited evidence for chronic pain than rTMS/tDCS.

Combining neuromodulation with behavioral therapies such as neurofeedback and systolic extinction training appears to produce clinically significant pain reduction and remission, unlike neuromodulation alone which tends to yield only short-term improvement.

The review proposes that neuromodulation may transiently increase neural plasticity within the pain network, with reactivation of the dorsal-medial nucleus tractus solitarius (dmNTS) potentially opening a window for adaptive learning during subsequent behavioral therapy.

The authors suggest neuromodulatory interventions act as neurophysiological facilitators of learning-based pain therapy rather than as standalone treatments, supporting integration with operant pain therapy and cognitive behavioral therapy.

Hot flashes, night sweating, and vaginal dryness were more common among migraineurs than controls, but this difference did not reach statistical significance.

Migraine with onset during perimenopause was characterized by throbbing pain of alternating laterality in orbito-fronto-temporal sites, moderate-to-severe intensity, high frequency, phonophobia and photophobia, rare autonomic symptoms, analgesic overuse, and unsatisfactory treatment response.
Lower estradiol levels correlated significantly with higher migraine severity as measured by the MIDAS score.
Lower estradiol levels correlated significantly with higher migraine pain intensity as measured by the VAS score.
FSH levels did not differ significantly among the perimenopausal-onset migraine, pre-perimenopausal-onset migraine, and healthy control groups.
FDG PET increases diagnostic sensitivity and supports syndrome-oriented metabolic pattern recognition in autoimmune encephalitis, where the clinical rationale for its use is currently strongest.
In viral encephalitis, FDG PET use is selective rather than routine.
In post-COVID condition and related postinfectious syndromes, FDG PET may support biological stratification and differential diagnosis in a subset of patients.

All 15 participants reported experiencing some element of body perception disturbance, with most reporting disturbances across multiple of six identified themes.
All 15 participants reported distorted perceptions of tension, size, weight, numbness, pressure, shape, temperature, and/or frailty in painful body parts.
Thirteen of 15 participants described painful body parts as feeling larger than their actual size.
A participant with Ehlers-Danlos syndrome perceived her shoulder as oversized during episodes of joint subluxation.
During a migraine episode, one participant perceived her head as elongated and her scalp as hairless, describing a 'Conehead' sensation illustrated in her body drawing.
Thirteen participants reported distortions of perceived weight, most commonly a sensation that painful body parts or the whole body felt heavier than normal.
One participant with a phantom leg reported that its perceived weight varied with pain intensity, feeling heavier during more painful periods and lighter during less painful periods.
All 15 participants reported issues with perceiving their body's movements, posture, or outline in space.
Fourteen of 15 participants described shifting attention toward (hypervigilance, n=13) or away from (disconnection, n=6) their painful body parts.

Fourteen participants reported perturbed emotions and beliefs about their body, including negative feelings (n=11), trust issues (n=11), altered attitudes/beliefs (n=12), and altered self-concept (n=5).
Two-thirds (10/15) of participants reported neglect-like symptoms, including motor neglect (delayed movement initiation, n=8) and cognitive neglect (limb foreignness/disownership, n=8).
A participant with fibromyalgia described a recent flare in which her hands felt detached and unrecognizable as her own.
A participant with 27 years of fibromyalgia reported not feeling in control of her body, reflecting a disrupted sense of agency.

A prior large observational study cited in the discussion found that respondents with complex regional pain syndrome were substantially more likely than those with other limb pain to report involuntary movements, consistent with the two CRPS cases observed here.
The present study found no apparent relationship between pain duration and the manifestation of body perception disturbances across participants.

A cited systematic review and meta-analysis found a positive association between pain intensity and Fremantle Back/Body Awareness Questionnaire scores, and another cited study found pain intensity predicted body perception disturbance scores in CRPS, though the present qualitative sample did not observe a clear intensity gradient except during pain flare-ups.

The incidence of SVV side exclusivity (a subclinical marker of lateralized vestibular imbalance) was significantly higher in migraine patients with balance disorders than in migraine patients without balance disorders.

No significant difference in SVV side exclusivity incidence was found between migraine patients without balance disorders and healthy controls.
SVV side exclusivity was significantly more frequent in migraine patients reporting episodic vertigo than in those reporting dizziness.

Cochlear symptoms (fullness, hearing loss, tinnitus) were significantly more prevalent in migraine patients with balance disorders than in those without.
Unilateral cochlear symptoms were significantly more frequent in migraine patients with balance disorders than in those without.
SVV side exclusivity was significantly more common in migraine patients with unilateral cochlear symptoms than in the remaining patients.

Conventional vestibular tests (positional, caloric, cVEMPs, vHIT) were normal in all migraine patients with balance disorders, with no significant differences from either control group in value or asymmetry ratio.

Although perceptual imbalance correlated significantly with migraine symptom laterality, no strict correlation was found between the direction of SVV tilt (left/right) and the predominant side of symptoms.
Galcanezumab treatment in the CONQUER trial significantly reduced monthly migraine headache days and interictal burden (MIBS-4 scores) in both episodic and chronic migraine subgroups.
At baseline, MIBS-4 total score showed only moderate-negligible correlations with migraine headache duration, monthly migraine headache day frequency, and presence of phonophobia/photophobia.

MIBS-4 total score showed negligible correlation with age, gender, race, comorbidity count, prior migraine duration, headache severity, number of prior preventive treatment failures, acute medication overuse, attack number, migraine with aura, and migraine with nausea/vomiting.
At baseline, the strongest correlations of MIBS-4 total score with other PROMs were seen with MSQ total score, MSQ Emotional Function domain, and PHQ-9 total score.

MIBS-4 showed only moderate-negligible to low correlation with monthly migraine headache days at both baseline and Month 6, suggesting interictal burden is not simply driven by headache frequency.
In the episodic migraine subgroup, the baseline correlation between MIBS-4 and MSQ total score was weaker than in the total study population.
Among galcanezumab-treated participants, the proportion achieving predefined responder criteria increased over time, with MIBS-4 showing the highest responder rate of all outcome measures by Month 6.

SCFAs induce regulatory T cell (Treg) differentiation in the colon and maintain peripheral immune tolerance via anti-inflammatory factors such as IL-10.
Butyric acid shows significant anti-inflammatory and analgesic potential in various visceral pain animal models, supporting a neuroprotective role for SCFAs in GBA communication.

Evidence for the SCFA "paradox" (analgesic vs pro-nociceptive effects) and concentration-dependence is derived almost entirely from animal models, with a severe lack of direct human data on SCFA concentrations in chronic pain patients.

FMT can significantly alleviate clinical symptoms and improve quality of life in some chronic pain patients by reshaping the intestinal microecological structure.

Microbial metabolites stimulate enterochromaffin cells to synthesize the majority of peripheral serotonin, indicating peripheral 5-HT signaling is predominantly microbe-regulated rather than solely microbe-derived.

Immune cytokines reciprocally activate enteroendocrine cells: IL-13 regulates EC proliferation and 5-HT synthesis, while IL-33 triggers calcium influx and directly drives 5-HT release, forming a local immune-epithelial feedback loop.

Substance P release, driven by TRPA1 activation under inflammatory/stress conditions, exacerbates intestinal immune-inflammatory responses via NK1 receptor activation and elevated TRPV1 expression, contributing to visceral hypersensitivity.

Pathological increases of substance P in cerebrospinal fluid induce internalization and abnormal responses of NK1 receptors within the dorsal anterior cingulate cortex, directly driving central sensitization.

CGRP mediates neurogenic inflammation and peripheral sensitization by lowering nociceptor threshold, and its pathological upregulation is controlled by epigenetic mechanisms including DNA methylation and miRNA regulation.
GLP-1 receptor agonists demonstrate analgesic potential by inhibiting microglial activation and modulating the central dopamine reward system.
Physiological estrogen concentrations downregulate TRPV1 channel expression in dorsal root ganglia and promote its intracellular translocation, producing analgesic effects.

Physiological estrogen concentrations downregulate TRPV1 channel expression in dorsal root ganglia and promote its intracellular translocation, producing an analgesic effect.
