Female IBS patients display enhanced activation and connectivity within the emotional arousal network and more robust stimulus-induced responses compared with males.
Persistent overactivation of the HPA axis under acute psychological stress further worsens abdominal pain symptoms in IBS.
Central and peripheral CRF-CRF1 receptor signaling is critical for mediating stress-induced visceral hypersensitivity in IBS.
Mast cell-released histamine and proteases directly sensitize sensory neurons via the CRF-TLR4 pathway in IBS.

IBS-associated microecological imbalance, marked by reduced Bifidobacteria and increased Firmicutes abundance, modulates enterochromaffin cell 5-HT release via SCFAs and lowers the visceral pain threshold.
Antibiotic intervention for IBS pain shows double-edged effects, with outcomes depending on the direction of bacterial remodeling and metabolic changes induced.

Probiotic supplementation combined with a low-FODMAP diet shows greater potential than antibiotics alone in restoring intestinal metabolic homeostasis and suppressing excessive immune activation in IBS.
Migraine patients frequently show reduced gut microbial diversity, including decreased coliform abundance, with a large proportion presenting comorbid IBS or Helicobacter pylori infection.

In migraine, gut dysbiosis disrupts intestinal barrier integrity, allowing LPS translocation and systemic inflammation that induces neurogenic inflammation in the trigeminovascular system and promotes CGRP release.

Gut microbiota modulates biosynthesis of tryptophan-derived 5-HT and GABA, disturbing central pain perception and descending inhibitory pathways, which contributes to migraine central sensitization and accompanying nausea/vomiting.

RCTs confirm that probiotic supplementation, H. pylori eradication, fecal microbiota transplantation, or the Mediterranean diet repair the intestinal barrier, improve mood comorbidities, and significantly reduce migraine attack frequency, pain intensity, and painkiller dependence.
In fibromyalgia patients, occurrence of small intestinal bacterial overgrowth (SIBO) and abnormal intestinal hydrogen production are positively correlated with pain severity.

Fecal microbiota transplantation from fibromyalgia patients into germ-free mice successfully recapitulates hyperalgesic phenotypes, directly demonstrating a pathogenic role of gut microbiota in fibromyalgia.

Fecal microbiota transplantation significantly alleviates pain and fatigue symptoms in fibromyalgia by reshaping gut microbiota composition and reducing pro-inflammatory cytokines such as IL-6 and TNF-alpha.

In neuropathic pain, gut barrier impairment allows translocation of endotoxins such as LPS into circulation, activating macrophages and increasing the excitability of primary dorsal root ganglion neurons.

Chemotherapy-induced peripheral neuropathy (CIPN) patients show significant alterations in gut microbial composition that closely correlate with pain sensitivity, suggesting gut microbiota drives neuropathic pain progression via neuroinflammation.

Supplementation with specific probiotics and ginger extract relieves mechanical pain in neuropathic pain models by preserving intestinal barrier integrity, suppressing neuroinflammation, and restoring mitochondrial homeostasis.
In burning mouth syndrome, gastrointestinal signals upregulate TRPV1 expression within the trigeminal system, facilitating oral nociception.

Probiotic and prebiotic supplementation reshapes gut microbiota composition, strengthens intestinal epithelial barrier integrity, and increases butyrate and other SCFA abundance, attenuating excessive HPA axis activation and improving visceral hypersensitivity in IBS and neuropathic pain.

Rifaximin, an antibiotic, reduces intestinal bacterial load and thereby decreases pro-inflammatory mediator production, alleviating mucosal inflammation, and is often combined with probiotics to maintain microecological stability.

Antibiotic treatment for chronic pain shows a controversial double-edged effect, as the microbiota remodeling it induces can increase pro-inflammatory metabolites such as LPS, thereby exacerbating pain sensitivity in some patients.
Linaclotide, a guanylate cyclase-C receptor agonist, promotes extracellular cGMP release from intestinal epithelial cells, inhibiting nociceptor activity and alleviating visceral hypersensitivity.
Lubiprostone improves intestinal secretion and barrier function by activating chloride channels, blocking abnormal immune sensitization along the gut-brain axis.

Prucalopride, a 5-HT4 receptor agonist, accelerates colonic motility and reflexes by inducing acetylcholine release from neurons, relieving constipation and related abdominal symptoms via the gut-brain axis.
Central regulatory drugs such as antidepressants exert distal analgesic effects by strengthening the descending pain inhibition system.

Novel modulators targeting the endocannabinoid system regulate visceral perception by activating CB1 receptors, providing a new approach for precise intervention in orofacial and gastrointestinal pain.
A low FODMAP diet restricts colonic fermentation and lowers LPS levels, restoring intestinal barrier function and alleviating visceral pain.
Functional foods such as ginger root extract have been shown to inhibit neuroinflammation, offering therapeutic potential for chronic pain via the gut-brain axis.

FMT shows clinical potential in improving visceral pain and fibromyalgia symptoms, and even delaying morphine tolerance, by reshaping recipient gut microbiota structure and regulating bile acid metabolism.
Psychological interventions such as cognitive behavioral therapy and meditation weaken pain perception at the level of the brain's higher centers by inhibiting excessive activation of the HPA axis.

Emerging neuroregulation technologies such as vagus nerve stimulation and transcutaneous electrical stimulation directly regulate gut-brain communicating fibers through electrical signals, exerting synergistic anti-inflammatory and analgesic effects.

SCFA-related G protein-coupled receptors GPR41/GPR43, the LPS-mediated microglial activation receptor TLR4, P2X7R involved in maintaining neuroinflammation, and lipid metabolite receptor FPR2 are proposed as candidate therapeutic targets in gut-brain axis pain regulation.

Host intestinal epithelial cells and enteroendocrine cells, particularly enterochromaffin cells, release classical endogenous endocrine peptides including Apelin-13 that participate in gut-brain axis pain signaling.
Among 103 patients with ICD-10-confirmed anxiety disorders, 77.67% were found to have a patent foramen ovale on agitated saline contrast echocardiography.
A strong positive correlation was found between the grade of right-to-left shunt through the PFO and the severity of anxiety symptoms.
Anxiety severity was greater in inpatients than in outpatients within the anxiety disorder cohort.
Patients with a positive right-to-left shunt via PFO had greater anxiety severity than patients with a negative shunt.

The authors propose that neurohumoral dysregulation, cerebrovascular compromise, and autonomic nervous system dysfunction may underlie the observed PFO-anxiety association, pending future investigation.
Esculetin administered systemically at 5, 10, and 20 mg/kg reduced NTG-induced mechanical hyperalgesia in a rat migraine model.
Esculetin treatment decreased trigeminal CGRP levels in NTG-induced migraine model rats in vivo.
Esculetin decreased cellular Fos proto-oncogene (c-Fos) expression, a marker of trigeminal neuronal activation, in NTG-induced migraine model rats.
Esculetin decreased meningeal mast cell degranulation and mast cell numbers in the NTG-induced migraine model.
Esculetin reduced NTG-stimulated CGRP release from trigeminal ganglion and trigeminal nucleus explants ex vivo.
Unlike trigeminal ganglion and nucleus explants, esculetin did not significantly reduce NTG-stimulated CGRP release from meningeal explants ex vivo.

Unlike the trigeminal ganglion and trigeminal nucleus explants, esculetin did not reduce NTG-stimulated CGRP release from meningeal explants, indicating a tissue-specific limitation of its direct ex vivo effect.
Esculetin was systemically tested at three doses (5, 10, and 20 mg/kg) in the NTG-induced migraine rat model, with sumatriptan used as a positive control comparator.

PUAL, a quantitative index of spontaneous pupillary oscillations (hippus) reflecting autonomic pupillomotor instability, showed a non-normal, right-shifted distribution in vestibular migraine patients compared to a Gaussian distribution in healthy controls, with a statistically significant between-group difference.
Using Youden's index derived from ROC analysis, an optimal PUAL cut-off of 0.325 was identified, above which values suggest the presence of vestibular migraine.

At the PUAL cut-off of 0.325, 111 of 137 vestibular migraine patients had values above threshold versus only 4 of 102 controls, while 26 migraine patients and 98 controls fell below threshold, indicating strong separation between groups.

Conventional vestibular testing (vHIT, caloric testing, VEMPs) was largely normal in vestibular migraine patients, whereas the functional head impulse test (fHIT) revealed subtle abnormalities suggestive of central vestibular dysfunction.

Prior studies cited by the authors reported a high prevalence of pupillary nystagmus in vestibular migraine patients, with sensitivity and specificity exceeding 90%, including during the interictal phase.

Spontaneous pupillary diameter oscillations (hippus) occur within an approximate 0.04-2 Hz frequency range and are thought to reflect brainstem noradrenergic activity, including the locus coeruleus, integrating sympathetic and parasympathetic control.

Among 186 children referred with an initial diagnosis of migraine or headache, 18.8% (n=35) ultimately received a possible, probable, or definite diagnosis of self-limited epilepsy with autonomic seizures (SeLEAS).
A definite diagnosis of SeLEAS, confirmed by clear symptomatic response to antiseizure medication, was established in 6.5% (n=12) of the 186 patients referred with migraine/headache.

Of 186 children referred for migraine or headache, 20.4% (n=38) showed (multi)focal interictal epileptiform discharges on initial EEG, with 2.2% (n=4) also showing focal slowing, while 77.4% (n=144) had unremarkable EEGs.
Attacks occurring during sleep were significantly more common among SeLEAS patients than among migraine patients.
Nausea, retching, vomiting, photophobia, phonophobia, visual disturbances, and family history of migraine or epilepsy did not differ significantly in frequency between SeLEAS and migraine patients.
Among 15 SeLEAS patients started on antiseizure medication (14 with sulthiame, 1 with ethosuximide), 80% experienced significant symptom improvement, 6.7% worsened, and 13.3% reported no change.
IEDs were found in 18.8% of patients with a final diagnosis of migraine versus 10% of patients with tension-type headache, a difference that did not reach statistical significance.
Among 3 patients whose headaches did not improve on a single antiseizure medication and were re-diagnosed as migraine, 2 reported improvement in attacks after starting magnesium.

Of the 186 patients, most (87.1%, n=162) were finally diagnosed with migraine, tension-type headache, or mixed migraine/TTH, while 8.6% (n=16) were diagnosed with SeLEAS and 4.3% (n=8) with secondary headache.
Prior literature reports that headache occurrence during SeLEAS seizures varies widely, from 4.6% to 55% of cases.
Vomiting, the most common autonomic manifestation of SeLEAS, occurs in approximately 75% of affected children and commonly leads to misdiagnosis as acute gastroenteritis or migraine.
In the PREVA trial, adjunctive cervical nVNS reduced weekly cluster headache attack frequency by 43% versus 13% with sham, with a significantly higher ≥50% responder rate.
Pooled ACT1/ACT2 data showed nVNS produced a higher rate of pain-free response within 15 minutes in episodic cluster headache compared with sham.
In the PRESTO trial, three times as many acute migraine patients receiving nVNS were pain-free by 30 minutes compared to sham.
The open-label EVENT study found prophylactic nVNS reduced headache days in chronic migraine with good safety and tolerability.
In the PREMIUM I trial, episodic migraine patients with good adherence had a significant reduction in monthly migraine days with nVNS versus sham.
The PREMIUM II trial found a higher ≥50% responder rate with nVNS than sham for migraine prevention, strongest in migraine with aura.
Open-label trials of perimenstrual nVNS reduced attack frequency, analgesic use, and disability scores in menstrual migraine.
A retrospective study found nVNS rapidly relieved vertigo and headache intensity in vestibular migraine, in all but one patient within 15 minutes.
In an adolescent pilot study, nearly half of treated migraine attacks responded to nVNS with no device-related adverse events.
In migraine patients, IL-1β rose over two months in the sham group but remained stable in the nVNS group.
In preclinical models, nVNS suppressed release of the neuroinflammatory peptides substance P and calcitonin gene-related peptide involved in the trigeminovascular reflex.
fMRI shows nVNS reduces activity in the spinal trigeminal nucleus, the brainstem relay for head and neck pain signaling.
A longitudinal case series found 65% of trigeminal autonomic cephalalgia patients considered nVNS a meaningful management tool, used for a median of 47 months.
In a sham-controlled RCT in healthy adults, nVNS significantly reduced pro-inflammatory cytokines including IL-1β, TNF-α, IL-8, MCP-1, and MIP-1α 24 hours after stimulation.
The same RCT found nVNS increased the anti-inflammatory cytokine IL-10 compared with sham.
Five days of nVNS reduced disease activity and lowered CRP, IFN-γ, and IL-8 in psoriatic arthritis and ankylosing spondylitis patients.
In the SAVIOR-I trial, five days of adjunctive nVNS in hospitalized acute COVID-19 patients produced significantly greater reductions in CRP and procalcitonin than standard care alone.
In a double-blind sham-controlled trial in Sjögren's syndrome, twice-daily nVNS for 54 days significantly improved fatigue and cognition, with EEG evidence of restored cholinergic signaling.
Evoked compound action potentials recorded from the cervical vagus during nVNS showed conduction velocities consistent with Aδ, B, and (at higher intensity) C fibers.
Vagal somatosensory evoked potentials were recorded in 80% of healthy subjects during cervical nVNS at 15V, but not when the same stimulation was applied to the sternocleidomastoid muscle.
In a controlled ERP trial, cervical nVNS increased P300b amplitude by about 40%, with effects persisting at least two hours; sham produced no change.
Advanced signal processing showed that nVNS blunted stress-induced increases in the reciprocal of pulse transit time (1/PTT), a surrogate marker of arterial stiffness and blood pressure load.
Healthy adults who received bilateral nVNS showed increases in cardiac vagal tone, a real-time measure of efferent vagal drive to the heart.
The same cohort of healthy adults receiving bilateral nVNS also showed reduced levels of the inflammatory marker TNF-alpha.

In preclinical models, nVNS suppressed release of neuroinflammatory peptides such as substance P and calcitonin gene-related peptide that are released during the trigeminovascular reflex underlying migraine and TAC head pain.
fMRI recordings show that nVNS reduces activity in the spinal trigeminal nucleus, the brainstem relay for head and neck pain signaling.
In the PRESTO trial, acute cervical nVNS produced a significantly higher rate of pain-free migraine responses at 30 minutes compared to sham stimulation.
The EVENT study found that prophylactic cervical nVNS reduced headache days in chronic migraine patients during open-label treatment.
In the PREMIUM I trial, episodic migraine patients with good treatment adherence had significantly fewer monthly migraine days with nVNS than with sham.
The PREMIUM II trial found a higher 50%-responder rate for migraine prevention with nVNS than sham, with the strongest benefit in patients with migraine with aura.
Open-label trials showed that perimenstrual nVNS reduced migraine attack frequency, analgesic use, and disability scores in women with menstrual migraine.
A retrospective study found that cervical nVNS rapidly relieved vertigo and headache intensity in nearly all vestibular migraine patients within 15 minutes.
A pediatric pilot study found that nearly half of migraine attacks treated with nVNS responded, with no device-related adverse events.
Across migraine trials, nVNS adverse events were consistently mild and transient (mostly skin or neck sensations), with no serious device-related adverse events.
Discontinuation due to adverse events is low across cervical nVNS randomized controlled trials, and no serious device-related adverse events have been observed.
Transient voice alteration or hoarseness is an infrequently reported adverse event of cervical nVNS, likely reflecting recruitment of adjacent laryngeal motor fibers.

A preliminary study using auricular vagus nerve stimulation reported positive effects in patients with postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome, and ongoing studies are evaluating cervical nVNS in POTS and related dysautonomias.
Early open-label studies suggest cervical nVNS may reduce symptom burden, particularly nausea and fullness, in idiopathic and drug-refractory gastroparesis.

Sham-controlled studies in healthy adults found that nVNS enhances cognitive performance and resilience, including visuospatial reasoning, multitasking, sustained attention under sleep deprivation, reduced fatigue, and accelerated second-language learning.
Preliminary human reports suggest nVNS may mitigate cognitive decline by enhancing cholinergic signaling and reducing neuroinflammation.

Early clinical studies in patients with rheumatoid arthritis and primary Sjögren's syndrome demonstrate that nVNS can suppress pro-inflammatory cytokine signaling while providing meaningful symptomatic relief.

Studies in large mammals show that dorsal motor nucleus-derived vagal efferent fibers have conduction velocities consistent with myelinated B- or Aδ-type fibers, in contrast to the largely unmyelinated efferents seen in small animal models.
Lie-to-stand produced larger immediate drops in systolic, diastolic, and mean arterial pressure than sit-to-stand.
Lie-to-stand produced greater heart rate increases than sit-to-stand.
Older adults showed larger drops in blood pressure than younger adults, particularly under higher gravitational load (lie-to-stand).
Older adults showed larger drops in systemic vascular resistance than younger adults, particularly under higher gravitational load.
Older adults showed blunted heart rate responses compared with younger adults, particularly under higher gravitational load.
Heart rate increases immediately upon standing were greater during lie-to-stand transitions than during sit-to-stand transitions.

The authors conclude that sit-to-stand and lie-to-stand maneuvers provide complementary physiological information, so transition type should be considered when clinically evaluating orthostatic cardiovascular regulation.

Sex-related differences in cardiovascular responses were modest overall and depended on the specific transition condition, in contrast to the stronger and more consistent effects of age and gravitational load.
Pain intensity measured with the McGill Pain Questionnaire was directly correlated with visual analogue scale scores for dryness in patients with Sjögren disease.
Pain score showed no significant relationship with patient age, disease duration, or disease activity.
More than 80% of patients endorsed McGill Pain Questionnaire domains describing pressure, sensory quality, dullness, tension, brightness, and the affective component of pain.
Sleep, rest, and mild exercise reduced pain in about half of the patients with Sjögren disease.
Damp weather changes, fatigue, and tension were reported to worsen pain in up to 81% of patients with Sjögren disease.
Thirty percent of patients reported that their pain worsened during intercourse.
Damp weather changes worsened pain in up to 81% of patients with Sjögren disease.
Fatigue worsened pain in up to 81% of patients with Sjögren disease, highlighting a relationship between fatigue and pain.
Tension worsened pain in up to 81% of patients with Sjögren disease.
Thirty percent of patients with Sjögren disease reported that pain worsened during intercourse.

Abrupt cessation of habitual caffeine intake in a hospitalized patient with overlap connective tissue disease produced a severe headache mimicking status migrainosus that resolved rapidly after caffeine ingestion.
The headache was refractory to six acute migraine therapies and a status migrainosus protocol before caffeine ingestion resolved it.
Participants who received the PORT brain/body intervention showed a large reduction in overall POTS symptom severity compared with the community care control group over the same period.
PORT participants showed improvement in anxiety symptoms relative to community care controls.
PORT participants showed improvement in depressive symptoms relative to community care controls.
PORT participants showed reduced symptom catastrophizing compared with community care controls.
Fatigue severity did not show meaningful change following PORT during the study period.
Pain-related outcomes did not show meaningful change following PORT during the study period.
General quality of life did not show meaningful change following PORT during the study period.
Of 19 consented PORT participants, 15 initiated and 14 completed treatment and all study activities, supporting feasibility of delivering PORT.
Therapists delivering PORT completed an average of 93.51% of identified key treatment components, indicating strong protocol adherence.

Baseline COMPASS-31 scores indicated substantial autonomic symptom burden in both study groups, comparable to values reported in other clinical POTS cohorts, with elevated orthostatic intolerance subscale scores.

Out of 181 prospective participants screened from a large autonomic clinic waitlist, 39 completed baseline consent/questionnaires and 29 completed the full study, supporting overall feasibility of recruitment despite attrition.
Participants in the PORT group reported overall high levels of treatment satisfaction, with mostly positive open-ended feedback.
Across pooled meta-analytic evidence, transcranial direct current stimulation (tDCS) showed efficacy for fibromyalgia among the seven neurological/pain conditions examined.
Adverse effects of tDCS were generally rare, but mood changes were reported specifically in the context of fibromyalgia treatment.
Pooled meta-analytic evidence indicated that tDCS was efficacious for migraine among the seven neurological conditions assessed.

Across 17 systematic reviews/meta-analyses comprising 358 RCTs and 7160 participants, tDCS significantly improved 34 distinct health outcomes spanning stroke, Parkinson's disease, Alzheimer's disease, cerebellar ataxia, fibromyalgia, disorders of consciousness, and migraine.
No statistically significant increased risk of migraine was observed following bivalent/quadrivalent or 9-valent HPV vaccination compared to unvaccinated periods.
No statistically significant increased risk of hypotension was observed following HPV vaccination compared to unvaccinated periods.
No statistically significant increased risk of postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome was observed following bivalent/quadrivalent or 9-valent HPV vaccination compared to unvaccinated periods.
No statistically significant increased risk of asthma was observed following HPV vaccination compared to unvaccinated periods.
No statistically significant increased risk of polycystic ovary syndrome was observed following HPV vaccination compared to unvaccinated periods.
No statistically significant increased risk of hypothyroidism was observed following HPV vaccination compared to unvaccinated periods.
No statistically significant increased risk of hyperthyroidism was observed following HPV vaccination compared to unvaccinated periods.
No statistically significant increased risk of epilepsy was observed following bivalent/quadrivalent or 9-valent HPV vaccination compared to unvaccinated periods.
Patients with hEDS/HSD had significantly lower polysomnographic sleep efficiency than matched OSA controls without hypermobility.
Insomnia prevalence was significantly higher among hEDS/HSD patients with OSA compared to matched controls.
Baseline (pre-CPAP) daytime sleepiness scores were similar between hEDS/HSD cases and OSA controls.
CPAP therapy significantly reduced daytime sleepiness scores in OSA control patients without hypermobility.
CPAP did not significantly reduce daytime sleepiness in hEDS/HSD patients despite effective apnea treatment, suggesting hypermobility-related factors beyond OSA contribute to residual sleepiness.
CPAP compliance rates were statistically similar between hEDS/HSD cases and matched OSA controls.
Baseline Apnea-Hypopnea Index did not differ significantly between hEDS/HSD cases and controls.
Lowest recorded oxygen saturation during sleep studies was similar between hEDS/HSD cases and controls.
Residual AHI while on CPAP therapy did not differ significantly between hEDS/HSD cases and controls, indicating comparably effective apnea treatment.
hEDS/HSD cases used nasal CPAP masks less frequently than controls.

The CAMS model's first dimension captured the overall presence/abundance of headache-associated symptoms, while the second dimension separated typical migraine symptoms (photophobia, phonophobia, nausea/vomiting, osmophobia) from vestibular symptoms (vertigo, imbalance, lightheadedness, tinnitus, diplopia), consistently across adult and pediatric datasets.

CAMS models generated from adult (n=350) and pediatric comparison (n=471) datasets were consistent with the original CAMS model built on 6,662 children and adolescents, demonstrating generalizability across the lifespan.
The number of CAMS symptoms increased throughout childhood and adolescence and reached a plateau in early adulthood.
A greater number of headache-associated symptoms, and specifically more autonomic and vestibular symptoms, were associated with greater headache burden and allodynia across the lifespan.

In children and adolescents, a greater number of headache-associated symptoms—particularly those reflecting autonomic and vestibular dysfunction—was associated with older age and greater headache burden.
Five of seven SIH patients (71%) met a pre-specified rubric of clinically meaningful improvement after starting CGRP-pathway therapy during the pre-EBP interval.
Across all seven patients with routinely charted NRS scores, pain intensity fell by a median of 3 points after CGRP-pathway therapy was started.
Despite improvement in overall headache pain scores with CGRP-pathway therapy, positional/orthostatic headache features generally did not resolve until after epidural blood patch.
Patients underwent targeted epidural blood patch a median of 7 days after starting CGRP-pathway therapy.

Prior exposure to CGRP-pathway agents before epidural blood patch was not associated with an apparent reduction in the clinical response to the patch, though the small sample and short follow-up limit this conclusion.
Diagnostic work-up with head-up tilt testing and heavily T2-weighted MR myelography identified predominantly cervicothoracic and/or multifocal spinal CSF leaks in this SIH cohort.
Patients with hEDS/HSD had significantly higher odds of chronic GI symptoms compared to controls.
Nearly two-thirds of hEDS/HSD patients reported at least one chronic GI symptom.
Heartburn was the most common individual chronic GI symptom reported by hEDS/HSD patients.
Nearly half of hEDS/HSD patients had a disorder of gut-brain interaction.
Functional dysphagia was the most common disorder of gut-brain interaction reported in hEDS/HSD patients.
Gastroesophageal reflux disease was reported in 41.3% of hEDS/HSD patients across pooled studies.
Chronic fatigue was the most common extraintestinal comorbidity in hEDS/HSD patients, present in 49% of cases.
Migraine was a common extraintestinal comorbidity in hEDS/HSD patients, present in 38.2% of cases.
Orthostatic intolerance was present in 35.9% of hEDS/HSD patients as an extraintestinal comorbidity.
Fibromyalgia was present in 27.9% of hEDS/HSD patients as an extraintestinal comorbidity.
Postural orthostatic tachycardia syndrome (POTS) was present in 21.9% of hEDS/HSD patients as an extraintestinal comorbidity, though with wide confidence intervals reflecting heterogeneity.
The MDS possible prodromal MSA (PP-MSA) criteria demonstrated 100% sensitivity for identifying eventual phenoconversion to MSA at year 1, decreasing to 92% by year 6.
Specificity of the PP-MSA criteria for predicting MSA phenoconversion in the PAF cohort was limited, ranging from 56% to 67% across follow-up.
The positive predictive value of the PP-MSA criteria for MSA phenoconversion in PAF patients was low, ranging from 21% to 34%.
Using a stricter olfactory threshold (UPSIT ≤28) as an exclusion criterion improved specificity to 90%-97% and PPV to 53%-83%, at the cost of a modest reduction in sensitivity to 83%.
Patients with PAF who later phenoconverted to MSA were younger than those who did not phenoconvert.
Patients with pure autonomic failure who phenoconverted to multiple system atrophy were younger at baseline than those who did not phenoconvert.
Patients with pure autonomic failure who phenoconverted to multiple system atrophy had more severe urinary dysfunction than those who did not phenoconvert.
Patients with pure autonomic failure who phenoconverted to multiple system atrophy showed greater orthostatic heart rate responses than those who did not phenoconvert.
DRQOL scores were positively correlated with depression severity as measured by the Self-rating Depression Scale.
DRQOL scores were positively correlated with anxiety severity as measured by the HADS-Anxiety subscale.
DRQOL scores were positively correlated with depression severity as measured by the HADS-Depression subscale.
DRQOL scores were positively correlated with autonomic dysfunction severity measured by the Orthostatic Dysregulation checklist.
DRQOL scores were not significantly correlated with patient age, vestibular handicap (DHI), or individual migraine indices.
Patients who screened positive for migraine had significantly higher (worse) DRQOL scores than migraine screener-negative patients.
DRQOL scores did not correlate with individual migraine severity/impact indices (POUNDing, MIDAS) among patients with dizziness and balance disorders.
Patients who screened positive for migraine had significantly higher (worse) DRQOL scores than migraine screener-negative patients.
DRQOL scores alone showed only modest ability to discriminate migraine screener-positive from migraine screener-negative patients, with an AUC of 0.65.
A multivariable model combining DRQOL with age and sex improved discrimination of migraine screener status to an AUC of 0.77.
CSI scores correlated strongly with all eight SPIDER questionnaire domains in patients with hEDS/HSD.
Fatigue was independently associated with increased odds of clinically significant central sensitization in hEDS/HSD patients.
Pain was independently associated with increased odds of clinically significant central sensitization in hEDS/HSD patients.
Cardiac dysautonomia was independently associated with increased odds of clinically significant central sensitization in hEDS/HSD patients.
Patients with hEDS/HSD who met criteria for clinical central sensitization were significantly younger and more often female than those without central sensitization.
Just over half of the enrolled hEDS/HSD patients (76 of 150) met criteria for clinical central sensitization, defined as a CSI score greater than 40.
The multivariable logistic regression model combining fatigue, pain, and cardiac dysautonomia predicted clinical central sensitization with excellent discriminative accuracy (AUC 0.98).
In fibromyalgia, the central nervous system is hyperresponsive to sensory stimuli in general.
Pharmacologic and nonpharmacologic interventions that successfully manage fibromyalgia act on the CNS to promote quiescence and restore homeostasis.
Fibromyalgia can occur alone, alongside other chronic overlapping pain conditions, or superimposed on other conditions such as autoimmune disorders as secondary pain.
Parosmia is associated with a higher rate of migraine compared with quantitative olfactory loss (anosmia).
Parosmia is associated with a higher rate of chronic pain compared with quantitative olfactory loss.
Parosmia is associated with a higher rate of fibromyalgia compared with quantitative olfactory loss.
Parosmia is associated with a higher rate of hypersomnia compared with quantitative olfactory loss.
Central sensitization-associated comorbidities differ between patients with parosmia and those with quantitative (non-qualitative) olfactory loss, distinguishing the two groups.
The authors conclude that parosmia represents a disorder of altered central sensory processing rather than a purely peripheral olfactory deficit.

Whole-exome sequencing of families with hereditary primary idiopathic hyperhidrosis showed gene-level enrichment of rare coding variants within the voltage-gated sodium channel gene family, with SCN10A (Nav1.8) the most strongly implicated gene.
A knock-in mouse carrying the clinically observed Na_v1.8 p.R14L substitution reproduced excessive sweating, functionally validating the human genetic finding.
Na_v1.8 was found in a subset of postganglionic neurons within thoracic sympathetic ganglia in both humans and mice, the site where the p.R14L variant exerted its effect.
The p.R14L Na_v1.8 substitution produced a gain-of-function electrophysiological profile that enhanced cholinergic responsiveness of sympathetic postganglionic neurons.
Excessive sweating in the Na_v1.8 p.R14L mutant mice was reversible with sodium channel inhibition, using both clinically used sodium channel agents and a Na_v1.8-preferential experimental compound.
Both the SEQUOIA run-in trial and the pivotal REDWOOD randomized withdrawal trial failed to meet their prespecified primary endpoints for ampreloxetine in the MSA subgroup.
After 16 weeks of open-label ampreloxetine treatment, OH Symptom Assessment (OHSA) composite domain scores improved by 2.6 points on average from pretreatment baseline.
In the randomized withdrawal phase, treatment failure at week 6 occurred in 40% of placebo-arm and 15% of ampreloxetine-arm participants, a difference that did not reach statistical significance.
At week 6 of randomized withdrawal, OHSA composite symptoms remained stable in patients continued on ampreloxetine but worsened significantly in those switched to placebo.
The OHSA item assessing ability to stand for a short time favored continued ampreloxetine treatment over withdrawal to placebo.
Among MSA patients maintained on ampreloxetine during the randomized withdrawal period, standing systolic and diastolic blood pressure remained essentially unchanged from open-label levels.
MSA patients withdrawn to placebo after open-label ampreloxetine treatment experienced a fall in standing systolic and diastolic blood pressure.
The catecholamine profile observed during treatment was consistent with pharmacologic inhibition of the norepinephrine transporter, the mechanism of action of ampreloxetine.
No increases in supine blood pressure were observed during ampreloxetine treatment, indicating no signal of supine hypertension.
Individuals with concussion showed blunted autonomic (HRV) modulation during cognitive and emotional tasks compared to control subjects.
Concussion patients exhibited atypical HRV responses that varied by emotional valence of stimuli, differing from typical control patterns.
Some studies reported compensatory increases in vagal (parasympathetic) activity among concussion patients relative to controls, suggested as a possible adaptive autonomic response.
